edits.html:
Sinusitis and Its Complications

double worsening · orbital and intracranial flags · preseptal vs orbital · image before lumbar punctureAre there orbital or intracranial flags, even with a nonfocal neurologic exam?

Source vignette Pt – child with acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in a double-worsening pattern, now with focal headache, early-morning vomiting and drowsiness; neurologic examination nonfocal · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned oral antibiotics, lumbar puncture and urgent neuroimaging
The decision point

A double worsening course indicates acute bacterial rhinosinusitis. Focal headache, early-morning vomiting and drowsiness are intracranial extension flags. Vomiting is worst in the early morning because ICP (intracranial pressure) rises in recumbency. These flags call for urgent imaging rather than oral antibiotics.

"Neurologic examination is nonfocal" does not exclude a brain abscess; frontal lobe abscesses are neurologically silent until late. When raised ICP is suspected, image before LP (lumbar puncture).

Sinusitis complications – features → next step
ComplicationFeaturesNext step
Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitisEyelid swelling; normal extraocular movement (EOM), normal vision, no proptosis; often from a skin break such as an insect bite, eczema or traumaOral antibiotics
Orbital (postseptal) cellulitisProptosis, pain with EOM, ophthalmoplegia, ↓ acuity; usual source is ethmoid or maxillary sinusitis (cheek tenderness), less often a maxillary dental infection or orbital traumaComputed tomography (CT) orbits and sinuses + IV antibiotics; surgical drainage for an abscess
Pott puffy tumorFrontal bone osteomyelitis with subperiosteal abscess – doughy forehead swellingCT/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) + IV antibiotics + surgery
Brain abscess EmergencyFocal headache, early-morning vomiting, drowsiness, ± focal deficitCT/MRI → ring-enhancing lesion; IV antibiotics + drainage
MeningitisDiffuse headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobiaImage first if ICP signs, then LP
Cavernous sinus thrombosisCranial nerve (CN) III, IV, V1–V2, VI palsies, proptosis, spreads bilaterallyMRI/magnetic resonance venography (MRV) + IV antibiotics
Where orbital cellulitis comes from Sinusitis – the most common source; ethmoid or maxillary, spreading contiguously into the orbit (streptococci, S aureus); cheek tenderness points to the maxillary sinus · Dental infection – only maxillary (upper) teeth sit near the sinus and orbit; a mandibular abscess, especially on the opposite side, does not explain it · Skin break (eczema, insect bite, trauma) – causes preseptal cellulitis, anterior to the orbital septum, without proptosis, vision change or painful eye movements · Otitis media – spreads to the mastoid or meninges, not the orbit
Signs of raised ICP & abscess essentials Early-morning headache and vomiting (recumbent CO₂ retention → cerebral vasodilation) · papilledema · altered mental status · late, the Cushing triad. Contiguous sinus spread means Streptococcus anginosus/milleri group and anaerobes; CT with contrast shows a ring-enhancing lesion, and MRI with restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging separates abscess from tumor. Treat with vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole plus drainage. Ring-enhancing differential: abscess, glioblastoma, metastasis, toxoplasmosis, tuberculoma, lymphoma.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Clinical course and neurologic historyFirstDouble worsening with no red flagsUncomplicated sinusitis: oral antibiotics, no imaging
Eye exam: movements, acuity, proptosisBy branchPain with eye movement or proptosisOrbital cellulitis: CT of the orbits and sinuses with contrast, which shows the source sinus and any abscess to drain
CT or MRI of the head with contrastNextRing-enhancing lesionBrain abscess; order for morning vomiting or drowsiness, even with a nonfocal exam
MRI with diffusion-weighted imagingSupportsRestricted diffusion in the lesionAbscess rather than tumor
MRI with magnetic resonance venographyBy branchCavernous sinus thrombosisCranial nerve palsies with proptosis, becoming bilateral
Drainage with Gram stain and cultureConfirmsStreptococcus anginosus group or anaerobesNames the organism; drainage is also treatment
Lumbar puncture before imagingSkipRisk of herniation with raised pressureImage first; LP without CT only when no pressure signs
Scenario bank
  1. Eyelid swelling but normal EOM and vision → Preseptal cellulitis → oral antibiotics
  2. Proptosis and painful eye movement → Orbital cellulitis → CT orbits + IV antibiotics
  3. Doughy swelling over the forehead → Pott puffy tumor → imaging + IV antibiotics + drainage
  4. CN VI palsy with proptosis becoming bilateral → Cavernous sinus thrombosis → MRV
  5. Fever + nuchal rigidity with no ICP signs → Lumbar puncture without prior CT
  6. A child has rhinosinusitis with a double-worsening course, focal headache, and 12 days of symptoms. The neurologic examination is nonfocal, and there is no vomiting or drowsiness. → Uncomplicated acute bacterial rhinosinusitis → amoxicillin-clavulanate
  7. Ring-enhancing lesions in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus and CD4 <100 → Toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma → multiple basal ganglia lesions favor toxoplasmosis
  8. Child with morning headache and vomiting plus ataxia, no infection → Posterior fossa tumor → same ICP syndrome, non-infectious cause
  9. Adult with a ring-enhancing lesion and recent dental infection → Brain abscess by contiguous spread
  10. 5 yo M, right eye pain since morning with blurred vision for several hours; history of frequent ear infections, recurrent sinusitis, many dental caries, atopic dermatitis and hives after mosquito bites; T 39.4, HR 120; right eye acuity 20/70 with proptosis, conjunctival injection, periorbital swelling and redness, and pain with limited adduction; normal fundus; right cheek tenderness; a large foul-smelling cavity in the left lower second molar → Bacterial sinusitis → Orbital cellulitis from contiguous ethmoid or maxillary spread
  11. 6 yo with a week of purulent rhinorrhea, now fever, proptosis, painful and limited eye movements, and falling visual acuity despite 2 days of IV antibiotics; CT shows ethmoid sinusitis with a large subperiosteal orbital abscess → Surgical drainage with continued IV antibiotics → Orbital abscess
  12. 7 yo with a week of nasal congestion and cough, now fever, a swollen red upper eyelid, proptosis and pain with eye movement; normal mental status and no neck stiffness → CT of the orbits and sinuses with contrast → Orbital cellulitis; start IV antibiotics
Pairs with Part II Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child covers the hordeolum and dacryocystitis that can spread into preseptal cellulitis. Ask: is the swelling a focal lump or the whole lid?
Transferable rule A normal neurologic exam is a low-sensitivity test for intracranial pathology. When the symptom pattern is positional and progressive (morning headache, morning vomiting, declining alertness), symptoms of raised ICP (intracranial pressure) outweigh a reassuring exam.
Test-overrides-findingsSequencing trap

edits.html:
Noisy Breathing in a Child

stridor vs wheeze · toxic vs well · the phase of the noise localizes · airway before imagingWhich phase is the noise in, and is the child toxic or well?

Pediatric noisy breathing – the differential
DiagnosisThe pictureThe tellCause & next step
Croup6 mo–3 yrBarky seal cough, hoarse, inspiratory stridor, worse at night, nontoxicSteeple signParainfluenza · dexamethasone for all; racemic epi if stridor at rest
Epiglottitis Emergency2–7 yr, unvaccinatedAbrupt, high fever, toxic, drooling, tripod, muffled voiceThumbprint sign – but never delay the airway for X-ray; don't examine the throatH. influenzae b · secure airway in the operating room (OR) → ceftriaxone + vanc
Bacterial tracheitis"Croup that got worse" – sudden toxicity, purulent secretionsNo response to racemic epiS. aureus · airway + IV antibiotics
Foreign body6 mo–3 yrSudden choke/stridor in a well, afebrile childUnilateral hyperinflation on EXPIRATORY film; R mainstemRigid bronchoscopy (dx + tx)
Retropharyngeal abscess<5 yrFever, drooling, refusal to extend the neckWidened prevertebral spacePolymicrobial · computed tomography (CT) + IV abx ± drainage
Peritonsillar abscessadolescentTrismus, unilateral bulge, hot-potato voiceUvula deviates awayNeedle aspiration / I&D + abx
Bronchiolitis<2 yr, winterUpper respiratory infection (URI) prodrome → wheeze + crackles, retractionsClinical dx – no routine chest x-ray or viral panelRespiratory syncytial virus · supportive ONLY – no albuterol, steroids, or antibiotics
PertussisParoxysms + inspiratory whoop, post-tussive emesis; infants: apneaMarked lymphocytosisAzithromycin (patient + contacts, within 21 days)
Laryngomalacianeonate–6 moChronic inspiratory stridor from the first weeks, worse supine, crying and feeding, loudest at 4 to 8 mo; many have reflux symptomsImproves PRONE; omega-shaped epiglottis and short aryepiglottic folds that collapse inward on inspirationReassure if feeding and growing, treat reflux; resolves by 18 mo · surgery for respiratory distress, cyanosis or failure to thrive
TracheomalaciainfantChronic noisy breathing on expiration with a brassy cough; common after tracheoesophageal fistula repairExpiratory stridor; no change with position or albuterolFloppy intrathoracic trachea collapses on expiration · bronchoscopy confirms; most outgrow it
Vascular ringChronic biphasic stridor + dysphagiaStridor + trouble swallowing togetherBarium swallow / CT angiography
The phase of the noise localizes the lesion
SoundWhere the narrowing isWhy that phaseCauses
Inspiratory stridorExtrathoracic, collapsible (supraglottis, glottis)Fast inspiratory flow lowers pressure inside the airway, pulling floppy tissue inwardLaryngomalacia, croup, epiglottitis, vocal cord dysfunction
Expiratory stridorIntrathoracic tracheaExpiration raises intrathoracic pressure and compresses a soft trachea; inspiration widens itTracheomalacia, tracheal compression by a vascular ring (often biphasic when tight)
Biphasic stridorFixed narrowing, usually subglotticThe complete cricoid ring cannot change caliber, so noise sounds in both phasesSubglottic stenosis, severe croup, a foreign body in the trachea
Expiratory wheezeSmall intrathoracic airwaysBronchioles narrow further on expirationAsthma, bronchiolitis
RhonchiLarger airways with secretionsCoarse sound that may clear with coughPneumonia, bronchitis
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
None: croup and bronchiolitis are clinicalConfirmsNo routine film or viral panelImaging only if the course is atypical
Laryngoscopy in the operating roomConfirmsSwollen cherry-red epiglottisEpiglottitis; intubate at the same sitting
Inspiratory and expiratory chest filmsBy branchUnilateral hyperinflation on expirationForeign body: the trapped lung stays inflated
Rigid bronchoscopyConfirmsForeign body seen and removedForeign body aspiration; diagnostic and therapeutic
Flexible laryngoscopy in the officeConfirmsSupraglottic tissue collapses inward on inspiration, mobile vocal cordsLaryngomalacia; normal cord movement excludes vocal cord paralysis
Laryngoscopy during a symptomatic episodeConfirmsCords adduct on inspirationVocal cord dysfunction
Barium swallow or CT angiographyBy branchPosterior indentation of the esophagusVascular ring: biphasic stridor with dysphagia
Lateral neck X-ray in a toxic, drooling childSkipDelays securing the airwayEpiglottitis: go to the operating room first
Mnemonic 4 Ds of epiglottitis: Drooling, Dysphagia, Dysphonia (muffled voice), Distress (tripod position)
Scenario bank
  1. 2 yo M, barky cough, inspiratory stridor, low-grade fever, steeple sign → Croup → dexamethasone
  2. 4 yo M, unvaccinated, drooling and tripoding with high fever and no cough → Epiglottitis → secure the airway in the operating room
  3. 2 yo M with sudden choking while eating peanuts and a unilateral wheeze → Foreign body aspiration → bronchoscopy
  4. 3 yo M, toxic with high fever and thick purulent tracheal secretions after a viral prodrome → Bacterial tracheitis
  5. 6 mo M in winter with wheeze and crackles following a URI → Bronchiolitis → supportive care
  6. 3 wk M with inspiratory stridor worse supine and better prone, well-appearing → Laryngomalacia → reassurance
  7. 4 mo M with paroxysmal cough, post-tussive vomiting and lymphocytosis → Pertussis → azithromycin
  8. 4 wk F, noisy breathing since birth, inspiratory vibratory sound louder supine and quieter prone, feeding well, no cyanosis → Laryngeal collapse on inspiration → Laryngomalacia – position-dependent, the commonest cause of neonatal stridor
  9. 14 yo F, episodic stridor she calls wheezing, normal voice between episodes, saturation 99% during an attack, no response to albuterol → Vocal cord dysfunction → Paradoxical vocal cord motion – inspiratory and expiratory stridor, not wheeze
  10. Adolescent with recurrent stridor unresponsive to albuterol and a normal saturation → Laryngoscopy during a symptomatic episode → Cords must be seen moving abnormally while symptomatic
  11. 2 yo M, barky cough and inspiratory stridor 3 days after coryza, low-grade fever → Subglottic narrowing from mucosal edema → Croup – the obstruction sits below the cords
  12. 4 yo M, unimmunized, 2 days of fever and rhinorrhea, now severe sore throat and refusing food, temperature 39.4 °C, leaning forward with the chin thrust out, tonsils only mildly erythematous, submandibular space soft → Absent Haemophilus influenzae type b immunization → the risk factor, not the finding
  13. 4 yo M, unimmunized, toxic and tripoding with drooling and a normal-looking pharynx → Intubation in the operating room → visualization happens where the airway can be secured; take him there with anesthesia and an otolaryngologist present
  14. The organism still isolated most often from pediatric epiglottitis despite universal vaccination → Haemophilus influenzae type b → rates fell sharply but the ranking did not change
  15. Preventing epiglottitis in a healthy infant → Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine → immunization is the whole of prevention here; the conjugate series, from 2 months
  16. Agitated 4 yo with suspected epiglottitis in the emergency department → Depressing the tongue to inspect the pharynx → anything that agitates him can complete the obstruction
  17. 3 mo girl with 2 weeks of squeaky noisy breathing when lying on her back, louder and more persistent over time, quieter when prone; gaining weight and breastfeeding well; no labored breathing or cyanosis; laryngoscopy shows patent nasal passages, small adenoids and tonsils, a normal palate, and arytenoid tissue that intermittently falls into the airway, worse with crying; both vocal cords move normally → Inspiratory stridor → laryngomalacia: inspiration lowers pressure in the collapsible extrathoracic airway
  18. 4 mo boy with noisy breathing since 1 month of age, a low-pitched sound heard mainly on expiration over the central chest, and a brassy cough; worse with crying and during colds; no change with position or with albuterol; feeding well without choking or vomiting; normal growth; afebrile → Tracheomalacia → expiratory stridor from a floppy intrathoracic trachea; bronchoscopy confirms
  19. 7 mo boy born at 26 weeks who was intubated for 6 weeks in the neonatal intensive care unit; now noisy breathing on both inspiration and expiration that is constant and worse with colds; no change with position; afebrile, feeding well → Subglottic stenosis → fixed subglottic narrowing after prolonged intubation gives biphasic stridor
  20. 5 mo girl with inspiratory stridor since 2 weeks of age, worse supine and with feeding; weight has fallen from the 50th to below the 5th percentile, with suprasternal retractions at rest and two episodes of perioral cyanosis during feeds; flexible laryngoscopy shows supraglottic collapse on inspiration with normal vocal cord movement → Referral for airway surgery → laryngomalacia with failure to thrive, distress and cyanosis
Decision spine 1. Stridor (upper) or wheeze (lower)? Then which phase: inspiratory is extrathoracic, expiratory is the intrathoracic trachea, biphasic is fixed and usually subglottic. 2. Sudden + afebrile → foreign body; the absence of fever is a key clue. 3. Toxic + drooling + tripod → epiglottitis, airway first in the OR (operating room). Getting a throat exam or X-ray first is an error. 4. Barky + nontoxic → croup. 5. Croup that is not behaving like croup → bacterial tracheitis. 6. Vaccination status always matters.
Risk factors, and the ones that are not Absent Hib immunization is the strongest risk factor for epiglottitis in a child · Immune deficiency raises the risk, but far less strongly · Diabetes mellitus raises the rate of epiglottitis in adults, not in children · Obesity raises postoperative and nosocomial infection risk and brings sleep apnoea, but is not associated with epiglottitis · Secondhand smoke causes middle ear disease, dental caries and lower respiratory infection, but not epiglottitis · Poor dental hygiene points instead at Ludwig angina, which needs tender bilateral submandibular induration and an elevated floor of mouth; a soft submandibular space excludes it
Paired pearls Croup improves with racemic epi, tracheitis doesn't · laryngomalacia better prone, croup worse at night · bronchiolitis gets nothing · expiratory film for foreign body because the trapped lung stays inflated.
Pairs with Part II Deep Neck Infections covers Ludwig angina and the retropharyngeal space. These are the two deep-neck mimics of a toxic child with a sore throat. Ask: is the submandibular space soft?
Sequencing trapThroat exam or lateral neck film in a toxic, drooling child: the airway is secured in the operating room first
Unchecked attributeExpiratory stridor: the sound of the floppy intrathoracic trachea (tracheomalacia); laryngomalacia is above the thoracic inlet, so it collapses on inspiration
Unchecked attributeBiphasic stridor: needs a fixed lesion such as subglottic stenosis; the arytenoid tissue in laryngomalacia is mobile and position-dependent

edits.html:
Anemia with Thrombocytopenia

hemolytic uremic syndrome triad · smear · Coombs test · coagulation studies · its four mimicsAre two cell lines down, is the smear sheared, and are the coagulation studies normal?

Source vignette Pt – 7 yo, bloody diarrhea a week ago, now anuric and icteric · Q – the expected laboratory value; options spanned a decreased platelet count, an increased serum haptoglobin and a positive direct Coombs test
The decision point

Scleral icterus with fatigue is hemolytic anemia, and anuria for 24 hours with pedal edema is acute kidney injury. The third feature of hemolytic uremic syndrome is thrombocytopenia. Shiga toxin damages endothelium, platelets are consumed into microthrombi, and red cells are sheared as they pass. The platelet count falls because of the same process that produces the schistocytes and the bilirubin. The exposure is bloody diarrhea a week ago, in a cluster of people who ate together and recovered.

Defining criteria HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) triad – microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury (rising blood urea nitrogen [BUN] and creatinine) · Microangiopathic hemolysis – red cells sheared by platelet microthrombi, giving schistocytes, increased indirect bilirubin, and decreased haptoglobin · The preceding illness – Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H7 or Shigella dysenteriae; bloody diarrhea first, with HUS appearing about a week later · Coombs in HUS – negative, because the red cells are destroyed mechanically rather than coated by antibody
Pertinent positives & negatives Bloody diarrhea one week ago – Shiga toxin colitis; the one-week latency between the diarrhea and the syndrome is characteristic · Shared meal with relatives who recovered – a point-source exposure that confirms the organism but does not explain the labs; most infected people never develop HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) · Anuria for 24 hours with normal intake, plus 2+ pedal edema – acute kidney injury with volume overload, the renal feature of the triad · Scleral icterus – indirect hyperbilirubinemia from hemolysis, the hemolytic feature of the triad · Fatigue and refusing to get out of bed – symptomatic anemia rather than ongoing volume loss; the diarrhea has resolved · No bruising or petechiae described – consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS is often not severe enough to bleed; its absence never argues against the diagnosis · No fever or neurologic change – the absent neurologic change argues against TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)
Anemia with thrombocytopenia: the differential
ProcessIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Hemolytic uremic syndromeChild, Shiga toxin colitis, then endothelial injury with platelet microthrombi ~1 week laterBloody diarrhea → anemia + low platelets + acute kidney injury (AKI), normal coags, negative Coombs(the answer)
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpuraUsually adult; ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves ultralarge von Willebrand multimersNeurologic changes, more common than in HUS; plasma exchange, not supportive careAge 7, no neurologic findings
Disseminated intravascular coagulationA severely ill patient (sepsis, trauma, malignancy); consumption of factors as well as plateletsProlonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with low fibrinogen alongside the schistocytesPT is normal in HUS; no critical illness described
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemiaImmunoglobulin G coats red cells; lupus, lymphoproliferative disease, or a drugDirect Coombs positive; spherocytes, not schistocytes; platelets and kidneys sparedRenal failure and edema, which antibody-mediated hemolysis does not cause
Isolated thrombocytopenia (immune)Low platelets alone after a viral illness; bruising and petechiae in a well childNormal hemoglobin and a normal smear: one cytopenia, not twoAnemia, jaundice and anuria are all present
Management, in one line HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) is treated supportively with fluid and electrolyte management, transfusion, and dialysis when needed. Withhold antibiotics and antimotility agents in suspected Shiga toxin infection.
Decision spine How many cell lines are down? – Anemia plus a consumed platelet count → the microangiopathy family, not a single-lineage problem · Is the hemolysis mechanical or immune? – Schistocytes with a negative Coombs → mechanical shearing · Are the coagulation studies normal? – Yes → HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) or TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura), not DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) · Which organ, and what came first? – Kidney, after bloody diarrhea in a child → HUS · Marker directions from the mechanism – haptoglobin consumed and falling, reticulocytes rising, indirect bilirubin rising, Coombs negative
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Complete blood count (CBC) with platelets and reticulocytesFirstAnemia with low platelets, reticulocytes highTwo cell lines down with hemolysis: consumption, not marrow failure
Peripheral smearNextSchistocytesMechanical shearing; spherocytes would point to an antibody
Direct Coombs testNextNegativeMechanical destruction; positive means autoimmune hemolysis
PT, aPTT and fibrinogenNextNormalHUS or TTP; prolonged times with low fibrinogen mean DIC
Bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and haptoglobinSupportsIndirect bilirubin and LDH up, haptoglobin lowHemolysis; haptoglobin is consumed binding free hemoglobin
BUN, creatinine and urinalysisConfirmsRising creatinine, little or no urineCompletes the HUS triad after bloody diarrhea; stool Shiga toxin testing names the cause
Bone marrow biopsySkipNot needed once the smear shows schistocytesThe platelets are consumed, not underproduced
Mnemonic TTP pentad (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura): microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, neurologic signs, renal injury. Most patients do not have all five; anemia with schistocytes plus low platelets is enough to act.
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo with bloody diarrhea a week ago, now anuric and icteric; which laboratory value is expected → A decreased platelet count → The third leg of the HUS triad
  2. 5 yo on day 3 of bloody diarrhea, stool culture pending, well hydrated and making urine → Supportive care with fluids, withholding antibiotics → Antibiotics may increase the risk of HUS
  3. 7 yo with hemolytic uremic syndrome, hemoglobin 6.2, urine output 10 mL/h, potassium 6.8 → Hemodialysis → Supportive care includes dialysis
  4. 42 yo F with fever, confusion, schistocytes, platelets 15,000, normal PT and normal creatinine → Plasma exchange → Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
  5. 42 yo F with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, platelets 12,000, no active bleeding → Platelet transfusion → It can worsen TTP; reserve for overt bleeding or an invasive procedure
  6. 60 yo M with gram-negative sepsis, schistocytes, platelets 40,000, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen → Treat the underlying sepsis → Disseminated intravascular coagulation is secondary
  7. 9 yo F with 2 weeks of jaundice and fatigue, spherocytes on smear, direct Coombs positive, normal platelets and creatinine → Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia → Antibody-coated cells rather than sheared ones
  8. Child with brisk hemolysis; why the serum haptoglobin falls rather than rises → It binds free hemoglobin and the complex is cleared → Consumed, unlike the acute-phase reactants
  9. 6 yo with bloody diarrhea 6 days ago, now pale with hemoglobin 8 and platelets 60,000; confirming the mechanism → Peripheral blood smear for schistocytes → Mechanical hemolysis
  10. 5 yo, well appearing, petechiae 2 weeks after a viral illness, platelets 20,000, hemoglobin 12.8, otherwise normal smear → Immune thrombocytopenia → One cytopenia with no hemolysis
Decoy note The cookout and the recovered relatives are epidemiology: they confirm a point-source Shiga toxin exposure but settle no laboratory value. The stool blood "has since resolved"; it stopped days ago and was never chronic, so it does not support iron deficiency. The absence of bruising or petechiae does not argue against a low platelet count. Consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) frequently produces no bleeding at all.
Pearls Bloody diarrhea a week ago plus anuria and jaundice is HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome): schistocytes, low platelets, rising creatinine and a negative Coombs test. · Two cytopenias with schistocytes mean mechanical destruction. In mechanical destruction the Coombs test is by definition negative, because no cell is antibody-coated. · Haptoglobin is consumed in hemolysis, while ferritin and other acute-phase reactants rise. A marker falls if the process uses it up and rises if the liver makes more of it. · Reticulocytes rise in hemolysis and fall in marrow failure. A reticulocyte count that fails to rise in a known hemolytic patient is a hematologic emergency. · Normal coagulation studies separate HUS and TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura) from DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation). Kidney injury after bloody diarrhea in a child points to HUS; brain involvement in an adult points to TTP. · Withhold platelet transfusion in TTP unless there is overt bleeding or an invasive procedure, because it can worsen TTP. Withhold antibiotics in suspected Shiga toxin colitis, because they may increase the risk of HUS.
Pairs with Part II Acute Kidney Injury in a Child covers the acute-kidney-injury compartments and carries the hemolytic uremic syndrome row from the renal side. Part II Hemolytic Anemia covers Coombs-negative hemolysis when the platelets and kidneys are normal. This brief covers the case where both cell lines fall together. Ask: is a second cell line down, and is the smear sheared or spherocytic? Part I Hemolytic Anemia covers hemolysis with a normal platelet count and an antibody rather than a clot. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child starts one step earlier, from the bruise, and sorts it by the platelet count.
Transferable rule For a laboratory abnormality "associated" with a stated mechanism, what matters is the direction each marker moves, not the marker's name. Derive the direction from the mechanism: consumed or produced, mechanical or immune. When the findings form a named syndrome, list its triad rather than re-deriving each component.
Unchecked attributeIncreased serum haptoglobin: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and is consumed, so it falls in hemolysis
True-fact-wrong-slotPositive direct Coombs test: Coombs detects antibody-coated cells; HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) destroys red cells mechanically, so the test is negative. Antibody hemolysis would not cause anuria and edema
Salient decoyDecreased ferritin level: The bleeding was acute and has resolved; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and rises with inflammation
Class-vs-memberIncreased PT: DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) also consumes clotting factors and needs a critically ill patient; in HUS the PT is normal
Unchecked attributeDecreased reticulocyte count: Hemolysis is expected to produce reticulocytosis, a rise, as the marrow responds to the anemia

Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth

trisomies, cri-du-chat and Turner · the newborn with multiple anomalies · the floppy newborn · the trisomy 18 murmurWhich finding belongs to only one syndrome: the hands, the tone, the nose or the eye?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Name the syndrome by its rarest finding, never its commonest: a heart defect, cleft palate and cryptorchidism sit on several lists.

  • Trisomy 18 (Edwards): overlapping fingers, hypertonia, micrognathia.
  • Trisomy 21 (Down): hypotonia, transverse palmar crease.
  • Cri-du-chat (5p deletion): the cat-like cry.
  • Turner (45,X): the webbed neck.
  • CHARGE (coloboma, heart defect, atresia choanae, retarded growth and development, genitourinary and ear anomalies): among these, the only one with choanal atresia; coloboma is CHARGE or trisomy 13.
  • Trisomy 13 (Patau): midline defects; a small head separates it from CHARGE.
  • VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, limb): no eye or nasal component.

Maternal age acts through meiotic nondisjunction: sporadic, not inherited.

Diagnosis
The feature map: one signature finding each
SyndromeSignatureAlso
Trisomy 18Clenched fists, overlapping fingers; hypertoniaGrowth restriction, microcephaly with prominent occiput, micrognathia, low-set pointed ears, absent palmar creases, limited hip abduction, rocker-bottom feet; ventricular septal defect (VSD); Meckel diverticulum, malrotation and omphalocele in over three quarters; about 95% die in the first year
Trisomy 13Cutis aplasia, microphthalmiaMicrocephaly, holoprosencephaly, omphalocele, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, coloboma, cryptorchidism; highly lethal
Trisomy 21Transverse palmar crease; hypotoniaUp-slanting fissures, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots, protruding tongue; under 2.5 kg; heart defects, intestinal atresia; young mothers too
Cri-du-chatCat-like cryMicrocephaly with protruding metopic suture, hypertelorism, flat nasal bridge, hypotonia
TurnerWebbed neckLow hairline, widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, short stature; coarctation
CHARGEChoanal atresia; colobomaCleft lip or palate, hypotonia, anosmia: common, not identifying
22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge)Hypocalcemic seizure, absent thymic shadowConotruncal defect such as truncus arteriosus, cleft palate
VACTERLImperforate anus or radial ray defectHemivertebrae, tracheoesophageal fistula, renal anomaly
Fanconi anemiaAbnormal thumbs with abnormal pigmentationCafé-au-lait macules, short stature, renal and ear anomalies; marrow failure later
CHARGE, letter by letter C: coloboma – a gap in an eye structure · H: heart defect – tetralogy of Fallot or VSD, commonly · A: atresia choanae – a 5-French catheter will not pass either naris · R: retarded growth and development – postnatal, not visible at an hour of life · G: genitourinary – cryptorchidism · E: ear – short, wide, lobeless; hearing loss
The floppy newborn Vertical suspension – held under the arms, the hypotonic infant slips through, limbs extended · Down syndrome – floppy from birth, low birth weight, up-slanting fissures · Prader-Willi syndrome – almond-shaped eyes, small genitalia, undescended testes; paternal chromosome 15 genes lost; hyperphagia later · Infant botulism – well for weeks to months, then constipation and descending weakness; soil, dust or honey; no dysmorphism · Fragile X syndrome – X-linked; may be floppy in infancy; normal birth weight, no newborn dysmorphism; long face, large ears, macroorchidism later · Congenital hypothyroidism – normal at birth; weeks later lethargy, constipation, prolonged jaundice; newborn screen
The trisomy 18 murmur, and the blue newborn VSD – the commonest; holosystolic, left lower sternal border, louder as pulmonary resistance falls · Atrial septal defect – fixed split second heart sound (S2), left upper sternal border · Patent ductus arteriosus – continuous, left infraclavicular · Transposition, truncus arteriosus – central cyanosis, single S2; not trisomy 18 lesions · Acrocyanosis – blue hands and feet, pink lips and tongue: normal
Management
What to do Bilateral choanal atresia – an airway emergency in an obligate nasal breather: oral airway until surgical repair · Trisomy 18 – multidisciplinary supportive and palliative care · Infant botulism – botulism immune globulin · Acrocyanosis – reassurance
Practice
  1. Newborn girl has fetal growth restriction and microcephaly hypertonia, with clenched fists second digit overlapping the third Prenatal ultrasound showed a ventricular septal defect Afebrile · HR 150/min · lips and tongue pink → Trisomy 18 → overlapping fingers with hypertonia is the trisomy 18 hand; trisomy 21 is hypotonic and trisomy 13 is the midline trisomy
  2. Newborn girl delivered for fetal growth restriction hypertonia; clenched fists second finger over third, fifth over fourth prenatal ultrasound: ventricular septal defect Mother 40 years old; further testing declined HR 148/min · weight and head circumference below 5th percentile → Micrognathia → micrognathia travels with a prominent occiput, low-set pointed ears and rocker-bottom feet; cutis aplasia is trisomy 13, a transverse crease trisomy 21
  3. 2-day-old girl, born at 38 weeks, has a murmur clenched fists, overlapping fingers, hypertonia low-set ears, small jaw, rocker-bottom feet Growth-restricted at birth HR 142/min · lips pink, hands and feet bluish · holosystolic, left lower sternal border → Ventricular septal defect → the trisomy 18 profile; its commonest lesion is a ventricular septal defect, louder as pulmonary vascular resistance falls; blue hands with a pink mouth are acrocyanosis; truncus arteriosus gives central cyanosis and a single S2 and belongs to 22q11 deletion
  4. 2-month-old girl with a 47,+18 karyotype feeds slowly soft systolic ejection murmur, left upper sternal border second heart sound widely split, fixed with breathing Lips and tongue pink HR 150/min · respiratory rate 44/min → Atrial septal defect → a fixed split from increased right-sided flow, heard at the left upper border, not the left lower
  5. 40-year-old woman delivers a girl with clenched, overlapping fingers hypertonia, micrognathia, prominent occiput rocker-bottom feet Infant karyotype: 47,+18 in every cell; no family history of chromosomal disease infant HR 150/min · afebrile → Meiotic nondisjunction in oogenesis → homologous chromosomes fail to separate in the egg, giving a disomic gamete; sporadic, not inherited
  6. 1-day-old girl has clenched fists with overlapping fingers growth restriction and marked microcephaly micrognathia, low-set pointed ears, rocker-bottom feet Rapid testing shows three chromosome 18 signals HR 155/min · holosystolic murmur → Full karyotype → rapid fluorescence in situ hybridization is fast but misses mosaicism; a full karyotype across multiple cells confirms and also finds translocations; the karyotype, not a microarray alone, is the confirming test
  7. 3-day-old boy has a large ventricular septal defect karyotype: 47,+18 in multiple cells abdominal ultrasound shows an omphalocele and malrotation Parents ask what care should follow HR 160/min · oxygen saturation 95% → Supportive and palliative care → about half die within 2 weeks and 95% within the first year; a multidisciplinary team plans supportive and palliative care
  8. 38-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has first-trimester screening low pregnancy-associated plasma protein A low human chorionic gonadotropin Ultrasound shows an enlarged nuchal translucency BP 118/72 mm Hg · HR 80/min → Chorionic villus sampling → a positive screen is never a diagnosis: a karyotype on chorionic villi or amniotic fluid confirms
  9. Newborn boy has a head circumference below the 3rd percentile cleft lip and palate, coloboma, microphthalmia punched-out scalp defects (cutis aplasia), postaxial polydactyly Omphalocele; cryptorchidism; holoprosencephaly on imaging HR 150/min · catheters pass both nares → Trisomy 13 → the midline trisomy: scalp, eye, forebrain and abdominal wall, with a small head and nares that are patent
  10. 2-day-old girl, born at term, has a high-pitched cry like a cat's microcephaly with a protruding metopic suture hypertelorism and a flat nasal bridge Low muscle tone; feeds slowly Afebrile · HR 140/min → Cri-du-chat syndrome → the cry names the 5p deletion; intellectual disability and short stature follow
  11. Newborn girl born at term is examined before going home webbed neck, low posterior hairline broad chest with widely spaced nipples Cubitus valgus at both elbows T 36.9 °C · HR 150/min · lips and tongue pink → Turner syndrome → 45,X: coarctation and gonadal dysgenesis go with it, so check the femoral pulses
  12. Newborn boy is floppy from birth up-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds Brushfield spots; a single transverse palmar crease Feeds with a weak suck Afebrile · HR 145/min · open hands, no overlapping fingers → Trisomy 21 → hypotonia with a transverse palmar crease is trisomy 21, not the hypertonia of trisomy 18
  13. 1-hour-old boy, 37 weeks, turns blue when calm pinks up with crying: saturation 97% crying, 80% at rest a catheter will not pass either naris Coloboma, cleft palate, short lobeless ears holosystolic murmur · testes not palpable · normal head size → CHARGE syndrome → choanal atresia and coloboma together belong to CHARGE alone; a normal head excludes trisomy 13
  14. 1-hour-old boy turns blue whenever he stops crying pinks up again with each cry a catheter will not pass either naris Bilateral choanal atresia confirmed at the bedside oxygen saturation 80% at rest · HR 150/min → Place an oral airway → an oral airway does what crying was doing until surgical repair; bilateral choanal atresia in an obligate nasal breather is an airway emergency
  15. Newborn girl turns blue in the delivery room unless crying a catheter will not pass either naris desaturates with every feed oxygen saturation 78% while feeding · 97% while crying · HR 150/min → Bilateral obstruction leaves no route but the mouth → feeding is when it fails; the obligate nasal breather opens the mouth only by crying; unilateral atresia often waits for a first upper respiratory infection
  16. 2-day-old boy has coloboma and bilateral choanal atresia short, lobeless ears; cleft palate undescended testes Oral airway in place; feeding by orogastric tube HR 150/min · oxygen saturation 97% · no murmur heard yet → Echocardiogram and renal ultrasonography → the heart and kidneys are letters the examination cannot see; audiology too
  17. 3-day-old girl has coloboma of the right eye bilateral choanal atresia, oral airway placed echocardiogram: ventricular septal defect Short, lobeless ears; normal head circumference and thumbs; genitalia normal HR 152/min · afebrile → CHD7 gene testing → genetic confirmation of a diagnosis usually made clinically; the gene and the syndrome share their first two letters
  18. Newborn girl has hypoplastic thumbs on both hands several café-au-lait macules length below the 3rd percentile Ultrasound shows a horseshoe kidney; nares patent, eyes normal HR 150/min · echocardiogram: ventricular septal defect → Fanconi anemia → abnormal thumbs with abnormal pigmentation; marrow failure comes later
  19. Newborn boy cannot be fed: a catheter coils in the upper esophagus imperforate anus absent radius on the left Radiograph shows hemivertebrae HR 155/min · holosystolic murmur; echocardiogram: ventricular septal defect → VACTERL association → vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb: no eye or nasal component in this one; Fanconi anemia does not explain the esophageal atresia, imperforate anus or hemivertebrae, and its tell is abnormal thumbs with abnormal pigmentation
  20. 2-day-old boy born at term has a generalized seizure echocardiogram shows an interrupted aortic arch chest radiograph: no thymic shadow Cleft palate; dysmorphic ears ionized calcium low · HR 160/min · T 36.8 °C → 22q11.2 deletion syndrome → parathyroid and thymic failure together with a conotruncal defect
  21. 18-hour-old boy, home-born at term, floppy since birth weak suck, soon asleep held under arms, slips through; legs extended Mother 19, no prenatal care Up-slanting fissures, protruding tongue, narrow intact palate Afebrile · 2.3 kg · normal heart, lungs, abdomen → Down syndrome → hypotonia and a weak suck from birth, low birth weight and up-slanting fissures; a karyotype shows the extra chromosome 21
  22. 2-day-old boy born at term is profoundly floppy since birth suck too weak to feed without a nasogastric tube almond-shaped eyes Small penis; both testes undescended 3.2 kg · HR 140/min · normal palmar creases and palpebral fissures → Prader-Willi syndrome → loss of paternal chromosome 15 genes; hyperphagia and obesity follow in childhood
  23. 10-week-old girl, well until 4 days ago, is constipated weak cry, poor suck, drooping eyelids weakness descends face to arms, trunk Normal newborn screen; family lives beside a construction site Afebrile · sluggish pupils · normal birth weight · no dysmorphic features → Infant botulism → spores from soil and dust in a previously well infant; constipation, then descending weakness; botulism immune globulin
  24. 1-day-old girl born at term has bluish hands and feet lips and tongue pink feeding well No murmur; pulses normal in all limbs oxygen saturation 98% in right hand and foot · HR 140/min → Normal peripheral vasoconstriction → acrocyanosis, normal in a healthy newborn; cyanotic heart disease turns the lips, tongue and trunk blue; reassure
Traps Wrong trisomy: right family, another trisomy's signature finding. Tone ignored: hypertonia rules out trisomy 21. Ready slot: VACTERL fits anomalies in several systems, but needs its own components. Head not read: trisomy 13 shares coloboma, cleft palate, cryptorchidism and a heart defect with CHARGE; microcephaly and choanal atresia separate them. Loud murmur: the most striking finding and the least useful; every option carries a heart defect. Blue hands, pink mouth: acrocyanosis, not a cyanotic lesion. Truncus arteriosus: real, but a 22q11 lesion with a single S2. Atrial septal defect: also seen in trisomy 18, but heard at the left upper border.
Pearls Mosaic trisomy arises after fertilization, so the parents carry no recurrence risk. Isolated choanal atresia still sends you looking for the other CHARGE features. VACTERL and CHARGE overlap only in cardiac and renal anomalies. The gene CHD7 and the syndrome share their first two letters.
Pairs with Teratogenic Exposures: acquired dysmorphology; what are the hands doing, and is tone up or down? Congenital Hypothyroidism: hypotonic from the first hour, or later? Cyanosis in the Newborn: the catheter test and the crying maneuver; are the lips and tongue pink? Hypotonia in an Infant: the full workup and the Down syndrome health supervision grid; weak, or only floppy? Imprinting Disorders: Angelman and Prader-Willi: which parent's copy is missing? 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome: that syndrome in depth. Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia: the VACTERL workup.
Transferable rule

Do not count the anomalies. Find the one finding that sits on the fewest syndrome lists and that you are certain belongs to this infant; shared findings show that a syndrome exists, never which one.

edits.html:
Bruising and Purpura in a Child

vessel, platelets, clotting factors or trauma · red flags · the platelet count removes branches · immunoglobulin A (IgA) vasculitisWhat failed, and is the platelet count normal in a well child?

Source case Pt – 6 yo with new bruising, Aquifer Pediatrics 21; the case works through purpura and petechiae to IgA vasculitis · Q – build the differential for purpura in a school-age child, then narrow it by history, examination and a first set of tests
The approach

Bruising is a finding, not a diagnosis. Ask what failed: the vessel wall (IgA vasculitis), the platelets (immune thrombocytopenia, leukemia, von Willebrand disease), the clotting factors (hemophilia), or the story (accidental or nonaccidental trauma). Each leaves a different bruise, history and first test. First check whether the child needs intervention now. Then use the history, the examination and the platelet count to remove whole branches at a time. Order the confirmatory test last, once one branch is left.

Red flags: act before the full history
FindingWhat it points to
Altered mental status, labored breathing, slow capillary refillUnstable: circulation, airway, breathing first
Fever with fast-spreading purpura, ill childSepsis or meningococcemia: antibiotics before the workup
Pallor, fatigue, bone pain, big spleen or nodesMarrow disease: complete blood count (CBC) and smear today
Headache or confusion with low plateletsIntracranial bleeding
Sudden severe belly pain, vomiting, bloody stoolIntussusception
The differential
DiagnosisWhat failedWhat the bleeding looks likeFirst clue
IgA vasculitisVessel wallRaised purpura, symmetric, on both legs and buttocksNormal platelets; sore joints, belly pain, blood in the urine
Immune thrombocytopeniaPlatelets: destroyed (antibody-coated, cleared in the spleen)Flat petechiae and bruises; nose and gum bleedingA well child; low platelets and nothing else
LeukemiaPlatelets: crowded out of the marrowPetechiae and bruises with pallorAn ill child: fever, bone pain, big spleen or nodes
Von Willebrand diseasePlatelets: normal count, poor stickingMucosal bleeding: nose, gums, heavy periodsNormal count; bleeding relatives of either sex
Hemophilia A and BClotting factorsDeep bleeding into joints and muscleBoys; bleeding after circumcision, shots or surgery
Meningococcemia or sepsisInfectionPurpura that spreads within hoursFever in an ill-looking child
Accidental traumaTraumaFlat bruises over shins, elbows, foreheadThe story fits the injury and the child’s age
Nonaccidental traumaTraumaFlat bruises on the back, buttocks, face or ears; patterned; different agesThe story does not fit, or the child cannot yet crawl
History: what each answer points to
ClueWhat it points to
A recent coldVessel or platelets: it comes before about half of IgA vasculitis and more than half of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), so it separates neither
Bleeding after circumcision, shots or dental work; bleeding relativesClotting factors or von Willebrand disease
Nose or gum bleedingPlatelets: about 40% of ITP
Sore knees and ankles with crampy belly painIgA vasculitis
Fever, weight loss, bone painLeukemia
A story that does not fit the injury or the child’s ageNonaccidental trauma
Examination: what each finding points to
FindingWhat it points to
Does not blanch when pressedBlood outside the vessel: purpura, not a rash
Raised, symmetric, on both legs and buttocksIgA vasculitis
Flat petechiae all overLow platelets
Flat bruises over shins, elbows, foreheadAccidental
Flat, patterned, on the back, ears or faceNonaccidental trauma
Swollen joint after little or no injuryJoint bleed: clotting factors
Spleen more than 2 cm below the ribsNot ITP or IgA vasculitis: leukemia or infection (Epstein-Barr virus is the commonest cause); a tip alone is normal in about 10%
Nodes over 2 cm, supraclavicular, or hard and mattedMalignancy
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CBC with platelet countFirstNormal plateletsVessel wall: IgA vasculitis
Low platelets, nothing else abnormalITP
Low platelets with anemia or an abnormal white countMarrow or consumption: smear next
Peripheral smearBy branchBlasts or schistocytesLeukemia, or hemolytic uremic syndrome
Urinalysis and blood pressureBy branchBlood or protein, or high blood pressureKidney involved: blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine
Prothrombin time (PT) and aPTTBy branchaPTT long, PT normalHemophilia or von Willebrand disease
Abdominal ultrasoundBy branchIntussusceptionA negative study does not exclude an intermittent one
Bone marrow biopsy with flow cytometryConfirms20% or more blastsLeukemia
Factor VIII, IX and von Willebrand studiesConfirmsLow levelNames the bleeding disorder
Skin biopsy, only if atypicalConfirmsIgA in the vessel wallsIgA vasculitis; rarely needed
Serum IgASkipHigh in only about halfCannot confirm or exclude IgA vasculitis
Finalists
On arrivalCBCNextConfirmsTreatment and follow-up
IgA vasculitisWell; raised purpura on the legs, sore ankles, belly painPlatelets normalUrinalysis and blood pressureClinical; biopsy only if atypicalSupportive; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) unless GI bleeding or nephritis; urine and BP checks for a year
Immune thrombocytopeniaWell; flat petechiae, nose or gum bleedingPlatelets low, nothing elseSmearLow platelets alone, in a typical storyObserve; intravenous immunoglobulin or steroids for serious bleeding; no NSAIDs, limit contact sports
LeukemiaIll; fever, bone pain, big spleen or nodesTwo or more cell lines abnormalSmearMarrow: 20% or more blasts; lumbar puncture for central nervous system spreadOncology
IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schönlein purpura) What it is – the commonest vasculitis of childhood, about half of cases; an IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis of the skin, gut, joints and kidneys that usually settles in about a month · Who – 4 to 6 years (range 2 to 17), boys about twice as often; about half follow an upper respiratory infection · Mechanism – an IgA-dominated immune response, often to an infection, inflames small vessels; biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits · Features – palpable purpura with a normal platelet count, symmetric and gravity-dependent, sometimes starting as macules or hives; arthritis of the knees and ankles; colicky belly pain, sometimes before the rash; hematuria; no big spleen · Diagnosis – clinical; the urinalysis is the one test it needs, with BUN and creatinine if the urine or blood pressure is abnormal · Treatment – acetaminophen or an NSAID unless there is GI bleeding or nephritis; steroids are debated, used for severe belly pain, and have not been shown to protect the kidney · Complications – kidney disease in about a third (about 5% chronic renal failure, under 1% end-stage); GI bleeding, with occult blood in about half; intussusception, usually ileoileal, so an enema cannot reduce it · Follow-up – urinalysis and blood pressure every 1 to 2 weeks for 1 to 2 months, then monthly to every other month for a year; about 30% recur, weeks to months later · Return for – severe belly pain, blood in the stool, vomiting that stops fluids, puffy face, hands or feet, severe headache, blurred vision or confusion
What sets it apart
VersusWhat separates it
ITPPlatelets normal, and the purpura is raised
LeukemiaA well child with normal counts and no big spleen
Hemolytic uremic syndromeNo anemia or schistocytes; platelets normal
AbuseRaised, symmetric, dependent lesions with joint, belly or kidney findings
Scenario bank
  1. 6 yo boy, a week after a cold, with raised, nonblanching red-purple spots on the backs of both legs and the buttocks, swollen tender ankles and crampy periumbilical pain; platelets 280,000 → IgA vasculitis → urinalysis next
  2. 6 yo with 3 days of new bruises and pinpoint red spots on the legs and trunk; afebrile, alert, normal vital signs, no history of injury → CBC with smear → the platelet count sorts every branch
  3. 4 yo, well-appearing, flat petechiae everywhere and a nosebleed two weeks after a viral illness; platelets 12,000, hemoglobin and white count normal, no organomegaly → Immune thrombocytopenia → low platelets and nothing else
  4. 5 yo with petechiae and platelets of 20,000 who otherwise looks like ITP, except that the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin → Bone marrow examination → a spleen this size is not ITP
  5. 8 yo girl with frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising and bleeding for a day after a tooth extraction; platelet count normal; her mother has heavy periods → Von Willebrand disease → platelets that do not stick, at a normal count
  6. 7 yo boy, afebrile, with a warm, tense, swollen knee after a minor fall, a deep thigh hematoma last year, and an uncle who bled after surgery; platelet count normal → Hemophilia → deep bleeding means a clotting factor
  7. 7 yo boy with a swollen knee after a minor fall; platelet count and PT normal, aPTT prolonged → Factor VIII and IX activity → names the missing factor
  8. 9-month-old who cannot yet crawl, with a bruise on the ear and another on the upper back; the parent says he bruises easily; CBC and coagulation studies are normal → Skeletal survey → a child who cannot crawl cannot bruise his back by accident
  9. 5 yo with purpura on the legs, abdominal pain and hematuria a week after bloody diarrhea; hemoglobin 7, platelets 40,000, schistocytes on the smear → Hemolytic uremic syndrome → low platelets and hemolysis; IgA vasculitis keeps both normal
  10. 6 yo diagnosed with IgA vasculitis on examination, platelet count normal → Urinalysis → the only test the diagnosis itself requires
  11. 6 yo with raised purpura on both legs, ankle pain and a normal platelet count, whose serum IgA level comes back normal → It does not exclude IgA vasculitis → serum IgA is high in only about half
  12. 6 yo with IgA vasculitis whose urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria → BUN and creatinine → measures the extent of renal disease
  13. 5 yo with IgA vasculitis who develops sudden severe colicky abdominal pain with vomiting → Abdominal ultrasound → looking for intussusception
  14. 5 yo with IgA vasculitis and an ileoileal intussusception that is still present on repeat ultrasound hours later, with ongoing pain → Surgical reduction → an enema cannot reach the small bowel
  15. 6 yo with IgA vasculitis whose purpura has faded; urinalysis and blood pressure were normal at diagnosis → Serial urine and BP checks → kidney disease can come after the rash
  16. 4 yo with ITP, platelets 15,000, skin petechiae only, no mucosal or other bleeding → Observation → with activity limits; the count alone does not call for treatment
  17. 4 yo with ITP and a painful sprained ankle → Ibuprofen → impairs platelet function
  18. Previously healthy 4 yo boy with 3 days of bruising that started on the arms and legs and has spread to the trunk; no injury recalled, and his parents call him very active; afebrile, normal vital signs; scattered petechiae and bruises of different ages, most on the limbs; hemoglobin 12 g/dL, white count 6,000, platelets 1,000, PT and aPTT normal → Increased platelet destruction → immune thrombocytopenia; antibody-coated platelets are cleared in the spleen
  19. 5 yo with 2 weeks of bruising, pallor, fever and leg pain; liver and spleen enlarged; hemoglobin 7 g/dL, white count 2,000, platelets 15,000; PT and aPTT normal → Decreased platelet production → marrow replacement, as in leukemia; peripheral smear next, and bone marrow examination confirms
Bleeding by mechanism Normal PT (prothrombin time) and aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) argue against a clotting factor deficiency and against DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation). A low platelet count with a normal hemoglobin and white count in a well child means increased platelet destruction. In ITP (immune thrombocytopenia), antibodies coat platelets and splenic macrophages clear them; the antibodies also reduce platelet production. Decreased production from leukemia or aplastic anemia usually lowers two or more cell lines. Abnormal platelet function (von Willebrand disease, Glanzmann thrombasthenia) causes bleeding at a normal or near-normal count.
How NBME framed it The key was a mechanism class, increased platelet destruction, not the name ITP (immune thrombocytopenia). Child abuse was the decoy, planted as an active boy with bruises in several stages of healing. Widespread petechiae, a platelet count of 1,000 and a normal PT (prothrombin time) and aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) explain the bruising.
Pairs with Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers the child with two cell lines down. Part II Acute Leukemia in a Child covers the marrow branch and its confirmatory biopsy. Part I Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome covers the glomerular workup that renal IgA vasculitis enters. Part II Suspected Child Abuse covers the fracture branch of nonaccidental trauma. Ask: does the fracture need a pull or a twist, and does the film show a bone disease?
Transferable rule For bruising in a child, decide whether the vessel, the platelets, the clotting factors or the story failed. The feel of the lesion, the platelet count and the spleen each remove a branch. Order the confirmatory test only after one branch is left.
Salient decoyThe recent cold is shared by ITP and IgA vasculitis and cannot separate them.
Unchecked attributePurpura read as a platelet problem without checking whether it is raised.
Mirror twinA child who looks like ITP but has a spleen more than 2 cm down is not ITP.
Test-overrides-findingsA normal serum IgA offered as exclusion, when it is high in only about half.
Salient decoyChild abuse: bruises of different colors on an active boy invite it, but bruise color cannot reliably date a bruise. Widespread petechiae, a platelet count of 1,000 and normal clotting times explain the bleeding; a platelet count and coagulation studies belong in most bruising workups for suspected abuse.
Unchecked attributeAbnormal platelet function: von Willebrand disease and Glanzmann thrombasthenia cause bleeding at a normal or near-normal count; this count is 1,000.
Unchecked attributeDecreased platelet production: leukemia and aplastic anemia usually lower more than one cell line; a hemoglobin of 12 and a white count of 6,000 are normal.
True-fact-wrong-slotDisseminated intravascular coagulation: it occurs in an ill patient and prolongs the clotting times, with low fibrinogen and high D-dimer; this boy is well and his clotting times are normal.

edits.html:
Headache in a School-Age Child

primary, or a mass, raised pressure, infection or bleeding · red flags · the fundi and cerebellar signs · posterior fossa tumorDoes the headache come and go or progress, and are the fundi or the gait abnormal?

Source case Pt – 7 yo with headache, Aquifer Neurology 10 / Pediatrics 20; the case works from red flags and the fundoscopic exam through cerebellar localization to a posterior fossa brain tumor · Q – separate primary from secondary headache, find raised intracranial pressure at the bedside, localize the lesion by site and time course, and name the likely tumor
The approach

Ask first whether a headache is primary (migraine, tension-type headache) or secondary. Causes of a secondary headache include a mass (posterior fossa or supratentorial tumor) and pressure without a mass (idiopathic intracranial hypertension). The others are blocked CSF flow (cerebrospinal fluid flow, as in hydrocephalus), infection (meningitis, abscess) and bleeding. Primary headaches come and go; secondary headaches progress. Check the vital signs for Cushing triad and fever first. Then use the pattern over time, the fundi and the neurologic exam to sort the causes. MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) finds the lesion. Tissue, CSF or the typical story confirms the diagnosis.

Red flags: act before the full history
FindingWhat it points to
High blood pressure, slow pulse, irregular breathingCushing triad: herniation; circulation, airway, breathing now
Fever, stiff neck, confusionInfection: meningitis, encephalitis, abscess
Wakes from sleep; vomits on waking; worse with cough or lying flatRaised intracranial pressure
Weakness, numbness, clumsiness or a new gait changeSpace-occupying lesion
Worst pain at the moment it startsBleeding or a vascular cause
Worse week by week, or a child under 6Secondary headache until proven otherwise
Headache in a child: the differential
DiagnosisWhat caused itWhat the headache looks likeFirst clue
MigrainePrimaryEpisodic, throbbing, frontal; nausea, light and sound both botherRelieved by sleep; a parent with migraine
Tension-type headachePrimaryBand-like pressure, mild to moderate, not progressiveLight or sound bothers, not both
Posterior fossa tumorMassProgressive; worse on waking, with vomitingClumsy gait; papilledema
Supratentorial or sellar tumorMassProgressive, with seizures or one-sided weaknessContralateral signs; field loss or slowed growth
HydrocephalusCSF flow blockedHeadache and vomiting, ataxia over weeksOften from a posterior fossa mass
Idiopathic intracranial hypertensionPressure, no massDaily, worse lying down; brief graying of visionPapilledema, exam otherwise normal; obesity or a drug
Meningitis, encephalitis or abscessInfectionHeadache with feverStiff neck or confusion; sinusitis or otitis before an abscess
Intracranial hemorrhageBleedingMaximal at onsetSudden, the worst ever
History: what each answer points to
ClueWhat it points to
Attacks with well days betweenPrimary headache
More often and worse over weeksSecondary headache
Wakes the child; worse with coughing or strainingRaised intracranial pressure
Throbbing, nausea, dark quiet room, better after sleepMigraine
VomitingA migraine feature and a pressure sign, so on its own it separates neither; vomiting on waking points to pressure
New stumbling, falls, messier handwritingCerebellum: posterior fossa
Isotretinoin, a tetracycline, recent weight gainIdiopathic intracranial hypertension
Examination: what each finding points to
FindingWhat it points to
Swollen, blurred optic disc margins, both eyesPapilledema: raised pressure; image before any lumbar puncture
One eye will not turn outSixth nerve palsy from raised pressure; it does not localize
Wide-based, swaying gait; slurred speech; limbs sparedVermis (midline)
Clumsy reaching, tremor and nystagmus on one side; falls to that sideCerebellar hemisphere on the same side
Romberg: sways with eyes open and closedCerebellum
Romberg: sways only with eyes closedPosition sense: dorsal columns or nerves
Wild lurching gait, sits without difficultyFunctional gait disorder
Normal exam, including the fundiPrimary headache likely
First tests
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Neurologic exam with fundoscopyFirstNormal, episodic historyPrimary headache: diary, no imaging
Papilledema with ataxia or a focal signMass: MRI next
Papilledema, exam otherwise normalPressure without a focal lesion: MRI with magnetic resonance (MR) venography
Fever and a stiff neckInfection: lumbar puncture, after imaging if papilledema or a focal sign
Headache diaryBy branchPattern, triggers, what helpedNames the primary headache
MRI of the brain with contrastBy branchPosterior fossa mass, dilated ventriclesTumor with hydrocephalus: neurosurgery
MRI with MR venographyBy branchNormal: no mass, hydrocephalus or sinus clotLumbar puncture next
Noncontrast head computed tomography (CT)By branchBloodHemorrhage; fast and rarely needs sedation
Resection with histologyConfirmsNames the tumorMedulloblastoma, pilocytic astrocytoma, ependymoma
Lumbar puncture with opening pressureConfirmsHigh pressure, normal CSFIdiopathic intracranial hypertension
CSF cell count, Gram stain, cultureConfirmsNeutrophils, organismBacterial meningitis
None for migraineConfirmsTypical story, normal examClinical diagnosis
Head CT for a suspected posterior fossa massSkipPosterior fossa poorly seenA normal CT does not exclude the tumor: MRI
Finalists
On arrivalExam and fundiNextConfirmsTreatment and follow-up
MigraineEpisodic throbbing headache, nausea, better after sleepNormalHeadache diaryClinical, typical storyEarly ibuprofen, dark quiet room; sleep, fluids, meals, screens
Posterior fossa tumorWeeks of worsening morning headache, vomiting, stumblingPapilledema with ataxiaMRI of the brainResection with histologyDexamethasone, neurosurgery, CSF diversion if needed; oncology
Idiopathic intracranial hypertensionDaily headache worse lying down, brief graying of visionPapilledema, otherwise normalMRI with MR venographyLumbar puncture: high pressure, normal CSFStop the drug, weight loss, acetazolamide; serial visual fields
Meningitis or abscessFever, headache, stiff neck or confusionFever; focal sign in abscessCultures and antibiotics; image first if papilledemaCSF culture; abscess on MRIIV antibiotics; drainage of an abscess
Posterior fossa tumor in a child What it is – brain tumors are the commonest solid tumor of childhood, second to leukemia among childhood cancers, and cause the most childhood cancer deaths; after age 2 and through the first decade most arise below the tentorium · Who – first decade; risk factors are ionizing radiation and genetic syndromes (neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis, Li-Fraumeni) · Mechanism – a cerebellar mass compresses the fourth ventricle, causing obstructive hydrocephalus; pressure carried along the optic nerve sheath blocks axoplasmic flow and swells the disc · Features – progressive headache on waking with vomiting, ataxia, papilledema; vermis: truncal ataxia and slurred speech; hemisphere: same-side limb ataxia, falls to that side · Types – medulloblastoma (about 20%): malignant, midline, spreads through the CSF, needs surgery, radiation and chemotherapy; pilocytic astrocytoma (about 20%): often cystic, the best prognosis, about 90% 5-year survival after complete resection, 50 to 70% after partial; ependymoma: fourth ventricle lining, hydrocephalus, surgery then radiation, about 50% 5-year survival; brainstem glioma: cranial nerve and long-tract signs · Diagnosis – MRI; CT sees the posterior fossa poorly; histology names the tumor · Treatment – dexamethasone for edema, CSF diversion for hydrocephalus, resection; radiation and chemotherapy by type · Complications – herniation; late effects mostly from radiation and chemotherapy: neurocognitive deficits, learning disabilities, endocrine deficits, stroke, epilepsy · Follow-up – oncology imaging, growth and endocrine checks, school and neuropsychological support; give the news to both parents together, in private, in plain words · Return for – worse headache, repeated vomiting, drowsiness, double vision, new weakness or gait change
What sets it apart
VersusWhat separates it
MigraineProgressive, wakes the child, abnormal exam or fundi
Idiopathic intracranial hypertensionAtaxia or a focal sign; a mass on MRI
Acute cerebellar ataxiaToddler, sudden, weeks after varicella; no papilledema; recovers
Drug or toxin ataxiaAcute, bilateral, with an exposure; no papilledema
Functional gait disorderErratic lurching that needs good balance; sits normally
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo with headaches for several weeks that are getting worse, now waking him from sleep and followed by vomiting on waking; he has started stumbling; both optic discs have swollen, blurred margins → Posterior fossa tumor → Progressive headache with papilledema and ataxia; MRI next
  2. 8 yo girl with throbbing frontal headaches two or three times a month for a year, with nausea; she lies down in a dark, quiet room and wakes up well; her mother has similar headaches; neurologic exam and fundi normal between attacks → Migraine without aura → Episodic, with light and sound sensitivity, relieved by sleep
  3. 11 yo with 3 months of mild, band-like pressure around the whole head most school afternoons; noise bothers him but light does not; no nausea or vomiting; never wakes him; normal exam and fundi → Tension-type headache → Nonprogressive pressure pain, light or sound but not both
  4. The mechanism by which raised intracranial pressure swells the optic disc → Blocked axoplasmic flow in the optic nerve → Pressure travels through the subarachnoid space around the nerve
  5. 9 yo with 3 weeks of new daily headaches that do not wake her; no vomiting, fever or visual complaints; alert with a normal gait, strength and coordination; the fundi have not yet been examined → Fundoscopic examination → Papilledema decides between imaging and a diary
  6. 8 yo with 6 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting, a wide-based unsteady gait and papilledema; a noncontrast head CT in the emergency department is read as normal → It does not exclude a mass → CT sees the posterior fossa poorly; obtain MRI
  7. 7 yo admitted with a cerebellar mass on MRI and dilated ventricles, stable overnight, who suddenly develops severe headache, repeated vomiting and increasing drowsiness → Noncontrast head CT → Fast, needs no sedation; looks for bleeding or worse hydrocephalus
  8. 7 yo with a known posterior fossa mass who becomes drowsy; blood pressure 158/94, pulse 52, and breathing that is slow and irregular → Impending brain herniation → Cushing triad; emergent measures to lower pressure
  9. 10 yo stands steadily with feet together and eyes open but sways and nearly falls when he closes his eyes; vibration and position sense are reduced in the toes; finger-to-nose testing is normal → Dorsal column lesion → A Romberg sign only with eyes closed means lost position sense
  10. 8 yo with 2 months of morning headaches, a clumsy right hand, and falls to the right; MRI shows a cyst in the right cerebellar hemisphere with an enhancing nodule in its wall → Pilocytic astrocytoma → Cystic cerebellar tumor with the best prognosis; resection
  11. 12 yo treated for medulloblastoma with resection, craniospinal radiation and chemotherapy 4 years ago, with no recurrence on imaging; his grades are slipping and his height has fallen from the 50th to the 15th percentile → Neurocognitive and endocrine testing → Late effects of radiation and chemotherapy
  12. 3 yo, well until today, now walks with a wide-based, staggering gait and has nystagmus; she had chickenpox 2 weeks ago; afebrile, alert, no headache, normal fundi; no medicines or alcohol in the home → Acute cerebellar ataxia → Post-infectious; CSF and imaging normal; recovers over weeks to months
  13. 18-month-old with 2 weeks of unsteady walking, jerking of the arms and legs, and rapid, chaotic, darting movements of both eyes; afebrile and alert → Urine catecholamine metabolites → Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome: look for neuroblastoma
  14. 9 yo with fever and a worsening headache for 5 days, 2 weeks after a sinus infection that was not treated; new weakness of the left arm; no neck stiffness → Brain abscess → Spread from the sinuses; MRI shows a ring-enhancing lesion
  15. 8 yo with 1 day of fever, headache and a stiff neck, now confused; bilateral papilledema → Blood cultures and IV antibiotics now → Treat first, then image, then lumbar puncture
  16. 14 yo girl with obesity, no medications, and 2 months of daily headache worse lying down with brief graying of vision; bilateral papilledema with full visual fields; MRI with MR venography normal; lumbar puncture opening pressure high with normal CSF → Weight loss and acetazolamide → Idiopathic intracranial hypertension; follow the visual fields
  17. 12 yo who, when asked to stand, sways at the waist and lurches wildly across the room without falling, then sits comfortably; strength, reflexes, finger-to-nose and fundi are normal → Functional gait disorder → Astasia-abasia: the lurching needs good balance
Pairs with Part II Brain Tumors in a Child covers localization by side and structure, and imaging before a lumbar puncture. Ask: which side, and which part of the cerebellum? Part I Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment covers when to image and the drug causes of intracranial hypertension. Part I Brain Tumors in a Child covers the supratentorial midline mass. Ask: is growth or vision failing? Part I Hydrocephalus and Shunt Complications covers hydrocephalus once a shunt is in. Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes covers neurofibromatosis and tuberous sclerosis. Part I Primary Headache in an Adult covers the adult primary headache types.
Transferable rule For headache in a child, decide first whether it is primary or secondary. A headache that progresses, wakes the child, or comes with papilledema or a focal sign needs an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging). The location of the signs shows where the lesion is.
Salient decoyVomiting fits migraine and raised pressure alike; only vomiting on waking, with a headache that wakes the child, points to pressure.
Test-overrides-findingsA normal head CT offered as reassurance, when CT sees the posterior fossa poorly.
Mirror twinPapilledema with an otherwise normal exam and a normal MRI is intracranial hypertension; papilledema with ataxia is a mass.
Unchecked attributeA positive Romberg read as cerebellar without asking whether the child also sways with eyes open.
