edits.html:
Fever in an Infant

urine, blood, meninges, lungs, or a virus · red flags · workup by age, appearance and vaccines · the culture confirmsDoes the infant look ill, and if well, how old and how vaccinated is the infant?

Source case Pt – 6-month-old with fever, Aquifer Pediatrics 10; the case works a fever without a source through the serious bacterial infection workup to a first febrile urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis) · Q – decide which tests the infant’s age, appearance and vaccines call for, read the urine, complete blood count (CBC) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), then choose the setting, the antibiotic, the dose and the imaging
The approach

Fever without a source means a complete history and examination found no focus. Most of these infants have a virus (roseola, other viral syndromes). A small minority have a serious bacterial infection. The urine is the commonest source: a UTI (urinary tract infection). Other sources are the blood (occult bacteremia, sepsis), the meninges (bacterial meningitis), the lungs (pneumonia), or rarely bone, joint or gut. Look at the child first: an ill-appearing infant gets the full workup. In a well infant, age and vaccine status decide how much testing is needed. The catheter urine culture, blood culture or CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) culture confirms the infection.

Red flags: act before the full history
FindingWhat it points to
Slow capillary refill, low blood pressure, altered mental statusSeptic shock: circulation, airway, breathing first
Fast heart or breathing rate in an ill childEarly sepsis: cultures and antibiotics now
Hypothermia in a young infantSepsis; fever may be absent
Bulging fontanelle, lethargy, seizureMeningitis: lumbar puncture
Workup by age, appearance and vaccines
InfantWorkup
21 days or youngerFull workup with lumbar puncture, whatever the appearance
22 to 60 days, ill-appearingFull workup with lumbar puncture
22 to 60 days, well-appearingLumbar puncture only if inflammatory markers are abnormal
Over 2 months, ill-appearingUrine, CBC, blood culture; consider lumbar puncture
3 to 36 months, well, fully immunizedUrine if at risk; nothing else
3 to 36 months, well, underimmunizedUrine, CBC and blood culture
Infant with fever: the differential
DiagnosisSourceWhat it looks likeFirst clue
Urinary tract infectionUrineFever, no focus; fussy, eating lessPositive leukocyte esterase and nitrite
Occult bacteremiaBloodFever in a well-appearing childUnderimmunized; positive blood culture
SepsisBlood, with a systemic responseIll-appearing; fast heart and breathingPoor perfusion; hypothermia in young infants
Bacterial meningitisMeningesIrritable or lethargic, bulging fontanelle, poor feedingCries when picked up; no neck signs
Viral meningitisMeningesMilder; loose stools, rash or cold symptomsEnterovirus; lymphocytes in the CSF
PneumoniaLungsCough, fast breathing, crackles, low saturationRarely silent; lower lobe can cause belly pain
RoseolaVirus (HHV-6)3 to 5 days of high fever, well childRash as the fever breaks; under age 2
Acute otitis mediaEarRed eardrum that bulges and moves poorlyRedness alone predicts nothing
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) gingivostomatitisMouthFever and fussiness, then oral vesicles and ulcers10 months to 3 years
Viral upper respiratory infectionNose and throatCongestion, cough, runny noseA source, so not fever without one
Kawasaki diseaseVesselsFever 5 days or more, red eyes, lips, rashInfants often have incomplete forms
History: what each answer points to
ClueWhat it points to
Fussy and eating less, nothing elseUTI, meningitis and viral illness all do this, so it separates nothing
Fewer than 2 doses of pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) and HibUnderimmunized: bacteremia risk higher
DTaP or PCV in the last few daysVaccine fever, within a few days
Girl under 2, or uncircumcised boy under 1UTI risk: test the urine
Circumcised boy 6 months or olderLow UTI risk if nothing else
Prior UTI, urinary tract anomaly, fever over 48 hoursUTI risk: test the urine
Cough, congestion, runny noseViral respiratory infection
Examination: what each finding points to
FindingWhat it points to
Ill appearanceFull workup for serious bacterial infection
Bulging fontanelle; cries when picked upMeningitis
No Kernig or Brudzinski sign under 12 monthsUsually absent in infant meningitis; excludes nothing
Fast breathing, crackles, low saturationPneumonia
Red eardrum that moves and does not bulgeNot otitis media
Vesicles and ulcers in the mouthHSV gingivostomatitis
Normal examination, well childFever without a source: age and vaccines set the tests
First tests
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Catheterized urinalysisFirstLeukocyte esterase and nitrite positiveUTI strongly suggested: culture, start antibiotics
Leukocyte esterase alone positivePyuria has other causes; the culture decides
Nitrite negativeDoes not exclude UTI; infants void often
NormalUTI unlikely; look elsewhere or follow closely
CBC with differentialBy branchHigh white count, bandsMore likely bacterial, if ill or underimmunized
Chest x-rayBy branchInfiltrateFor chest findings, or fever over 39 C with white blood cell (WBC) count 20,000 or more
Lumbar puncture: cells, glucose, protein, Gram stainBy branchNeutrophils, low glucose, high proteinBacterial meningitis; lymphocytes with normal glucose: viral
Urine culture, catheter specimenConfirmsGrowth of one uropathogenUTI; E. coli in 85 to 90%
Blood cultureConfirmsGrowth in a well-appearing childOccult bacteremia; in an ill child, sepsis
CSF cultureConfirmsOrganism grown; Gram stain may be negativeBacterial meningitis
None: clinicalConfirmsRash as the fever breaksRoseola
CBC in a well, immunized childSkipA high count is almost always a false positiveBacteremia is now too rare to predict
Bag urine for cultureSkipHigh contamination rateScreening only; catheterize to culture
Group A strep test under age 3SkipStrep throat and rheumatic fever rareNot recommended at this age
Finalists
On arrivalUrinalysisNextConfirmsTreatment and follow-up
PyelonephritisFever, fussy, eating less; no focusEsterase and nitrite positiveDecide oral or IVCatheter urine cultureOral cephalexin if well; IV ceftriaxone if toxic; ultrasound under age 2
Bacterial meningitisIrritable or lethargic; bulging fontanelleNormalLumbar puncture; blood cultureCSF cultureAdmit; IV antibiotics
Occult bacteremiaWell; underimmunized; high feverNormalCBC and blood cultureBlood culture in a well childRecall and reexamine if the culture grows
RoseolaWell; 3 to 5 days of high feverNormalObserveClinical: rash as fever breaksReassurance; no treatment
Febrile urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis) in an infant What it is – bacterial infection of the kidney; the commonest serious bacterial infection behind fever without a source · Who – girls under 2, uncircumcised boys under 1, circumcised boys under 6 months; prior UTI or a urinary tract anomaly · Mechanism – bowel flora ascend the urethra to the bladder and kidney; E. coli in 85 to 90% of first episodes, the rest Klebsiella, Proteus or enterococcus · Features – fever with no focus, fussiness and poor appetite; an infant cannot report dysuria or flank pain · Diagnosis – catheterized urinalysis: pyuria over 5 WBC/hpf, and esterase and nitrite positive, strongly suggest it; the catheter culture confirms. Collect by catheter in a child not toilet trained; suprapubic aspiration only if catheterization fails; a bag specimen is never cultured · Setting – most are treated orally at home; IV and admission for a toxic child, one who cannot keep oral medicine down, or doubtful adherence · Treatment – oral cephalexin or another cephalosporin by local resistance; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and amoxicillin-clavulanate work but are not first choices; IV ceftriaxone after the first month (it displaces bilirubin in neonates; no calcium in the same line); ampicillin plus gentamicin also works, and ampicillin covers enterococcus, which ceftriaxone misses; nitrofurantoin reaches only the urine, so it treats cystitis, not pyelonephritis · Dosing – mg/kg per day times weight, divided by doses per day; prefer fewer daily doses and a whole-number volume · Follow-up – improvement expected in 48 to 72 hours; renal and bladder ultrasound after a first febrile UTI under age 2, usually after the course; voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) if the ultrasound is abnormal, fever of 39 C or more with an organism other than E. coli, or a second febrile UTI · Complications – renal scarring; vesicoureteral reflux behind recurrences · Return for – fever or fussiness after 2 to 3 days of antibiotics, vomiting that stops the medicine, lethargy, any new fever later
What sets it apart
VersusWhat separates it
Occult bacteremiaA positive urine names the source
Bacterial meningitisWell child, normal fontanelle: no lumbar puncture needed
RoseolaRoseola has a normal urine and a rash as fever ends
CystitisFever puts the infection in the kidney
Scenario bank
  1. 6-month-old girl with 2 days of fever to 39.4 C, fussier than usual and taking less formula; no cough, runny nose, vomiting or diarrhea; vaccines up to date; well-appearing with a normal examination, including a flat fontanelle, clear lungs and normal eardrums; catheterized urinalysis shows positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite with many white cells → Pyelonephritis → a febrile UTI in an infant is an upper-tract infection; catheter culture next
  2. 7-month-old girl with 2 days of fever to 39.2 C and no other symptoms; vaccines up to date; playful and well hydrated, with a normal fontanelle, clear lungs, normal eardrums and no rash → Urinalysis by catheter → UTI is the commonest serious bacterial infection behind a fever without a source
  3. 10-month-old circumcised boy with 1 day of fever to 38.9 C; vaccines up to date; no prior urinary infection or known urinary tract anomaly; playful and drinking well, with a normal examination → Clinical follow-up alone → low UTI risk and well-appearing: no testing needed
  4. 9-month-old boy whose parents declined all vaccines, with 1 day of fever to 39.6 C and no other symptoms; alert and playful, with a flat fontanelle, supple neck and normal examination → CBC, blood culture, and urine → underimmunized: bacteremia is more likely, so blood tests join the urine
  5. 12-month-old unvaccinated boy with fever to 39.8 C and no source on examination; a blood culture drawn in clinic grows gram-positive diplococci the next day, when he is afebrile, playful and eating well, with a normal fontanelle and no rash → Occult bacteremia → a positive blood culture in a well-appearing child; recall and reexamine
  6. 5-month-old boy with 1 day of fever, irritability and poor feeding; neck supple; Kernig and Brudzinski signs absent → Does not exclude meningitis → these signs are usually absent in infants with meningitis
  7. 7-month-old girl with fever to 39.3 C, no source on examination and a normal fontanelle; vaccines up to date; catheterized urinalysis shows pyuria with positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite → Urine culture → the catheter culture confirms the UTI and names the organism
  8. 8-month-old girl with 2 days of fever, lethargy and vomiting and a bulging fontanelle; cerebrospinal fluid shows a high white cell count, mostly neutrophils, low glucose and high protein; Gram stain shows no organisms → Bacterial meningitis → a negative Gram stain does not exclude it; the culture confirms
  9. 10-month-old boy with 4 days of fever to 40 C who stayed playful and fed well throughout; the fever stopped yesterday and today he has a pink, blanching rash on the trunk; examination otherwise normal → Reassurance → roseola (HHV-6): no tests or treatment needed
  10. 9-month-old fully immunized girl with fever to 39 C for 1 day; well-appearing and playful, with a normal examination; a CBC obtained at urgent care shows a white count of 17,000 with a mild left shift → Probably a false positive → bacteremia is rare in a well, immunized child, so the count predicts little
  11. 6-month-old girl with fever and no source on examination, not toilet trained; a urine specimen is needed to rule out infection → Culture of a bag specimen → high contamination rate; a bag specimen is for screening only
  12. 6-month-old girl with pyelonephritis on catheterized urinalysis, culture pending; well-appearing, taking formula and keeping it down; reliable parents with a phone and transportation → Oral cephalexin at home → most febrile UTIs are treated orally
  13. 6-month-old girl started on oral cephalexin for pyelonephritis 1 day ago now vomits every dose, is sleepier and has cool hands with a capillary refill of 3 seconds → Admit for IV ceftriaxone → toxic, or unable to keep oral medicine down
  14. 7-month-old boy with fever to 39.5 C and a catheter urine culture growing E. coli susceptible to all oral agents tested; well-appearing and ready to go home on oral therapy → Nitrofurantoin → therapeutic levels in the urine only, not the kidney
  15. 5-month-old girl admitted on IV ceftriaxone for pyelonephritis is still febrile after 48 hours; the catheter urine culture grows Enterococcus faecalis susceptible to ampicillin → Switch to ampicillin → ceftriaxone does not cover enterococcus
  16. 8-kg infant is prescribed an oral antibiotic at 50 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours; the suspension contains 250 mg per 5 mL → 4 mL twice daily → 400 mg a day, 200 mg a dose, at 50 mg per mL
  17. 6-month-old girl with her first febrile UTI, E. coli on catheter culture, afebrile within 48 hours on oral therapy and now finishing the course; normal growth and blood pressure → Renal and bladder ultrasound → first febrile UTI under age 2; VCUG only if abnormal or recurrent
  18. 9-month-old boy with 2 days of fever to 39.6 C, no cough, fussy with feeds and a mildly uncomfortable belly; vaccines up to date; well-appearing, breathing comfortably, lungs clear; catheterized urinalysis normal; white count 22,000 → Chest x-ray → occult pneumonia: high fever and a white count of 20,000 or more with no other source
Pairs with Part II Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn covers the decision to tap once other sources are closed: is there a meningeal sign, or only a fever? Part I Urinary Tract Infection in a Child covers the imaging rules after a febrile UTI (urinary tract infection) and the child not improving by 72 hours. Part I Urinary Tract Infection in a Child covers the child once the VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram) shows reflux. Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) grid. Part II Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn covers the first month of life. Part II Fever and Rash in a Child covers roseola among the rashes. Part I Kawasaki Disease covers fever of 5 days or more with red eyes and lips.
Transferable rule In an infant with fever and no source, appearance, age and vaccine status decide how much testing is needed. Test the urine of any child at risk, and collect it by catheter. The culture, not the dipstick, confirms the infection.
Salient decoyFussiness and poor feeding come with UTI, meningitis and viral illness alike and cannot separate them.
Unchecked attributeA supple neck and no Kernig or Brudzinski sign under 12 months do not exclude meningitis.
Test-overrides-findingsA high white count in a well, fully immunized infant is almost always a false positive.
Class-vs-memberNitrofurantoin treats bladder infection but never reaches the kidney, so it cannot treat a febrile UTI.

edits.html:
Hypotonia in an Infant

brain, anterior horn cell, neuromuscular junction or muscle · strength and reflexes · genetic confirmation · Down syndrome careIs the infant floppy but strong, or weak with absent reflexes, and which test confirms the level?

Source case Pt – infant with low tone, Aquifer Pediatrics 29; the case works from the hypotonia differential to Down syndrome, its confirmation and its health supervision · Q – decide whether the low tone comes from the brain or from the motor unit, confirm the chromosomal cause, then plan the child’s care for the first years
The approach

Hypotonia is a finding, not a diagnosis. Localize where it starts. Causes in the brain include Down syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, congenital hypothyroidism and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. Other levels are the anterior horn cell (spinal muscular atrophy), the neuromuscular junction (infant botulism) and the muscle (congenital myotonic dystrophy, congenital myopathies). A central cause produces an infant who is floppy but strong for the tone, often dysmorphic or sleepy, with normal or brisk reflexes. A peripheral cause produces a weak, alert infant with low or absent reflexes. Check breathing and feeding first. Send the confirmatory test, usually genetic, once the level is known.

Red flags: act before the full history
FindingWhat it points to
Weak cry, pooled secretions, belly breathing, falling saturationRespiratory or bulbar failure: circulation, airway, breathing first
Seizures or a sleepy infant after a hard deliveryBrain injury: glucose, then imaging
Ptosis, weak suck and constipation in a previously well infantInfant botulism: admit and watch the airway
Tongue fasciculations with absent reflexesSpinal muscular atrophy: breathing fails next
Infant with hypotonia: the differential
DiagnosisLevelWhat it looks likeFirst clue
Down syndromeBrain: extra chromosome 21Floppy from birth, upslanting fissures, flat midfaceDysmorphic features on the first examination
Prader-Willi syndromeBrain: chromosome 15Severe hypotonia, poor suck, almond-shaped eyesSmall genitals, undescended testes
Congenital hypothyroidismBrain: thyroid hormoneNormal at birth, sluggish weeks laterAbnormal newborn screen; big tongue, constipation
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathyBrain: injuryFloppy, lethargic, seizures on day 1Hard delivery, low Apgar scores
Spinal muscular atrophyAnterior horn cellWeak but alert; frog-leg postureTongue fasciculations, absent reflexes
Infant botulismNeuromuscular junctionDescending weakness, ptosis, weak suckWell for weeks; constipation first
Congenital myotonic dystrophyMuscleWeak face, tented upper lip, clubfeetPolyhydramnios; an affected mother
Congenital myopathy or muscular dystrophyMuscleWeak from birth, low reflexesHigh creatine kinase (CK) in the dystrophies
History: what each answer points to
ClueWhat it points to
Floppy from the first hourCongenital: chromosomal, brain or muscle
Well for weeks, then floppyAcquired: botulism, missed hypothyroidism, metabolic
Hard delivery, low Apgar scores, seizuresHypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Polyhydramnios, reduced fetal movementWeakness before birth: neuromuscular disease or Prader-Willi
Parents related by bloodAutosomal recessive disease; ask whether the grandparents are siblings, with sensitivity
Mother with a grip she cannot quickly releaseMyotonic dystrophy, passed from the mother
Mother under 35Most Down infants have younger mothers, so it separates nothing
Examination: what each finding points to
FindingWhat it points to
Slips through the hands when held under the armsHypotonia; it says nothing about the level
Moves limbs against gravity, reflexes normal or briskCentral cause
Weak, reflexes absent, bright alert faceAnterior horn cell: spinal muscular atrophy
Ptosis, sluggish pupils, weak suckNeuromuscular junction: botulism
Upslanting fissures, flat midface, small ears, single palmar creaseDown syndrome; hypotonia is its most consistent infant finding
Almond-shaped eyes, small penis, undescended testesPrader-Willi syndrome
Tented upper lip, weak face, clubfeetCongenital myotonic dystrophy
First tests
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Bedside strength and reflex examinationFirstStrong for the tone, reflexes normal or briskCentral: karyotype, thyroid tests, imaging by story
Weak, reflexes absent, alertAnterior horn cell or muscle: CK and gene testing
Descending weakness with ptosis, previously wellJunction: stool toxin
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (T4)By branchHigh TSH, low T4Congenital hypothyroidism
Serum creatine kinaseBy branchHighMuscular dystrophy; normal or near normal in spinal muscular atrophy and botulism
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)By branchWatershed or deep gray matter injuryHypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Chromosomal microarrayBy branchSmall deletion or duplicationDysmorphic infant with a normal karyotype
Lymphocyte karyotypeConfirms47,+21, a translocation, or mosaicismDown syndrome; a translocation means karyotypes for both parents
DNA methylation of 15q11-q13ConfirmsMaternal pattern onlyPrader-Willi syndrome
SMN1 deletion testingConfirmsNo functional copiesSpinal muscular atrophy
DMPK repeat testing, infant and motherConfirmsExpanded CTG repeatCongenital myotonic dystrophy
Stool botulinum toxin or organismConfirmsPositiveInfant botulism; treat before the result
Rapid fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for chromosome 21Skip as the final testThree signalsFast, but has not replaced the karyotype and cannot show a translocation
Head MRI in Down syndromeSkipNo consistent findingNot indicated
Finalists
On arrivalBedside examinationNextConfirmsTreatment and follow-up
Down syndromeFloppy from birth; upslanting fissures, single palmar creaseStrength and reflexes preservedEchocardiogram and complete blood count (CBC)Lymphocyte karyotypeEarly intervention; health supervision grid below
Prader-Willi syndromeSevere hypotonia, poor suck; almond eyes, small genitalsStrength preserved, profoundly floppyKaryotype often normalDNA methylation studyTube feeding early; growth hormone; food security later
Spinal muscular atrophyAlert, frog-legged, belly breathingWeak, areflexic, tongue fasciculationsCK normal or near normalSMN1 deletion testingGene-targeted therapy; respiratory and feeding support
Down syndrome (trisomy 21) What it is – the commonest chromosomal cause of intellectual disability, about 1 in 700 US births · Who – any couple; risk climbs from the mid-30s, but most affected infants have mothers under 35 because younger women have more pregnancies · Mechanism – extra chromosome 21 material: free trisomy (most likely at any maternal age), an unbalanced translocation (relatively likelier with a younger mother), or mosaicism, with features from classic to almost none · Features – hypotonia, upslanting fissures, epicanthal folds, flat midface, small ears, loose nuchal skin; Brushfield spots, single palmar crease, clinodactyly, sandal gap; intellectual disability usually mild (intelligence quotient (IQ) 50 to 70) or moderate (35 to 50) · Diagnosis – prenatal serum analytes, nuchal ultrasound and cell-free DNA estimate risk; CVS (chorionic villus sampling) or amniocentesis diagnose; after birth a lymphocyte karyotype · Treatment – early intervention at diagnosis; an IEP (individualized education program) at school entry, with parents as advocates · Complications – heart disease in about half, some silent; duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease; hypothyroidism at any age; hearing and vision loss; transient myeloproliferative disorder and leukemia; atlantoaxial instability · Follow-up – the grid below · Return for – neck pain, head tilt, a change in walking, new weakness or wetting; pallor, bruising or fever; poor feeding or weight gain
Down syndrome: health supervision
CheckWhenWhy
CBCFirst 3 days, then yearlyPolycythemia, leukemoid reaction, transient myeloproliferative disorder; later iron deficiency
EchocardiogramFirst month, read by pediatric cardiologyHeart disease in about half, some not heard on auscultation
HearingNewborn, then repeatedHearing loss is more common
EyesCataract check from birth; ophthalmology at least yearlyCataracts and other vision problems
TSHNewborn screen, then yearlyHypothyroidism can appear after a normal screen
Early interventionAt diagnosisTherapies before delay shows
NeckHistory and examination every visit; positioning precautions discussed at least every 2 yearsAtlantoaxial instability; imaging for symptoms, not routinely
Gut and growthPediatric gastroenterology for feeding or weight problems; celiac serology for symptomsStructural anomalies, celiac disease
SleepSleep study for all at ages 3 to 4Obstructive sleep apnea
ImmunologyIf infections recurImmunodeficiency
Head MRINot indicatedNo consistent finding
What sets it apart
VersusWhat separates it
Prader-Willi syndromeAlmond eyes, small genitals, no Down facies; normal karyotype
Trisomy 18Hypertonia with clenched, overlapping fingers
Congenital hypothyroidismNormal at birth, floppy weeks later; abnormal newborn screen
Spinal muscular atrophyTruly weak, areflexic, alert, not dysmorphic
Other chromosomal and intellectual disability syndromes
SyndromeGeneticsSignature findingsIntellect
Fragile X syndromeFMR1 CGG repeat, over 200; X-linkedLong face, large ears, lax joints; large testes after pubertyIntellectual disability in boys; girls variable
Turner syndrome45,XWebbed neck, puffy hands and feet; coarctation in about 20%Usually normal
Klinefelter syndrome47,XXYNormal at birth; small testes, infertility, gynecomastiaLow normal
Trisomy 1347,+13Cutis aplasia, microphthalmia, cleft lip, polydactylySevere disability
Trisomy 1847,+18Overlapping fingers, prominent occiput, rocker-bottom feetSevere disability
When to send chromosome studies Features of a known chromosome disorder or an unrecognized malformation syndrome · developmental disability with other unusual findings · a stillborn infant with multiple malformations · some tumors, including leukemia · in adults, recurrent pregnancy loss · submicroscopic deletions need FISH or a microarray · Fragile X needs FMR1 repeat testing, not a karyotype; mothers of affected sons carry at least a premutation · Sharing the diagnosis: in person, privately, both parents present; ask what they know, give a warning and a short headline, respond to emotion, then plan the next visit; this sequence is SPIKES (setting, perception, invitation, knowledge, emotions, strategy and summary)
Scenario bank
  1. 1-day-old boy, floppy since birth and slow to feed; upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, a flat midface, small ears, loose skin at the back of the neck, a single transverse palmar crease and a wide gap between the first and second toes; strength and reflexes are preserved; the parents ask whether a future child could be affected → Lymphocyte karyotype → Down syndrome; only the karyotype shows free trisomy, a translocation or mosaicism, which sets the recurrence risk
  2. 5-week-old girl who slips through the examiner's hands when held under the arms; she lifts her arms and legs against gravity and kicks vigorously; knee reflexes are 3+; no fasciculations; flat midface and upslanting palpebral fissures → Brain → Central hypotonia: strong for the tone, reflexes preserved; chromosomal cause likely
  3. 3-month-old girl, born at term after a normal pregnancy, whose parents are first cousins; over 6 weeks she has stopped kicking and now lies with her legs flopped outward; alert and follows faces; fine quivering movements of the tongue; knee and ankle reflexes absent; the chest sinks as the belly rises with each breath; no ptosis, pupils react briskly, stools normal → Spinal muscular atrophy → Anterior horn cell loss; autosomal recessive, so consanguinity raises the risk
  4. 3-month-old with progressive symmetric weakness of the limbs, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculations and paradoxical breathing; face and eye movements normal; alert and social → SMN1 deletion testing → Spinal muscular atrophy; CK is normal or near normal
  5. Newborn boy, pregnancy with polyhydramnios and reduced fetal movement, intubated at birth for weak breathing; weak face with a tented upper lip, poor suck, bilateral clubfeet and low reflexes; his mother has a long thin face and cannot quickly let go after a handshake → Congenital myotonic dystrophy → Muscle; DMPK CTG repeat expanded, passed from the mother
  6. 2-day-old boy, profoundly floppy since birth with a suck too weak to feed without a tube; almond-shaped eyes, a small penis and bilateral undescended testes; palpebral fissures and palmar creases normal; standard karyotype normal → DNA methylation analysis → Prader-Willi syndrome; methylation detects deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects
  7. 5-week-old girl born at home with no newborn screen; increasingly sleepy, feeds poorly, constipated, still jaundiced; large tongue, umbilical hernia, wide posterior fontanelle; tone low, face otherwise typical, reflexes present → TSH and free T4 → Congenital hypothyroidism; start levothyroxine without waiting for imaging
  8. Newborn girl with trisomy 21 confirmed on karyotype, floppy but feeding with support; the parents ask which tests she will need in the coming weeks → Brain MRI → No consistent finding in Down syndrome; not indicated
  9. Newborn boy with the features of Down syndrome born to a 24 yo mother; karyotype shows 46 chromosomes with the extra chromosome 21 material joined to chromosome 14 → Karyotype of both parents → Translocation Down syndrome; a balanced carrier parent changes the recurrence risk
  10. 2-week-old with Down syndrome, feeding well and gaining weight; no murmur; pulse oximetry 98% in the right hand and in a foot → Echocardiogram now → Heart disease in about half, some silent; echo in the first month
  11. 3 yo boy with Down syndrome at a well visit; normal newborn screen, growing along his curve, no symptoms, normal examination → TSH level → Hypothyroidism can develop after a normal newborn screen
  12. 7 yo girl with Down syndrome and 3 weeks of neck pain, holding her head tilted, falling more often and new daytime wetting; brisk knee reflexes, sustained ankle clonus and upgoing toes → Atlantoaxial instability → Cord compression at C1-C2; urgent cervical spine imaging and neurosurgery
  13. 3-day-old with Down syndrome, feeding well and afebrile; liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin; white count 45,000 with 30% blasts, hemoglobin and platelets normal → Transient abnormal myelopoiesis → Transient myeloproliferative disorder; usually resolves on its own, but later leukemia risk calls for CBC follow-up
  14. 6 yo boy with intellectual disability, poor eye contact and hand flapping; long face, large protruding ears, lax finger joints and flat feet; his mother's brother also has intellectual disability; a karyotype last year was normal → FMR1 CGG repeat analysis → Fragile X syndrome; over 200 repeats; the mother carries at least a premutation
  15. 7-week-old boy, well until 3 days ago, now constipated with a weak cry, drooping eyelids, a poor suck and weakness spreading from the face to the arms; afebrile; the team plans empiric antibiotics while cultures are pending → Gentamicin → Infant botulism; aminoglycosides worsen neuromuscular blockade; botulism immune globulin
  16. 2-month-old girl with Down syndrome, lifting her head briefly and smiling socially; the parents ask what they should do now for her development → Early intervention referral → Referral at diagnosis, before any delay appears; an IEP follows at school entry
Pairs with Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers the trisomy feature map and the prenatal screen. Ask: are the hands clenched or open, and is the tone up or down? Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism covers the floppy infant found on the newborn screen. Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers the malformation syndromes without an aneuploidy. Part I Cerebral Palsy covers hypoxic-ischemic injury and its imaging. Part I The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease in Down syndrome. Part II Abnormal Growth in a Child covers Turner syndrome in the short girl. Part I Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth covers the early intervention referral for delay.
Transferable rule For a floppy infant, first decide whether the problem is in the brain or the motor unit. An infant who is strong for the tone with normal reflexes has a central cause, often chromosomal. A weak infant with absent reflexes has a peripheral cause. Then send the genetic test for that level.
Unchecked attributeLow tone read as weakness without testing strength and reflexes, which is the step that separates central from peripheral causes.
Salient decoyA mother under 35 argues against Down syndrome, yet most affected infants are born to younger mothers.
Mirror twinPrader-Willi syndrome is as floppy as Down syndrome from birth but has almond-shaped eyes, small genitals and a normal karyotype.
Test-overrides-findingsA positive FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization) taken as the final answer, when only the karyotype shows a translocation that changes the parents’ recurrence risk.

edits.html:
Child with Puffy Eyes

local to the eye, or the first sign of edema everywhere · red flags · the dipstick splits the branches · minimal change diseaseDoes the swelling belong to the eye or to the whole child, and what does the urine dipstick show?

Source case Pt – 5 yo with puffy eyes, Aquifer Pediatrics 31; the case works from periorbital swelling through generalized edema, fatigue and a growing belly to nephrotic syndrome from minimal change disease · Q – build the differential for periorbital swelling, decide whether the edema is generalized, then diagnose, treat and follow nephrotic syndrome and its complications
The approach

Ask first whether the swelling belongs to the eye or to the whole child. Local swelling comes from allergy (allergic conjunctivitis, an acute allergic reaction) or infection (periorbital cellulitis, conjunctivitis, sinusitis). Generalized edema means protein is lost (nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy), not made (liver failure, malnutrition), or salt and water are retained (acute glomerulonephritis, heart failure). Check the airway and the orbit first. In the generalized branch, the urine dipstick eliminates most of the differential at once; the confirmatory test comes last.

Red flags: act before the full history
FindingWhat it points to
Stridor, wheeze, low blood pressure, poor perfusionUnstable: circulation, airway, breathing first
Swollen lips or tongue, or a hoarse voiceAnaphylaxis: intramuscular epinephrine
Proptosis, pain with eye movement, blurred visionOrbital cellulitis: computed tomography (CT) and IV antibiotics
Edema with fever, belly pain and reboundSpontaneous peritonitis: cultures, then antibiotics
High blood pressure with headache, vomiting or confusionHypertensive encephalopathy from nephritis
Flank pain with blood in the urine, or one swollen legThrombosis in a nephrotic child
Puffy eyes in a child: the differential
DiagnosisWhy it swellsWhat it looks likeFirst clue
Allergic conjunctivitisLocal: allergyBoth eyes, itchy, watery, ropey mucusSneezing, clear runny nose; seasonal
Acute allergic reactionLocal: allergy, suddenAbrupt swelling of lids, lips or tongueHives, minutes after a food, drug or sting
Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitisLocal: infected lidOne eye; red, warm, tender lidBite, scratch or sinusitis; eye moves freely
Infectious conjunctivitisLocal: infected conjunctivaRed eye, mild lid swelling, pus crusting the lidsStarts in one eye; under 6, usually bacterial
Sinusitis or a coldLocal: venous drainage blockedPainless puffiness, little rednessCongestion, cough, headache
Nephrotic syndromeProtein lost in the urineBoth eyes, worse on waking; then legs, belly, scrotumNormal blood pressure; 4+ protein, no blood
Acute glomerulonephritis (PSGN)Salt and water retainedPuffy eyes with cola-colored urineHigh blood pressure; strep 1 to 3 weeks earlier
Heart failurePump failureEdema is uncommon; big liverTires or breathes fast with activity; gallop
Liver failureAlbumin not madeAscites with jaundiceRare in a healthy child
Protein-losing enteropathyProtein lost in the gutEdema with chronic diarrheaLow albumin, clean urine
MalnutritionToo little protein eatenEdema with thin hair, poor growthDiet history
History: what each answer points to
ClueWhat it points to
Puffiness worst on waking, better by afternoonLying flat moves fluid to the lids in allergy and edema alike, so it separates neither; test the urine
Itchy eyes and sneezing in the same season each yearAllergic conjunctivitis
Minutes after a food, drug or sting, with hivesAcute allergic reaction
Insect bite, scratch or sinus infection near one eyePeriorbital cellulitis
Sore throat or skin sores 1 to 3 weeks ago; dark urineGlomerulonephritis
Tight shoes and waistband, weight gain, tired, eating lessGeneralized edema and ascites
Chronic diarrhea or a poor dietProtein lost in the gut or never eaten
Examination: what each finding points to
FindingWhat it points to
One red, warm, tender lid; full painless eye movements, normal visionPreseptal cellulitis
Dark circles under the eyes, an extra lower-lid crease, bumpy conjunctivaAllergy
Pitting over the shins; swelling of the scrotum or labiaGeneralized edema
Fluid wave: tap one flank, feel the wave at the other; an assistant's hand on the midline stops fat carrying itAscites
Blood pressureHigh in nephritis; usually normal in nephrotic syndrome, whose plasma volume is low
Gallop and a big liverHeart failure; an S4 is always abnormal, an S3 can be normal in a child
JaundiceLiver failure
First tests
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Urinalysis (dipstick and microscopy)First3+ to 4+ protein, no bloodNephrotic syndrome: albumin, lipids, creatinine
Protein with blood or red cell castsGlomerulonephritis: creatinine and C3
NormalNot the kidney: allergy, infection, or albumin lost elsewhere
Serum albumin, cholesterol, creatinineBy branchAlbumin below 2.5 g/dL, cholesterol high, creatinine normalNephrotic syndrome
Liver tests, bilirubin, international normalized ratio (INR)By branchBilirubin and INR highLiver failure
Stool alpha-1 antitrypsinBy branchHigh, with a clean urineProtein-losing enteropathy
Chest radiograph and echocardiogramBy branchBig heart, poor functionHeart failure
CT of the orbits and sinusesBy branchOnly with orbital signsOrbital cellulitis or abscess
Spot urine protein/creatinine ratioConfirmsAbove 2 mg/mg with low albuminNephrotic syndrome
Daily prednisoneConfirmsProtein clears within weeksMinimal change disease, presumed without biopsy
Renal biopsy, only if atypicalConfirmsFoot process effacement, otherwise normalMinimal change disease; focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) if steroid resistant
Serum immunoglobulin E (IgE) or allergy testingSkipOften high in atopic childrenCannot exclude a kidney cause
Finalists
On arrivalUrinalysisNextConfirmsTreatment and follow-up
Allergic conjunctivitisBoth eyes itchy and watery; sneezingNormalNothing furtherClinicalAvoid the allergen; antihistamine eye drops or oral antihistamine
Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitisOne red, tender lid; fever; eye moves freelyNot neededCheck movement, vision, proptosisClinical; CT only with orbital signsOral antibiotics; recheck in 1 to 2 days
Nephrotic syndrome (minimal change disease)Puffy eyes, then legs, belly, scrotum; BP normal4+ protein, no bloodAlbumin, lipids, creatinineProtein/creatinine ratio; remission on prednisonePrednisone; salt restriction; home dipstick for relapse
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisPuffy eyes, dark urine, high BPBlood, casts, some proteinCreatinine, C3Low C3; antistreptolysin O or anti-DNase BSalt and fluid restriction, furosemide; C3 normal by 8 weeks
Nephrotic syndrome from minimal change disease What it is – heavy proteinuria, albumin below 2.5 g/dL, edema and high lipids; minimal change disease causes 70 to 90% of cases under age 10 · Who – preschool and school-age children; boys about twice as often, a gap that closes by adolescence · Mechanism – the filter loses its negative charge, so albumin and immunoglobulin G (IgG) leak; low oncotic pressure moves fluid into the tissues, leaving the plasma volume low, which is why the blood pressure stays normal; the liver makes more lipoprotein and urinary loss of lipoprotein lipase slows clearance · Features – periorbital edema worst on waking, then dependent edema of the legs, scrotum or labia and ascites; tiredness and poor appetite; no blood in the urine, normal blood pressure and creatinine · Diagnosis – dipstick 3+ to 4+ protein, protein/creatinine ratio in the nephrotic range, low albumin, high cholesterol; biopsy only for steroid resistance after 8 weeks, hematuria, hypertension, a high creatinine, or age over 10 to 12 · Treatment – daily prednisone for 4 to 6 weeks, then a taper; salt restriction; albumin with furosemide only for severe edema, since diuretics alone can drop an already low plasma volume · Complications – infection during relapse (spontaneous peritonitis, usually pneumococcal; pneumonia, cellulitis, urinary infection) from urinary loss of IgG and factor B; venous thrombosis, including renal vein thrombosis, from urinary loss of antithrombin III and hemoconcentration; steroid effects: weight gain, hypertension, mood change, high glucose, slowed growth · Follow-up – home urine dipstick; relapse is common and treated with prednisone again; more than 95% respond to steroids, and relapses stop by the end of the second decade without kidney damage; frequent relapsers get a steroid-sparing drug; pneumococcal and yearly influenza vaccines in remission, and no live vaccines on high-dose steroids · Return for – fever or belly pain, swelling that returns, protein on the dipstick, little urine or dizziness, flank or leg pain
What sets it apart
VersusWhat separates it
Allergic conjunctivitisItch, sneezing and a clean urine
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisBlood in the urine, high blood pressure, low C3
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosisHematuria, hypertension, steroid resistance, an older child
Heart failureBig liver, gallop, no protein in the urine
Liver failure or protein-losing enteropathyLow albumin with a clean urine; jaundice or diarrhea
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo boy with a week of puffy eyelids on both sides, worst when he wakes and better by afternoon, now with swollen ankles, a bigger belly, tiredness and a poor appetite; no itching, redness or discharge; blood pressure normal; urine dipstick 4+ protein and negative for blood → Minimal change disease → Nephrotic syndrome: protein without blood at a normal blood pressure
  2. 5 yo girl with 4 days of puffiness around both eyes, worst on waking; no itching, redness, discharge or fever; her shoes have felt tight since yesterday → Urinalysis → The dipstick shows whether the kidney is leaking protein
  3. 6 yo with hay fever and 5 days of puffy eyelids on both sides each morning, now with ankle swelling; a serum IgE level is high; no urine has been tested → It does not exclude a kidney cause → Atopy is common; the urine dipstick is still the next test
  4. 7 yo with puffy, itchy eyes on both sides every spring, clear watery discharge, sneezing and a runny nose; dark circles and an extra crease below both lower lids; afebrile; urine dipstick negative → Allergic conjunctivitis → Itch and a clean urine separate it from edema; antihistamine eye drops
  5. 3 yo whose eyelids and lips swell within 20 minutes of eating a cashew for the first time, with raised, itchy wheals on the chest; no hoarseness, wheeze or vomiting; blood pressure and oxygen saturation normal → IgE-mediated food allergy → Abrupt swelling with hives; hereditary angioedema brings no hives
  6. 4 yo with 2 days of swelling and redness of the right upper eyelid, which is warm and tender, around a scratch from the family cat; T 38.3 C; full, painless eye movements, normal vision, no proptosis → Periorbital cellulitis → One eye, warm and tender, orbit spared: oral antibiotics
  7. 4 yo with 2 days of a red left eye, thick yellow discharge and lids stuck together each morning, with mild lid puffiness; the eyelid skin is not red, warm or tender; afebrile; vision normal → Bacterial conjunctivitis → Pus and crusting; under 6, bacterial is more likely than viral
  8. 5 yo with puffy eyes and swelling of the ankles and scrotum; BP 96/58; urine dipstick 4+ protein, no blood; serum albumin 1.8 g/dL → Spot urine protein/creatinine ratio → Above 2 mg/mg with low albumin is nephrotic syndrome
  9. 3 yo with 2 weeks of puffy eyelids who tires after a few minutes of play and sweats and breathes fast with meals; RR 44, HR 150; liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin; gallop rhythm; urine dipstick negative for protein → Heart failure → Big liver and a gallop with a clean urine: echocardiogram next
  10. 2 yo with 3 weeks of swollen eyelids and legs and 2 months of loose stools; weight has fallen from the 50th to the 10th percentile; albumin 1.7 g/dL; urine dipstick negative for protein; bilirubin and INR normal → Protein-losing enteropathy → Albumin lost in the gut; stool alpha-1 antitrypsin is high
  11. 4 yo with periorbital and leg edema; BP 132/88; urinalysis 4+ protein with 30 red cells per high-power field; creatinine 1.1 mg/dL; C3 normal → Renal biopsy → Hematuria, hypertension and a high creatinine are atypical for minimal change disease
  12. 6 yo with minimal change disease that went into remission on prednisone, off steroids for 5 months; his home urine dipstick has shown 3+ to 4+ protein for 3 days and his eyes are puffy again; blood pressure normal, no blood in the urine → Restart daily prednisone → A relapse in a steroid-responsive child; relapses are common and do not harm the kidney
  13. 5 yo in a relapse of nephrotic syndrome, before steroids have been restarted, who develops pneumococcal peritonitis → Urinary loss of immunoglobulin and factor B → Opsonins for encapsulated organisms leak into the urine
  14. 5 yo with nephrotic syndrome in relapse and ascites, now with T 39.2 C, severe abdominal pain, guarding and rebound tenderness; HR 140, BP 90/54 → Cultures and IV antibiotics → Spontaneous peritonitis, usually pneumococcal; blood and peritoneal fluid cultures, then broad Gram-positive and Gram-negative cover
  15. 6 yo with severe nephrotic syndrome, albumin 1.4 g/dL, who develops sudden left flank pain, gross hematuria and an enlarged, palpable left kidney; creatinine has risen from 0.4 to 0.9 mg/dL; afebrile → Renal vein thrombosis → Urinary loss of antithrombin III and hemoconcentration; Doppler ultrasound
  16. 5 yo in week 3 of daily prednisone, 2 mg/kg, for a first episode of nephrotic syndrome; his kindergarten vaccines are due → Varicella vaccine → Live vaccines wait until the child is off high-dose steroids
  17. 5 yo discharged in remission from a first episode of minimal change disease; the parents ask how a relapse will be caught early → Home urine dipstick testing → Protein on the morning dipstick comes before the swelling
Pairs with Part I Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child covers the lesion: minimal change disease versus membranous and FSGS (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis). It also covers starting steroids without a biopsy. Part II Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome covers PSGN (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis) and its C3 clock. Part II Anaphylaxis covers the acute allergic reaction and angioedema without hives. Part I Sinusitis and Its Complications covers preseptal versus orbital cellulitis and the orbital CT (computed tomography). Part I The Red Eye covers the conjunctivitis types.
Transferable rule For puffy eyes in a child, decide first whether the swelling belongs to the eye or to the whole child. If it is generalized, the urinalysis sorts it: protein alone means nephrotic syndrome, and blood with high blood pressure means nephritis.
Salient decoyPuffiness worst in the morning in an allergic child, treated as allergy without a urine dipstick.
Mirror twinPSGN also starts with puffy eyes; blood in the urine and a high blood pressure separate it.
Unchecked attributeA swollen lid called cellulitis without checking whether one eye or both, or whether the legs are swollen too.
Treat-the-numberFurosemide alone for nephrotic edema, when the plasma volume is already low.

edits.html:
Acute Rheumatic Fever

Jones criteria · recent strep evidence · carditis on echo · a setting is not a mechanism · penicillin prophylaxisDid a sore throat come 2 to 4 weeks before, and do the findings meet the Jones criteria?

The decision point

A sore throat 2 weeks ago was followed by migratory large-joint arthritis and a new holosystolic apical murmur with fever. That is 2 major Jones criteria on a strep foundation. A travel or camping detail is a setting, not a mechanism. There is no tick bite and no rash, and the 2–4 week latency belongs to the pharyngitis.

Jones criteria – 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, plus evidence of strep
  • Major (JONES): Joints (migratory polyarthritis) · O carditis · Nodules (subcutaneous) · Erythema marginatum · Sydenham chorea
  • Minor: fever, arthralgia, ↑erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)/C-reactive protein (CRP), prolonged PR
Pearls Type II hypersensitivity via molecular mimicry against M protein · Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells on pathology · the acute attack affects the mitral valve as regurgitation; decades later the valve disease presents as mitral stenosis · treatment is penicillin plus aspirin, then monthly benzathine penicillin for years · treating the pharyngitis prevents ARF (acute rheumatic fever) but not PSGN (post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Throat culture or rapid strep testFirstOften negative by the time ARF appearsA negative swab does not exclude it; serology next
Antistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B titersNextElevated or rising titerEvidence of recent group A strep, required by the Jones criteria
ESR and CRPSupportsElevatedMinor criterion
ElectrocardiogramSupportsProlonged PR intervalMinor criterion
EchocardiographyStagingMitral regurgitationCarditis, a major criterion, even when no murmur is heard
None: Jones criteriaConfirms2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, with strep evidenceAcute rheumatic fever; no single test confirms it
Lyme serology after a camping tripSkipNo erythema migrans or tick biteLyme gives late monoarthritis and atrioventricular (AV) block, not a new valve murmur
Scenario bank
  1. 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis → Acute rheumatic fever → penicillin plus anti-inflammatories
  2. 9 yo M with suspected acute rheumatic fever → Anti-streptolysin O titer
  3. 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever; which valve is most often involved → Mitral
  4. 9 yo M with arthritis 10 days after a diarrheal illness, with conjunctivitis and urethritis → Reactive arthritis
  5. 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever and new choreiform movements → Sydenham chorea – a major criterion
  6. 9 yo M recovering from acute rheumatic fever → Long-term penicillin prophylaxis
  7. 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis; history mentions a recent camping trip → Acute rheumatic fever → the trip is a setting, not a mechanism; no tick bite, no rash, and the latency belongs to the pharyngitis
Mimics Lyme needs erythema migrans. Its arthritis is late (months) and monoarticular, and its cardiac finding is AV block (atrioventricular block), not a valvular murmur. RMSF (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) needs headache and a rash involving palms and soles; it is a vasculitis, not an arthritis. JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) needs ≥6 weeks by definition.
How NBME framed it No sore throat was mentioned, only a recent refugee camp, which also invited the travel-fever decoys; Kawasaki disease appeared as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, and the mitral murmur was described, not named.
Salient decoyLyme carditis: the camping trip is a setting, not a mechanism; there is no tick bite or erythema migrans, and Lyme gives atrioventricular block, not a new valve murmur.

edits.html:
Bone Lesions in a Child

childhood bone lesions by site · age and periosteum · what each does next · imaging before biopsy · Ewing or infectionWhere does it sit, how old is the child, and is the periosteum quiet or aggressive?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Read the plain film by site and periosteum; then recall what that lesion does next.

  • Painless hard bump near a joint, spur continuous with the cortex and medulla: osteochondroma. It grows until the physes close, then stops. Observe; no biopsy. About 1% of solitary lesions turn malignant.
  • Night pain relieved by NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), small lucent nidus: osteoid osteoma. It involutes over years.
  • Central metaphyseal lucency, no periosteal reaction: unicameral bone cyst. Observe with serial films; the risk is fracture.
  • Sunburst periosteum, often with a Codman triangle, in a metaphysis: osteosarcoma. Onion skin in the shaft, pelvis or spine, sometimes with fever: Ewing sarcoma.

Night pain that wakes the child, with fever or weight loss, points to malignancy, not a benign lesion.

An aggressive film gets MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) before biopsy; chest CT (computed tomography) stages the lungs. Fever does not exclude a tumor: Ewing sarcoma can raise the ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), CRP (C-reactive protein) and WBC (white blood cell count).

Diagnosis
Where it sits, and the clue
LesionSiteAge and clue
ChondroblastomaEpiphysisTeens, physes open; well-defined lucency, thin sclerotic rim
Giant cell tumorEpiphysisOver 20, mature; soap bubble
OsteochondromaMetaphysisTeens; most common benign; painless spur; multiple if hereditary
Unicameral bone cystMetaphysis (humerus, femur)Physes open; painless, incidental; central lucency, no periosteal reaction
OsteosarcomaMetaphysisTeens; sunburst; high ALP (alkaline phosphatase); rarely febrile
Osteoid osteomaLong bone (often proximal femur) or spineTeens; night pain gone with NSAIDs; nidus
Ewing sarcomaShaft, pelvis, axialPeak 10 to 15; may be febrile; onion skin
ChondrosarcomaPelvis, proximal femur or humerusAdults over 40 to 50
Ewing sarcoma or osteomyelitis Ewing – weeks; shaft, pelvis or spine; small round blue cells · Osteomyelitis – days; long-bone metaphysis; trauma or immunodeficiency support it when present; inflammatory cells and necrotic bone
Management and treatment
By lesion Observe – osteochondroma; unicameral bone cyst with serial films; osteoid osteoma with NSAIDs · Curettage – chondroblastoma and giant cell tumor, both locally aggressive; giant cell tumor has high local recurrence · Malignant – osteosarcoma: chemotherapy plus resection; Ewing sarcoma: chemotherapy plus resection, radiation or both
Practice
  1. 12-year-old girl: pelvic film shows a moth-eaten lytic lesion of the right ilium with lamellated periosteal reaction Tender mass over the right buttock, growing for 6 weeks T 38.4 °C · leukocytes 12,800/mm³ · biopsy: sheets of small round blue cells → Ewing sarcoma → a pelvic lytic lesion over weeks with layered periosteum is Ewing sarcoma: MRI maps it, and biopsy shows uniform small round blue cells in sheets, little cytoplasm, fibrous septa; osteomyelitis can also bring fever but favors long bones, and its biopsy shows inflammatory cells and necrotic bone, and osteosarcoma is metaphyseal, rarely pelvic and rarely febrile
  2. 13-year-old girl, painless hard bump above the left knee 3 weeks; unchanged no trauma, fever or weight loss Firm, nontender distal femoral mass Vital signs normal · film: metaphyseal spur pointing away from the joint, continuous with cortex and medulla → Grows until the growth plates close, then stops → a spur continuous with the cortex and medulla is an osteochondroma, the most common benign bone tumor: it grows with the skeleton until physeal closure, then stops; transformation is about 1% and involution belongs to osteoid osteoma
  3. 15-year-old boy with 2 months of right thigh pain worst at night; unrelated to activity ibuprofen relieves it completely No weight loss or limp Afebrile · film: small round lucency with a sclerotic rim, proximal femur → Osteoid osteoma → night pain relieved by NSAIDs with a small lucent nidus in a sclerotic rim is osteoid osteoma, most often in the proximal femur
  4. 16-year-old boy was diagnosed with osteoid osteoma of the femur 2 months ago night pain controlled by ibuprofen no other complaints Parents ask what happens if nothing more is done Afebrile · repeat film unchanged → Spontaneous involution → osteoid osteoma involutes on its own over years, so NSAIDs and serial films are reasonable
  5. 14-year-old boy was diagnosed with osteoid osteoma of the tibia last week pain wakes him at night one ibuprofen dose stops it within an hour Parents ask why the medicine works so well Afebrile · nidus under 2 cm on film → Prostaglandin production by the nidus → the nidus makes prostaglandins, which NSAIDs block, so the response is nearly diagnostic
  6. 13-year-old girl with 6 weeks of worsening pain below the knee firm mass over the proximal tibia no trauma Pain now present at rest Afebrile · film: mixed lytic and dense metaphyseal lesion, sunburst periosteal reaction → Osteosarcoma → a metaphyseal mixed lesion with a sunburst reaction in a teenager is osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone malignancy of childhood; prior radiation and hereditary retinoblastoma raise the risk
  7. 15-year-old boy with 6 weeks of progressive pain above the right knee now wakes him at night firm, tender distal thigh swelling Film: ill-defined mixed lytic-sclerotic distal femoral metaphysis Afebrile · sunburst reaction, Codman triangle · ALP elevated → MRI of the right femur → an aggressive film gets MRI of the affected bone before biopsy: it maps soft tissue and vessels and plans the biopsy; chest CT stages the lungs
  8. 12-year-old boy with 6 weeks of worsening thigh pain wakes him at night intermittent fevers; lost 2 kg; no trauma or recent infection Film: moth-eaten mid-shaft femoral lysis, onion-skin periosteum T 38.2 °C · ESR 55 mm/h → Ewing sarcoma → a permeative diaphyseal lesion with onion-skin layers over weeks, with weight loss, is Ewing sarcoma; the shaft and the 6-week course argue against osteomyelitis; fever, when present, often means it has spread
  9. 7-year-old boy, febrile 4 days won't bear weight on left leg warm, point-tender distal femoral metaphysis; full, painless knee motion MRI: marrow edema, small subperiosteal collection T 39.2 °C · WBC 16,000/mm³, neutrophils · hemoglobin, platelets normal · CRP markedly high · film normal → Osteomyelitis → days of fever with metaphyseal point tenderness and an early normal film is osteomyelitis: blood culture, intravenous antibiotics, drain the abscess; Ewing sarcoma runs for weeks
  10. 9-year-old boy with arm pain after a minor fall no pain before the fall tender upper arm Fracture through a well-defined central proximal humeral metaphyseal lucency Afebrile · thin sclerotic margin; no periosteal reaction → Unicameral bone cyst → a central metaphyseal lucency with no periosteal reaction that fractures is a unicameral bone cyst; medullary expansion thins the cortex; chondroblastoma is also a lucency with a sclerotic rim, but it sits in the epiphysis
  11. 10-year-old girl, mild shoulder pain after a fall on an outstretched hand full range of motion no weight loss No fracture on film Afebrile · incidental well-defined central proximal humeral metaphyseal lucency · thin cortex; narrow transition; no periosteal reaction → Observation with serial radiographs → an incidental unicameral bone cyst is observed with serial films; it resolves by physeal closure, and the risk is pathologic fracture
  12. 28-year-old woman with 4 months of knee pain and swelling skeletally mature no trauma, fever or weight loss Eccentric expansile lytic lesion of the distal femoral epiphysis Afebrile · soap-bubble appearance on film → Giant cell tumor of bone → an expansile soap-bubble epiphyseal lesion after skeletal maturity is giant cell tumor: locally destructive, curettage or excision, high local recurrence
  13. 16-year-old boy with 3 months of constant knee pain physes still open; no weight loss mild joint swelling Well-circumscribed epiphyseal lucency, thin sclerotic rim, crossing the physis Afebrile · no periosteal reaction → Chondroblastoma → an epiphyseal lucency before skeletal maturity is chondroblastoma; age separates it from giant cell tumor; curettage
Pairs with Leg Pain in a Child: one-sided night pain needs a film. Muscle Contusion and Myositis Ossificans: the post-injury mass. Acute Leukemia in a Child: bone pain from marrow. The Limping Child: the febrile limp.
Transferable rule

To predict a lesion's course, name it first, then recall what it does. To name it, check site, age and fever before reading the film.

edits.html:
Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia and Urinary Retention

three-stage history · retention, infection and kidney injury as complications · 1+ blood is not a stone · catheter firstWhich process came first, and does it explain every other finding?

The decision point

The underlying cause is the primary process that produces the other findings, not one of its complications. Six months of hesitancy and dribbling came first. Five days of frequency and incomplete emptying followed, then one day of anuria with suprapubic pain. The retention, the UTI (urinary tract infection) and the creatinine of 3.4 all result from prostatic obstruction.

Why 1+ blood does not change the diagnosis Trace-to-1+ hematuria is expected with UTI (urinary tract infection), bladder distension and BPH (benign prostatic hyperplasia) itself. Nephrolithiasis needs the pain syndrome of colicky flank pain radiating to the groin. It also does not explain six months of hesitancy. A single nonspecific dipstick finding does not outweigh a six-month history.
Scenario bank
  1. 72 yo M with 6 months of hesitancy, now anuric for a day with suprapubic fullness → Acute urinary retention from BPH → catheterize
  2. 72 yo M in retention; the question asks the underlying cause → Benign prostatic hyperplasia
  3. 72 yo M after catheter relief; first-line medical therapy → Alpha-blocker
  4. 72 yo M with a very large prostate seeking long-term volume reduction → Add a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor
  5. 72 yo M with BPH started on oxybutynin for urgency, now in retention → Anticholinergic-induced retention → stop the drug
  6. 72 yo M in retention with a hard nodular prostate and prostate-specific antigen 40 → Prostate cancer → biopsy
The management sequel Acute retention → bladder catheterization first (suprapubic if the urethra is impassable). Then treat the UTI (urinary tract infection) and watch for post-obstructive diuresis. Expect the creatinine to fall; the fall proves the AKI (acute kidney injury) was post-renal. Renal ultrasound shows hydronephrosis if confirmation is needed. Long-term, give tamsulosin ± finasteride, with TURP (transurethral resection of the prostate) if refractory.
Transferable rule A single lab value should change the diagnosis only if it is incompatible with it, not merely compatible with another diagnosis.
Treat-the-number

edits.html:
Abdominal Mass in a Young Child

organ of origin · age · Wilms tumor vs neuroblastoma · cystic newborn masses · ultrasound, then computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)Where does the mass arise, and how old is the child?

Source vignette Pt – 3 yo F at a well-child visit, normal development and immunizations; BP 156/96; mild right upper and lower quadrant tenderness with a palpable right-sided abdominal mass · Imaging – ultrasound shows a 12-cm heterogeneous solitary mass arising within the upper pole of the right kidney · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Wilms tumor, neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma, polycystic kidney disease and renal cell carcinoma
The decision point

Ask two questions of any solid abdominal mass in a child: which organ does it arise from, and how old is the child. A mass within the kidney in a 2- to 5-year-old is Wilms tumor. The hypertension fits Wilms tumor and comes from renin secretion or compression of the renal vessels.

Neuroblastoma is the nearest mimic and also causes hypertension, through catecholamines. It arises from neural crest in the adrenal or sympathetic chain and displaces the kidney rather than growing inside it. It usually presents before age 2 and may cross the midline. Pheochromocytoma is also adrenal and presents with episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations.

Abdominal mass in a young child: the differential
DiagnosisAge and originThe NBME tellWhy less likely here
Wilms tumorPeak age 2 to 5; arises within the kidney; child usually looks wellSmooth unilateral flank mass that does not cross the midline; hypertension, hematuria; WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann, Denys-Drash; alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) not raised – (the answer)
NeuroblastomaUsually under 2; neural crest of the adrenal medulla or sympathetic chainIrregular mass that may cross the midline, calcifications, raised urine vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA); periorbital ecchymoses (raccoon eyes), opsoclonus-myoclonus; often an ill childMass lies within the kidney; age 3
PheochromocytomaOlder child or adult; adrenal medulla, often syndromicEpisodic headache, sweating, palpitations with hypertension; raised metanephrinesAdrenal sits on the kidney, not within it; no paroxysms
Hydronephrosis or multicystic dysplastic kidneyNewborn or infant; the commonest neonatal abdominal massesFluid-filled on ultrasound: a dilated collecting system, or noncommunicating cysts with no functioning kidneySolid heterogeneous mass at 3 years
Polycystic kidney diseaseRecessive form in newborns; dominant form in adultsBilateral enlarged cystic kidneys; the newborn form shows large echogenic kidneys and hepatic fibrosisSolitary, unilateral, solid
Renal vein thrombosisNewborn under stress: infant of a diabetic mother, asphyxia, dehydration, polycythemia; clot in the renal veinEnlarged kidney with hematuria and thrombocytopeniaAge 3; well child with a solid mass
HepatoblastomaInfant or toddler; arises in the liver; Beckwith-Wiedemann associationRight upper quadrant hepatic mass with a raised AFPMass arises from the kidney
Renal cell carcinomaAdults; hereditary forms such as von Hippel-Lindau present earlierFlank pain, hematuria and a mass in an adultAge 3
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Abdominal ultrasoundFirstSolid mass within the kidneyWilms tumor; a suprarenal calcified mass suggests neuroblastoma; a cystic mass suggests hydronephrosis or multicystic dysplastic kidney
CT or MRI of the abdomenNextExtent of the tumor, nodes, the other kidneyLocal staging and surgical planning
Urine VMA and HVABy branchRaised catecholamine metabolitesNeuroblastoma; normal in Wilms tumor
Serum AFPBy branchRaised with a liver massHepatoblastoma; not raised in Wilms tumor
Chest CTStagingLung nodulesMetastatic Wilms tumor; the lung is its usual distant site
Excision with pathologyConfirmsNephroblastoma on histologyWilms tumor, staged for chemotherapy with or without radiation
Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo F at a well-child visit, BP 156/96, palpable right abdominal mass; ultrasound shows a 12-cm heterogeneous solid mass arising within the upper pole of the right kidney → Wilms tumor → excision with chemotherapy, with or without radiation
  2. 14 mo M, irritable for weeks, with rapid chaotic eye movements, jerking of the limbs, and a firm irregular abdominal mass crossing the midline; ultrasound shows calcifications → Neuroblastoma → urine VMA and HVA
  3. 18 mo M with weight loss, bruising around both eyes and a firm left upper quadrant mass lying above the kidney on ultrasound → Urine VMA and HVA → neuroblastoma
  4. 2 yo F, well, whose mother felt a firm painless mass in her left flank while bathing her; BP 118/76, mass smooth and does not cross the midline → Abdominal ultrasound → suspected Wilms tumor
  5. 3-day-old boy with a smooth left flank mass; ultrasound shows multiple noncommunicating cysts of varying size replacing the left kidney with no normal parenchyma, right kidney normal → Multicystic dysplastic kidney → nonfunctioning kidney; the other kidney must be checked
  6. 15 yo F with episodes of pounding headache, sweating and palpitations, BP 172/104 during an episode, and a 4-cm mass above the left kidney → Pheochromocytoma → plasma free metanephrines
  7. 6 mo F with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, 1 week of intermittent vomiting and fussiness, macroglossia, right-sided hemihypertrophy and a firm right upper quadrant mass; serum alpha-fetoprotein 15,678 ng/mL, urine homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid normal → Hepatoblastoma → liver mass with a very high alpha-fetoprotein
  8. 3 yo M with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome; a screening ultrasound shows a 7-cm solid mass arising within the left kidney; serum alpha-fetoprotein and urine catecholamine metabolites are normal → Wilms tumor → kidney origin with a normal alpha-fetoprotein
  9. 9 mo F, fussy, with a firm right upper quadrant mass that ultrasound places within the right lobe of the liver; the kidneys and adrenals are normal → Serum alpha-fetoprotein → hepatoblastoma
  10. Male newborn at 38 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, Apgar scores 8 and 9, normal examination except bilateral flank masses; hematocrit 50%, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, urine with moderate blood and trace protein; ultrasound shows both kidneys enlarged with mixed echogenicity → Polycystic kidney disease → the recessive form; look for hepatic fibrosis
  11. 2-day-old boy whose mother has poorly controlled diabetes, with a new right flank mass, gross hematuria and a platelet count of 70,000/mm3; ultrasound shows one enlarged kidney and a normal left kidney → Renal vein thrombosis → confirm with Doppler ultrasound of the renal vein
Management, in one line Wilms tumor is treated with excision plus chemotherapy, with or without radiation; about 90% of children survive. Tissue at excision or biopsy makes the diagnosis. Ultrasound, not CT (computed tomography), is the first study.
Pearls Establish the origin before weighing age: a mass within the kidney is Wilms tumor; an adrenal or paraspinal mass is neuroblastoma or pheochromocytoma · Hypertension does not separate the two tumors: Wilms raises renin, neuroblastoma releases catecholamines · A well child with a smooth flank mass favors Wilms; an irritable child with weight loss, bone pain or raccoon eyes favors neuroblastoma · Rapid chaotic eye movements with myoclonic jerks in a toddler is opsoclonus-myoclonus, a paraneoplastic sign of neuroblastoma · Two enlarged kidneys in a well newborn suggest ARPKD (autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease); ultrasound shows large echogenic kidneys · ARPKD comes from PKHD1 mutations and brings congenital hepatic fibrosis and Caroli syndrome · Severe ARPKD in utero causes oligohydramnios and Potter sequence · ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease) is the adult form, with kidney and liver cysts and cerebral aneurysms · A creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL on day 1 mirrors the mother's creatinine and does not prove neonatal kidney failure · Neonatal renal vein thrombosis also gives a flank mass and hematuria, usually with thrombocytopenia, in a stressed infant · Avoid repeated deep palpation of a suspected Wilms tumor, because rupture of the capsule spreads tumor · Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome raises the risk of both Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma, so the syndrome alone cannot pick between them · A firm right upper quadrant mass with a very high AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) in an infant is hepatoblastoma · How NBME framed it: the stem names the syndrome and hides the answer in a lab panel, a very high AFP with normal urine HVA (homovanillic acid) and VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) · A syndrome that carries Wilms risk earns surveillance ultrasounds, covered in Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes
How NBME framed it For the newborn with two flank masses, the key reads only polycystic kidney disease, and the ultrasound says mixed echogenicity rather than cysts · The options are a mass family sorted by age, three tumors plus one vascular mimic, and the labs plant hematuria and a raised creatinine to fit the decoys
Pairs with Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes covers WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann and the surveillance that follows. Part II Posterior Urethral Valves covers the neonatal flank mass, where hydronephrosis and multicystic dysplastic kidney come first. Part II Acute Leukemia in a Child shares neuroblastoma through marrow infiltration and periorbital ecchymoses. Part I Maternal Effects in the Newborn covers the day-1 creatinine that reflects the mother's kidneys: is the value the mother's or the baby's? Ask: does the mass arise within the kidney, and is the child older than 2?
Transferable rule For a solid mass in a child, name the organ it arises from before naming the tumor, then use age to decide among the rest. A finding two tumors share, such as hypertension, cannot distinguish them.
Unchecked attributeNeuroblastoma is the famous childhood abdominal tumor, but it arises from the adrenal or sympathetic chain and usually before age 2.
Salient decoyPheochromocytoma matches the hypertension and the upper-pole location, but it is adrenal and episodic.
Unchecked attributePolycystic kidney disease gives bilateral cystic kidneys, not one solid mass.
Unchecked attributeRenal cell carcinoma arises within the kidney too, but in adults.
Salient decoyWilms tumor (nephroblastoma): the best-known Beckwith-Wiedemann tumor, but it is a flank mass within the kidney and does not raise AFP (alpha-fetoprotein).
Test-overrides-findingsNeuroblastoma: age 6 months fits it better than Wilms tumor, but urine HVA (homovanillic acid) and VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) are normal.
Unchecked attributeGerm cell tumor: a yolk sac tumor also raises AFP, but in a young child it presents as a pelvic mass, not a firm upper abdominal one.
True-fact-wrong-slotSpina bifida occulta: a raised AFP goes with open neural tube defects in pregnancy, not the closed form, and it makes no abdominal mass.
Unchecked attributeNephroblastoma (Wilms tumor): it shares the flank mass and hematuria; it is usually unilateral and peaks at ages 2 to 5, and this newborn has two masses.
Salient decoyNeuroblastoma: it is the most common solid tumor of infancy; it arises in the adrenal, displaces the kidney rather than enlarging it, and is rarely bilateral.
Unchecked attributeRenal cell carcinoma: it shares a mass within the kidney and hematuria; it is a tumor of adults and adolescents, not newborns.
Unchecked attributeRenal vein thrombosis: it shares a newborn flank mass, hematuria and an enlarged kidney; this baby has no risk factor, with an uncomplicated delivery, good Apgar scores and a normal hematocrit.
