edits.html:
High Blood Pressure in a Child or Adolescent

device vs auscultation · adult cutoffs from age 13 · staging · recheck interval by stage · ambulatory monitoringHas auscultation confirmed the device reading, and what stage does the averaged value set?

Source vignette Pt – 17 yo M at a pre-participation examination for football; feels well; no illnesses, medications or family history; body mass index (BMI) 29; automated oscillometric reading 138/88 mm Hg, stated as the 95th percentile for age and height, then 140/89 mm Hg on the same device; rest of the examination normal · Q – the most appropriate next step in diagnosis; options spanned auscultatory measurement, echocardiography, 24-hour ambulatory monitoring and repeat device readings daily for 3 days or in 2 weeks
The decision point

Automated oscillometric devices tend to read higher than auscultation for both systolic and diastolic pressure. A high device reading needs confirmation by auscultation, even after the same device has repeated it. Take at least two auscultatory readings at that visit and average them. The averaged auscultatory value sets the category and the recheck interval.

From age 13, the 2017 AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) guideline uses fixed cutoffs that match the adult categories. By those cutoffs, 138/88 mm Hg falls in stage 1 and 140/89 mm Hg in stage 2. Device readings are not staged until auscultation confirms them. Ambulatory monitoring, echocardiography and drug therapy all come after that confirmation.

Defining criteria, age 13 and older Confirming a high reading – repeat by auscultation at the same visit and average the readings; a device reading alone is not staged · Elevated blood pressure – systolic 120 to 129 mm Hg with diastolic below 80 mm Hg · Stage 1 hypertension – 130/80 to 139/89 mm Hg · Stage 2 hypertension – 140/90 mm Hg or higher · Hypertension diagnosis – auscultatory-confirmed readings of 130/80 mm Hg or higher at 3 separate visits
Management ladder – high blood pressure in an adolescent
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Screening reading at a routine visit; an oscillometric device is acceptable. Yearly from age 3, and at every visit with obesity, kidney disease, diabetes, prior coarctation or a drug that raises blood pressureReading of 120/80 mm Hg or higher
2Repeat by auscultation at the same visit, at least 2 readings, and average themAveraged auscultatory value in the elevated or hypertensive range; that value sets the stage
3Recheck by auscultation on a schedule set by stage: elevated, lifestyle advice and recheck in 6 months; stage 1, lifestyle advice and recheck in 1 to 2 weeks; stage 2, lifestyle advice and specialty referral within 1 weekElevated readings for 1 year, or stage 1 readings at 3 visits
424-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring to confirm hypertensionHypertension confirmed: evaluate for secondary causes and end-organ damage
5Lifestyle change first: the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet and moderate to vigorous activity 3 to 5 days a week. Echocardiography for left ventricular hypertrophy when drug therapy is consideredLifestyle change fails, especially with left ventricular hypertrophy, symptoms or stage 2 without a modifiable cause: start a drug
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo M at a football pre-participation examination, well, BMI 29, automated oscillometric blood pressure 138/88 mm Hg and 140/89 mm Hg on repeat with the same device, otherwise normal examination → Blood pressure measurement by auscultation → the averaged auscultatory readings set the stage
  2. 15 yo F at a well visit with an automated reading of 136/82 mm Hg; two auscultatory readings at the same visit average 132/78 mm Hg → Stage 1 hypertension → a systolic of 130 to 139 mm Hg sets stage 1 even with a diastolic below 80
  3. 14 yo M at a well visit whose auscultatory readings average 124/76 mm Hg, with a normal examination → Lifestyle advice and recheck in 6 months → elevated blood pressure
  4. 16 yo F with obesity whose auscultatory averages are 134/84, 132/82 and 136/86 mm Hg at three visits over 3 months → 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring → confirms hypertension before workup and treatment
  5. 17 yo M, asymptomatic with a normal examination, whose auscultatory readings at one visit average 146/94 mm Hg → Lifestyle advice and referral within 1 week → stage 2 hypertension
  6. 16 yo M with obesity and hypertension confirmed by ambulatory monitoring whose blood pressure stays high after a trial of diet and exercise, so drug therapy is planned → Echocardiography → measures left ventricular mass before drug therapy
Guideline history The 2004 Fourth Report defined hypertension as a reading at or above the 95th percentile at every age, and older questions still use that definition. The 2017 AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) guideline set fixed adult cutoffs from age 13 and kept percentiles only for children under 13. Under 13, stage 1 starts at the 95th percentile for sex, age and height, or at 130/80 mm Hg if that is lower. From age 13, stage 1 starts at 130/80 mm Hg regardless of percentile.
Exit ramps A symptomatic adolescent, or a reading above 180/120 mm Hg, goes to the emergency department · Stage 1 or stage 2 readings call for a leg blood pressure; an arm reading higher than the leg suggests coarctation of the aorta · Confirmed hypertension opens a search for secondary causes and end-organ damage
Pearls Electrocardiography is not used to look for left ventricular hypertrophy in a hypertensive child; echocardiography is · Lifestyle change aimed at obesity is the first treatment for most adolescent hypertension · How NBME framed it: with the device reading already repeated, the key is a measurement method, not a diagnosis, heart test or later recheck
Pairs with Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers confirmation, baseline tests and drug choice in adults. Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers the causes to test for once hypertension is confirmed.
Transferable rule A high blood pressure from an automated device is confirmed by averaged auscultatory readings before it is staged, monitored, imaged or treated.
Sequencing trapEchocardiography looks for left ventricular hypertrophy once drug therapy is considered, and this reading is not yet confirmed.
Sequencing trapAmbulatory monitoring is accurate, but it follows auscultatory office readings that stay elevated for 1 year or in stage 1 across 3 visits.
Unchecked attributeDaily device readings for 3 days repeat the same overestimate; the method must change, not the number of readings.
True-fact-wrong-slotA 1 to 2 week recheck follows stage 1 confirmed by auscultation, but a repeat device reading in 2 weeks confirms nothing.

edits.html:
Adolescent Confidentiality

the exceptions · services protected without parental consent · CRAFFT and brief counseling · encouraging self-disclosureWhat would have to be true to break confidentiality, and is any of it present?

Source vignette Pt – 16 yo M, well, discloses weekend marijuana use during the confidential portion of the visit · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned confidential counseling with CRAFFT screening, informing his parents and ordering a urine drug screen
The decision point

A minor discloses substance use during a confidential interview. In this case, keep it confidential and counsel him directly. Substance use is a confidential service in essentially every state, and nothing he describes meets an exception. Confidentiality is what makes honest disclosure possible at all; adolescents who don't expect it don't disclose.

Set the frame before he talks by saying "what you tell me stays between us, unless someone's safety is at risk". Then screen with CRAFFT (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Family/Friends, Trouble), deliver brief counseling, and encourage him to tell his parents himself. Encouraging voluntary disclosure is not the same as disclosing.

Defining criteria Suicidal or homicidal intent – harm to self or others; break confidentiality · Physical or sexual abuse – including statutory abuse by partner age; break confidentiality and report · Imminent danger – specific and serious; imminence is the word that decides · Not an exception – vagueness, a parent asking, an embarrassing diagnosis, or risky behavior that is not imminently lethal
Adolescent confidentiality – what is protected
Confidential without parental consent
Sexually transmitted infection diagnosis and treatment (all 50 states)
Contraception
Pregnancy care (abortion varies – many states require notification or consent)
Substance use evaluation and treatment
Mental health services (age and state vary)
Emancipated / mature minors: married, military, parenting, self-supporting, court-declared → consent as adults
Distractors "Inform his parents": parental authority is the higher principle for most care, but the confidential-services carve-outs exist to override it (trump-card inversion) · "Tell him you can't promise confidentiality": this sounds true but is harmful; frame confidentiality as conditional, naming the specific exceptions, not as a blanket refusal · "Refer to a substance-use program": escalating before you have screened severity is a sequencing trap; occasional use gets brief counseling, not a program · "Order a urine drug screen": he already told you. Testing to confirm a disclosure is redundant, and a non-consented screen is its own ethics violation.
Mnemonic HEEADSSS (Home, Education and employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide and depression, Safety) is the adolescent psychosocial history, asked privately.
Scenario bank
  1. 16 yo M discloses weekend marijuana use, otherwise well → Confidential counseling, CRAFFT, encourage self-disclosure to parents
  2. 16 yo M discloses use and says he's been thinking about killing himself → Break confidentiality – safety exception
  3. 16 yo M who drives after drinking → Maintain confidentiality and counsel about the driving → escalate only if he describes an imminent plan to drive impaired
  4. 15 yo F requesting contraception, doesn't want her mother told → Provide it confidentially
  5. 15 yo F at 15 weeks, sexual partner is 24 years old → Report it → the age gap converts this to statutory abuse
  6. 17 yo M with chlamydia → Treat confidentially; partner notification is a public-health obligation and does not breach his confidentiality
  7. 17 yo F, married, needs surgery → She is emancipated and consents herself
  8. 16 yo M whose mother calls to ask what was discussed → Decline to disclose; redirect to encouraging the conversation at home
  9. 14 yo M with an appendectomy needed → Parental consent required → surgical care is not a confidential service
  10. 16 yo M, opioid use with withdrawal symptoms and IV track marks → Severity now warrants treatment referral, still discussed with him first
  11. 16 yo M in a state where billing goes to the parent's insurance → Address the practical confidentiality limit up front; this is the real-world failure point
Paired pearls Set the frame before the disclosure; confidentiality cannot be promised retroactively · CRAFFT (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Family/Friends, Trouble) is the validated adolescent screen; ≥2 is positive · emergency care never waits for consent · Management almost always includes "encourage him to tell his parents", which preserves confidentiality and the family relationship.
Pairs with Elder Abuse above covers the same axis in the opposite direction. There, impaired capacity forces reporting over the patient's wishes. Here, a minor with a confidential service forces confidentiality over the parent's wishes. Both turn on who holds decisional authority for this specific decision, not on who is older.
Transferable rule Maintain confidentiality unless the disclosure satisfies a named exception (harm to self, harm to others, abuse). Do not weigh how serious the behavior sounds; without a named exception, confidentiality holds no matter how alarming the disclosure.
Trump-card inversionSequencing trap

edits.html:
Anaphylaxis

organ-system criteria · hypotension not required · mast cell mechanism · bradykinin angioedema · delayed drug reactionsHow many organ systems are involved, and how soon after the exposure?

Source vignette Pt – 12 yo M, 30 minutes of burning, swollen eyes, a scratchy, tight throat and crampy abdominal pain; seen earlier the same day for several days of sore throat and started on amoxicillin; no known drug allergies · Exam – T 37.2, BP 116/68, HR 92; bilateral periorbital swelling, mild conjunctival redness, scattered wheals on the trunk · Q – the pathogenesis of his symptoms; options spanned Epstein-Barr virus infection, immune complex formation, impaired bradykinin degradation, mast cell activation and systemic vasculitis
The decision point

Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis based on the number of organ systems involved and the time since exposure; hypotension is not required. Within minutes to hours of a likely allergen, skin or mucosal findings plus one more system (respiratory, gastrointestinal or cardiovascular) meet criteria. This boy has wheals and periorbital swelling (skin), throat tightness (respiratory) and cramps (gut) 30 minutes after amoxicillin. He therefore has anaphylaxis despite a normal blood pressure. The mechanism is immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation releasing histamine, prostaglandins and leukotrienes. A history of no known drug allergies does not argue against it. An earlier exposure sensitized him without a reaction, and re-exposure triggers the release.

The exception is angioedema without hives. Swelling of the lips, tongue, face or bowel wall with no wheals and no itch from an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or hereditary angioedema is bradykinin-mediated. It builds over hours and responds poorly to epinephrine and antihistamines. Rashes that arrive days into a drug or an infection are delayed reactions, not anaphylaxis.

Defining criteria Anaphylaxis is likely with acute onset (minutes to hours) and any 1 of: · 1 – skin or mucosal involvement (hives, flushing, swollen lips, tongue or eyes) plus respiratory compromise or hypotension · 2 – 2 or more systems after a likely allergen: skin or mucosa, respiratory, cardiovascular, persistent gastrointestinal symptoms · 3 – hypotension alone after a known allergen for that patient
Anaphylaxis and its mimics – the differential
DiagnosisTiming after exposureMechanismThe NBME tell
AnaphylaxisMinutes to a few hoursIgE-mediated mast cell activation (type I)Skin plus a second system: wheeze, stridor, throat tightness, vomiting or cramps, hypotension
Acute urticaria aloneMinutes to hoursMast cell activation, often IgEHives and itch with no second system; normal airway, gut and blood pressure
Bradykinin angioedema (ACE inhibitor, hereditary angioedema)Hours; ACE inhibitor reactions can start months or years into therapyImpaired bradykinin degradation (ACE inhibitor); C1 inhibitor deficiency (hereditary, low C4)Lip, tongue or bowel-wall swelling with no hives or itch; little response to epinephrine or antihistamines
Serum sickness-like reaction5 to 14 days into a drugDelayed drug hypersensitivity; true serum sickness is immune complexUrticarial rash with fever, arthralgia and nodes
Epstein-Barr virus with an aminopenicillinDays into amoxicillinVirus-driven drug rash, not IgEMaculopapular rash with fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior nodes, left upper quadrant pain
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisDays to weeks after pharyngitisImmune complex (type III)Edema building over days with hypertension and cola-colored urine
Systemic vasculitis (immunoglobulin A [IgA] vasculitis)DaysImmune complex vessel inflammationPalpable purpura, fever, arthralgia, colicky abdominal pain
Vasovagal syncopeSeconds, with pain or fear (needles)Vagal surgeBradycardia, pallor and sweating; no hives, no wheeze
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo M, 30 minutes of burning, swollen eyes, a scratchy, tight throat and crampy abdominal pain; earlier today diagnosed with pharyngitis after several days of sore throat and started on amoxicillin; no known drug allergies; T 37.2, BP 116/68, HR 92; bilateral periorbital swelling, mild conjunctival redness, scattered wheals on the trunk → Mast cell activation → anaphylaxis: skin, respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement within 30 minutes of amoxicillin, after sensitization by an earlier course; intramuscular (IM) epinephrine
  2. 7 yo F at a birthday party, 10 minutes after eating a cookie made with peanut butter, develops hives on the face and trunk, wheezing and 2 episodes of vomiting; no previous reactions to food; T 37.0, BP 98/60, HR 128, RR 30, SpO2 94% on room air; diffuse expiratory wheezes → Intramuscular epinephrine → anaphylaxis by skin plus respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement; blood pressure need not fall
  3. 9 yo M, itchy raised wheals on the trunk and arms 1 hour after eating strawberries for the first time this season; no lip or tongue swelling, throat symptoms, cough, vomiting or abdominal pain; BP 104/66, HR 90, SpO2 99%; lungs clear; blanching urticarial plaques → Oral cetirizine → acute urticaria alone: one system, so criteria for anaphylaxis are not met
  4. 15 yo M treated in the emergency department for hives, throat tightness and wheezing 20 minutes after eating cashews, his first reaction to food; one dose of intramuscular epinephrine was given, and after 6 hours of observation he is asymptomatic with normal vital signs and clear lungs → Epinephrine autoinjector prescription → anaphylaxis, observed for a biphasic reaction; discharge with self-injectable epinephrine, an action plan, avoidance and allergy referral
  5. 58 yo M with hypertension and diabetes, 6 hours of progressive swelling of the lips and tongue; no itching, hives, wheezing or abdominal pain; takes lisinopril, which he started 2 years ago, and metformin; no new foods or medications; swelling did not improve after intramuscular epinephrine and diphenhydramine → Impaired bradykinin degradation → ACE inhibitor angioedema: no urticaria and little response to epinephrine; stop the ACE inhibitor permanently
  6. 16 yo F with recurrent episodes over 3 years of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the hands, face and once the throat, each lasting 2 to 3 days, and separate episodes of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes no medications; her mother has similar episodes; antihistamines and epinephrine have not helped; examination between episodes is normal → Serum C4 level → hereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency; low C4, bradykinin-mediated, so epinephrine disappoints
  7. 17 yo F, 5 days of fever, sore throat and fatigue, treated with amoxicillin for presumed strep pharyngitis; 4 days later, a diffuse, mildly itchy maculopapular rash on the trunk and limbs; T 38.4, BP 112/70; tonsillar exudates, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, left upper quadrant tenderness; no wheals, no lip swelling, lungs clear → Infectious mononucleosis → an aminopenicillin rash during Epstein-Barr virus infection; not an IgE-mediated penicillin allergy
  8. 34 yo F with a known severe shellfish allergy becomes lightheaded 15 minutes after eating a dish she later learns contained shrimp; no rash, flushing, lip swelling, wheeze or vomiting; BP 76/44, HR 132, warm extremities; lungs clear → Anaphylaxis → hypotension alone after a known allergen meets criteria; give IM epinephrine
  9. 22 yo F with recurrent episodes since adolescence of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the lips and one hand lasting 2 to 3 days, the latest starting the day after a dental extraction; separate bouts of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes a combined oral contraceptive and no other medications; her father has similar episodes; epinephrine and diphenhydramine in the emergency department did not help; serum C4 low → C1 inhibitor deficiency → hereditary angioedema: bradykinin-mediated swelling without urticaria; confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function
  10. 19 yo M with known hereditary angioedema, 4 hours of progressive swelling of the face and tongue with a hoarse voice after a facial injury in a basketball game; no stridor; SpO2 98% on room air; no hives; no improvement after intramuscular epinephrine and intravenous diphenhydramine → Intravenous C1 inhibitor concentrate → acute hereditary angioedema attack with laryngeal involvement: give specific therapy and be ready to secure the airway
  11. 45 yo F with hereditary angioedema, low C4 and a family history, now with blood pressure 152/96 on three separate visits; no diabetes or kidney disease → Lisinopril → ACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown and provoke attacks
Management First – IM epinephrine in the anterolateral thigh, 0.01 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL solution (max 0.5 mg adult, 0.3 mg child); lie the patient flat with legs raised · Repeat – every 5 to 15 minutes if symptoms persist; persistent hypotension gets isotonic fluid boluses and then an epinephrine infusion; glucagon if the patient takes a beta-blocker · Adjuncts only – H1 and H2 antihistamines for itch and hives, albuterol for residual wheeze, glucocorticoids; none of them treats airway obstruction or shock, and none replaces or delays epinephrine · Observe – for a biphasic reaction, symptoms returning hours later without re-exposure; 1 symptom-free hour may be reasonable without severe risk features; extended observation up to 6 hours or longer, including admission, may be appropriate at higher risk · Discharge – epinephrine autoinjector with training and an action plan, avoidance of the trigger, and allergy referral
Hereditary angioedema Mechanism – autosomal dominant C1 inhibitor deficiency; unchecked kallikrein makes excess bradykinin · The tell – recurrent nonpitting swelling of the face, lips, limbs or bowel wall (colicky abdominal attacks) with no urticaria and no itch, often with a family history · Triggers – dental work, trauma, stress, estrogen (oral contraceptives, pregnancy) · Avoid – ACE inhibitors, which block bradykinin breakdown and worsen attacks · Tests – screen with C4 (low), confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function · Acute attack – secure the airway if the larynx is involved; give C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor blocker) or ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor); epinephrine, antihistamines and steroids do not work
Pearls Waiting for hypotension is a deadly delay; in children hypotension is a late sign. Throat tightness or wheeze with hives is enough to give epinephrine · Diagnosis is clinical; a serum tryptase drawn early can support mast cell activation afterward but never delays treatment · Bradykinin swelling is the one angioedema in which epinephrine works poorly. Stop the ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor for life, and check C4 when swelling recurs without a drug · Most childhood anaphylaxis is from food (peanut, tree nuts, milk, egg); insect stings and drugs such as beta-lactams follow
Pairs with Part II Fever and Rash in a Child covers the serum sickness-like reaction: did the hives start 5 to 14 days into the drug, with joint pain? Part I Transfusion Reactions covers anaphylaxis during transfusion: is the recipient IgA deficient? Aquifer Shock in Children covers anaphylactic shock as a distributive subtype: is perfusion abnormal? Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome), the non-IgE mimic: is it hours of vomiting without hives? Part I Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications covers anaphylaxis after a vaccine dose as a contraindication. Aquifer Child with Puffy Eyes places the acute allergic reaction among the other causes of swollen eyelids: is it one eye or both, and does the urine contain protein?
Transferable rule Skin or mucosal involvement plus any second system within minutes to hours of an exposure is anaphylaxis. Treat it with IM (intramuscular) epinephrine first. Swelling with no hives points to bradykinin. A rash that arrives days later points to a delayed drug or immune complex reaction.
Unchecked attributeImpaired bradykinin degradation: the swollen eyes suggest angioedema, but bradykinin swelling has no wheals or itch; he has wheals on the trunk plus throat and gut symptoms, which is mast cell release.
Unchecked attributeImmune complex formation: the sore throat invites poststreptococcal disease or serum sickness, but immune complexes take days to form; this began 30 minutes after the drug.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus infection: mononucleosis really does cause a rash after amoxicillin, but that rash is maculopapular, comes days later and brings fever and nodes; he is afebrile with wheals.
Salient decoySystemic vasculitis: crampy abdominal pain recalls IgA vasculitis, but vasculitis develops over days with fever and palpable purpura, not wheals within minutes.

edits.html:
Brachial Plexus Injury at Birth

upper vs lower plexus vs fracture · Moro, biceps and grasp by lesion · Horner syndrome rides with T1 · prognosisWhich of Moro, biceps and grasp is lost, and are ptosis, miosis or crepitus present?

Source vignette Pt – 1-day-old boy, 4.4 kg, 39 wk forceps delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia, mother with insulin-treated gestational diabetes and obesity; right hand barely moves, held with the wrist extended, metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints hyperextended and interphalangeal (IP) joints flexed; grasp absent, Moro and biceps reflexes intact; no crepitus; slight right ptosis and a smaller right pupil · Q – the most likely cause; options spanned clavicle fracture, humerus fracture, C5-C6 injury, C8-T1 injury, perinatal asphyxia and perinatal ischemic stroke
The decision point

Three reflexes localize a weak newborn arm. The Moro reflex needs shoulder abduction and elbow extension (C5-C6) and a pain-free arm. The biceps reflex runs through C5-C6, and the grasp runs through C8-T1. Here the grasp is absent while Moro and biceps are intact. The hand is clawed, and the same side has ptosis and miosis. This is a lower plexus (Klumpke, C8-T1) injury. Horner syndrome occurs because the sympathetic fibers to the eye leave the cord with T1.

Erb palsy (C5-C6) is the most common birth palsy and shows the reverse pattern: Moro and biceps lost, grasp kept. A clavicle or humerus fracture lowers the Moro only through pain. It keeps biceps and grasp and has crepitus.

Newborn arm weakness: reflexes by lesion
MoroBicepsGraspPosture and other tellInjury
Decreased (pain)IntactIntactCrepitus or a bony step over the clavicle; a callus lump laterClavicle fracture
Decreased (pain)IntactIntactCrepitus and swelling of the upper armHumerus fracture
DecreasedDecreasedIntactWaiter's tip: arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, wrist and fingers flexedErb-Duchenne palsy, upper plexus (C5-C6)
IntactIntactAbsentClaw hand (wrist extended, MCP hyperextended, IP flexed) with ipsilateral Horner (ptosis, miosis)Klumpke palsy, lower plexus (C8-T1)
AbsentAbsentAbsentFlail arm, often with HornerTotal plexus palsy (C5-T1)
VariablePreserved or briskPreservedFocal seizures and later upper motor neuron signsPerinatal ischemic stroke
Depressed on both sidesDepressed on both sidesDepressed on both sidesAltered mental status, poor tone, poor feeding or breathing, seizuresPerinatal asphyxia
Scenario bank
  1. 1-day-old boy, 4.4 kg, delivered with forceps after shoulder dystocia; mother has insulin-treated gestational diabetes; the right hand is held with the wrist extended, MCP joints hyperextended and IP joints flexed; grasp absent; Moro and biceps reflexes intact; no crepitus; mild right ptosis and a smaller right pupil → Lower brachial plexus (C8-T1) injury → Klumpke palsy
  2. 1-day-old girl, 4.6 kg, after shoulder dystocia; the left arm lies adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended, forearm pronated and wrist flexed; left Moro and biceps reflexes absent; left grasp strong; no crepitus; pupils equal → Erb-Duchenne palsy → Physical therapy with gentle range of motion
  3. 2-day-old boy after shoulder dystocia, moves the right arm less; right Moro diminished and he cries when the arm is moved; biceps reflex and grasp present on both sides; crepitus midway between the sternal notch and the right shoulder → Clavicle fracture → Gentle handling and pain control
  4. 3-week-old girl with an Erb palsy from a shoulder dystocia delivery; she has begun to flex the elbow a little; no crepitus; radiographs of the clavicle and humerus are normal → Range-of-motion exercises with physical therapy → Upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury
  5. 7-month-old boy with a left upper brachial plexus injury from birth who has had physical therapy since the first weeks; he still has no elbow flexion or shoulder abduction on the left → Referral for surgical nerve repair → Upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury without recovery
  6. 3-day-old girl with weakness of the right arm after a difficult vaginal delivery → Ipsilateral ptosis and miosis → Horner syndrome from a T1 injury
Management and prognosis Gentle massage and range-of-motion exercises with physical therapy to prevent contractures; most infants recover within months. No improvement by 3 to 9 months: refer for surgical nerve repair. Horner syndrome marks a T1 injury and predicts a poorer outcome. A clavicle fracture needs only gentle handling and pain control.
Pearls Risk factors: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and maternal diabetes, with obesity and instrumented delivery adding to them · Traction on the head and neck during shoulder dystocia stretches the upper roots (Erb); traction on a raised arm, as in delivering the posterior arm, stretches C8-T1 (Klumpke) · An intact, symmetric Moro does not exclude a plexus injury, because Klumpke spares the shoulder; check the grasp
Pairs with Arm Injury in a Young Child: its pediatric elbow neighbors line names these palsies; this brief covers the reflex split. Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: the other birth-position injury; it lists clavicle fracture only as a neck-mass mimic, and the clavicle question is in this brief. Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: perinatal stroke presents with focal seizures and upper motor neuron signs, not a limp arm with one lost reflex. Ask: are the signs upper or lower motor neuron?
Transferable rule When a newborn will not move one arm, read three reflexes before the posture. A lower Moro alone with crepitus is a fracture. Lost Moro and biceps with a kept grasp is C5-C6. A lost grasp with Moro and biceps kept is C8-T1. In C8-T1 injury, ptosis and miosis confirm T1 and predict slower recovery.
Mirror twinC5-C6 injury is the commonest birth palsy and shares the shoulder dystocia, but it loses Moro and biceps and keeps grasp, the reverse of this infant.
Salient decoyClavicle fracture: suggested by a 4.4 kg infant after shoulder dystocia. It lowers the Moro from pain, keeps the grasp and gives crepitus; none of these is present.
True-fact-wrong-slotPerinatal ischemic stroke causes one-sided weakness, but with seizures and upper motor neuron signs, not a clawed hand with Horner.
Unchecked attributePerinatal asphyxia is global and bilateral, with altered mental status and poor tone; this infant has one weak hand.

edits.html:
Infectious Diarrhea

timing gates · organism by food source · stool culture, blood culture or neither · who gets an antibioticWhat did the patient eat, how soon did it start, and does that organism need a blood culture or an antibiotic?

Source vignette Pt – 14-year-old girl with 2 days of cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, today with fever and blood in the stool; home from a week-long summer camp, well while there; common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) on immunoglobulin replacement; sinusitis a month ago treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate · Exam – T 38.2 C, HR 102; mild diffuse tenderness, no peritoneal signs · Labs – stool ova and parasites negative; stool culture grows Salmonella · Q – the most likely underlying cause of her illness; options spanned food handling, seafood, contaminated infusions, antibiotic disruption of gut flora and typhoid vaccine failure
The decision point

Identify the organism from the exposure. Nontyphoidal Salmonella comes from undercooked poultry and eggs. Food left unrefrigerated lets it multiply. Symptoms start within 3 days with fever, vomiting, cramps and diarrhea, which can be bloody in children. Camp food fits this source, and her stool culture confirms Salmonella.

The organism then determines the workup and treatment. Invasive diarrhea needs a stool culture. A fever-first illness after travel is typhoid and needs a blood culture. Most bacterial diarrhea needs only rehydration.

Timing gates 1 to 6 hours, vomiting first, no fever – preformed toxin: S aureus or B cereus · Within about 3 days, fever and diarrhea – invasive bacteria: nontyphoidal Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella; Shiga toxin E coli with little fever · Fever for days to weeks after travel, diarrhea minor – typhoid · During or after antibiotics, watery – C difficile
Diarrhea by source: the differential
OrganismSource and settingThe NBME tellTest and treatment
Nontyphoidal SalmonellaUndercooked poultry and eggs, poor refrigeration; reptiles and backyard poultryFever, vomiting, cramps; bloody stools possible in childrenStool culture; supportive; antibiotics only for infants under 3 months, immunocompromise, sickle cell disease or bacteremia
Typhoid (S Typhi)Travel to areas with poor sanitation; contaminated food or waterFever and bacteremia first; abdominal pain, rose spots, relative bradycardia; later splenomegaly, intestinal perforationBlood culture; ceftriaxone; the vaccine covers only typhoidal strains
CampylobacterUndercooked poultry, unpasteurized milkFever, bloody diarrhea, pain that can mimic appendicitis; Guillain-Barre weeks laterStool culture; supportive unless severe or prolonged
Shiga toxin E coli (O157:H7)Undercooked ground beef, petting zoosBloody diarrhea with little fever; hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) about a week laterStool culture and Shiga toxin test; no antibiotics, no antimotility drugs
ShigellaDay care; spreads person to person from a very small inoculumHigh fever, bloody diarrhea, seizures in young childrenStool culture; azithromycin shortens illness and spread
Vibrio parahaemolyticusRaw or undercooked seafood, shellfishWatery diarrhea and cramps after raw oystersSupportive
S aureus and B cereus toxinToxin already in the food: S aureus in ham, mayonnaise or custard; B cereus in reheated riceVomiting within 1 to 6 hours, no fever, several diners illClinical; supportive
C difficileRecent antibioticsWatery diarrhea at onset, cramps, leukocytosisStool toxin or polymerase chain reaction (PCR); oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Stool culture, with Shiga toxin testing if bloodyFirstNames the organismFor fever with bloody diarrhea, immunocompromise, severe or prolonged illness, or an outbreak
Blood cultureBy branchS Typhi or other bacteremiaFever-first illness after travel, infants under 3 months, immunocompromise
C difficile toxin or PCRBy branchPositiveWatery diarrhea during or after antibiotics
Stool ova and parasites or Giardia antigenBy branchGiardiaProlonged watery, greasy diarrhea after untreated water; common in CVID and immunoglobulin A deficiency
Stool studies for brief watery diarrhea without fever or bloodSkip Self-limited; rehydrate
Scenario bank
  1. 6-week-old boy has 1 day of fever to 38.4 C and loose stools with streaks of blood; both parents had fever and diarrhea after a family picnic with undercooked chicken; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella; he feeds well and is well hydrated → Blood culture and antibiotic therapy → infants under 3 months with Salmonella are at risk of bacteremia and meningitis, so they are treated
  2. 14-year-old girl with CVID on immunoglobulin replacement has 2 days of cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, and today fever and bloody stools; she just returned from a week-long summer camp; she took amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis a month ago; T 38.2 C, HR 102, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs; stool ova and parasites negative; stool culture grows Salmonella → Inadequate cooking and refrigeration of chicken and eggs → nontyphoidal Salmonella from undercooked poultry or eggs starts within 3 days, and warmth lets it multiply; bloody stools are common in children
  3. 10-year-old boy and his sister begin vomiting repeatedly 2 hours after a lunch of fried rice left out overnight from a takeout meal and reheated; mild cramps, no fever, no diarrhea yet; normal vital signs apart from mild tachycardia → Bacillus cereus food poisoning → vomiting within hours from a toxin already in the food; reheated rice is the classic source; supportive care
  4. 16-year-old boy develops watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps 18 hours after eating raw oysters at a coastal cookout; temperature 37.9 C; no blood in the stool; he ate no poultry or eggs → Vibrio parahaemolyticus infection → raw or undercooked shellfish; self-limited, supportive care
  5. 6-year-old girl has 2 days of crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody diarrhea 3 days after eating an undercooked hamburger at a barbecue; temperature 37.4 C; mildly dry mucous membranes; stool testing for Shiga toxin is pending → Oral azithromycin → antibiotics and antimotility drugs raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome in Shiga toxin E coli infection; rehydrate and watch hemoglobin, platelets and creatinine
  6. 17-year-old girl returned 12 days ago from visiting family in rural South Asia; for 6 days she has had fever rising to 39.8 C, headache, abdominal pain and constipation; heart rate 82 at that temperature; faint pink macules on the upper abdomen; she is alert and hemodynamically stable → Blood cultures → typhoid presents as fever and bacteremia; the blood culture confirms it before empiric ceftriaxone
  7. 11-year-old girl has 3 days of fever, cramps and loose stools with some blood after a summer barbecue where chicken was undercooked; she is otherwise healthy; today she is afebrile, drinking well, and her stools are fewer; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella → Oral rehydration and supportive care → antibiotics do not shorten uncomplicated nontyphoidal Salmonella in a healthy child and prolong carriage
Management Rehydrate first – oral rehydration for nearly everyone · Antibiotics only for – typhoid; Shigella; C difficile; nontyphoidal Salmonella in infants under 3 months, immunocompromise, sickle cell disease or bacteremia, since treating others prolongs carriage · Suspected Shiga toxin E coli – never antibiotics or antimotility drugs, which raise the risk of HUS
Pearls Exposures to know: a pet turtle, reheated rice, raw oysters, a hamburger · Humoral immunodeficiency such as CVID (common variable immunodeficiency) raises the risk of Salmonella, Campylobacter and Giardia infection; it does not change which food carries which organism · A vaccine exists for typhoid, not for nontyphoidal Salmonella · In sickle cell disease, Salmonella is the organism of osteomyelitis, which is why these children are treated
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers CVID (common variable immunodeficiency): are immunoglobulin G and at least one other isotype low, with poor vaccine responses? Part I Right Lower Quadrant Pain covers Campylobacter and Yersinia pseudoappendicitis and its list of who gets antibiotics: is the pain from the appendix or the ileocecum? Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome), which follows Shiga toxin E coli infection: is a second cell line down a week after bloody diarrhea? Part II Sickle Cell Disease and Trait covers Salmonella osteomyelitis: is it trait or disease?
Transferable rule In infectious diarrhea, name the organism from the exposure and the timing. That organism then determines the culture and whether to treat. A risk factor for a different organism is not the exposure.
Salient decoyAntibiotic disruption of gut flora: the recent amoxicillin-clavulanate is real, but it predisposes to C difficile, which starts watery; the culture grew Salmonella.
Class-vs-memberTyphoid vaccine failure: the vaccine covers only typhoidal strains, and there is no vaccine for nontyphoidal Salmonella; CVID blunting the response does not matter here.
True-fact-wrong-slotRaw or unrefrigerated seafood: a real foodborne source, but of Vibrio parahaemolyticus, not Salmonella.
Salient decoyContaminated immunoglobulin infusions: rare, and they cause bacteremia with high fever and chills found on blood culture, not gastroenteritis with a positive stool culture.

edits.html:
Genital Ulcers

painless vs painful ulcers · syphilis vs herpes vs chancroid · test for syphilis, herpes and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) · penicillinDoes the ulcer hurt, and are there vesicles or suppurating nodes?

Source vignette Pt – 17 yo F, 5 days of a nontender vulvar lesion; three male partners, condoms used inconsistently; afebrile, normal vital signs · Exam – 2 cm ulcer with raised borders on the right labium majus · Q – the most likely causal organism; options were organism classes: gram-negative bacillus, gram-negative diplococcus, obligate intracellular bacterium, protozoan, spirochete and virus
The decision point

A single painless genital ulcer with a firm, raised border and no systemic signs is a primary syphilis chancre. The cause is Treponema pallidum, a spirochete. Genital herpes and chancroid both cause painful ulcers. HSV (herpes simplex virus) starts as grouped vesicles that break into shallow ulcers. Chancroid causes deep ulcers, often with tender suppurative inguinal nodes.

A chancre can also be multiple or painful, and the exam alone often misleads. Test every genital ulcer for syphilis and HSV, and test for HIV. Early in primary syphilis the RPR (rapid plasma reagin) can still be nonreactive. Darkfield microscopy or a molecular test of the ulcer exudate detects the spirochete directly.

Genital ulcer in a sexually active patient: the differential
DiagnosisUlcerNodes and courseThe NBME tell
Primary syphilis: Treponema pallidum, a spirocheteUsually single, painless, clean base, firm raised borderPainless, rubbery inguinal nodes; heals in weeks even untreated, and secondary syphilis can followPainless ulcer with an indurated, raised border; no vesicles
Genital herpes: herpes simplex virus type 2 or herpes simplex virus type 1, a virusPainful grouped vesicles on a red base that break into shallow ulcers, then crustTender inguinal nodes; a first episode can bring fever and dysuria; recursVesicles first, painful, often multiple
Chancroid: Haemophilus ducreyi, a gram-negative bacillusOne or more deep, painful ulcers with ragged, undermined edges and a purulent baseTender suppurative inguinal nodes (buboes) that can rupture; rare in the United StatesPainful ulcer with a suppurating node
Lymphogranuloma venereum: Chlamydia trachomatis L1 to L3, an obligate intracellular bacteriumSmall papule or ulcer that heals on its own and often goes unnoticedTender, usually unilateral inguinal or femoral nodes; proctocolitis after rectal exposureThe nodes, not the ulcer, bring the patient in
Discharge infections: N. gonorrhoeae (gram-negative diplococcus), C. trachomatis (obligate intracellular), Trichomonas vaginalis (protozoan)No ulcerCervicitis, urethritis and pelvic inflammatory disease; trichomoniasis gives a frothy, malodorous dischargeDischarge without an ulcer
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Nontreponemal test (RPR or VDRL, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) plus a treponemal testFirstBoth reactiveSyphilis; a nonreactive nontreponemal test does not exclude early primary syphilis
HSV NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test, usually PCR, polymerase chain reaction) of a lesion swabFirstPositiveGenital herpes
HIV testScreenReactiveCo-infection; test everyone with a genital ulcer
Darkfield microscopy or PCR of ulcer exudateConfirmsMotile spirochetes or T. pallidum DNAPrimary syphilis, including before serology turns reactive
H. ducreyi culture on special mediaBy branchPositive in under 80%Chancroid; probable when ulcers are painful and syphilis and HSV tests are negative
Tzanck smearSkipInsensitive and nonspecificReplaced by HSV NAAT
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo F, 5 days of a nontender vulvar lesion; three male partners, condoms used inconsistently; afebrile, normal vital signs; 2 cm ulcer with raised borders on the right labium majus → Spirochete → Treponema pallidum, primary syphilis chancre
  2. 18 yo F, 3 days of painful vulvar sores beginning a week after a new partner; dysuria, T 38.3 C; clusters of small vesicles and shallow ulcers on a red base on both labia; tender bilateral inguinal nodes → Genital herpes → HSV NAAT of a lesion; acyclovir or valacyclovir for 7 to 10 days
  3. 19 yo F, 1 week of two deep, painful vulvar ulcers with ragged, undermined edges and a purulent base; a tender, fluctuant left inguinal node; syphilis serology and HSV NAAT negative → Haemophilus ducreyi → chancroid; azithromycin 1 g orally once or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM (intramuscular) once
  4. 17 yo F, 6 days of a painless vulvar ulcer with a firm, raised border; nonreactive RPR; rubbery, nontender inguinal nodes; no vesicles → Darkfield microscopy of the ulcer exudate → primary syphilis; the RPR can be nonreactive this early
  5. 16 yo F, 1 week of a painless labial ulcer with a raised, indurated border; RPR and treponemal antibody test reactive; no rash; no drug allergies; negative pregnancy test → Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once → primary syphilis; also test for HIV
  6. 20 yo F at 14 weeks of gestation with a painless vulvar ulcer; RPR and treponemal antibody test reactive; hives after amoxicillin as a child → Penicillin desensitization, then benzathine penicillin G → penicillin is the only recommended treatment in pregnancy
  7. 17 yo F given benzathine penicillin G for primary syphilis 6 hours ago; now T 38.6 C, headache and myalgia; no hives, wheeze or hypotension → Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction → antipyretics; not a penicillin allergy
  8. 18 yo F, 2 weeks of a tender, enlarging left inguinal node mass; a small painless vulvar bump 3 weeks ago that healed on its own; no current ulcer → Lymphogranuloma venereum → Chlamydia trachomatis L1 to L3; doxycycline for 21 days
Management Primary syphilis – benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM (intramuscular) once for adults and adolescents; children get 50,000 units/kg, up to 2.4 million units · Penicillin allergy, not pregnant – doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days · Pregnancy – penicillin only; desensitize a patient with penicillin allergy, then treat · Genital herpes, first episode – oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir for 7 to 10 days · Chancroid – azithromycin 1 g orally once or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once
Organism classes Spirochete – Treponema pallidum: painless chancre · Virus – herpes simplex virus: painful vesicles, then ulcers · Gram-negative bacillus – Haemophilus ducreyi: painful ulcer, suppurative nodes · Obligate intracellular bacterium – Chlamydia trachomatis: cervicitis, or lymphogranuloma venereum with prominent nodes · Gram-negative diplococcus – Neisseria gonorrhoeae: cervicitis and discharge · Protozoan – Trichomonas vaginalis: frothy, malodorous discharge
Pearls In the United States, most genital ulcers in young, sexually active patients are genital herpes or syphilis · Treat presumptively for syphilis when the ulcer looks like a chancre, before results return · The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is fever, headache and myalgia within 24 hours of treating syphilis; it is not a penicillin allergy · How NBME framed it: every option was an organism class, so the ulcer had to be named as syphilis and then matched to spirochete.
Pairs with Part II Fever and Rash in a Child covers secondary syphilis. Ask: is there a rash on the palms and soles? Part I Cervicitis and Pelvic Inflammatory Disease covers gonorrhea and chlamydia. Ask: is there a discharge instead of an ulcer?
Transferable rule For a genital ulcer, ask first whether it hurts. A painless, indurated ulcer is primary syphilis until proven otherwise. A painful ulcer is herpes when vesicles came first and chancroid when the inguinal nodes suppurate.
Unchecked attributeGram-negative bacillus: Haemophilus ducreyi causes a genital ulcer, but the chancroid ulcer is painful and comes with tender suppurative nodes.
Unchecked attributeVirus: HSV (herpes simplex virus) is the most common cause of genital ulcers, but its lesions are painful and start as grouped vesicles.
True-fact-wrong-slotObligate intracellular bacterium: Chlamydia trachomatis is common in sexually active adolescents, but it causes cervicitis, and its lymphogranuloma venereum strains cause only a small transient ulcer.
Salient decoyGram-negative diplococcus: multiple partners suggest gonorrhea, but gonorrhea causes cervicitis and discharge, not an ulcer.
True-fact-wrong-slotProtozoan: Trichomonas vaginalis causes a frothy, malodorous discharge with itching, not an ulcer.

edits.html:
Constipation and Fecal Impaction in an Adult

firm stool in the vault · overflow diarrhea · anticholinergic cause · enema, then manual disimpaction · treat the causeWhat does the rectal exam find, and which drug is slowing the colon?

Source vignette Pt – 77 yo F taking oxybutynin; last bowel movement 5 days ago, and it was loose stool; colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnormalities; no hematochezia · Exam – afebrile, warm dry skin, soft abdomen without distension, diffuse tenderness, firm stool in the rectal vault · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned fecal impaction, adhesions, colon cancer, diverticulitis, ischemic bowel and volvulus
The decision point

Rectal examination shows firm stool in the rectal vault. This confirms fecal impaction and is incompatible with adhesive small bowel obstruction, which gives an empty rectum, a distended abdomen, and high-pitched or absent bowel sounds.

The last bowel movement, 5 days ago, was loose stool. Loose stool in a constipated patient is overflow diarrhea: liquid stool passing around a hard impaction. It is near-pathognomonic.

Stem findings → options ruled out
OptionThe sentence that kills it
AdhesionsFirm stool in the rectal vault (small bowel obstruction empties the rectum); soft, undistended abdomen
Colon cancer"Colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnormalities"
DiverticulitisNo fever; diffuse, not focal left lower quadrant (LLQ), tenderness
Ischemic bowelNo hematochezia; no atrial fibrillation or atherosclerotic risk factors
VolvulusSoft abdomen without distension; no coffee-bean film
Details that change management Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic that slows colonic transit and is the cause here, so treatment includes addressing it. The patient's warm, dry skin is an anticholinergic sign. Constipating drugs: anticholinergics (oxybutynin, TCAs [tricyclic antidepressants], antihistamines, antipsychotics), opioids, verapamil, iron, calcium, aluminum antacids, ondansetron.
Management ladder – fecal impaction
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Enema (in-context: first-line)Fails to clear
2Manual disimpactionEnema unsuccessful
3Treat the cause – stop or reduce the oxybutynin; then maintenance polyethylene glycol (PEG), fluids, mobilityAlways, after clearing
Scenario bank
  1. 77 yo F, 5 days without a bowel movement (BM), empty rectal vault, distended abdomen, high-pitched bowel sounds, prior laparotomy → Adhesive small bowel obstruction → nasogastric decompression + imaging
  2. 77 yo F, sudden severe pain, distended tympanitic abdomen, coffee-bean sign → Sigmoid volvulus → endoscopic decompression
  3. 68 yo M, LLQ pain with fever 38.5 and focal tenderness → Diverticulitis → CT
  4. 72 yo F with atrial fibrillation, crampy pain and hematochezia → Ischemic colitis
  5. 60 yo M, progressive constipation with iron deficiency anemia and weight loss, no recent colonoscopy → Colon cancer → colonoscopy
  6. 77 yo F, impaction cleared by enema, still constipated → Stop the oxybutynin, start PEG
  7. 80 yo M on chronic opioids, 6 days without a BM, hard stool in the vault → Disimpaction + methylnaltrexone or naloxegol
Exceptions Impaction can sit distal to a second lesion, such as a slow-growing tumor or partial obstruction. Here, a normal colonoscopy 3 years ago and no weight loss or anemia mean no further workup is needed. If any one of these is missing, relieve the impaction and also investigate.
Pairs with Part I Constipation in a Child covers the pediatric case, where the rectal vault is empty and an anal fissure rules out the rectal route that is first-line here.
Transferable rule Change an answer only when a new detail makes the current choice impossible, not when another option merely becomes plausible. Check whether the stem contains a finding that excludes the new option. Here, firm stool in the rectal vault excludes small bowel obstruction.
Salient decoy

edits.html:
Urinary Incontinence

stress, urge, overflow, fistula · the postvoid residual splits the differential · cough stress test · drug pairingsWhat is the postvoid residual, and which diagnosis does that number make impossible?

Source vignette Pt – woman with urinary leakage; no pelvic surgery, obstetric injury, malignancy or radiation · Labs – postvoid residual 800 mL · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned overflow, stress and urge incontinence and vesicovaginal fistula
The decision point

Postvoid residual 800 mL. Retention of 800 mL points to overflow incontinence. The PVR (postvoid residual) splits the entire differential before any symptom is weighed.

Fistula is not merely unsupported but mechanically impossible. A bladder draining continuously through a fistula cannot hold 800 mL. Two further findings exclude it. Fistula requires pelvic surgery, obstetric injury, malignancy, or radiation, and all are absent. Fistula shows urine pooling in the vagina, but the examination shows no abnormalities.

A positive cough stress test A positive cough stress test normally means stress incontinence. However, a chronically overdistended bladder leaks with any rise in intra-abdominal pressure, so the test loses specificity once the PVR (postvoid residual) is high. A positive test can fail to mean what it usually means, just as a negative test can fail to exclude. In each case, context sets a test's operating characteristics.
Urinary incontinence types
TypeMechanismPresentationPVRTreatment
StressUrethral hypermobility / sphincter deficiencyLeaks with cough, sneeze, liftingLowPelvic floor → pessary → midurethral sling
Urge (OAB)Detrusor overactivitySudden urge then leakage, frequency, nocturiaLowBladder training → antimuscarinic or mirabegron → Botox
OverflowDetrusor underactivity or outlet obstructionHesitancy, weak stream, dribbling, recurrent urinary tract infection (UTI)HIGHIntermittent catheterization; bethanechol; α-blocker if obstructive; stop anticholinergics
FunctionalCognitive or mobility barrierCan't reach the toilet; tract normalNormalScheduled toileting
FistulaAbnormal communicationContinuous leakage, vaginal urine poolingNormal/lowDye test, cystoscopy → repair
The causal chain & a drug pairing T1DM (type 1 diabetes mellitus) since age 6 causes diabetic autonomic neuropathy. The neuropathy causes detrusor underactivity and retention. Retention causes overflow leakage and the recurrent UTIs (urinary tract infections) from stasis. Oxybutynin treats urge incontinence and would worsen overflow. The same drug causes fecal impaction. Gut motility down, bladder emptying down: when oxybutynin appears on an elderly or diabetic patient's medication list, check both.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
UrinalysisFirstPyuria and nitritesUTI: treat; not chronic incontinence
Postvoid residualSupportsHigh residual volumeOverflow: detrusor underactivity or outlet obstruction
Cough stress testBy branchLeakage with cough, low residualStress incontinence
UrodynamicsBy branchMixed retention and urgencyNeurogenic bladder, such as multiple sclerosis
Dye test and cystoscopyBy branchDye in the vaginaVesicovaginal fistula after surgery, delivery or radiation
Autonomic neuropathy screenCauseOrthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, resting tachycardiaDiabetic autonomic neuropathy behind detrusor underactivity
Cough stress test with a high residualSkipPositive from overdistension aloneDoes not establish stress incontinence
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo F, leaks only when coughing, PVR 30, four vaginal deliveries → Stress incontinence → pelvic floor exercises first
  2. 68 yo F, sudden urge then leakage with nocturia, PVR 40 → Urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity
  3. 72 yo M, hesitancy and weak stream, PVR 350, enlarged prostate → Overflow incontinence from outlet obstruction → α-blocker ± 5-α-reductase inhibitor
  4. 28 yo F, continuous leakage two weeks after a difficult delivery, vaginal urine pooling → Vesicovaginal fistula
  5. 84 yo F with dementia, wets before reaching the bathroom, tract normal → Functional incontinence
  6. 68 yo F on oxybutynin with rising PVR and retention → Anticholinergic-induced retention → stop the drug
  7. 45 yo F, urgency and frequency with dysuria, pyuria and nitrites → Urinary tract infection → not chronic incontinence
  8. 40 yo F with multiple sclerosis, mixed retention and urgency → Neurogenic bladder → urodynamics
  9. 32 yo F, T1DM, PVR 800 → Screen for autonomic neuropathy → gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension and resting tachycardia
Boundary conditions A high PVR (postvoid residual) suggests that overflow is present, not that it is the only mechanism; mixed incontinence is common. A positive cough test may reflect a real coexisting stress component. A PVR is only interpretable when measured after a normal void. PVR thresholds in adults: under 50 mL argues against overflow; over 200 mL suggests overflow as a main contributor.
Transferable rule When a quantitative measure of organ function is given, check whether each candidate diagnosis is compatible with that number before weighing symptoms. Exclude a diagnosis the physiology forbids without arguing from symptoms.
Test-overrides-findings

edits.html:
School Difficulty in a Child

behavior confined to school · the child's private interview · learning vs behavioral disorders · hearing and visionDoes the behavior stay at school, and what does the child say when interviewed alone?

Source vignette Pt – 9 yo M, irritable and fighting at school since third grade began, with school refusal; privately reports classmates call him a baby because he counts on his fingers and reads slowly; behavior normal at home · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned specific learning disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, social anxiety disorder and oppositional defiant disorder
The decision point

The mother's chief complaint is irritability, a fight and school refusal. In a private interview, the child says his classmates call him a baby because he counts on his fingers and reads slowly. This private disclosure identifies the diagnosis. Each behavioral disorder in the differential explains the behavior, but only specific learning disorder also explains the failing grades.

Onset coincides with an academic transition: third grade, where learning to read becomes reading to learn. The symptoms are confined to school, with normal behavior at home.

Defining criteria Specific learning disorder – achievement below intellectual potential in reading, writing or math for at least 6 months despite support · attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) – symptoms in at least 2 settings with onset before age 12, so school-only behavior excludes it · Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder – severe outbursts at least 3 times weekly for at least 12 months with persistently irritable mood between them · Oppositional defiant disorder – a pattern of defiance, argumentativeness and vindictiveness toward authority for at least 6 months · Social anxiety disorder – fear of scrutiny across situations, and not diagnosed when better explained by another disorder
The school-age child with behavior change – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Specific learning disorderBehavior downstream of an academic skill deficitThe child names the deficit himself when interviewed privately
ADHDInattention and hyperactivity carried everywhereSchool and home both complain
Disruptive mood dysregulationChronic angry mood between frequent outburstsOutbursts three times weekly for a year; explains no academic decline
Oppositional defiant disorderDefiance toward authorityArgumentative and vindictive, not avoidant
Social anxiety disorderFear of scrutiny generallyFear of eating, speaking or performing anywhere, not only where a weakness shows
Absence seizuresBrief lapses many times dailyStaring spells provoked by hyperventilation
Hearing or vision impairmentSensory barrier misread as inattentionSits close, turns the head, mishears
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Private interview with the childFirstChild names the deficit: slow reading, counting on fingersBehavior is downstream of an academic problem
Hearing and vision screeningNextAbnormal screenSensory barrier, not a learning disorder: audiology or eye referral
Parent and teacher ADHD rating scalesBy branchSymptoms in two or more settingsADHD; behavior confined to school argues against it
ElectroencephalographyBy branch3 Hz spike-and-wave provoked by hyperventilationAbsence seizures behind staring spells and falling grades
Psychoeducational testing (cognitive and achievement)ConfirmsAchievement below age and intellect for 6 months despite supportSpecific learning disorder: school-based support
Scenario bank
  1. 9 yo M, irritable and fighting only at school since third grade began, reads slowly and counts on fingers, normal behavior at home → Specific learning disorder → educational testing
  2. 9 yo M with suspected specific learning disorder, initial evaluation → Educational testing plus hearing and vision screening → rule out psychiatric and medical causes
  3. 8 yo M, inattentive and disruptive at school and at home, loses things, since age 5 → Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
  4. 10 yo M, argumentative and vindictive with all adults for a year, grades normal → Oppositional defiant disorder
  5. 9 yo F, severe temper outbursts 4 times weekly for 18 months, persistently angry between outbursts → Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder
  6. 12 yo F, fear of speaking or eating in front of others in every setting, blushing and trembling → Social anxiety disorder
  7. 7 yo F, brief staring spells many times daily, declining grades, provoked by hyperventilation → Absence seizures → electroencephalogram
  8. 8 yo M, declining grades, turns his head to listen, frequently says what → Hearing impairment → audiology evaluation
  9. 13 yo M stays home on most school days, stomachaches on school mornings that resolve on weekends → School refusal
Behavior is a symptom, not a diagnosis Before naming a behavioral disorder in a school-age child, ask what the child is avoiding. Learning disorder, hearing or vision loss, absence seizures, bullying and abuse all present as acting out.
Pearls Count the settings: behavior in one setting means something about that setting; behavior in two or more settings is a disorder the child carries · Symptoms starting at a school transition point to an academic-demand mismatch rather than a primary mood disorder · Early intervention improves self-esteem and social skills as well as grades · Social anxiety is explicitly not diagnosed when the avoidance is better explained by another disorder
Pairs with Related conditions without their own brief: ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) diagnosis and stimulant management.
Transferable rule In a child with a behavior problem, the parent's history gives the chief complaint and the child's private disclosure gives the diagnosis.
Class-vs-memberSocial anxiety is a real disorder whose own criterion excludes it when another disorder explains the avoidance.
Mirror twinOppositional defiant disorder is the defiant version of the same complaint; he is avoidant.

edits.html:
Acute Leukemia in a Child

pancytopenia with bone pain · counts down vs up · screen versus confirm · marrow before steroidsAre two or more cell lines down, and has the marrow been sampled before any steroid?

Source vignette Pt – 5 yo M, 2 weeks of fatigue, 1 week of leg pain, 1 day of fever with petechiae; pale, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, cervical and axillary adenopathy · Q – the most useful test; options spanned complete blood count with differential and smear, C-reactive protein and partial thromboplastin time
The decision point

Together, tri-lineage cytopenia, diaphyseal bone pain and diffuse nontender adenopathy with splenomegaly fit only one disease. They indicate marrow replacement, which is confirmed in the marrow.

The complete blood count is the initial and most useful first test: cheap, fast, and enough to convert a vague illness into an oncologic emergency. It raises the suspicion of leukemia; the bone marrow aspirate is the diagnostic test that confirms it.

Defining criteria Pancytopenia – reduction in all three lineages, the word that eliminates every single-lineage disease · acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) diagnostic gate – at least 20% lymphoblasts of marrow nucleated cells · M1, M2, M3 marrow – under 5%, 5 to 25%, over 25% blasts, a burden and response category rather than the diagnostic gate · Leukemic bone pain – diaphyseal or metaphyseal tenderness from marrow expansion, distinct from joint-line pain · Petechiae – a platelet problem, so prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) are normal
The pale child with bone pain – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Acute lymphoblastic leukemiaPeak 2 to 5 yr; marrow replaced by lymphoblastsPancytopenia with diaphyseal pain and nontender adenopathy; counts go down
Sickle cell aplastic crisisParvovirus B19 arrests erythropoiesisIsolated anemia with reticulocytopenia; platelets and white blood cell (WBC) normal
Infectious mononucleosisAdolescent, prolonged fever and fatigueTender posterior cervical nodes, atypical lymphocytosis, transaminitis
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritisQuotidian fever, evanescent rashCounts go up – leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, ferritin high
Aplastic anemiaMarrow failure without infiltrationPancytopenia with an empty exam: no adenopathy, no organomegaly, no bone pain
Neuroblastoma Can't missUnder 5 yr; marrow metastases give identical cytopenia and bone painPeriorbital ecchymoses, proptosis, midline-crossing abdominal mass
Immune thrombocytopeniaPost-viral, well-appearing childIsolated thrombocytopenia with normal PT and PTT
Nonaccidental traumaVague or shifting history, bruises in areas that are not injury-prone (trunk, ears, neck)Normal blood counts; trauma never lowers them
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Complete blood count (CBC) with differential and peripheral smearFirstTwo or more cell lines low, with or without blastsMarrow replacement; a normal white count does not exclude ALL
Uric acid, potassium, phosphate, calcium, creatinineNextHigh uric acid, potassium and phosphateTumor lysis risk; hydrate before and during induction
Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with flow cytometryConfirms20% or more lymphoblastsALL and its lineage; obtain before any corticosteroid
Chest radiographStagingAnterior mediastinal massT-cell ALL
Lumbar punctureStagingBlasts in the cerebrospinal fluidCentral nervous system (CNS) disease
C-reactive protein or PTTSkipC-reactive protein nonspecific; PTT normal with petechiaeNeither selects or excludes leukemia
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M with 2 wk of fatigue, 1 wk of leg pain and 1 day of fever with petechiae, pale, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, cervical and axillary adenopathy → Complete blood count with differential and peripheral smear → bone marrow confirms afterwards
  2. 5 yo M whose complete blood count shows hemoglobin 7, platelets 22,000 and WBC 3,100 → Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy → greater than 20% lymphoblasts
  3. 4 yo M, 3 wk fever, pallor, petechiae, nontender diffuse adenopathy, splenomegaly, midshaft femoral tenderness, WBC 2,800 and platelets 18,000 → Acute lymphoblastic leukemia → bone marrow aspirate and biopsy
  4. 4 yo M with fever, limp and pancytopenia in whom a colleague proposes empiric prednisone for presumed systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) → Obtain bone marrow before any corticosteroid → steroids partially treat ALL and destroy the specimen
  5. 5 yo M with 4 wk of fatigue and pallor, pancytopenia, no adenopathy, no organomegaly and no bone pain → Aplastic anemia → bone marrow biopsy showing a hypocellular marrow
  6. 6 yo F, 5 wk of daily spiking fever, evanescent salmon rash, WBC 24,000 and platelets 700,000 → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
  7. 4 yo M with petechiae and bruising 2 wk after a viral illness, well-appearing and afebrile, platelets 12,000 with normal hemoglobin and WBC → Immune thrombocytopenia → observation
  8. 8 yo M with sickle cell disease, hemoglobin 4.2, reticulocytes 0.2%, normal platelets and WBC → Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis → transfuse and supportive care
  9. 3 yo M with fever, refusal to walk, pancytopenia, periorbital ecchymoses and proptosis, and an abdominal mass crossing the midline → Neuroblastoma → urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid
  10. 16 yo M, 3 wk fever, sore throat, tender posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes → Infectious mononucleosis → avoid contact sports for 3 to 4 weeks
  11. 6 yo F with petechiae and gum bleeding, platelets 9,000, PT and PTT normal, otherwise well → No further coagulation testing is needed → petechiae are a platelet problem
  12. 5 yo M with pancytopenia and adenopathy in whom a normal white count on an earlier CBC is offered as reassurance → Accepting a normal white count as excluding leukemia → some ALL presents with under 1% circulating blasts
  13. 7 yo M, day 3 of ALL induction, potassium 6.8, phosphate 8.1, uric acid 14, calcium 6.8 and creatinine 2.1 → Tumor lysis syndrome → intravenous hydration and urate-lowering therapy
  14. 7 yo M on day 3 of ALL induction with rising potassium, phosphate and uric acid, a low calcium and a rising creatinine → IV hydration and urate-lowering therapy → tumor lysis syndrome
  15. 14 yo M with pancytopenia, marrow lymphoblasts and an anterior mediastinal mass on chest film → T-cell lineage → a mediastinal mass points to T-cell ALL
  16. 5 yo F brought by her mother and the mother's boyfriend a week after a fall from the couch, now leg pain worse at night and refusing to walk; a month of dry cough, temperature 38.3 C, pale, liver 3 cm below the costal margin, bilateral proximal tibial tenderness, scattered bruises on the chest and back; hemoglobin 8, platelets 30,000, WBC 3,000 → Acute lymphoblastic leukemia → bone pain plus pancytopenia
  17. 2 yo with bruises of different ages on the ears, neck and trunk, a history that changes between caregivers, and a normal CBC and coagulation profile → Nonaccidental trauma → normal counts; bruises away from injury-prone areas
  18. 5 yo with ALL and scattered truncal bruises whose family links them to a recent fall → Marrow replacement by blasts → thrombocytopenia, not trauma
  19. 4 yo M with 1 month of bruises on the chest, back and legs, more fatigue and longer naps, poor appetite, and 1 week of gum bleeding with brushing; tonsillectomy last year without complications; a paternal uncle has hemophilia; normal vital signs; pale; buccal mucosal hematomas; bruises and petechiae on the shins, chest and back; nontender bilateral anterior cervical nodes; hepatosplenomegaly; no joint swelling → Platelet production → Acute lymphoblastic leukemia replacing the marrow
  20. 3 yo M with a warm, swollen, painful knee after a minor fall; prolonged bleeding after circumcision as a newborn; a maternal uncle has a bleeding disorder; no pallor, adenopathy or organomegaly; hemoglobin, platelets and WBC normal; PT normal, PTT prolonged → Hemophilia A → Factor VIII activity level
Never steroids before the marrow Corticosteroids partially treat ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia). They transiently improve the child while destroying the diagnostic specimen and degrading risk stratification. Separate systemic JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) from ALL before treatment, not after. A normal white count does not exclude ALL; the cytopenias are the clue, not the blasts.
Leukemic bone pain blamed on a fall The story – families often date leukemic bone pain to a fall; the pain is dull, in the long-bone shafts, worse at night, and the child limps or refuses to walk · What makes it systemic – fever, hepatomegaly, bilateral tibial tenderness and two or more cytopenias · The bruises – thrombocytopenia explains truncal bruising; trauma cannot depress three cell lines · When to think abuse – a vague history with bruising away from injury-prone areas, and normal counts · The white count – often low early, since normal production falls; later high as blasts spill into the blood · Versus aplastic anemia – pancytopenia from a hypocellular marrow, so no bone pain and rarely hepatomegaly · Versus immune thrombocytopenia – hemoglobin and white count normal, no bone pain or organomegaly · Workup – marrow biopsy with flow cytometry (20% or more blasts), then lumbar puncture for CNS (central nervous system) disease · Prognosis – 5-year survival above 85% in children with multidrug chemotherapy
A paternal family history of hemophilia Paternal uncle with hemophilia – hemophilia A is X-linked recessive, so a boy inherits it through his mother; his father's brother cannot pass it to him · Uneventful tonsillectomy last year – a surgical challenge passed without bleeding argues against any inherited bleeding disorder · New bleeding plus pallor, nodes and hepatosplenomegaly – an acquired marrow problem: blasts crowd out megakaryocytes, so platelet production fails · Hemophilia – joint and muscle bleeds after trauma, prolonged PTT (partial thromboplastin time), normal counts and no organomegaly · Von Willebrand disease – lifelong mucosal bleeding with a normal platelet count and a normal exam
Pearls Leukemia lowers blood counts; systemic JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) raises them, with ferritin, platelets and WBC (white blood cell count) all rising · Neuroblastoma and ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia) are confirmed by the same test; periorbital ecchymoses and a midline-crossing mass separate them · A mediastinal mass points to T-cell ALL and can compress the airway or cause superior vena cava syndrome; a normal chest film does not exclude B-cell ALL · About half of children with ALL present with bleeding (petechiae, bruising, gum oozing) from thrombocytopenia · Extramedullary spread also shows as testicular enlargement and as leptomeningeal disease with cranial nerve deficits or meningismus, which is why a lumbar puncture is part of the workup · Inflammatory markers monitor disease; they do not distinguish between diagnoses that all raise them · Tumor lysis: potassium up, phosphate up, uric acid up, calcium down, with acute kidney injury
Pairs with Part I Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis is the mirror twin, and Part I The Limping Child shares the presenting complaint. Ask: are the counts up or down? Part I Leg Pain in a Child covers the benign nocturnal limb pain whose normal examination excludes this diagnosis. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child places leukemia among the other causes of bruising in a child. Part I Hemophilia covers the bleeding-pattern-to-lab table: is the PT (prothrombin time) or the PTT (partial thromboplastin time) long, and are the platelets normal?
How NBME framed it A systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis diagnosis made 2 months earlier, partly improved on ibuprofen, was the anchor; new pancytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly still meant bone marrow aspiration, not imaging or liver biopsy.
Transferable rule Choose laboratory tests by what a result could change, not by their sophistication. A test that is abnormal in every diagnosis on the differential discriminates nothing. A test of an uninvolved compartment does not address the clinical question.
Salient decoyEthnicity and travel are epidemiologic priors, not findings, and cannot outrank the blood count.
True-fact-wrong-slotSplenomegaly and generalized adenopathy are not features of Kawasaki or of leukemia's mimics in the way offered.
Class-vs-memberPTT is the right class of hematologic test on the wrong compartment.
Salient decoyThe fall and the mother's boyfriend pull toward abuse, but trauma cannot explain fever, hepatomegaly or three low cell lines.
