edits.html:
Suspected Child Abuse

fractures that mean abuse · red flags · the bone-disease mimics · a risk factor is not a findingDoes the fracture need a pull, twist or squeeze, and does the film or exam give a bone disease its own sign?

Source vignette Pt – 13-month-old boy brought by an aunt for left leg pain; irritable, refuses to stand, cries when the leg is touched; born at home without prenatal care, exclusively breastfed without vitamin D, no routine care; his mother broke her forearm and wrist as a child · Exam – weight 5th percentile, height 50th; swelling and point tenderness of the distal left thigh; no bruises; beefy red diaper plaques with satellite papules · Imaging – medial metaphyseal corner fracture of the distal femur · Q – the most likely cause of the x-ray findings; options spanned abuse, two metabolic or genetic bone diseases, an infection and a histiocytic disorder
The decision point

In a young child, three fractures are abuse until proven otherwise. A metaphyseal corner (bucket-handle) fracture needs a forcible pull or twist of the limb. A posterior rib fracture comes from squeezing the chest. The third is a femur fracture in a child who does not yet walk. The bone-disease mimics each need their own finding on the film or exam. Rickets needs osteopenia with cupped, frayed metaphyses. Osteogenesis imperfecta needs blue sclerae and many low-energy fractures. Langerhans cell histiocytosis needs a punched-out lytic lesion.

A risk factor in the history (breastfeeding without vitamin D, no prenatal care, a parent's single childhood fracture) is not that finding. A film with normal bone density and a classic abuse fracture outweighs that risk factor; the fracture stays abuse until proven otherwise.

Red flags for abuse History – injury inconsistent with the child's developmental stage, delay in seeking care, a story that changes or conflicts between caregivers · Bruises – patterned (belt, buckle, hand), any bruise in an infant who is not yet mobile, or bruises over the ears, neck or trunk rather than shins and forehead · Burns – linear or sharply demarcated, such as immersion burns with a clean line · Fractures – metaphyseal corner, posterior rib, femur before walking, multiple in different stages of healing, skull · Head – subdural and retinal hemorrhages
Fracture in an infant or toddler: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellWhy less likely here
Child abuseHistory that does not fit the injury or the child's development; delay in careMetaphyseal corner, posterior rib, or femur fracture before walking, on a film with normal bone densityThe key: a pull-or-twist fracture with no sign of bone disease
Osteogenesis imperfectaType I collagen defect, usually autosomal dominant; fractures with minimal traumaBlue sclerae, easy bruising, short stature, hearing loss, a family history of many fractures; osteopenia on filmNo blue sclerae, normal height; a parent's single childhood fracture is not that history
RicketsVitamin D deficiency in an exclusively breastfed infant without supplements; X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets looks similar on filmFilm: osteopenia, cupped and frayed metaphyses, widened physes; exam: bowed legs, widened wrists, rachitic rosaryRisk factor present, film findings absent; the metaphysis is fractured, not frayed
Congenital syphilisUntreated maternal infection; early (under 2 years): snuffles, palm and sole rash, hepatosplenomegaly, periostitis; late: saber shin, frontal bossing, saddle noseRash, snuffles, big liver; later saber shinNone of its findings; it does not cause corner fractures
Langerhans cell histiocytosisA rash that looks seborrheic or candidal but is petechial or crusted and persists; sometimes diabetes insipidusPunched-out lytic skull or long-bone lesionThe film shows a fracture, not a lytic lesion
Toddler's fracture (accidental)A child who has started walking; new limp after a minor, often unwitnessed twistNondisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibiaWrong bone and wrong pattern
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Radiograph of the painful limbFirstCorner fracture, normal bone densityA pull-or-twist injury: suspect abuse
Skeletal surveyNextOccult fractures: multiple, different ages, posterior rib, skull, metaphysealRequired for suspected abuse under age 2
Head computed tomography (CT)NextSubdural hemorrhage or skull fractureAbusive head trauma, which can be silent on exam in an infant
Dilated funduscopic examNextRetinal hemorrhagesAbusive head trauma
Complete blood count, prothrombin time and aPTTBy branchNormalWhen bruising is present: excludes a bleeding disorder before calling bruises inflicted
Calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone (PTH), 25-hydroxyvitamin DBy branchLow phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase; high PTH and low vitamin D in nutritional ricketsOnly when the film shows osteopenia, cupping or fraying: rickets
Genetic or collagen testing for osteogenesis imperfectaSkip Not needed without blue sclerae, osteopenia, hearing loss or a family history of many fractures
Scenario bank
  1. 13-month-old boy brought by an aunt for 1 day of left leg pain; irritable, refuses to stand, cries when the leg is touched; born at home without prenatal care, exclusively breastfed without vitamin D supplements, no routine medical care; his mother broke her forearm and wrist as a child; weight 5th percentile, height 50th; swelling and point tenderness of the distal left thigh; no bruises; beefy red diaper plaques with satellite papules; radiograph shows a medial metaphyseal corner fracture of the distal femur → Child abuse → a corner fracture needs a forcible pull or twist of the limb; admit for safety, report to child protective services, and obtain a skeletal survey, head CT and funduscopy
  2. 4-month-old boy with a swollen right thigh; his father says the leg got caught in the crib rails while he was out of the room; the infant cannot yet roll over; no bruises, white sclerae, normal growth; radiograph shows a midshaft femur fracture with normal bone density → Skeletal survey → a femur fracture in a child who does not walk is abuse until proven otherwise; head CT, funduscopy and a report to child protective services go with it
  3. 7-month-old girl brought in for fussiness; exam shows bruises on both ears; skeletal survey shows two healing posterior rib fractures; the parents say she bruises easily and ask to take her home tonight → Discharge home with outpatient follow-up → safety comes first: admit, report to child protective services, and complete the head CT and funduscopy
  4. 8-month-old boy with his third fracture, a humerus fracture after being lifted from his crib; blue sclerae; length 5th percentile; his father has hearing loss and had many fractures as a child; radiographs show diffuse osteopenia and several healed long-bone fractures → Osteogenesis imperfecta → type I collagen defect: blue sclerae, hearing loss, osteopenia and a family history of many low-energy fractures
  5. 14-month-old girl, exclusively breastfed, no vitamin D supplements, with bowed legs, widened wrists and beading along the costochondral junctions; wrist radiograph shows osteopenia, cupped and frayed distal radial and ulnar metaphyses and widened physes, with no fracture; phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase high, PTH high → Nutritional rickets → vitamin D deficiency: treat with vitamin D; X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets looks the same on film but runs in families and does not respond to vitamin D
  6. 18-month-old boy with a crusted, petechial rash in the diaper area and scalp that has not cleared with 4 weeks of topical nystatin; new polyuria and polydipsia; skull radiograph shows a well-defined punched-out lytic lesion → Langerhans cell histiocytosis → a punched-out lytic lesion with a treatment-resistant rash and diabetes insipidus; biopsy confirms
  7. 6-month-old boy seen for cough; chest radiograph shows a healing posterior rib fracture; the mother says he has never been injured; a small bruise is on the left ear; the physician is not certain the injury was inflicted → Report to child protective services → physicians are mandated reporters on reasonable suspicion, not proof; admit and obtain the skeletal survey, head CT and funduscopy alongside the report
Management Safety first – admit the child to the hospital rather than discharge to the suspected caregivers while the workup runs · Report – to child protective services on reasonable suspicion; physicians are mandated reporters and do not need proof, and the report is not delayed for the skeletal survey or other results · Evaluate – skeletal survey, head CT and funduscopy, plus the by-branch labs above
Pearls Abuse also presents as a posterior rib fracture or a femur fracture before walking, or with an added bruise on the ear or trunk · A walking toddler with a spiral distal tibial fracture after a minor twist has an accidental injury. The same child with a corner fracture does not · Caregivers who were themselves abused or neglected, an unstable home and a child with chronic medical problems raise the risk. The diagnosis rests on the fracture pattern
Pairs with Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child covers bruising. Ask: is the bruise somewhere a child of this age could bump, and are the platelets normal? Part I The Limping Child master table covers the toddler's fracture. Ask: does the child walk, and is it a spiral tibial fracture or a corner fracture? Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin D deficiency rickets and the 400 international units supplement for breastfed infants. Part I Bone Lesions in a Child covers the lytic lesion. Ask: is the bone destroyed, or broken?
Transferable rule Some fractures in a young child need a force the child could not generate. Treat these as abuse until the film or exam shows a sign specific to a bone disease. A risk factor in the history is not that sign.
Unchecked attributeRickets: exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D is a real risk factor, but the film never showed osteopenia, cupping, fraying or widened physes.
Salient decoyLangerhans cell histiocytosis: the beefy diaper rash with satellite papules is ordinary candida; Langerhans cell histiocytosis causes punched-out lytic lesions, not corner fractures.
Salient decoyOsteogenesis imperfecta: the mother's one childhood forearm fracture is common; without blue sclerae, short stature, bruising or many fractures, this is not osteogenesis imperfecta.
True-fact-wrong-slotCongenital syphilis: no prenatal care is a real risk, but saber shin, frontal bossing and saddle nose are late findings, and none of its signs is a corner fracture.

edits.html:
Stroke in a Child or Adolescent

find the arteriopathy · constitutional symptoms plus unequal pulses make it inflammatory · its mimicsWhat made the artery fail: constitutional symptoms with unequal pulses, a murmur, or neck strain?

Source vignette Pt – 15 yo with weeks of constitutional symptoms and episodic light-headedness, now an acute focal neurologic deficit, with asymmetric upper-extremity pulses · Q – the most likely cause of the stroke; options spanned the pediatric stroke categories: vasculitis, bacterial endocarditis, fibromuscular dysplasia and others
The decision point

A stroke in a teenager is never "just a stroke"; find what made the artery fail. Weeks of fever, weight loss and aches indicate systemic inflammation. Unequal pulses or arm pressures indicate that several large arteries are narrowed at once. Inflammation plus multiple fixed large-artery stenoses is a large-vessel vasculitis; in an adolescent, that is Takayasu arteritis.

Endocarditis is the exception. It also brings fever and stroke, but emboli occlude one vessel at a time and never narrow the aorta's branches, so the pulses stay equal. Look for the murmur and the embolic skin findings instead.

Pediatric stroke, by category Cardiac – congenital heart disease with a right-to-left shunt, endocarditis, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia · Vascular, noninflammatory – arterial dissection, moyamoya, fibromuscular dysplasia · Vascular, inflammatory – Takayasu arteritis, lupus, primary central nervous system vasculitis, post-varicella arteriopathy, meningitis · Hematologic – sickle cell disease, inherited thrombophilia such as factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid antibodies · Takayasu arteritis – granulomatous vasculitis of the aorta and its primary branches in a young patient, most often female; a systemic phase (fever, weight loss, arthralgia) then an occlusive phase (arm claudication, weak or absent pulses, unequal arm pressures, bruits, renovascular hypertension, transient ischemic attack (TIA) and stroke)
Stroke in a young patient: the causes and their tells
CauseIllness scriptThe tell
Vasculitis (Takayasu)Adolescent with weeks of fever, weight loss and arthralgia; high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)Unequal arm pulses or pressures, bruits, long smooth stenoses of the aorta and branches
Bacterial endocarditisFever with a damaged valve or injection drug useNew regurgitant murmur, embolic skin lesions, positive blood cultures; pulses equal
Fibromuscular dysplasiaYoung woman, renovascular hypertension, no inflammationString of beads on angiography, normal ESR
Arterial dissectionNeck trauma, contact sports, neck manipulationNeck pain or headache, Horner syndrome, one tapered vessel
Moyamoya diseaseDown syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, sickle cell diseaseDeficits provoked by hyperventilation (crying, blowing); puff-of-smoke collaterals
Sickle cell diseaseKnown disease or unexplained anemiaLarge-artery vasculopathy; exchange transfusion for the acute stroke
Factor V LeidenFamily history of clotsVenous thrombosis; arterial stroke only by paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale
AtherosclerosisDiabetes, smoking, hyperlipidemia in adultsRare in adolescents without familial hypercholesterolemia; no systemic inflammation
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Brain magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion, or head computed tomography (CT)FirstAcute infarct, no hemorrhageArterial stroke; now find what made the artery fail
Pulses and blood pressure in both armsFirstUnequal arm pressures or pulsesSeveral large arteries narrowed: large-vessel vasculitis
ESR and C-reactive proteinSupportsElevatedInflammatory arteriopathy; normal in fibromuscular dysplasia
CT or magnetic resonance (MR) angiography of the aorta and branchesConfirmsLong smooth stenoses of the aorta and its branchesTakayasu arteritis
Blood cultures and echocardiographyBy branchVegetation with positive culturesEndocarditis: fever with a murmur, pulses equal
Angiography of the head and neckBy branchA single tapered vessel, beading, or puff-of-smoke collateralsDissection, fibromuscular dysplasia or moyamoya
Temporal artery biopsySkipGiant cell arteritis occurs over 50Takayasu is diagnosed by angiography
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo with weeks of fatigue, weight loss and joint aches and episodes of light-headedness, now an acute focal deficit; the arm pulses are unequal → Vasculitis → Takayasu arteritis narrowing the aorta and its branches
  2. 15 yo with fever, weight loss, a 20 mm Hg difference in arm pressures and a carotid bruit → Aortic angiography → CT or MR angiography of the aorta and branches
  3. 15 yo F whose angiogram shows long smooth stenoses of both subclavian arteries; ESR is high and she is still losing weight → High-dose glucocorticoids → then a steroid-sparing agent
  4. 15 yo with Takayasu arteritis who becomes light-headed whenever she exercises her left arm → Subclavian steal → reversed vertebral flow feeds the arm beyond the stenosis
  5. 16 yo who injects drugs, febrile with a new regurgitant murmur and splinter hemorrhages, then sudden aphasia → Infective endocarditis → septic embolus; draw blood cultures
  6. 14 yo struck in the neck during hockey, with neck pain and a left Horner syndrome, then right arm weakness the next day → Carotid dissection → a single tapered vessel on angiography
  7. Young woman with severe hypertension, an abdominal bruit, a normal ESR and a string of beads on renal angiography, who has a TIA → Fibromuscular dysplasia → noninflammatory; no constitutional symptoms
  8. 7 yo with Down syndrome who develops transient arm weakness when crying hard or blowing out candles → Moyamoya disease → hyperventilation constricts the collateral vessels
Pearls Check both arm pressures and every pulse in any young stroke with constitutional symptoms; the older name is pulseless disease · Takayasu and giant cell arteritis share the granulomatous large-vessel histology and are split by age, with giant cell arteritis over 50 · diagnose with CT or MR angiography of the aorta and its branches, and treat with high-dose glucocorticoids plus a steroid-sparing agent · renal artery involvement makes it a cause of secondary hypertension in a young patient · light-headedness or syncope comes from carotid, vertebral or subclavian narrowing, including subclavian steal.
Pairs with Part I Polymyalgia Rheumatica has a giant cell arteritis row, the same vasculitis in patients over 50. Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers fibromuscular dysplasia and the abdominal bruit, the noninflammatory twin. Part II Sickle Cell Disease and Trait covers the sickle cell stroke and its exchange transfusion. Part I Tall Stature and Marfanoid Habitus covers thrombotic stroke in a tall, thin child with learning problems: check plasma homocysteine.
Transferable rule When a young patient has a stroke, name what made the artery fail. Systemic inflammation with unequal pulses is vasculitis; fever with a murmur is an embolus; neck strain with Horner syndrome is a dissection; a string of beads with no inflammation is fibromuscular dysplasia.
Salient decoyBacterial endocarditis: fever plus stroke looks embolic, but emboli do not narrow several arteries or unequalize the pulses.
Mirror twinFibromuscular dysplasia: a young woman with arterial stenoses, but no fever, weight loss or raised ESR.
Class-vs-memberThe options name the class (vasculitis), not the member (Takayasu); answer at the level offered.

edits.html:
Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant

corrected age · milestones at corrected age · growth faltering thresholds · vaccines at chronological ageWhat is the corrected age, and do growth and milestones fit it?

Source vignette Pt – 18 mo F, former 26-week preterm infant, just walking, 10 words, imitates and scribbles; height, weight and head circumference all at the 15th percentile · Q – the most likely assessment; options spanned normal growth and development for corrected age, global developmental delay and failure to thrive
The decision point

Calculate the corrected age first. Born at 26 weeks, she was 14 weeks early. At 18 months chronological age, her corrected age is about 14 and a half months. Judge every milestone against that age. She has just started walking, which is on time. Her vocabulary of 10 words is ahead of the three to five words expected at 15 months. Following a call, imitating and scribbling are age-appropriate.

All three parameters sit together at the 15th percentile. They are proportionate, symmetric and well within normal. Faltering growth requires a parameter below about the 2nd percentile or a downward crossing of two major lines, and she has neither.

Defining criteria Corrected age – chronological age minus the weeks born before 40 weeks · How long to correct – through 24 months for growth and development; newer data support 36 months in extremely and very preterm children · What is never corrected – immunizations, given at chronological age regardless of gestational age or birth weight; the one weight rule is the birth hepatitis B dose at 2 kg or more, and it is a weight threshold rather than an age correction · Normal percentile range – the 15th percentile is normal; faltering growth needs under about the 2nd percentile or a crossing of two major lines
Assessing the former preterm infant – the differential
AssessmentIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Normal for corrected agePreterm child meeting milestones and tracking a normal percentile once correctedCorrected-age milestones met, parameters proportionate above the 2nd percentile
Global developmental delaySignificant delay in two or more domains at corrected ageNot walking or no words at 18 months corrected, often with a falling head circumference
Isolated growth falteringWeight crosses percentiles downward with intact developmentWeight disproportionately low with length and head preserved
Failure to thriveInadequate calories, malabsorption or increased demandParameter below the 2nd percentile or crossing two major lines
Constitutional smallnessSmall but healthy child on a low-normal curveNormal growth velocity along their own percentile
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Growth plotted at corrected ageFirstAll three parameters together, above the 2nd percentileNormal growth; weight alone low points to inadequate calories
Developmental screen at corrected ageNextMilestones met for corrected ageNormal; delay in two or more domains needs early intervention referral
Retinopathy of prematurity exam and hearing screenScreenRetinopathy or failed hearing screenRequired by gestational age and birth weight, however well the infant looks
Cranial ultrasound, all born under 32 weeksConfirmsGerminal matrix or intraventricular bloodIntraventricular hemorrhage; screen at 1 to 2 weeks, repeat to follow progression
Complete blood count with reticulocyte countBy branchNormocytic anemia with no reticulocytosis for its degreeAnemia of prematurity; microcytosis or brisk reticulocytes point elsewhere
Failure-to-thrive laboratory workupSkipThe 15th percentile is normalProportionate, steady growth needs routine surveillance only
Scenario bank
  1. 18 mo F, former 26-week preemie, just walking, 10 words, imitates and scribbles, with height, weight and head circumference all at the 15th percentile corrected → Normal growth and development for corrected age → corrected age about 14 and a half months
  2. Former 26-week premature infant now 12 months chronological, how to plot her growth → Plot at corrected age until 24 months → chronological plotting overstates the deficit
  3. 6 mo old former 28-week premature infant due for routine immunizations → Immunize at chronological age on the standard schedule → prematurity is never corrected for vaccines
  4. 18 mo F, former 26-week preemie, not sitting, no words, head circumference below the 2nd percentile → Refer for developmental evaluation and early intervention → delay across multiple domains at corrected age
  5. Former 26-week premature infant at neonatal intensive care unit discharge, required screening → Retinopathy of prematurity screening – plus a hearing screen → screening driven by gestational age and birth weight
  6. 18 mo former premature infant with all growth parameters at the 15th percentile and tracking steadily → Continue routine surveillance → the 15th percentile is normal
  7. 15 mo M, former 30-week preemie, weight at the 2nd percentile with length at the 25th and head circumference at the 30th, corrected → Inadequate caloric intake → not explained by prematurity
  8. Why growth and development in a preterm child are assessed at corrected rather than chronological age → She has had fewer weeks of growth and brain development → uncorrected assessment falsely labels delay
  9. 24 mo former 26-week premature infant with normal growth and development → Stop correcting for prematurity → plot chronologically from here
  10. 6 wk old former 31-week infant, medically stable and gaining weight, parents asking about the 2-month vaccines → Give them at 2 months of chronologic age on the standard schedule → prematurity is never corrected for vaccines
  11. Why medically stable preterm infants are vaccinated on time rather than deferred → They are at high risk from vaccine-preventable disease and mount an adequate antibody response → immature is not immunocompromised
  12. Preterm infant weighing 1.8 kg at 12 h of life, mother hepatitis B surface antigen negative, due for the birth dose → Delay until the weight reaches 2 kg → the only weight-gated vaccine
  13. 1 wk old girl born at 29 weeks, birth weight 1.51 kg, tolerating feeds, normal vital signs, nondysmorphic, soft anterior fontanelle, moving all four limbs → Screening head ultrasound → all preterm infants under 32 weeks, at age 1 to 2 weeks
  14. Why prematurity under 32 weeks is the threshold for intraventricular hemorrhage screening → The germinal matrix involutes by 32 weeks → before then its thin-walled vessels rupture with swings in cerebral perfusion
  15. 3-day-old born at 28 weeks, 1.04 kg, Apgar scores 8 and 9, afebrile, no maternal fever, membranes ruptured 3 hours before birth; an hour of lethargy and hypotonia, apnea with bradycardia, a tense fontanelle, head circumference up 3 cm since yesterday, then a generalized seizure → Intraventricular hemorrhage → germinal matrix bleed; confirm with cranial ultrasound
  16. Neonate born at 29 weeks who on day 2 develops apnea, lethargy and a bulging anterior fontanelle → Cranial ultrasound → sees blood in the germinal matrix and ventricles through the open fontanelle
  17. 7 wk old born at 32 weeks, feeding and gaining well on fortified formula and ferrous sulfate, pulse 150 with a soft systolic flow murmur; hemoglobin 8, reticulocytes 1.4%, normal platelets and white count, normocytic normochromic smear → Impaired erythropoietin production → anemia of prematurity; the marrow is not asked to respond
  18. 10 wk old term infant, thriving and asymptomatic, hemoglobin 10 with a normocytic smear and normal platelets and white count → Physiologic anemia of infancy → the normal erythropoietin nadir at 2 to 3 months
  19. 6 wk old former 28-week infant with new apnea spells and flat weight gain; hemoglobin 6.5, low reticulocytes, no hemolysis → Red cell transfusion → symptomatic anemia of prematurity
Reading the neonatal history Former 26-week premature sets the age correction; it is not the problem. Mild bronchopulmonary dysplasia with normal head ultrasounds looks like a list of morbidities but is reassuring. Normal cranial imaging excludes the intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia that drive adverse neurodevelopmental outcome at this gestational age.
Intraventricular hemorrhage Mechanism – fragile germinal matrix vessels rupture with swings in cerebral perfusion (hypotension, hypoxia, hypo- or hyperventilation), and the blood can extend into the lateral ventricles · Who – under 32 weeks gestation or under 1500 g · When – the first few days of life, and often asymptomatic · Symptomatic signs – lethargy, hypotonia, seizures, apnea, bradycardia, a bulging fontanelle, a rapidly rising head circumference, acute anemia · Diagnosis – cranial ultrasound, repeated to follow progression; routine screening under 32 weeks · Versus hypoglycemia or hypocalcemia – lethargy, hypotonia and seizures, but never a growing head · Versus hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy – needs perinatal asphyxia and acidosis, not a day-3 onset after Apgar scores of 8 and 9 · Versus meningitis – needs fever or risk factors such as maternal fever or prolonged rupture of membranes
Anemia of prematurity Mechanism – oxygenation at birth (breathing, ductus closure) switches off erythropoietin; a preterm infant has also missed the third-trimester shift of erythropoietin production from liver to kidney · Why worse than term – lower hematocrit at birth, shorter red cell life span, frequent NICU (neonatal intensive care unit) blood draws, iron depletion · Timing – term physiologic anemia bottoms out at 9 to 11 g/dL at 2 to 3 months; the preterm nadir is deeper (about 7 g/dL) and earlier (1 to 2 months) · Presentation – often asymptomatic; tachycardia, a flow murmur, apnea, poor weight gain · Labs – normocytic, normochromic, normal platelets and white count; the absolute reticulocyte count may be normal for age, but there is no reticulocytosis for the degree of anemia · Management – iron supplementation and fewer blood draws; red cell transfusion if severe or symptomatic · Versus thalassemia – microcytic and hypochromic with target cells · Versus hemolysis – erythropoietin rises and the reticulocytes climb · Versus iron deficiency – microcytic, and unlikely on fortified formula with ferrous sulfate · Versus anemia of chronic disease – iron trapped in macrophages by chronic inflammation, infection or malignancy, in older children and adults
Pearls Head circumference is the parameter that predicts neurodevelopment, so preserved head growth in a former preemie is the most reassuring single measurement · A percentile by itself is not a pathology; the concerning patterns are crossing lines downward and disproportion between parameters · Retinopathy of prematurity and hearing screening are required by gestational age, however well the infant looks · A preterm infant is more vulnerable to vaccine-preventable disease, so the vaccine schedule is never delayed
Pairs with Part II Abnormal Growth in a Child covers the contrasting case. Ask: are the three parameters together or apart? Parameters that are together and steady are normal. Parameters that are apart, with weight lowest, indicate inadequate calories. Part I Cerebral Palsy covers the imaging diagnosis when the delay does not resolve with corrected age. Part I Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers apnea of prematurity, the diagnosis for the spells once intraventricular hemorrhage and anemia are excluded. Ask: did the spells start on day 2 to 3 in an infant who is well between episodes?
Transferable rule When a gestational age is given, do the arithmetic before interpreting anything. An option claiming that assessment is impossible is almost always wrong.
Uniform-answer doubtDeclining to assess is not caution; correction exists to make the assessment possible.
Treat-the-numberThe 15th percentile sounds low only against an unexamined assumption that normal means the 50th.
Class-vs-memberGlobal delay is a valid framework, but here it is judged against chronological rather than corrected age.

edits.html:
Deep Neck Infections

trismus with a deviated uvula needs no imaging · deep neck spaces by age · epiglottitis and Ludwig angina: airway firstHow old is the child, and is it trismus, pain on neck extension, or tripoding with stridor?

Source vignette Pt – 14 yo M, a week of worsening unilateral sore throat, trismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated left · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess and infectious mononucleosis
The decision point

A week of worsening unilateral sore throat with trismus, a muffled voice and a uvula deviated away from the swelling is a peritonsillar abscess. It is a clinical diagnosis, so imaging adds nothing. The next step is needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics.

The deep neck spaces sort by age and by what the child cannot do. Trismus and uvular deviation are peritonsillar; pain on neck extension with a bulging posterior wall is retropharyngeal; tripoding with stridor and a normal-looking pharynx is epiglottitis.

Defining criteria Peritonsillar abscess – trismus, muffled hot-potato voice, uvula deviated to the contralateral side, unilateral tonsillar bulge · Retropharyngeal abscess – pain on neck extension, bulging posterior pharyngeal wall, typically under 5 years · Epiglottitis – toxic, tripoding, drooling, stridor, with a deceptively normal oropharynx
The child or adolescent with a severe sore throat - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Peritonsillar abscessAdolescent or young adult, days of worsening unilateral painTrismus with uvular deviation; no imaging required
Retropharyngeal abscessUnder 5 years, often after a pharyngeal infectionPain on neck extension, bulging posterior wall; computed tomography (CT) neck with contrast
EpiglottitisUnvaccinated child, hours not daysTripoding with stridor and a normal pharynx; secure the airway in theatre
Infectious mononucleosisBilateral exudates, posterior cervical nodesSplenomegaly; avoid amoxicillin and contact sports
Ludwig anginaDental source, floor of mouthTongue elevation and submental induration; airway first
Lemierre syndrome Can't missAfter oropharyngeal infectionPersistent fever with nodular lung opacities; internal jugular thrombophlebitis
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Oropharyngeal examFirstTrismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated away from the swellingPeritonsillar abscess; a clinical diagnosis, no imaging needed
Needle aspirationConfirmsPus aspiratedAbscess, drained in the same step; send for culture
Intraoral ultrasoundBy branchPhlegmon versus abscess unclear: fluid collectionAbscess to drain
Heterophile antibody testBy branchBilateral exudates and splenomegaly: positiveMononucleosis; avoid amoxicillin and contact sports
CT neck with contrastBy branchNew neck swelling or torticollis: deeper collectionParapharyngeal or retropharyngeal spread
Lateral neck radiographSkipDoes not show a peritonsillar collectionDelays drainage; it is a retropharyngeal or epiglottitis study
Scenario bank
  1. 14 yo M, week of worsening unilateral sore throat, trismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated left → Peritonsillar abscess → no imaging - needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics
  2. 14 yo M with a peritonsillar abscess, what must the antibiotics cover → Group A Streptococcus and respiratory anaerobes
  3. 4 yo M, fever and drooling with pain on neck extension and a bulging posterior pharyngeal wall → Retropharyngeal abscess → CT neck with contrast
  4. 5 yo M, unvaccinated, toxic and tripoding with stridor and a normal-looking pharynx → Epiglottitis → secure the airway in the operating room
  5. 17 yo F back from camp, bilateral exudative tonsils, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly → Infectious mononucleosis → heterophile antibody, avoid amoxicillin and contact sports
  6. 14 yo M whose drained abscess is followed by persistent fever, pleuritic chest pain and nodular lung opacities → Lemierre syndrome → contrast CT and anaerobic coverage
  7. 50 yo M with a dental infection, floor-of-mouth induration and tongue elevation → Ludwig angina → airway first
  8. 14 yo M with tonsillar swelling where phlegmon versus abscess is uncertain → Intraoral ultrasound
  9. 14 yo M with tonsillar swelling who develops new neck swelling and torticollis → Parapharyngeal extension → CT neck with contrast
  10. 14 yo M with a third peritonsillar abscess this year → Tonsillectomy
  11. 6 yo F with bilateral exudates, no trismus, no uvular deviation, positive rapid strep → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → penicillin or amoxicillin
Airway before anything In Ludwig angina and epiglottitis, the airway is the emergency. Examination can precipitate obstruction, so do not depress the tongue or instrument the pharynx of a tripoding child outside the operating theatre. Recurrent peritonsillar abscess, three or more in a year, is an indication for tonsillectomy.
Pearls Peritonsillar abscess is diagnosed clinically; intraoral ultrasound only helps when phlegmon versus abscess is genuinely uncertain · Retropharyngeal abscess hurts on extension; meningitis hurts on flexion · Amoxicillin in undiagnosed mononucleosis produces a florid morbilliform rash · Lemierre syndrome is Fusobacterium necrophorum with septic pulmonary emboli after an oropharyngeal infection
Pairs with Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the uncomplicated end of this spectrum. Ask: is anything unilateral?
Transferable rule When a diagnosis is clinical and the complication is airway compromise, imaging is almost always the wrong next step. It cannot change what is already known, and it costs time the airway may not have.
Sequencing trapImaging before drainage in a clinically obvious abscess.
Mirror twinRetropharyngeal abscess is the younger child's version, separated by extension versus trismus.

edits.html:
Foot Puncture Wounds and Osteomyelitis

exposure and clock name the organism · shoe vs fresh or salt water · film, then magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) · debridement and bone cultureWas the puncture through a shoe or in water, and is this the first days or weeks later?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

After a foot puncture, the exposure and the clock name the organism:

  • First 1 to 4 days, spreading redness: cellulitis from Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci.
  • Nail through a shoe, pain and redness persisting a week or more, little fever, often a normal WBC (white blood cell count): osteomyelitis or osteochondritis (bone or cartilage infection) from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, carried in from the shoe's foam sole.
  • Wound soaked in fresh water at injury (NBME adds soil), then a fast-spreading infection: Aeromonas hydrophila. Salt water: Vibrio vulnificus.

A normal film does not exclude bone infection; MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) does better. Treat with debridement and bone culture, covering Pseudomonas and S. aureus.

Diagnosis
How NBME framed it: question 1

7-year-old boy, follow-up 3 weeks after a nail went through his shoe into the right foot wound thoroughly cleaned and bandaged; moderate pain persists tetanus vaccine at age 5; otherwise healthy Red, warm skin over the wound, tender to touch T 37.2 °C · other vital signs normal

Most likely causal organism?

Competing answers
  • Aeromonas hydrophila: a wound pathogen that also causes diarrhea and infections in immunocompromised hosts; but it needs fresh water or soil in the wound at injury; this stem gives a shoe and a 3-week course.
  • Group A streptococcus: causes cellulitis; but as a fast-spreading skin infection in the first days, not a deep infection weeks after a puncture.
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae: a gram-negative rod like the key; but it causes aspiration pneumonia, not puncture-wound bone infection.
  • Staphylococcus aureus: the most common cause of osteomyelitis; but a nail through a shoe with a deep infection weeks later points to Pseudomonas.

Down to two: Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus. Pseudomonas aeruginosa: a nail through a shoe, then pain, redness and warmth still present at 3 weeks with a near-normal temperature, is osteomyelitis by direct inoculation. The stem never names osteomyelitis. NBME calls Pseudomonas the puncture-wound organism; that holds for the deep infection weeks after a shoe puncture, while the first days are S. aureus or streptococci. Tetanus at age 5 is 2 years ago: no booster, and no organism.

Management and treatment
By situation Osteomyelitis – surgical debridement, bone cultures, empiric antibiotics covering Pseudomonas and S. aureus · Through a shoe – past 72 hours with signs of infection, add Pseudomonas coverage · Tetanus – a puncture is tetanus-prone: booster if the last dose was over 5 years ago; it names no organism · Fever – a near-normal temperature does not argue against bone infection after a puncture
Practice
  1. 10-year-old boy, 10 days after a nail went through his sneaker into the heel improved at first; heel pain now returning limps; mild swelling and tenderness No water exposure Afebrile · WBC normal · MRI: calcaneal marrow edema → Pseudomonas aeruginosa → a deep infection 1 to 2 weeks after a nail through a sneaker, often afebrile with a normal white count, is Pseudomonas osteomyelitis; S. aureus and streptococci cause the early cellulitis
  2. 9-year-old girl stepped barefoot on a tack on the kitchen floor 2 days ago spreading redness around the puncture warm and tender No water or soil exposure T 38.1 °C · foot radiograph normal → Staphylococcus aureus → a puncture infection in the first days is cellulitis, most often Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci; through a sneaker, a deep infection that appears 1 to 2 weeks later points to Pseudomonas
  3. 15-year-old boy cut his sole on a branch while wading barefoot in a lake 1 day later: rapidly spreading painful redness foot swollen Fresh water, not the sea T 38.9 °C · HR 112/min → Aeromonas hydrophila → a fast-spreading wound infection soon after fresh-water exposure is Aeromonas hydrophila; salt water or raw shellfish points to Vibrio vulnificus
  4. 8-year-old boy, 2 weeks after a nail went through his sneaker into the heel worsening heel pain and swelling tender over the calcaneus Walks on his toes T 37.4 °C · foot radiographs normal → MRI of the foot → early radiographs are often normal in osteomyelitis; MRI is more sensitive and shows marrow edema
  5. 11-year-old girl was diagnosed with calcaneal osteomyelitis by MRI today a nail went through her sneaker 3 weeks ago heel pain and swelling persist Afebrile and otherwise well T 37.3 °C · foot film normal → Surgical debridement with bone cultures and antipseudomonal antibiotics → osteomyelitis after a puncture through a shoe needs surgical debridement with bone cultures and antipseudomonal antibiotics, plus S. aureus coverage until cultures return
Pairs with The Limping Child: a limp after a nail through a shoe routes here. Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child: joint organisms by host. Diabetes Complications and Annual Care: diabetes also carries a high risk of Pseudomonas osteomyelitis.
Transferable rule

Name the organism from the exposure and the clock: a shoe and weeks mean Pseudomonas; the first days mean S. aureus or streptococci.

edits.html:
Encephalopathy and Cerebral Edema in a Child

cause of the cerebral edema, not of the illness · Reye syndrome · only ammonia swells astrocytes · the vitals eliminateWhich option causes edema rather than only encephalopathy, and do the vitals exclude the rest?

Source vignette Pt – 5 yo F, viral illness treated with over-the-counter medications; improved, then vomiting and lethargy; hepatomegaly with a normal spleen; no hypertension, no peripheral edema · Vitals – T 36.8 °C, pulse 110, BP 98/60 · Imaging – cerebral edema · Q – the most likely cause of the imaging findings; options spanned hyperammonemia, hypoglycemia, uremia, adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism
The decision point

The sequence is a viral prodrome, then "over-the-counter medications" (the aspirin, never named). A biphasic course follows (better, then vomiting and lethargy). Then come hepatomegaly without splenomegaly and cerebral edema. This is Reye syndrome. The cause of the imaging finding lies one level down, at the mechanism.

Hyperammonemia, hypoglycemia, uremia, adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism can all cloud consciousness, but only hyperammonemia causes edema. In astrocytes, glutamine synthetase combines ammonia with glutamate to form glutamine. Glutamine is osmotically active and cannot leave. Water follows, and the astrocytes swell, causing cytotoxic cerebral edema. Hypoglycemia, uremia and adrenal crisis produce encephalopathy by other routes and leave the brain the same size.

Option audit – which options cause encephalopathy?
OptionEncephalopathy?Why it fails here
HyperammonemiaYesCorrect – the only one that swells astrocytes
HypoglycemiaYesGenuinely occurs in Reye (failing hepatic gluconeogenesis) but causes no edema – a true fact in the wrong slot
UremiaYesUremic encephalopathy without edema; expect hypertension and peripheral edema, not hepatomegaly
Adrenal insufficiencyYesDysfunction is from hypoperfusion; BP is 98/60 – normal, which kills it outright
HypothyroidismYesMyxedema coma is hypothermic and bradycardic; this child is 36.8 °C with a pulse of 110
The vitals do most of the eliminating BP 98/60 (normal) – excludes adrenal crisis, which is a hypotension diagnosis · pulse 110, temp 36.8 – excludes myxedema coma, which is slow and cold · no hypertension, no peripheral edema – excludes uremia · hepatomegaly with a normal spleen – points to acute hepatic steatosis, not congestion or storage disease.
Toxic-metabolic encephalopathies & precipitants
Toxic-metabolic encephalopathyPrecipitant
Hypoxic-ischemicNear-drowning, choking episode
Diabetic ketoacidosisPoorly controlled diabetes; edema often follows fluid resuscitation
HyponatremiaSyndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion; or rapid correction of hypernatremia
Liver failureViral or autoimmune hepatitis; hepatotoxic drugs such as acetaminophen
Reye syndromeAspirin given for a viral illness in a child
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Serum ammonia and liver enzymesFirstHigh ammonia with raised aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferaseReye syndrome; a neonate with normal liver tests points to a urea cycle defect
Serum glucoseFirstLow glucoseFailing gluconeogenesis; does not cause the edema
Prothrombin time (PT) and international normalized ratioSupportsProlonged PTHepatic dysfunction
Head computed tomographyNextDiffuse cerebral edemaManage intracranial pressure; image before any lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture, when safeBy branchNormal cerebrospinal fluid apart from raised pressureExcludes meningitis and encephalitis
Liver biopsyConfirmsMicrovesicular steatosisReye syndrome; supportive, rarely needed
Salicylate levelSkipOften undetectable by the time of encephalopathyA negative level does not exclude Reye; the history does
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo F, viral upper respiratory infection treated with an over-the-counter medicine, now vomiting and lethargic with hepatomegaly and cerebral edema → Reye syndrome → supportive care and intracranial pressure management
  2. 5 yo F with Reye syndrome; the question asks the cause of the imaging finding → Hyperammonemia → astrocyte glutamine draws in water
  3. 5 yo F with Reye syndrome; what was in the over-the-counter medicine → Aspirin
  4. 5 yo F, liver biopsy performed → Microvesicular steatosis → supportive of the diagnosis but not required
  5. Which children may still receive aspirin → Kawasaki disease and rheumatologic disease such as JIA
  6. 6 yo F, altered after an infection, hypotensive with hyperkalemia and hyponatremia → Adrenal crisis → stress-dose hydrocortisone
  7. 12 yo M with type 1 diabetes, glucose 620, becomes obtunded hours into fluid resuscitation → DKA-associated cerebral edema → hypertonic saline or mannitol
  8. 2 yo M with hypernatremic dehydration corrected too rapidly → Cerebral edema from the osmotic shift
  9. 3 yo M pulled from a pool, now unresponsive → Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
  10. 3 day old with hyperammonemia, normal LFTs and no hepatomegaly, after feeds began → Urea cycle defect → ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
Distractors Hypoglycemia: the sharpest trap in the set, because it is true; Reye does cause hypoglycemia through failing hepatic gluconeogenesis. It simply is not what swells the brain. Uremia: a neurotoxin, but nothing here suggests renal failure. Adrenal insufficiency: plausible until you read the blood pressure. Hypothyroidism: the pulse and temperature contradict it.
Paired pearls Aspirin is contraindicated in children except for Kawasaki disease and rheumatologic disease such as JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis); Kawasaki is the reason the exception exists · the mechanism is mitochondrial injury → impaired β-oxidation. This causes microvesicular steatosis, which is why the liver is big but not scarred · treatment is supportive; there is no antidote · hyperammonemia without hepatomegaly in a neonate is a urea cycle defect, not Reye; the neurotoxin is the same, but the disease is different.
Pairs with Diabetes Complications and Annual Care also turns on reading the outcome noun (morbidity versus mortality). Here this stem says "cause of this patient's imaging findings," not "cause of this patient's presentation." Ask: "which effect am I being asked to explain?"
Transferable rule When a stem names a specific finding and asks what caused it, the answer must explain that finding, not the illness. Options that are true of the disease but cannot produce the named finding are the intended traps. They are the hardest to reject precisely because they are true.
True-fact-wrong-slotSalient decoy

edits.html:
Shock in Children

four categories by mechanism, not appearance · cold shock in children · perfusion before pressure · septic shock ladderIs perfusion abnormal, and what is wrong with the circulation rather than with the skin?

Source vignette Pt – 4 yo F, fever to 40 C, petechial rash, obtundation, capillary refill 4 seconds, no response to three fluid boluses; no blood pressure reported · Q – the category of shock; options spanned distributive, cardiogenic, hypovolemic and obstructive
The decision point

Fever, a petechial rash and shock in a preschooler indicate septic shock. Septic shock is by definition distributive. Inflammatory mediators produce vasodilation and capillary leak, so blood is maldistributed rather than absent, inadequate or obstructed.

She does not look vasodilated. Capillary refill of 4 seconds is cold shock, which is how children usually present. Children compensate by vasoconstricting and raising the heart rate, so the bedside picture mimics hypovolemia. The vignette gives no blood pressure, because in children hypotension is a late, pre-arrest finding.

Defining criteria Distributive shock – vasodilation and capillary leak with maldistributed flow despite normal or high cardiac output · Shock in a child – a perfusion diagnosis: mental status, capillary refill above 2 seconds, weak pulses, urine output under 1 mL/kg/h · Hypotension – not required, and marks decompensation when present · Fluid-refractory shock – persistent after 40 to 60 mL/kg, the trigger to start a vasoactive infusion
The four categories of shock – what to look for
CategoryMechanismThe NBME tell
DistributiveVasodilation and capillary leakFever with a source, urticaria, or a spinal injury; wide pulse pressure when warm
HypovolemicVolume loss – gastrointestinal, hemorrhage, burns, ketoacidosisA stated route of loss, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes
CardiogenicPump failure – myocarditis, arrhythmia, congenital lesionGallop, hepatomegaly, crackles; worsens with fluid
ObstructiveMechanical block – tamponade, tension pneumothorax, ductal-dependent lesionDistended neck veins with clear or asymmetric lungs, muffled sounds
Anaphylactic distributive subtypeImmunoglobulin E-mediated vasodilationUrticaria, angioedema, wheeze within minutes of exposure
Neurogenic distributive subtypeLoss of sympathetic tone above T6Hypotension with bradycardia, warm dry skin
Management ladder – pediatric septic shock
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Recognise, obtain access, balanced crystalloid 10 to 20 mL/kg per bolus up to 40 to 60 mL/kg in the first hour, reassessing after eachShock persists after 40 to 60 mL/kg, or rales or hepatomegaly appear, which stops the fluid
2Start a vasoactive infusion – epinephrine or norepinephrineCatecholamine-resistant shock
3Hydrocortisone for catecholamine-resistant shock or suspected adrenal insufficiencyNo response; consider extracorporeal support
ParallelAntimicrobials within 1 hour for septic shock, cultures first only if they cause no substantial delay –
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo F with fever to 40 C, a petechial rash, obtundation, capillary refill 4 seconds and no response to three fluid boluses → Distributive shock → septic shock, cold phenotype
  2. 4 yo F in septic shock still hypoperfused after 60 mL/kg of isotonic fluid → Start a vasoactive infusion → fluid-refractory septic shock
  3. 4 yo F with septic shock whose blood cultures are pending → Give antimicrobials within 1 hour → cultures first only if they cause no delay
  4. 9 mo M with 5 days of vomiting and diarrhea, sunken eyes, capillary refill 3 seconds and tachycardia → Give a 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid bolus → hypovolemic shock
  5. 8 yo M with viral myocarditis, a gallop, hepatomegaly, crackles and capillary refill 4 seconds → Give small 5 to 10 mL/kg fluid aliquots with an inotrope → cardiogenic shock
  6. 16 yo M with a penetrating chest wound, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and hypotension → Pericardiocentesis → obstructive shock from tamponade
  7. 5 yo F with meningococcemia who remains shocked on an epinephrine infusion → Give hydrocortisone → Waterhouse-Friderichsen adrenal insufficiency
  8. 16 yo M with urticaria, wheeze and hypotension minutes after eating peanuts → Anaphylactic shock → a distributive subtype
  9. 17 yo M after a cervical spine injury, hypotensive with bradycardia and warm dry skin → Neurogenic shock → also a distributive subtype
Exceptions Where intensive care is not available and the child has sepsis without hypotension, bolus fluid is recommended against. This is a strong, high-certainty recommendation. Also, adolescence is never itself a reason to admit; the same hospitalization thresholds apply as for adults.
Pearls Hypotension is a late sign in children; they defend pressure with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, then decompensate abruptly · Children get cold shock and adults get warm shock; a vasoconstricted child's shock is still distributive · Anaphylactic and neurogenic shock are distributive subtypes, so classify the shock as distributive, not as the subtype, unless the subtype's trigger is present · Neurogenic shock is the one form of shock with hypotension and bradycardia; all other shock is tachycardic · Fever plus petechiae plus toxicity is meningococcemia until excluded; petechiae in a well child point instead at immune thrombocytopenia
Pairs with Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) grid and meningococcal disease; this brief covers only recognition and resuscitation. Ask: is perfusion abnormal? If yes, resuscitate before you investigate.
Transferable rule Shock is classified by mechanism rather than appearance, so ask what is wrong with the circulation instead of what the skin looks like.
True-fact-wrong-slotFluid refractoriness in sepsis reflects leak and vasodilation, not pump failure.
Class-vs-memberAnaphylaxis: it is in the right class but is the wrong member, with no exposure and no urticaria.

edits.html:
Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia

choking on the first feed · pass a tube before you order a picture · fistula type by abdominal gas · age at presentationDid it start with the first feed, and will a nasogastric tube pass?

Source vignette Pt – 3 h old term boy born at home, coughs and vomits on his first breastfeed, formula mixed with saliva in his mouth, coarse breath sounds with retractions, soft systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned nasogastric tube placement, lateral neck radiography and echocardiography
The decision point

Formula mixed with saliva means the milk filled a blind proximal pouch and overflowed without reaching the stomach. With choking on the very first feed and coarse lungs from aspiration, this is esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.

The first step is to pass a nasogastric tube at the bedside. It meets resistance at the pouch, and the film shows it coiled. The murmur, maternal drug history and absent prenatal care do not call for imaging or drug treatment first.

Defining criteria Type C – proximal pouch with a distal fistula, about 85% of cases · Gas in the abdomen – a distal fistula is present · Gasless abdomen – pure atresia with no distal fistula · H-type – no atresia, presenting months later with recurrent pneumonia
Neonatal choking and vomiting – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Esophageal atresia (EA) with distal tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF)Choking on the first feed, copious frothy secretions, polyhydramnios in uteroFormula mixed with saliva; tube will not pass
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaSevere distress at deliveryScaphoid abdomen, bowel gas in the chest, shifted heart sounds
Congenital heart diseaseFeeding difficulty with cyanosisCyanosis and diaphoresis with feeds, no excess secretions
EpiglottitisFebrile stridor with droolingSchool-aged child, never a newborn
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosisNonbilious projectile vomitingAge 3 to 6 weeks, hungry after vomiting, olive mass
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiencyGround-glass with air bronchograms, low lung volumes
Neonatal abstinence syndromeMaternal opioid useOnset at or beyond 24 hours, hypertonia and irritability
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Nasogastric tube passageFirstMeets resistance at the pouchEsophageal atresia likely: film with the tube in place
Chest and abdominal x-ray with the tubeConfirmsTube coiled in the upper chestEsophageal atresia
Gas below the diaphragmDistal fistula present (type C)
Gasless abdomenPure atresia, no distal fistula
Echocardiogram and renal ultrasoundNextVACTERL anomaliesScreen after the diagnosis, before repair
Bronchoscopy or prone contrast esophagramBy branchH-type fistulaTube passes; months of cough with feeds and recurrent pneumonia
Barium esophagram or endoscopySkipContrast can aspirate from the blind pouchThe coiled tube on film already confirms atresia
Scenario bank
  1. 3 h old term boy born at home, coughs and vomits on his first breastfeed, formula mixed with saliva in his mouth, coarse breath sounds with retractions, soft systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border → Nasogastric tube placement → Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
  2. 2 h old term girl drooling frothy secretions who choked on her first feed; a nasogastric tube meets firm resistance and will not advance → Chest x-ray with the tube in place → A coiled tube confirms atresia; gas below the diaphragm means a distal fistula
  3. Term newborn girl, maternal polyhydramnios, drooling; the feeding tube coils in the upper chest on x-ray and the abdomen is completely gasless → Esophageal atresia without a fistula → No tracheal connection, so no air reaches the stomach
  4. 8 mo old boy with three right upper lobe pneumonias and coughing and choking with liquid feeds since birth; a feeding tube passes easily into the stomach → H-type tracheoesophageal fistula → Bronchoscopy or prone contrast esophagram
  5. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, before surgical repair → Echocardiogram and renal ultrasound → VACTERL association
  6. 4 wk old boy with a week of nonbilious projectile vomiting, hungry after each episode, ultrasound showing a thickened elongated pylorus, low chloride and high bicarbonate → IV fluids and electrolyte repletion → Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; pyloromyotomy once the alkalosis corrects
  7. Newborn girl with upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease, maternal polyhydramnios, bilious vomiting on day 1, abdominal x-ray with a double bubble and no distal gas → Nasogastric decompression and IV fluids → Duodenal atresia; repair after stabilization and an echocardiogram
  8. 30 wk preterm boy grunting and retracting at 1 h of life, x-ray with diffuse ground-glass opacities, air bronchograms and low lung volumes → Respiratory distress syndrome → continuous positive airway pressure, then surfactant if the oxygen requirement rises
  9. 36 h old girl, irritable and tremulous with a high-pitched cry, sneezing and feeding poorly; mother maintained on methadone → Swaddling, low stimulation and rooming-in → Neonatal abstinence syndrome; morphine only if nonpharmacologic care fails
  10. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, saturating 96% in room air, awaiting surgical repair → NPO, head elevated, continuous pouch suction → Keeps pooled saliva out of the lungs and gastric acid out of the fistula
Age at presentation Age at presentation narrows the differential. Minutes to hours: TEF (tracheoesophageal fistula) with EA (esophageal atresia), choanal atresia, diaphragmatic hernia, respiratory distress syndrome, Potter sequence. Beyond 24 hours: neonatal abstinence, sepsis, ductal-dependent lesions as the PDA (patent ductus arteriosus) closes, bilious vomiting and malrotation. 3 to 6 weeks: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Months: H-type fistula, laryngomalacia.
Pearls Polyhydramnios in utero, because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid · Diagnosis is made by passing the tube: resistance at roughly 9 to 11 cm, confirmed on film · The abdominal gas pattern shows the anatomic type without endoscopy · VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) screening after diagnosis: echocardiogram and renal ultrasound at minimum · A soft systolic murmur on day one is usually a closing ductus, not structural disease
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves shares the mechanism in reverse: a fetus that cannot make urine has oligohydramnios and Potter sequence, and a fetus that cannot swallow has polyhydramnios and foregut or duodenal atresia. Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn covers cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying, which is choanal atresia, not a fistula. Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) alongside the syndromes it is mistaken for and what excludes each.
Transferable rule When a newborn chokes or vomits with the first feed, first check whether a nasogastric tube reaches the stomach, before any imaging or drug. Imaging only confirms what the tube found.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpiglottitis is a febrile school-age disease; a 3-hour-old cannot have it.
Sequencing trapEchocardiography is indicated for VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) screening after the diagnosis, not before it.
True-fact-wrong-slotPyloric stenosis needs 3 to 6 weeks for the muscle to hypertrophy, and it gives projectile vomiting, not coughing with saliva-mixed formula at 3 hours.
True-fact-wrong-slotSurfactant treats respiratory distress syndrome in the preterm lung; this is a term newborn whose retractions come from aspirated secretions, which surfactant does not fix.
Salient decoyThe maternal drug history points at neonatal abstinence syndrome, but withdrawal typically begins at 24 hours or later, never pools saliva or causes coughing with feeds, and is treated first without drugs.

edits.html:
Spinal Dysraphism

grade the reflexes first · a number outranks a story · upper vs lower motor neuron · bladder, back, pes cavusAre the reflexes brisk or diminished, and is the bladder involved?

Source vignette Pt – 6 yo M, 2 months of progressive gait difficulty and back pain, new incontinence, pes cavus and hammer toes, 1+ lower extremity reflexes · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned tethered cord, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and spastic diplegia
The decision point

1+ reflexes are the key finding. Hyporeflexia is a lower motor neuron sign that localizes at or below the anterior horn cell. It eliminates spastic diplegia outright, since cerebral palsy is by definition an upper motor neuron disorder. Three findings then pick the lesion. Bladder involvement counts because muscle and peripheral nerve diseases spare the bladder. Back pain points at a structural spinal lesion. Pes cavus is chronic denervation of the intrinsic foot muscles.

One lesion explains all four findings: a tethered cord from closed spinal dysraphism, stretched by two months of growth.

Defining criteria Reflex grading – 0 absent, 1+ diminished, 2+ normal, 3+ brisk, 4+ clonus · Lower motor neuron signs – weakness with hypotonia, hyporeflexia and atrophy, localizing at or below the anterior horn cell · Upper motor neuron signs – weakness with spasticity, hyperreflexia and Babinski, localizing above the anterior horn cell · Secondary incontinence – continence achieved and held, then lost; always pathologic · Low-lying conus – the conus reaches L1 to L2 by about 3 months, so below mid-L2 is low; a filum over 2 mm is thickened
The child with progressive leg weakness - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Tethered cordCord anchored caudally and stretched by growthLower motor neuron signs with bladder dysfunction, pes cavus and back pain together
Duchenne muscular dystrophy3 to 5 yo boy, progressive degenerationProximal weakness, Gower sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, pes planus; no bladder involvement
Spastic diplegiaStatic perinatal insult, often prematurityHypertonia and hyperreflexia, scissoring gait, nonprogressive
Transverse myelitisPost-infectious cord demyelinationAcute over hours to days with a sensory level
Charcot-Marie-ToothHereditary neuropathy, autosomal dominantPes cavus with foot drop and family history; no bladder involvement
Friedreich ataxiaAutosomal recessive, teensPes cavus with ataxia and areflexia with upgoing toes, cardiomyopathy
Spinal cord tumor Can't missAstrocytoma or ependymomaNight-waking back pain with progressive deficits; same magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) answers both
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Reflex grading and neurologic examFirst1+ reflexes with bladder dysfunctionLower motor neuron signs plus bladder: spinal cord
Inspection of the lower backFirstHair tuft, lipoma or dimple above the gluteal cleftClosed dysraphism; a normal back does not exclude it
Spinal ultrasound, infant under about 3 monthsBy branchLow-lying conus or thick filumClosed dysraphism; MRI after the posterior elements ossify
MRI of the lumbosacral spineConfirmsConus below mid-L2, filum over 2 mmTethered cord: surgical detethering; also shows a cord tumor
Creatine kinase (CK)By branchVery high CKDuchenne: proximal weakness, Gower sign, bladder spared
Brain MRI for suspected spastic diplegiaSkipReflexes are decreased, not briskHyporeflexia localizes below the brain
Scenario bank
  1. 6 yo M, 2 mo of progressive gait difficulty and back pain, new incontinence, pes cavus and hammer toes, 1+ lower extremity reflexes → Tethered cord → MRI of the spine
  2. 5 yo M, difficulty climbing stairs, Gower sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, CK 18,000, continent → Duchenne muscular dystrophy → genetic testing
  3. 3 yo, former 27-week preemie, toe-walking with a scissoring gait, hypertonia, 3+ reflexes, nonprogressive → Spastic diplegic cerebral palsy
  4. 12 yo F, 3 days of leg weakness, a sensory level at T8, urinary retention, 2 wk after a viral illness → Transverse myelitis → MRI and high-dose intravenous steroids
  5. 14 yo M, distal weakness, foot drop with steppage gait, pes cavus, absent ankle reflexes, father has the same feet → Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
  6. 13 yo M, progressive ataxia and dysarthria, pes cavus, areflexia with upgoing toes, scoliosis, cardiomyopathy → Friedreich ataxia → echocardiogram
  7. Newborn with a lumbosacral hair tuft and a dimple above the gluteal cleft, normal neurologic exam → Closed spinal dysraphism → ultrasound of the spine
  8. 8 yo F, back pain that wakes her at night, progressive leg weakness, bladder dysfunction, normal feet → Spinal cord tumor → MRI of the spine
  9. 7 yo M, bedwetting at night only, never been dry, normal exam and urinalysis → Primary nocturnal enuresis → reassurance
  10. 6 yo M with tethered cord on MRI and progressive symptoms → Surgical detethering
Occulta means hidden A normal-looking back does not exclude dysraphism. Cutaneous stigmata are common but not universal. Look for a hair tuft, lipoma, hemangioma, sacral appendage, or a dimple above the gluteal cleft; a simple dimple within the cleft with a visible base is benign. Image with ultrasound before about 3 months, while the posterior elements are cartilaginous, and MRI after.
Pearls Pes cavus is a neurologic sign, not an orthopedic one: Charcot-Marie-Tooth, Friedreich ataxia, and tethered cord · Secondary enuresis is never assumed functional; consider infection, diabetes, constipation, neurologic disease, stress and sleep apnea · Back pain in a child under 10 is pathologic until proven otherwise · Occulta – skin intact, no herniation · Meningocele – meninges herniate, cord normal · Myelomeningocele – meninges and neural tissue, with Chiari II and hydrocephalus · Folate prevents neural tube defects: 0.4 mg periconceptionally, 4 mg with a prior affected pregnancy
Pairs with Part I Enuresis is the mirror twin: it shares the complaint of a school-age child wetting, and the classification flips from functional to neurologic. Ask: was the child ever dry, and is anything else abnormal? Part I Constipation in a Child screens for this condition on every perineal examination; a sacral dimple or hair tuft converts constipation into imaging.
Transferable rule Grade the reflexes before you name the disease. Hyperreflexia and hyporeflexia split the weakness differential into halves that share no members. That split holds however compelling the history.
Class-vs-memberDuchenne: the right age and sex, with proximal weakness, flat feet and no bladder involvement.
Mirror twinSpastic diplegia: the upper motor neuron version of the same complaint.
True-fact-wrong-slotTransverse myelitis: a real cord syndrome on the wrong timeline.
