edits.html:
22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome

the syndrome is given; find the missing piece · CATCH · which syndrome has which finding · read the last sentence firstWhich component did the vignette leave out, and which bedside sign in the exam shows it?

Source vignette Pt – 3 h old F, 38 wk by cesarean for nonreassuring tones, Apgars 8 and 8, moved to the nursery for a dusky appearance; cyanotic and tremulous, with low-set ears, micrognathia and a cleft palate · Labs – pulse oximetry 72% in the right hand and the leg, unchanged after 10 minutes of 100% oxygen by hood · Imaging – chest radiograph shows an absent thymus; echocardiography shows truncus arteriosus · Q – which condition this patient most likely has; options spanned anemia, duodenal atresia, horseshoe kidney, hypocalcemia, hypoglycemia, myelomeningocele and neutropenia
The decision point

The vignette already gives the diagnosis. Conotruncal defect plus absent thymus plus cleft palate plus low-set ears and micrognathia is 22q11.2 deletion. Every answer option is a condition, not a syndrome. CATCH lists the components: Cardiac outflow anomaly, Anomalous face, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia. Four of the five are printed in the vignette; the missing one is hypocalcemia. The clue is in the physical examination: tremulous is neonatal hypocalcemia. This matters because these infants are at real risk of tetany, seizures and arrhythmia.

Defining criteria CATCH-22 – Cardiac outflow tract anomaly such as truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot or interrupted aortic arch; Anomalous face with prominent nasal bridge, low-set ears and micrognathia; Thymic hypoplasia or aplasia reducing T-cell immunity; Cleft palate; and Hypoparathyroidism producing hypocalcemia · DiGeorge versus velocardiofacial syndrome – both are 22q11.2 phenotypes; DiGeorge requires thymic involvement, with a CD3+ T-cell count under 500/mm3, while velocardiofacial requires facial abnormalities · Pathogenesis – loss of genes controlling third and fourth pharyngeal pouch derivation and neural crest migration, which is why the thymus, parathyroids, palate, face and cardiac outflow tract fail together
Pertinent positives & negatives Absent thymus on chest radiograph – third and fourth pouch failure; the most specific finding in the stem and the reason this is DiGeorge rather than isolated truncus · Truncus arteriosus – a conotruncal defect, the cardiac C · Cleft palate, low-set ears, micrognathia – the C and the A; with the thymus, four of five CATCH letters are printed · Tremulous – neonatal hypocalcemia before it becomes tetany · Saturation 72% in right hand and leg – no differential cyanosis, which excludes severe coarctation and interrupted arch physiology, and with them Turner syndrome · Refractory to 100% oxygen for 10 minutes – a fixed right-to-left shunt, confirming cyanotic structural heart disease rather than lung disease · Apgars 8 and 8, uncomplicated pregnancy, primigravida – no asphyxia and no maternal diabetes, closing the usual setups for hypoglycemia · No abdominal or spinal findings – nothing pointing at duodenal atresia or a neural tube defect
The dysmorphic neonate with a heart defect – which syndrome has which finding
SyndromeIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge)Pouch 3 and 4 failure; conotruncal defect, hypoplastic thymus and parathyroidsAbsent thymus plus conotruncal defect plus cleft palate; hypocalcemia is the fourth member – (the answer)
Down syndrome (trisomy 21)Commonest aneuploidy; atrioventricular septal defect, hypotoniaDuodenal atresia with a double bubble, single palmar crease, upslanting fissuresThymus present; no gastrointestinal malformation described
Turner syndrome (45,X)Female, short stature, gonadal dysgenesisHorseshoe kidney, coarctation, webbed neck, wide-spaced nipplesEqual pre- and postductal saturations; no renal or neck findings
CHARGE associationColoboma, choanal atresia, ear anomaliesColoboma and choanal atresia alongside the heart defectNo eye or nasal findings; thymic loss is not its signature
Infant of a diabetic motherMacrosomia, transposition, septal hypertrophyHypoglycemia in the first hours with a high birth weightPregnancy uncomplicated in a primigravida, no macrosomia
Management, in one line Once 22q11.2 is suspected, send an ionized calcium and get an echocardiogram. Confirm the deletion with chromosomal microarray or FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization). Treat symptomatic hypocalcemia with intravenous calcium. Until normal T-cell immunity is confirmed, these infants get irradiated blood products and no live vaccines.
Decision spine Read the last sentence first. – It asks for a condition, not a diagnosis · Name the syndrome from the cluster. – Conotruncal defect plus absent thymus plus cleft palate is 22q11.2 · Recite CATCH and cross off what is printed. – Cardiac, face, thymus and cleft are all given, so H is missing · Look for its bedside tell. – Tremulous means hypocalcemia · Assign each remaining option to its own syndrome. – Horseshoe kidney to Turner, duodenal atresia to Down, hypoglycemia to the infant of a diabetic mother, myelomeningocele to folate · Check the cell line. – DiGeorge takes lymphocytes, not neutrophils or red cells
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Pulse oximetry on 100% oxygenFirstSaturation unchanged, equal in hand and legFixed intracardiac shunt: cyanotic heart disease
EchocardiographyNextConotruncal defect: truncus, tetralogy or interrupted archRaises suspicion for 22q11.2 deletion
Chest radiographSupportsAbsent thymic shadowThymic hypoplasia or aplasia
Ionized calciumNextLowParathyroid hypoplasia; IV calcium if tremulous or seizing
Chromosomal microarray or FISH for 22q11.2ConfirmsMicrodeletion at 22q11.222q11.2 deletion syndrome
T-cell subsetsStagingCD3 count under 500/mm3DiGeorge immune phenotype: irradiated blood, no live vaccines
Standard karyotypeSkipNormal; the deletion is too small to seeUse microarray or FISH instead
Scenario bank
  1. 3 h old F, cyanosis refractory to 100% oxygen, saturation 72% in right hand and leg, low-set ears, micrognathia, cleft palate, absent thymus on chest film, truncus arteriosus on echocardiography, tremulous on examination → Hypocalcemia → parathyroid hypoplasia in 22q11.2 deletion
  2. Term neonate with truncus arteriosus, cleft palate and an absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph → Chromosomal microarray for the 22q11.2 deletion → a standard karyotype does not resolve a microdeletion
  3. Neonate with known 22q11.2 deletion who develops a generalized seizure; ionized calcium is low → Intravenous calcium gluconate → hypocalcemic seizure from parathyroid hypoplasia
  4. 4 mo old with 22q11.2 deletion and a CD3+ T-cell count of 210/mm3, presenting for routine immunizations → The live attenuated rotavirus vaccine → live vaccines are withheld until CD3 and CD4 exceed 500/mm3 and CD8 exceeds 200/mm3 with a normal mitogen response
  5. Newborn with a double-bubble sign on abdominal radiograph, a single transverse palmar crease and an atrioventricular septal defect → Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
  6. Newborn girl with coarctation of the aorta, a webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples and a horseshoe kidney → Turner syndrome → 45,X
  7. Why the thymus, parathyroids, palate and cardiac outflow tract fail together in this syndrome → Failed third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development with abnormal neural crest migration → one embryologic field, four organs
  8. 6 yo with 22q11.2 deletion, recurrent sinopulmonary infections and poor responses to polysaccharide vaccines → T-cell subsets with quantitative immunoglobulins → humoral failure follows defective T-cell help
Decoy note Tremulous is the bedside sign of both neonatal hypoglycemia and neonatal hypocalcemia. An uncomplicated pregnancy in a primigravida with Apgars of 8 closes off the hypoglycemia route. The equal right-hand and leg saturations read as an incidental vital sign, but they exclude differential cyanosis, and with it coarctation and Turner syndrome.
Pearls Syndrome with a missing component: when a vignette describes most of a syndrome, recite the mnemonic and cross off what is printed. Answer with the remainder; CATCH, JONES and CREST are tested this way · Hypocalcemia and hypoglycemia share a neonatal presentation of jitteriness, tremor and seizure, and the pregnancy history separates them · Differential cyanosis means ductal or arch pathology; equal pre- and postductal saturations mean a fixed intracardiac shunt, which is what truncus produces · DiGeorge takes lymphocytes, so an option of neutropenia or anemia tests which lineage the thymus governs · Until normal T-cell immunity is confirmed, these infants need irradiated blood and no live vaccines · The same deletion has two names: thymic involvement makes it DiGeorge, and facial abnormality makes it velocardiofacial
Pairs with Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers truncus arteriosus within the cyanosis differential, and the oxygen-refractory shunt logic that leads to it. Antibody Deficiencies covers the downstream question of which immunodeficiency the absent thymus produces. Ask: is the thymic shadow present, and does the face carry a syndrome? Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth places this syndrome beside CHARGE, VACTERL, trisomy 13 and Fanconi anemia. There, the deciding finding is the one on the fewest lists.
Transferable rule Read the last sentence before the vignette. When a vignette assembles a recognizable syndrome, the diagnosis is given, and the question asks for the component it left out. That component usually has a one-word bedside sign in the physical examination.
True-fact-wrong-slotHorseshoe kidney: a real and memorable syndrome pairing, but it belongs to Turner, and the equal limb saturations already exclude Turner's coarctation.
True-fact-wrong-slotDuodenal atresia: congenital heart disease with low-set ears reads as Down syndrome, but that is where duodenal atresia belongs and Down has no thymic aplasia.
Unchecked attributeNeutropenia: DiGeorge genuinely causes a cytopenia, but the lineage is lymphocytes; red cell and neutrophil counts are unaffected.
Mirror twinHypoglycemia: a tremulous neonate is the classic hypoglycemia cue and also the hypocalcemia cue, but this pregnancy was uncomplicated with normal Apgars.

edits.html:
Ectopic Pregnancy

transvaginal ultrasound first · discriminatory zone · serial hCG · methotrexate eligibility · unstable means surgeryWhere is the pregnancy, and is the patient stable enough to image?

The decision point

The urine test has already confirmed pregnancy. The next step is to find where the pregnancy is. Only transvaginal ultrasound can localize it. A single serum β-hCG localizes nothing.

Defining criteria Methotrexate eligibility – unruptured, hCG <5,000, <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, reliable follow-up · Unstable ectopic – hypotension, rebound, or shoulder pain → emergent laparoscopy/laparotomy
Where β-hCG actually belongs
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Urine or serum hCGFirstPositivePregnant: the question becomes where the pregnancy is
Transvaginal ultrasoundNextIntrauterine gestational sac with a yolk sacIntrauterine pregnancy: stop; heterotopic pregnancy is rare outside in vitro fertilization (IVF)
ConfirmsExtrauterine sac, or adnexal mass with free fluidEctopic pregnancy: methotrexate if eligible, otherwise surgery
Quantitative serum β-hCGBy branchAbove 1,500 to 2,000 with an empty uterusIndeterminate scan: presumed ectopic
Serial β-hCG every 48 hoursBy branchRise of less than 35 to 50%Abnormal pregnancy, likely ectopic; a normal one doubles, a miscarriage falls
Emergent laparoscopyConfirmsTubal pregnancy or hemoperitoneumUnstable patient: operate without waiting for imaging
Single serum β-hCG before ultrasoundSkipA number cannot localize the pregnancyTransvaginal ultrasound answers the location question
  1. Symptomatic + positive pregnancy test → Transvaginal ultrasound now
  2. Intrauterine pregnancy seen → Stop the workup → heterotopic pregnancy is rare outside IVF
  3. Adnexal mass or free fluid → Ectopic pregnancy → treat
  4. Transvaginal ultrasound indeterminate → Check the β-hCG against the discriminatory zone → above 1,500 to 2,000 with an empty uterus is a presumed ectopic, and below it serial hCG q48h (a normal intrauterine pregnancy doubles; ectopic rises <35–50%; miscarriage falls)
Unstable ectopic Hypotension, rebound or shoulder pain (diaphragmatic irritation from hemoperitoneum) → skip the rest of the workup and go to emergent laparoscopy/laparotomy. Image the stable patient and operate on the unstable one, the same logic as in PE (pulmonary embolism).
Pearls The biggest acquired risk factor is prior PID (pelvic inflammatory disease), through tubal scarring. Others are prior ectopic, tubal surgery, IUD (intrauterine device) in place and smoking, which impairs ciliary transport · half of ectopics have no palpable adnexal mass · methotrexate if unruptured, hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) <5,000, <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, reliable follow-up · Rh-negative mother with any bleeding in pregnancy → RhoGAM.
Transferable rule When two tests both seem reasonable, choose the one whose result changes management. A single hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) does not change management tonight; the ultrasound does.

edits.html:
Atopic Dermatitis

vesicles on eczema · punched-out erosions vs honey crust · mucosa and failed antibiotics exclude mimics · acyclovir nowAre these vesicles on eczema, and what do the mucosa and the failed antibiotic exclude?

The decision point

Atopic dermatitis with vesicles is eczema herpeticum until proven otherwise. The atopic dermatitis is the precondition. A disrupted barrier plus local immune dysfunction lets HSV (herpes simplex virus) spread across the skin instead of staying a single cold sore. Treatment is immediate systemic acyclovir, because the infection can disseminate to the liver and brain.

Findings that exclude the mimics "Conjunctiva and oropharynx are clear" excludes the drug reaction. SJS (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and TEN (toxic epidermal necrolysis) require mucosal involvement (classically ≥2 sites) plus symmetric target lesions. "Progressive worsening on TMP-SMX" (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) excludes impetigo. TMP-SMX covers staph, including MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus). So failure on appropriate antibacterial therapy eliminates the bacterial hypothesis, exactly as a failed antihistamine eliminates upper airway cough syndrome.
Atopic dermatitis complications
Complication of atopic dermatitisPathogenPresentationTreatment
Eczema herpeticum Can't missHerpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1)Painful monomorphic vesicles → punched-out erosions, hemorrhagic crusting; fever, lymphadenopathySystemic acyclovir immediately
ImpetigoS. aureus, S. pyogenesHoney-colored adherent crustMupirocin or oral cephalexin
Molluscum contagiosumPoxvirusSkin-colored papules with central umbilicationSelf-limited; curettage/cantharidin
Tinea corporisT. rubrumAnnular, central clearing, raised scaly borderTopical azole or terbinafine
Eczema coxsackiumCoxsackie A6Vesicles concentrated in eczematous skinSupportive
Morphology tell & workup Herpes causes monomorphic vesicles that evolve into "punched-out" erosions with hemorrhagic crust and scalloped coalescing borders. Impetigo causes honey-colored crust, not hemorrhagic crust. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed with HSV PCR of vesicle fluid (herpes simplex virus polymerase chain reaction). A Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells but is less sensitive. Give IV acyclovir if the eruption is widespread, the patient is ill-appearing, or the patient is a young infant; ophthalmology consult if periocular.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Exam of the eyes and mouthFirstConjunctiva and oropharynx clearNot SJS or TEN, which needs mucosa at 2 or more sites
HSV PCR of vesicle fluidConfirmsHSV-1 detectedEczema herpeticum; start acyclovir before the result returns
Tzanck smearSupportsMultinucleated giant cellsHSV or varicella-zoster virus; less sensitive than PCR and does not separate them
Ophthalmology slit-lamp examBy branchDendritic corneal lesions with periocular vesiclesHSV keratoconjunctivitis, which threatens vision
Culture of nares, conjunctiva or throatBy branchS. aureus at a distant focusStaphylococcal scalded skin syndrome; the bullae themselves are sterile
Skin swab for bacterial cultureSkipS. aureus colonizes eczematous skinA positive swab does not explain failure on TMP-SMX
Scenario bank
  1. A child with atopic dermatitis and monomorphic vesicles evolving into punched-out erosions has periocular lesions. → Emergent ophthalmology (HSV keratoconjunctivitis threatens vision)
  2. Widespread, ill-appearing, poor oral intake → Admit for IV acyclovir
  3. Honey-colored crust, afebrile, no vesicles → Impetigo → mupirocin
  4. Fever + mucositis at two sites + targetoid lesions after a new drug → Stevens-Johnson syndrome → stop the drug, admit
  5. Nikolsky positive with spared mucosa in a toddler → Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome → IV anti-staph; culture the distant focus, not the skin
  6. Lesions in different stages simultaneously → Varicella
  7. Umbilicated papules in an eczematous child → Molluscum → observe
  8. Eczema + recurrent skin and lung infections + very high immunoglobulin E + retained primary teeth → Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome
  9. Child with atopic dermatitis, fever and painful monomorphic vesicles evolving into punched-out erosions with hemorrhagic crust, worsening on TMP-SMX; conjunctiva and oropharynx clear → Eczema herpeticum → systemic acyclovir immediately
Transferable rule The past medical history can contain the deciding fact. Sometimes it is a risk factor that overrides a benign reading (prior cancer → spinal mets). Sometimes it is a risk factor masquerading as an explanation (Klinefelter → gynecomastia). Sometimes it is the precondition that makes the right diagnosis possible at all. Read the past medical history as information that enables a diagnosis.
True-fact-wrong-slotTest-overrides-findings

edits.html:
Elder Abuse

reasonable suspicion is enough · findings that build suspicion · reporting pathways · capacity determines whether to reportIs the suspicion reasonable, and is the victim a competent adult or a cognitively impaired elder?

The decision point

Reasonable suspicion → report to Adult Protective Services. You do not need proof, and you do not investigate first. Confounders such as warfarin (easy bruising) and dementia (unreliable historian) are real but irrelevant to the decision to report. Adult Protective Services investigates; you do not adjudicate.

Scenario bank
  1. 82 yo F with bruises in multiple stages of healing and a vague mechanism → Report now, on suspicion alone → proof is not required, and confirming it is not the physician's job
  2. 82 yo F on warfarin with easy bruising and an implausible history → Report to Adult Protective Services → anticoagulation explains bruising, not the implausible history; suspicion alone obligates the report
  3. 82 yo F with dementia who denies abuse while her caregiver is present → Interview her alone
  4. 34 yo F disclosing intimate partner violence, fully competent, who declines reporting → Support and safety planning, respecting her autonomy
  5. 6 yo M with a spiral femur fracture and an inconsistent history → Mandatory report to child protective services
  6. 82 yo F with suspected abuse; who investigates → Adult Protective Services → the physician reports suspicion; the agency investigates
The findings that build suspicion Bruises in multiple stages of healing (the single most tested physical finding, as in child abuse) · implausible or vague mechanism · caregiver who cannot explain the injuries · patient who becomes uncomfortable and minimizes when asked alone · risk profile: dementia, dependency, caregiver stress. Interview technique: separate the patient from the caregiver, ask direct nonjudgmental questions, and do not confront the suspected abuser.
Reporting pathways
SituationPath
Elder / dependent adult abuseAPS – report on suspicion, mandated in most states
Child abuseChild Protective Services – report on suspicion, no parental consent needed
Intimate partner violence in a competent adultNOT reportable without consent in most states → safety assessment, safety plan, resources, document
Gunshot / stab wounds, certain infectionsReportable regardless
The asymmetry rule Capacity determines whether to report. Report abuse of children and cognitively impaired elders over anyone's objection. For a competent adult experiencing IPV (intimate partner violence), offer support and respect autonomy. Once abuse is suspected, never "document and re-ask at the next visit". Doing so sends a dependent patient back into the home you suspect.

edits.html:
Hemophilia

refractory bleeding on replacement: alloantibodies · the mixing study proves it · bleeding to lab pattern · arthropathyIs the partial thromboplastin time still long on adequate factor, with normal platelets and prothrombin time?

The decision point

A patient with known severe hemophilia A on factor VIII replacement has bleeding that does not respond to increased dosing. The aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) is 112 seconds, massively prolonged despite daily infusions that should be correcting it. The infused factor VIII is being neutralized by alloantibodies. This is inhibitor development, which occurs in ~25% of patients with severe hemophilia A.

An aPTT of 112 on replacement therapy means the intrinsic pathway remains uncorrected even though the missing factor is being given. Platelets of 150K and a normal PT (prothrombin time) exclude every platelet and common-pathway cause.

Defining criteria Inhibitor development – alloantibodies (IgG) against infused factor VIII; ~25% of severe hemophilia A patients · Clinical clue – bleeding refractory to adequate factor replacement therapy · Lab clue – prolonged aPTT that does not correct on a mixing study · Bethesda assay – quantifies inhibitor titer; guides treatment (low <5 Bethesda units (BU) vs high ≥5 BU)
Refractory bleeding in a hemophiliac – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded by
Inhibitor developmentKnown hemophilia on replacement; increasing bleedsRefractory bleeding + prolonged aPTT on replacement + mixing study does not correct –
Acquired von Willebrand diseaseAutoimmune, lymphoproliferative; mucocutaneous bleedingMucosal bleeding; low vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactorHemarthrosis, not mucocutaneous
Fibrinogen dysfunctionDisseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), liver failure; diffuse bleedingBoth PT and aPTT prolonged; low fibrinogenPT is normal
Heparin-induced thrombocytopeniaHeparin exposure; thrombosis + falling plateletsThrombocytopenia + thrombosis; 4T score, platelet factor 4 antibodyPlatelets 150K (normal)
Platelet dysfunctionUremia, aspirin; mucocutaneous bleedingNormal coagulation studies + prolonged PFA-100aPTT 112; hemarthrosis, not petechiae
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
PT, aPTT and platelet countFirstaPTT prolonged; PT and platelets normalIntrinsic pathway defect, not platelets or the common pathway
Mixing study, incubated at 37 CNextaPTT does not correctAn inhibitor; correction means a simple factor deficiency
Factor VIII and IX activityConfirmsLow factor VIII or IX, when the mix correctsNew diagnosis: hemophilia A or B
Bethesda assayConfirmsInhibitor titer, 5 BU or more is highHigh titer: bypassing agents; low titer: high-dose factor VIII
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the kneeBy branchSynovial thickening and cartilage damageEarly hemophilic arthropathy when radiographs are still normal
Platelet function assay (PFA-100)SkipNormal in hemophiliaJoint bleeding with a long aPTT is a factor problem, not a platelet problem
Bleeding pattern first Factor (clotting) defect – deep bleeding: hemarthroses, muscle hematomas, large ecchymoses, excess bleeding after surgery; the PT or aPTT is prolonged · Platelet defect – mucocutaneous bleeding: nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy periods, petechiae, small bruises; the count is low or aggregation is abnormal · PT – factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen; factor VII is the only one the PT measures alone · aPTT – factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen · Hemophilia by age – easy bruising in infancy; hemarthroses and deep hematomas once the toddler walks · Factor XI deficiency – the hemophilia lab pattern, but bleeding mainly with surgery or major trauma
Bleeding pattern to lab pattern
DisorderWho bleeds, and howLab pattern (platelets, PT, aPTT)Separating clue
Hemophilia A or B (factor VIII or IX)X-linked, boys; joints, deep muscle, large ecchymosesPlatelets normal, PT normal, aPTT prolonged; aggregation normalA joint or deep bleed in a boy; factor VIII and IX levels confirm
Factor VII deficiencyRare; factor-type bleedingPlatelets normal, PT prolonged, aPTT normalAn isolated long PT
Vitamin K deficiencyNewborn without vitamin K at birth, malabsorption, broad-spectrum antibioticsPlatelets normal, PT prolonged first, then aPTT tooFactor VII has the shortest half-life, so the PT lengthens first; corrects with vitamin K
DICAn ill patient (sepsis, trauma); oozing from lines, petechiae and deep bleedingPlatelets low, PT and aPTT prolonged; fibrinogen low, D-dimer highSick patient; platelets and factors consumed together
Immune thrombocytopeniaWell child; petechiae, small bruises, nose or gum bleedingPlatelets low, PT and aPTT normalIsolated thrombocytopenia
Glanzmann thrombastheniaMucocutaneous bleeding from infancyPlatelets normal, PT and aPTT normal, aggregation abnormalA qualitative platelet defect at a normal count
Von Willebrand diseaseEither sex; nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy periods; severe forms bleed like hemophiliaPlatelets normal, PT normal, aPTT normal or mildly prolongedvWF carries factor VIII, so low vWF lowers VIII; the vWF panel confirms
Factor XII deficiencyNo bleedingPlatelets normal, PT normal, aPTT markedly prolongedA long aPTT on preoperative screening in a child who has never bled
Factor XIII deficiencyUmbilical stump bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage soon after birthAll normalXIII cross-links fibrin after the clot forms, so the PT and aPTT miss it
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo M with hemophilia A on prophylactic factor VIII, 5 days of right elbow swelling despite daily infusions, aPTT 112, PT normal, platelets normal → Inhibitor development → bypassing agent for acute bleed
  2. 12 yo M with hemophilia A and a known high-titer inhibitor (35 Bethesda units), acute hemarthrosis of the knee → Recombinant activated factor VII → bypasses factor VIII in the coagulation cascade
  3. 8 yo M with hemophilia A and a newly detected low-titer inhibitor (2 Bethesda units), long-term management → Immune tolerance induction with regular high-dose factor VIII → inhibitor eradication
  4. 10 yo M with hemophilia A on replacement therapy, recent increase in bleeding episodes, aPTT prolonged → Mixing study followed by Bethesda assay → confirm and quantify inhibitor
  5. Why a mixing study fails to correct the aPTT in a patient with a factor VIII inhibitor → The inhibitor is a time- and temperature-dependent antibody that neutralizes the normal factor VIII added in the mix
  6. 60 yo F with no bleeding history, new-onset large ecchymoses, aPTT 85, PT normal, mixing study does not correct after 2-hour incubation → Acquired hemophilia A → anti-factor VIII antibody titer
  7. 15 yo M with hemophilia A and inhibitor, life-threatening intracranial hemorrhage not responding to recombinant factor VIIa → Activated prothrombin complex concentrate → second-line bypassing agent
  8. 3 yo M with immediate right knee swelling after a fall, a large hip ecchymosis last week and scattered shin bruises; hemoglobin 13, platelets 187,000, leukocytes 8,500; radiograph shows a large effusion without fracture → Coagulation studies → hemarthrosis after minor trauma suggests a factor deficiency
  9. 4 yo M with recurrent hemarthroses; prothrombin time and platelet count are normal and the activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged → Factor VIII and factor IX activity levels → separates hemophilia A from B
  10. 3 yo M with suspected severe hemophilia presenting with hemarthrosis and easy bruising → Bone marrow biopsy → contraindicated in severe hemophilia because of bleeding risk
  11. 16 yo M with past episodes of sudden knee swelling without injury and prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction, now 6 months of worsening knee pain with a boggy swelling and a knee he cannot fully extend → Hemosiderin deposition and fibrosis → hemophilic arthropathy after recurrent hemarthroses
  12. 3 yo M with severe hemophilia A and a second spontaneous knee hemarthrosis this year → Regular factor VIII prophylaxis → prevents the bleeds that build arthropathy
  13. 14 yo M with hemophilia A, repeated bleeds into the same knee and persistent swelling, with normal radiographs → MRI of the knee → shows synovial and cartilage damage before radiographs
  14. Adult with mild hemophilia A due for a dental extraction → Desmopressin → releases stored factor VIII and von Willebrand factor
  15. 15 mo M, walking since 12 months and bruising after minor bumps since then; now a swollen, tender left ankle with reduced motion after play and no fever; large ecchymoses on both thighs at recent vaccination sites; nares and oropharynx clear, no organomegaly; ankle radiograph shows no fracture → Normal platelet count, normal PT, prolonged PTT, normal platelet aggregation → Hemophilia A or B: deficiency of intrinsic factor VIII or IX
  16. 3-week-old M born at home whose parents declined newborn injections, exclusively breastfed, well-appearing and afebrile, now oozing from the circumcision site with a large scalp bruise → Normal platelet count, prolonged PT, prolonged PTT → Vitamin K deficiency bleeding: factors II, VII, IX and X are low
  17. 6-day-old M who received vitamin K at birth, bleeding from the umbilical stump; platelet count, PT and aPTT all normal → Factor XIII deficiency → XIII cross-links fibrin after the clot forms, so the PT and aPTT stay normal
  18. 5 yo M whose preoperative labs before tonsillectomy show a markedly prolonged aPTT with a normal PT and platelet count; a circumcision and a dental extraction caused no abnormal bleeding, and no relative bleeds → Factor XII deficiency → a long aPTT with no bleeding tendency
Hemophilic arthropathy Hemophilia – X-linked recessive deficiency of factor VIII (A) or factor IX (B); prolonged aPTT with normal PT and platelets; severity tracks factor activity · Hemarthrosis – spontaneous or trivial-trauma bleeding into a large joint, often a knee, with sudden severe swelling · The link – iron from the extravasated red cells is stored as hemosiderin in the synovium, which inflames it · Then – the synovium thickens and turns boggy, fibroses, and the cartilage and subchondral bone are destroyed · Result – chronic pain, swelling and loss of motion, including a joint that will not fully extend actively or passively · Imaging – radiographs show only late disease; MRI detects damage earlier · Prevention – early prophylaxis with factor concentrate lowers the risk · Treatment – factor replacement; desmopressin for mild hemophilia A · Versus juvenile idiopathic arthritis or rheumatoid arthritis – autoimmune cartilage destruction, no bleeding history · Versus disseminated gonococcal infection – acute onset, not 6 months · Versus avascular necrosis – sickle cell disease, or Legg-Calvé-Perthes at the hip between 4 and 12 · Versus Lyme arthritis – knee effusion, but no bleeding history
Pearls Mixing study – mix patient plasma 1:1 with normal plasma. Correction of the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) means factor deficiency; no correction means an inhibitor. A factor VIII inhibitor is time- and temperature-dependent (incubate at 37°C for 1–2 hours before reading) · Bethesda assay – low-titer (<5 BU) may respond to high-dose factor VIII; high-titer (≥5 BU) requires bypassing agents: rFVIIa (recombinant activated factor VII) or activated PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate) · Immune tolerance induction – repeated high-dose factor VIII to desensitize the immune system; the long-term eradication strategy · Acquired hemophilia A – the adult analogue: autoantibodies in a patient with no prior bleeding history, often autoimmune, malignancy, or postpartum · Hemarthrosis versus petechiae – hemarthrosis indicates a factor problem and petechiae a platelet problem; this division sorts most bleeding disorders before any lab is read
Pairs with Anemia with Thrombocytopenia also uses the coagulation workup. Ask: does the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) correct on mixing? Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin K deficiency. Ask: is the PT (prothrombin time) long first, and is factor V normal (vitamin K) or low (liver)?
Transferable rule Bleeding on factor replacement therapy that does not respond to dose escalation, with an aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) still prolonged despite adequate dosing, means the infused factor is being neutralized. The mixing study proves it.
Unchecked attributePlatelet dysfunction: platelets are normal, and the abnormal value is the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time), which is not a platelet test.
True-fact-wrong-slotAcquired vWD (von Willebrand disease): it can lower factor VIII but presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, not hemarthrosis. The patient already has a known factor deficiency.
Unchecked attributeFibrinogen dysfunction: the PT (prothrombin time) is normal, and a fibrinogen (common pathway) defect would prolong both the PT and the aPTT.

edits.html:
Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness

groin vs lateral vs buttock · tendon vs nerve · which nerves have motor fibers · when to imageWhere is the pain, and is there tenderness, weakness or only numbness?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Sort by location, then trust findings over descriptors:

  • Groin: the joint itself (osteoarthritis, avascular necrosis, fracture, labral tear).
  • Lateral hip: trochanter and its tendons, greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS), or the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
  • Buttock: spine, sacroiliac joint or piriformis.

Point tenderness over the trochanter with a normal neurologic exam is GTPS, however burning the pain sounds.

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory: a numb upper lateral thigh with normal strength is meralgia paresthetica, and normal strength confirms it.

Diagnosis
Defining findings GTPS – overuse tendinopathy of gluteus medius and minimus at the greater trochanter (trochanteric bursitis is a misnomer); point tenderness, normal range of motion; worse lying on that side, stairs, uphill, getting out of a car; age 50 or more, women, obesity, lower-limb or low-back disorders · Meralgia paresthetica – lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, from the L2 (second lumbar) and L3 (third lumbar) roots, compressed under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine); upper lateral thigh patch, no bony tenderness, no motor loss; tight belts, straining, obesity, pregnancy
Hip and thigh: the mimics
DiagnosisWhere and whatThe tell
Hip osteoarthritis (OA)Groin or medial, to thigh or knee; internal rotation reduced, groin pain on FABER (flexion, abduction, external rotation)Crepitus; morning stiffness under 30 minutes
Femoral neck stress fractureGroin or anterior; pain with hopping and log-rollRunner or recruit; female athlete triad: MRI
Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral headGroin; motion reduced in all planesSteroids, alcohol, sickle cell: MRI
Gluteal tendon tearLateral hip; abductor weakness, Trendelenburg gaitSevere end of GTPS: MRI
Osteoid osteomaProximal femur; often no focal finding in adultsNight pain dramatically relieved by an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug); children and young adults
Iliotibial (IT) band syndromeLateral knee at the femoral condyle; Noble testA knee diagnosis, not a hip one
L2 to L3 radiculopathyDermatomal with back pain; hip flexion weaknessFemoral stretch test positive
Femoral neuropathyAnterior thigh and medial leg; quadriceps weaknessReduced patellar reflex
Diabetic amyotrophyProximal weakness, wasting; asymmetricSevere pain and weight loss
Piriformis syndromeButtock, down the back of the thigh; worse sittingPiriformis tenderness, normal neurologic exam
Diabetic polyneuropathyStocking-glove, feet first; motor lateBilateral, symmetric; vibration lost first
Management and treatment
Management ladder: GTPS
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Activity modification, an NSAID and physical therapy (abductor strengthening)Refractory
2Corticosteroid injectionRefractory to injection: refer to investigate the underlying cause
Any tierAbductor weakness or Trendelenburg gaitMRI for a gluteal tendon tear
By diagnosis Meralgia paresthetica – weight loss, loosen restrictive belts; conservative care resolves over 90% · Metformin neuropathy – vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency over years gives a distal symmetric neuropathy, never a focal thigh patch · Peroneal palsy – foot drop after leg-crossing or rapid weight loss, at the fibular head · Other sensory-only nerves – sural (lateral foot), superficial peroneal (foot dorsum), saphenous (medial leg), digital (Morton neuroma, third interspace between the third and fourth toes, Mulder click)
Practice
  1. 54-year-old woman has 3 months of lateral hip pain she calls burning worse lying on that side and on stairs point tenderness over the bony lateral hip Hip range of motion full; neurologic exam normal Afebrile · body mass index 33 → Greater trochanteric pain syndrome → tenderness over the trochanter with a normal neurologic exam outweighs the word burning: greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS); activity modification, an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and physical therapy
  2. 58-year-old woman was diagnosed with greater trochanteric pain syndrome 2 months ago still tender over the trochanter 8 weeks of an NSAID and abductor-strengthening therapy No weakness or limp Afebrile · hip range of motion full → Corticosteroid injection → refractory to an NSAID and physical therapy: corticosteroid injection; MRI is for suspected tendon tear
  3. 66-year-old woman has 6 months of lateral hip pain weak hip abduction Trendelenburg gait Tender over the greater trochanter; worse lying on that side Afebrile · no back pain · sensation and reflexes normal · hip internal rotation full → Gluteus medius tendon tear → abductor weakness with a Trendelenburg gait is the severe end of the GTPS spectrum, a gluteus medius tendon tear: MRI; weakness separates a tear from uncomplicated GTPS, which has normal strength
  4. 67-year-old man has 2 years of groin pain pain radiates to the knee, worse after walking internal rotation reduced, with crepitus Morning stiffness under 30 minutes Afebrile · body mass index 29 · no trochanteric tenderness → Hip OA → groin pain with reduced internal rotation and crepitus is the joint itself, hip osteoarthritis: radiograph
  5. 26-year-old woman training for a marathon has groin pain pain when she hops on that leg log-roll of the leg reproduces the groin pain Hip radiograph normal; irregular periods Afebrile · body mass index 18 → Femoral neck stress fracture → groin pain on hopping in a runner with a normal film is a femoral neck stress fracture: MRI; irregular periods and low weight suggest the female athlete triad
  6. 30-year-old man, a cyclist, has lateral knee pain tender over the lateral femoral condyle Noble test reproduces it Hip examination normal; rides 200 km a week Afebrile · BP 118/70 mm Hg · no knee effusion → IT band syndrome → lateral knee pain at the femoral condyle with a positive Noble test is iliotibial (IT) band syndrome, a knee diagnosis, not a hip one
  7. 40-year-old man has numbness over the upper lateral thigh a patch that burns when he wears a tight belt no tenderness over the trochanter; no back pain Strength normal; reflexes normal Afebrile · body mass index 36 → Meralgia paresthetica → a sensory-only patch on the upper lateral thigh with normal strength is meralgia paresthetica; a radiculopathy usually brings back pain, a dermatomal pattern or weakness
  8. 16-year-old boy has 3 months of thigh pain pain wakes him at night ibuprofen relieves it dramatically No trauma; no weight loss Afebrile · radiograph: small lucency with sclerosis in the proximal femur → Osteoid osteoma → night pain dramatically relieved by NSAIDs in a young patient is an osteoid osteoma; CT (computed tomography) shows the nidus
  9. 45-year-old man on prednisone for 2 years has progressive groin pain drinks heavily range of motion reduced in all planes Hip radiograph normal; no trauma Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg · hemoglobin normal → AVN → steroids or alcohol with groin pain and a normal film is avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)
  10. 38-year-old woman has 2 months of right buttock pain pain runs down the back of the thigh worse sitting, tender deep in the buttock No back pain; straight-leg raise negative Afebrile · strength, reflexes and sensation normal → Piriformis syndrome → buttock pain sorts to the spine, sacroiliac joint or piriformis; worse sitting with piriformis tenderness and a normal neurologic exam fits piriformis syndrome
  11. 44-year-old man, obese, has burning numbness over the upper lateral thigh wears a tight work belt every day no back pain Strength 5/5 throughout Afebrile · BP 136/86 mm Hg · reflexes normal · body mass index 37 → Meralgia paresthetica → the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory, so full strength confirms meralgia paresthetica: weight loss and loosening restrictive belts
  12. 44-year-old man has numbness over the anterior thigh and medial leg weak knee extension reduced patellar reflex Began after a long procedure in the lithotomy position; no back pain Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg → Femoral neuropathy → anterior thigh and medial leg numbness with quadriceps weakness and a reduced patellar reflex is a femoral neuropathy
  13. 44-year-old man has 2 months of lateral thigh numbness back pain radiating to the knee reduced patellar reflex, weak hip flexion Femoral stretch test positive; no bladder symptoms Afebrile · BP 132/84 mm Hg → L2–L3 radiculopathy → back pain with weakness, a reduced reflex and a positive femoral stretch test is an L2 to L3 radiculopathy; meralgia has no motor or reflex loss
  14. 56-year-old woman has 2 months of lateral hip pain point tenderness over the bony lateral hip no numbness Worse lying on that side and climbing stairs Afebrile · strength normal · knee examination normal → Trochanteric bursitis → trochanteric tenderness without numbness is trochanteric bursitis, the older, misnamed label for greater trochanteric pain syndrome; the exam may still use it
  15. 60-year-old man with diabetes has severe right thigh pain proximal leg weakness and thigh wasting lost 7 kg in 2 months Asymmetric; the left leg is spared Afebrile · hemoglobin A1c 9.1% → Diabetic amyotrophy → severe asymmetric thigh pain, proximal weakness and weight loss in diabetes is diabetic amyotrophy; polyneuropathy is symmetric and starts in the feet
  16. 44-year-old man has burning numbness over the upper lateral thigh since he started wearing a tool belt strength and reflexes normal No back pain Afebrile · sensory loss in a patch on the upper lateral thigh → No testing; it is a clinical diagnosis → meralgia paresthetica is a clinical diagnosis; no imaging or electrodiagnostic testing is needed
Transferable rule

When the pain quality and the findings disagree, rely on the findings. A nerve's motor content sets what its lesion can look like: if it has no motor fibers, a normal motor exam confirms rather than refutes.

edits.html:
Male Breast Enlargement

gynecomastia vs male breast cancer · image first · Klinefelter is the risk factor, not the explanationDoes the mass behave like the known condition, or like something it only made more likely?

The decision point

A unilateral, firm, progressive, nontender subareolar mass has only features of cancer. Klinefelter syndrome is the risk factor, not the explanation. It increases male breast cancer risk 20–50× through a chronically elevated estrogen/androgen ratio. Always image first.

Gynecomastia vs male breast cancer
GynecomastiaCancer
LateralityUsually bilateralUnilateral
PositionConcentric to the nippleEccentric, off-center
TextureRubbery, mobileFirm, fixed
TendernessOften tender earlyNontender
MarginsBlends into fatWell-defined or spiculated, ± calcifications
Skin / nippleNormalDimpling, retraction, ulceration, discharge
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Diagnostic mammography, with or without ultrasoundFirstEccentric mass, spiculated or with calcificationsSuspicious for cancer: core biopsy; concentric subareolar tissue is gynecomastia
Core needle biopsyConfirmsInvasive ductal carcinoma, usually estrogen receptor (ER)-positiveMale breast cancer, even with known Klinefelter syndrome
Genetic testingCauseBRCA2 variantOffered to every man with breast cancer
Testicular exam and scrotal ultrasoundBy branchTesticular mass in a man with gynecomastiaGerm cell or Leydig cell tumor
Serum hCG and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)By branchHigh hCGhCG-secreting germ cell tumor
Hormone levels before imaging a unilateral hard massSkipKlinefelter labs do not explain the massImage and biopsy first; Klinefelter is the risk factor
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo M with a unilateral firm nontender subareolar mass and nipple retraction → Male breast cancer → mammography and biopsy
  2. 16 yo M with bilateral tender subareolar discs → Pubertal gynecomastia → reassurance
  3. 62 yo M with a breast mass and known Klinefelter syndrome → Klinefelter is the risk factor, not the explanation → biopsy anyway
  4. 55 yo M on spironolactone with bilateral tender breast enlargement → Drug-induced gynecomastia → change the agent
  5. 30 yo M with gynecomastia and a testicular mass → HCG-secreting germ cell tumor → ultrasound and tumor markers
  6. 62 yo M with soft symmetric fatty enlargement and no discrete mass → Pseudogynecomastia
Male breast cancer Risk factors: Klinefelter, BRCA2 (>BRCA1), family history, cirrhosis, obesity, chest radiation, exogenous estrogen · workup: mammography ± ultrasound → core biopsy · usually invasive ductal, >90% ER-positive → mastectomy + tamoxifen · every man with breast cancer gets genetic testing.
When it really is gynecomastia
  • Physiologic – three windows only: newborn, puberty (13–14, resolves in 1–2 yrs), elderly. Prepubertal gynecomastia is always pathologic.
  • Drugs (largest category): spironolactone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, finasteride, antipsychotics, digoxin, protease inhibitors, anabolic steroids, marijuana, alcohol
  • Cirrhosis · hyperthyroidism (↑sex hormone-binding globulin → ↓free testosterone) · chronic kidney disease · refeeding · hypogonadism
  • Tumors: hCG-secreting germ cell, Leydig/Sertoli, adrenal – gynecomastia + testicular mass → testicular ultrasound, hCG, AFP
Klinefelter 47,XXY; most common cause of primary hypogonadism and male infertility; tall with long limbs, small firm testes, sparse body hair; ↑follicle-stimulating hormone, ↑luteinizing hormone, ↓testosterone, ↑estradiol; seminiferous tubule hyalinization; also associated with mediastinal germ cell tumors, systemic lupus erythematosus, osteoporosis. Testosterone replacement does not restore fertility.
Transferable rule A known condition in the past medical history raises the prior probability but does not make the diagnosis. If the lesion behaves differently from the known disease, the known disease is the risk factor and something else is the diagnosis.
True-fact-wrong-slot

edits.html:
Oral Lesions in a Child

vesicles vs exudate · front of the mouth or back · herpangina vs herpetic gingivostomatitis · the palm and sole rashAre the lesions vesicles or exudate, and do they sit at the front of the mouth or the back?

Source vignette Pt – 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with 2 days of throat pain and poor intake; T 38.3, HR 108 · Exam – scattered 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars with gray shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula; tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared; no rash · Q – the most likely associated pathogen; options spanned adenovirus, coxsackievirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus and Streptococcus pyogenes
The decision point

The lesions are vesicles and ulcers, not exudate. This removes every bacterial and mononucleosis-type pharyngitis. Adenovirus, EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) and S. pyogenes all produce tonsillar exudate, and none produces oral vesicles. The lesions are posterior (soft palate, uvula, anterior palatine pillars), with the tongue, lips and buccal mucosa explicitly spared. Herpangina, from coxsackievirus A, affects the back of the mouth. In herpetic gingivostomatitis, lesions affect the front, with red swollen gums. The spared structures are exactly those HSV (herpes simplex virus) would involve.

Defining criteria Herpangina – coxsackievirus A; ages 3 to 10; late summer and early fall; fever and pharyngitis with gray vesicles progressing to fibrin-coated ulcers on the posterior oropharynx, and no rash; treatment is supportive · Herpetic gingivostomatitis – herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1); 6 months to 5 years; no seasonality; clusters of vesicles on the anterior oral mucosa and lips with erythematous, edematous gingiva; treated with oral acyclovir · Hand-foot-and-mouth disease – also coxsackievirus, but anterior oral lesions plus vesicles on palms and soles; herpangina's defining negative is the absent rash
Pertinent positives & negatives Vesicles and ulcers, not exudate – excludes adenovirus, EBV and group A streptococcus in one move · Soft palate, uvula and palatine pillars involved – the posterior distribution, herpangina territory · Tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared – a stated negative that excludes HSV gingivostomatitis, whose distribution is precisely those structures · No rash – separates herpangina from hand-foot-and-mouth disease · No gingival erythema or edema described – a second strike against HSV, whose gingivitis is near-universal · Age 5, starting the fall term in 2 weeks – age 3 to 10 and late summer, both epidemiological features; the school detail is dating the season, not flagging exposure · No adenopathy or splenomegaly – nothing to support mononucleosis
Oral lesions in a child – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Herpangina (coxsackievirus A)3 to 10 yrs, late summer and early fall, abrupt high feverPosterior gray vesicles becoming ulcers: soft palate, uvula, pillars; no rash – (the answer)
Herpetic gingivostomatitis (HSV-1)6 months to 5 years, any season; drooling, refuses to drinkAnterior clusters on buccal mucosa, tongue and lips; swollen red gingivaThose exact sites are stated as spared
Hand-foot-and-mouth diseaseSame virus family, same seasonAnterior oral lesions plus palms and solesThe skin has no rash
Streptococcal pharyngitisFever, sore throat, no coughTonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes, palatal petechiaeVesicles and ulcers rather than exudate
Infectious mononucleosisAdolescent with prolonged fatigueExudate plus posterior cervical nodes plus splenomegalyNo exudate, no adenopathy, no splenomegaly
Adenoviral tonsillitisFever, cough, sore throat, sometimes conjunctivitisExudate without vesiclesVesicular lesions are not its picture
Decision spine Vesicles and ulcers, or exudate? – Vesicles means a viral enanthem, and the bacterial and EBV options fall · Front of the mouth or back? – Back means herpangina · Are the gums red and swollen? – Not described, which argues against HSV · Is there a rash on palms and soles? – No, so not hand-foot-and-mouth · Age and season? – Five years in late summer corroborates · So what is the management? – Supportive; it self-resolves within a week
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with throat pain, 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars and gray shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula, tongue and lips and buccal mucosa spared, no rash → Coxsackievirus A → herpangina
  2. 2 yo with fever, drooling and refusal to drink; clusters of vesicles on the gingiva, tongue and lips with erythematous edematous gums → Herpetic gingivostomatitis → oral acyclovir
  3. 3 yo with fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles → Hand-foot-and-mouth disease → supportive care
  4. 5 yo with posterior oral vesicles and ulcers, drinking less but with moist mucous membranes and normal vital signs → Cold non-acidic fluids with analgesia → herpangina resolves within a week
  5. 8 yo with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes, without cough or oral vesicles → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → rapid antigen testing before treating
  6. 16 yo with 2 weeks of fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly → Epstein-Barr virus infection → avoid contact sports
  7. 5 yo with gray vesicles and ulcers confined to the soft palate and uvula, no rash, well hydrated → Oral acyclovir → herpangina is an enteroviral illness, not a herpesvirus one
  8. 4 yo with herpangina now refusing all fluids, with dry mucous membranes and no urine output for 10 hours → Intravenous rehydration → dehydration is the principal complication
  9. 5 yo in late summer with abrupt fever and sore throat; gray vesicles and shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and anterior pillars; gums, lips and tongue normal; no rash → Herpangina → coxsackievirus A; supportive care
Pearls Anterior is herpes, posterior is coxsackie – both diseases otherwise present with fever, sore throat and a miserable child · Vesicles and ulcers exclude exudate-producing pathogens wholesale: strep, EBV and adenovirus make exudate, not blisters · Herpangina has no rash; hand-foot-and-mouth does – same virus family, separated by the skin · Red swollen gingiva is the HSV signature, and its absence is as informative as any positive finding · Starting the fall term in two weeks is dating the season, not describing an exposure · The virus can stay in stool for weeks after infection, so hand hygiene is the public-health answer
Pairs with Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the exudative pharyngitis fork and the Centor rule; this brief covers vesicular lesions. Ask: are the lesions exudate or vesicles, and are they front or back? Part II Fever and Rash in a Child sorts hand-foot-and-mouth disease among the other rashes with fever.
Transferable rule When two diseases share a lesion type, the discriminating attribute is usually anatomical, not clinical. Ask where the lesions are before asking what they are. Treat a stated spared structure as an active exclusion, not as background.
Unchecked attributeHerpes simplex virus: oral vesicles in a child retrieves HSV automatically, but HSV is anterior and those sites are explicitly spared, with no gingival swelling.
Class-vs-memberAdenovirus: a common cause of pediatric fever with sore throat, but it produces exudative tonsillitis, not vesicles or ulcers.
Class-vs-memberStreptococcus pyogenes: exudate with tender anterior nodes; vesicles and ulcers argue against it.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus: exudate, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and adolescent age; none present.

edits.html:
Hip Injury in an Adult

fracture vs posterior dislocation by leg position · the mnemonic · the shoulder mirror · reduction within about 6 hoursIs the leg externally rotated and abducted, or internally rotated, adducted and flexed?

The decision point

Shortened + externally rotated + abducted = hip fracture (femoral neck / intertrochanteric). Shortened + internally rotated + adducted + flexed = posterior hip dislocation. It is the dashboard injury, accounts for ~90% of hip dislocations, and puts the sciatic nerve at risk.

Mnemonic and the shoulder mirror Fracture = Falls outward (external). Posterior dislocation = Points inward (internal). The shoulder mirrors it: anterior dislocation (95%) = abducted + externally rotated; posterior dislocation (seizures, electrocution) = adducted + internally rotated. In both joints the common and rare forms are mirror images.
Scenario bank
  1. 78 yo F after a fall, leg shortened and externally rotated → Femoral neck fracture → X-ray, then arthroplasty
  2. 28 yo M after a head-on collision, leg shortened, internally rotated, adducted and flexed → Posterior hip dislocation → reduction within 6 hours
  3. 28 yo M with foot drop after a posterior hip dislocation → Sciatic nerve injury
  4. 78 yo F with a displaced femoral neck fracture → Arthroplasty → retinacular vessel disruption risks avascular necrosis (AVN)
  5. 28 yo M whose hip dislocation was reduced at 10 hours → Increased risk of femoral head osteonecrosis
  6. 70 yo M after a fall, leg shortened and externally rotated but abducted, groin pain → Intertrochanteric fracture
Time-critical Posterior dislocation needs reduction within ~6 hours to avoid femoral head AVN (avascular necrosis). In the elderly, femoral neck fracture carries AVN risk from retinacular vessel disruption; treat it with arthroplasty.

edits.html:
Hypercalcemia

parathyroid hormone first in every case · calcium and phosphorus patterns · normal labs that rule out alternativesIs the parathyroid hormone high or suppressed, and which way is the phosphorus going?

The decision point

Calcium high + phosphorus low = PTH-driven until proven otherwise. The first step in any confirmed hypercalcemia is PTH (parathyroid hormone), because it splits the entire differential before anything else is ordered.

  • PTH high or inappropriately normal → primary hyperparathyroidism (most likely) or familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (separate with urine calcium)
  • PTH suppressed → then hunt: malignancy (PTHrP, bone mets), vitamin D excess or granulomatous disease, milk-alkali, thiazides, hyperthyroidism, immobilization
Calcium and phosphorus patterns Ca↑ / Phos↓ = PTH (parathyroid hormone) or PTHrP (parathyroid hormone-related protein) · Ca↑ / Phos↑ = vitamin D–mediated · Ca↓ / Phos↑ = renal failure or hypoparathyroidism · Ca↓ / Phos↓ = vitamin D deficiency. Symptoms: "stones, bones, groans, thrones, psychiatric overtones." In hypercalcemia, polyuria with a dilute urine is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Serum calcium with albumin and phosphorusScreenCalcium high, albumin normalTrue hypercalcemia; no correction needed
PTHFirstPTH high or inappropriately normalPTH-dependent: primary hyperparathyroidism or familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH)
PTH suppressedPTH-independent: PTHrP and vitamin D levels next
24-hour urine calciumConfirmsCalcium/creatinine clearance ratio under 0.01FHH, no surgery; a higher ratio fits primary hyperparathyroidism
PTHrPBy branchPTHrP highMalignancy: imaging next
25-OH and 1,25-OH vitamin DBy branch1,25-OH vitamin D highGranulomatous disease or lymphoma; high 25-OH means vitamin D excess
Sestamibi scan to make the diagnosisSkipA negative scan does not exclude itDiagnosis is biochemical; imaging only localizes before surgery
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo F with calcium 11.6 and phosphorus 2.1, found incidentally → Check PTH first
  2. 58 yo F with calcium 11.6 and an elevated PTH → Primary hyperparathyroidism
  3. 58 yo F with calcium 13.4, suppressed PTH and weight loss → Malignancy → PTHrP and imaging
  4. 24 yo M with lifelong mild hypercalcemia, normal PTH and a urine calcium-creatinine clearance ratio under 0.01 → Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia → no surgery
  5. 58 yo F with hypercalcemia, suppressed PTH, high 1,25-OH vitamin D and hilar adenopathy → Granulomatous disease
  6. 58 yo F with calcium 14.5, confusion and dehydration → Isotonic saline first, then calcitonin and a bisphosphonate
Normal labs that rule out alternatives A normal albumin means the calcium is truly elevated, with no correction needed · a specific gravity of 1.005 rules out diabetes mellitus, because glucosuria raises the specific gravity · low phosphorus argues against vitamin D excess, which raises both calcium and phosphorus · enalapril rather than a thiazide removes the drug confounder.
Pairs with Part I Polyuria covers the polyuria hypercalcemia causes. It results from an acquired, reversible resistance to vasopressin at the collecting duct, which corrects when the calcium does. Ask: does the kidney concentrate after desmopressin?

edits.html:
Hypoxemia

five mechanisms · A-a gradient · response to oxygen · shunt vs ventilation-perfusion mismatch · saturation gapIs the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia correct when inspired oxygen rises?

Source vignette Pt – 28 wk preterm, 1 hour old, cyanosis with grunting and increased work of breathing, bilaterally decreased breath sounds · Q – the mechanism of the hypoxemia; options spanned five mechanisms – intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypoventilation, diffusion limitation and low inspired oxygen
The decision point

Grunting with bilaterally decreased breath sounds at one hour of life in a 28-weeker indicates diffuse alveolar collapse. Surfactant deficiency raises alveolar surface tension, and the alveoli close. Those units stay perfused while their ventilation falls to zero, so blood crossing them reaches the left heart unoxygenated. This is intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt. Of the five mechanisms listed, it is the only one that produces cyanosis with increased work of breathing and bilaterally reduced air entry.

Defining criteria A-a gradient – alveolar minus arterial PO2 (partial pressure of oxygen). Widened in shunt, V/Q mismatch, and diffusion limitation; normal in hypoventilation and in low inspired PO2. Normal value approximately (age/4) + 4 · Shunt vs V/Q mismatch – shunt is the limiting case of mismatch (V/Q = 0). The gate is the oxygen response: mismatch corrects with modest supplemental oxygen; true shunt barely moves, because blood bypassing ventilated alveoli never sees the higher FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) · Saturation gap – pulse oximetry (SpO2) far below what the measured PaO2 (arterial partial pressure of oxygen) predicts → the hemoglobin is the problem (methemoglobin levels near 30% to 35% give a reading of about 85%, and the reading often stays low even on supplemental oxygen; carboxyhemoglobin is read as oxygenated, so the pulse oximeter is falsely reassuring)
Pertinent positives & negatives Grunting with bilaterally decreased breath sounds – auto-PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) against closed alveoli; locates the lesion in the parenchyma and excludes both cardiac shunt and central hypoventilation · Increased work of breathing at 1 hour – excludes apnea of prematurity, which appears days later with apnea and bradycardia and no respiratory effort · No murmur, regular rhythm – does not by itself exclude cyanotic heart disease, but with loud parenchymal findings it makes an intracardiac cause the second explanation, not the first · Normal CBC (complete blood count) – no anemia to lower content, no leukocytosis. The sepsis workup already running does not explain the hypoxemia; the CBC is typically normal in RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) · Still hypoxemic on 30% oxygen by CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) – the shunt fraction is large enough that a modest FiO2 cannot overcome it; recruit alveoli rather than raise the oxygen concentration
Hypoxemia: sorting by A-a gradient and oxygen response
MechanismIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt (V/Q = 0)Alveoli perfused but unventilated: RDS, lobar atelectasis/mucus plug, pneumonia, ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome), pulmonary edemaWidened A-a, hypoxemia refractory to raising FiO2, corrected by recruitment (CPAP, PEEP, surfactant)(the answer)
V/Q mismatch (low but non-zero)Asthma, COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), early pneumonia, atelectasis in evolutionWidened A-a that corrects on a few liters of oxygen; the commonest mechanism in adult medicineThe question keys the extreme: collapsed alveoli with zero ventilation
Right-to-left shunt outside the lungCyanotic CHD (congenital heart disease); hepatopulmonary syndrome; PFO (patent foramen ovale) opened by high right-sided pressuresNo rise in PaO2 on 100% oxygen; lungs clear, work of breathing normal or minimalGrunting and bilaterally decreased breath sounds: the lungs are abnormal
Dead space (ventilated, not perfused)Pulmonary embolism, low cardiac outputSudden dyspnea with a clear chest; hypercapnia is the primary consequenceBilateral decreased breath sounds; PE (pulmonary embolism) is vanishingly rare in young children
Normal-A-a hypoxemia: hypoventilation or low inspired PO2Opioids, neuromuscular disease, obesity hypoventilation, apnea of prematurity · altitude, hypoxic gas mixtureNormal A-a gradient; hypoventilation adds a high PaCO2 (arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide), altitude does not; both fully correct with a little oxygenTachypnea and grunting: effort is increased, not depressed; he is already receiving 30% oxygen
Abnormal hemoglobin affinity or carryingCO (carbon monoxide) poisoning, methemoglobinemia, fetal hemoglobinNormal PaO2 with cyanosis or a saturation gap; cyanosis unmoved by oxygenNormal Hb (hemoglobin), no exposure; fetal hemoglobin's left shift is physiologic and does not cause distress
Management, in one line Diffusion limitation is a seventh category and has no row in the table. It is a chronic, exertional finding (interstitial disease, emphysema) with a low DLCO (diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide). The resting saturation is often normal. The typical patient desaturates only on the walk down the hall. Shunt from collapsed alveoli is treated by reopening them with surfactant plus CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure), not by turning the oxygen up.
Decision spine Is the PaO2 low, or only the saturation? – Saturation-only → hemoglobin problem (carbon monoxide, methemoglobin) · Is the A-a gradient normal? – Normal → hypoventilation (high PaCO2) or low inspired PO2 (normal PaCO2) · Widened: what happens on oxygen? – Corrects → V/Q mismatch. Refractory → shunt · Shunt: are the lungs abnormal? – Grunting, decreased breath sounds, infiltrate → intrapulmonary. Clear lungs, no distress → intracardiac or intravascular · Any reason to think dead space? – Sudden onset, clear chest, risk factors; without them, embolus is unlikely
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to

Co-oximetryConfirmsMethemoglobin or carboxyhemoglobin raisedMethemoglobinemia or carbon monoxide poisoning
A-a gradient from the blood gasNextNormal gradientHypoventilation if PaCO2 high; low inspired PO2 if PaCO2 low
Response to supplemental oxygenBy branchWidened gradient that corrects on modest oxygenV/Q mismatch; little change means shunt
Chest X-rayBy branchClear lungs with oxygen-refractory hypoxemiaIntracardiac shunt or embolism: echocardiogram or CT (computed tomography) angiography
DLCO with a walk testBy branchLow DLCO, desaturation only on exertionDiffusion limitation: interstitial disease or emphysema
Pulse oximetry alone in suspected CO poisoningSkipReads falsely normalCarboxyhemoglobin is counted as oxygenated; get co-oximetry
Scenario bank
  1. 27 wk preterm M, 3 h old, grunting, ground-glass film with air bronchograms, SpO2 85% on CPAP FiO2 0.6 and rising → Intubate and give intratracheal surfactant → Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
  2. 24 yo M, postoperative day (POD) 1, RR 6, pinpoint pupils, PaO2 55, PaCO2 68, normal A-a gradient → Naloxone → Opioid-induced hypoventilation
  3. 4 mo F, cyanosis after topical teething gel, chocolate-brown blood, SpO2 fixed at 85% on 100% oxygen, PaO2 96 → Methylene blue IV → Methemoglobinemia
  4. 34 yo F and two housemates with headache and nausea after a furnace failure, COHb (carboxyhemoglobin) 18%, no syncope, normal neurologic exam → High-flow 100% oxygen by nonrebreather → Carbon monoxide poisoning
  5. 58 yo M with ARDS, PaO2 58 on FiO2 0.8 with PEEP 8, diffuse bilateral opacities → Increase PEEP → Refractory intrapulmonary shunt
  6. 68 yo M, COPD exacerbation, baseline PaCO2 62, now receiving oxygen → Titrating oxygen to a saturation of 100% → Oxygen-induced hypercapnia
  7. 62 yo F, 8 months of exertional dyspnea, resting SpO2 96% falling to 86% with ambulation, clear lungs, normal chest film → Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide → Diffusion limitation
  8. 44 yo F, POD 5 from knee arthroplasty, sudden dyspnea, clear lungs, normal film, widened A-a gradient → CT pulmonary angiography → Pulmonary embolism
  9. 29 yo M trekker at 4,500 m, dyspnea with SpO2 84%, clear lungs, PaCO2 30, normal A-a gradient → Reduced inspired oxygen tension → Descent; acetazolamide
  10. 72 yo F, POD 2 laparotomy, febrile, SpO2 88%, absent breath sounds at the left base, film shows left lower lobe collapse → Intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt → Incentive spirometry and mobilization
Decoy note The umbilical line and the started antibiotics reflect a sepsis workup. They do not explain the hypoxemia: the CBC (complete blood count) is normal and no fever or instability is reported. Apgar 7 at both marks argues against perinatal depression, which would present as hypoventilation. The absent murmur does not exclude cyanotic heart disease on its own; the parenchymal findings do.
Pearls Normal A-a means hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen; widened and oxygen-responsive means V/Q mismatch; widened and oxygen-refractory means shunt. · Shunt is the hypoxemia that oxygen will not fix. When the FiO2 goes up and the saturation does not follow, stop titrating and start recruiting. Recruit with PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure), surfactant, drainage, or a diuretic for the edema behind it. · RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) hypoxemia is clinically responsive to oxygen administration. The reason is that partially collapsed alveoli are recruitable by the CPAP delivering that oxygen, not that shunted blood responds to FiO2. · Hypoventilation is the one hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient and a high PaCO2; low inspired PO2 is the one with a normal gradient and a low PaCO2 from the compensatory hyperventilation. · A normal or high PaO2 in a cyanotic patient means the hemoglobin cannot carry or release oxygen. Causes are methemoglobin, carbon monoxide, or cyanide (where the tissue, not the blood, is the problem). · Boundary: refractory hypoxemia with clear lungs and no cardiac history can still be an embolus. If it raises right-sided pressures enough to open a PFO (patent foramen ovale), a dead-space disease presents as a right-to-left shunt. Look for the cause of the raised pressure, not just the shunt.
Pairs with Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers the parenchymal differential by chest film (ground glass and air bronchograms versus retained fluid, meconium, or air leak). Congenital Heart Disease covers the lesions themselves. Cyanosis in the Newborn covers sorting at-rest physiology in the delivery room. This brief covers the mechanism categories above all three. Ask: is the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia respond to oxygen?
Transferable rule Treat hypoxemia as a physiology question. Compute the A-a gradient, then check what happens on supplemental oxygen. Those two answers name the mechanism before the illness is named.
True-fact-wrong-slotUnderdeveloped medullary respiratory center: Apnea of prematurity appears days later as apnea with bradycardia and no respiratory effort; this infant is grunting and tachypneic at one hour
Salient decoyObstructed pulmonary arterial blood flow: Obstruction creates dead space, not bilaterally reduced breath sounds; embolus is nearly nonexistent in neonates
True-fact-wrong-slotGreater red blood cell oxygen affinity: It is the normal neonatal state; it is physiologic and does not cause respiratory distress
Class-vs-memberIncreased intracardiac left-to-right shunting: Left-to-right recirculates already-oxygenated blood; systemic saturation is unaffected, so it cannot desaturate a newborn

edits.html:
Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis

high-risk cardiac conditions · high-risk procedures · conditions removed in 2007 · the drug if both gates openDoes the patient have both a high-risk cardiac condition and a high-risk procedure?

The decision point

Prophylaxis requires a high-risk cardiac condition AND a high-risk procedure. MVP (mitral valve prolapse) with regurgitation, bicuspid valve, rheumatic valve disease and HCM (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) all came off the list in 2007. A patient with MVP having a dental visit needs no prophylaxis.

Gate 1 – high-risk cardiac conditions (the whole list)
  • Prosthetic valve or prosthetic material used in valve repair
  • Prior infective endocarditis
  • Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease; repaired with residual defect near prosthetic material; or fully repaired with prosthetic material for the first 6 months
  • Cardiac transplant with valvulopathy
Gate 2 – high-risk procedures
  • Dental work with gingival manipulation or mucosal perforation
  • Respiratory procedures breaching mucosa; procedures on infected skin or tissue
  • Not routine gastrointestinal/genitourinary procedures – that indication died in 2007 too
Scenario bank
  1. 45 yo F with mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation, due for a dental cleaning → No prophylaxis
  2. 45 yo M with a prosthetic aortic valve, due for a dental extraction → Amoxicillin 2 g one hour before
  3. 45 yo M with prior infective endocarditis and penicillin allergy, dental cleaning → Cephalexin, azithromycin or doxycycline
  4. 45 yo M with a prosthetic valve undergoing screening colonoscopy → No prophylaxis → GI and GU procedures are no longer covered
  5. 45 yo M with unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, due for dental work → Prophylaxis is indicated
  6. 45 yo M with a bicuspid aortic valve, due for a dental cleaning → No prophylaxis → bicuspid aortic valve was removed from the list in 2007
If both gates open Give amoxicillin 2 g PO (by mouth) 30–60 min before the procedure. If the patient is penicillin-allergic, give a macrolide or doxycycline. If the patient cannot take oral drugs, give IV (intravenous) cefazolin or ceftriaxone. Clindamycin is out because of C. difficile risk. Its removal is the newest edit.
Transferable rule When a case details a patient-specific factor that only matters if the intervention is indicated (an allergy, a dose adjustment), verify the indication. The detail does not confirm the indication.
Trump-card inversion
