edits.html:
Antibody Deficiencies

infection pattern · B-cell count first · isotype panel · class-switch failure · what each defect predictsAre B cells present, and which isotype is preserved or elevated?

Source vignette Pt – toddler with intensive care unit (ICU)-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic membrane perforation with otorrhea, weight below the 3rd percentile · Labs – immunoglobulin M (IgM) 450, immunoglobulin G (IgG) 250, immunoglobulin A (IgA) 24; neutropenia (15% of 9,000) · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned CD40 ligand deficiency, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
The decision point

ICU-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic perforation with otorrhea, and weight below the 3rd percentile establish a primary immunodeficiency rather than ordinary toddler illness. The infection history does not show which one. The panel shows IgM 450 against IgG 250 and IgA 24. XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) requires IgM to be low, and CVID (common variable immunodeficiency) requires it to be low or normal. Selective IgA deficiency and Job syndrome require a normal IgM. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) require a non-immunologic finding this child does not have: microthrombocytopenia and an inverted CD4/CD8, respectively. An isolated elevation of IgM with everything downstream absent is class-switch failure. CD40 ligand on the T cell cannot engage CD40 on the B cell, so the B cell stays locked on its native isotype. The neutropenia (15% of 9,000) is a confirmatory detail: it accompanies CD40 ligand deficiency and does not belong to XLA or CVID.

Defining criteria Class switching (isotype switch recombination) – the CD40L(T cell)–CD40(B cell) interaction that lets an IgM-committed B cell rearrange to IgG, IgA, or immunoglobulin E (IgE); when it fails, IgM is preserved or elevated and every other isotype falls · The CD40L signature – B cells normal, IgM ↑, IgG ↓, IgA ↓, IgE ↓. B and T cell counts are normal; they are dysfunctional, not absent · The B-cell count is the first gate – low or absent CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia; normal B cells → the block is downstream of B-cell development, and the isotype pattern names it
Pertinent positives & negatives IgM 450 with IgG 250 and IgA 24 – class-switch failure; simultaneously excludes XLA (all isotypes low) and CVID (IgM low or normal, never elevated) and selective IgA deficiency (requires normal IgG and IgM) · Neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count, ANC ≈1,350) – common in CD40L deficiency; not a feature of XLA or CVID · Lymphocytes 75%, CD4/CD8 2.2 – normal lymphocyte compartment; excludes HIV, where leukopenia and an inverted ratio are expected · Platelets 260,000 – excludes Wiskott-Aldrich, which requires small, low platelets · Age 14 months with disease since early infancy – argues against CVID, which surfaces in adolescents and young adults · Vaccinations up to date, yet invasive pneumococcal disease – vaccine failure from absent opsonizing IgG, not from missed doses · Lymphadenopathy – separates HIV from SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency): HIV causes generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly from chronic immune activation, while SCID has absent or tiny lymph nodes because there are no lymphocytes to populate them
Antibody deficiencies: reading the isotype panel
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficiency)X-linked recessive boy, infancy; recurrent AOM (acute otitis media)/sinusitis/pneumonia from encapsulated bacteria, plus opportunistic infection (Pneumocystis) because the T-cell–APC (antigen-presenting cell) limb is also brokenIgM high, IgG/IgA/IgE low, B cells normal, plus neutropenia(the answer)
X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemiaBoy, infections begin at 4 to 6 months as maternal IgG wanes; recurrent sinopulmonary and enteroviral diseaseB cells absent/low with ALL isotypes low; scant tonsils and lymph nodesIgM 450 (high) with a normal lymphocyte compartment
Common variable immunodeficiencyNormal early childhood, then onset at puberty or age 20 to 40; sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria → bronchiectasis; chronic lung disease including asthma and fibrosis; gastrointestinal (GI) infection (Giardia, Salmonella, Campylobacter) with low IgA, and chronic diarrhea; failure to thrive in children; atopic and autoimmune associations, granulomas, and lymphoma riskLow IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM, low vaccine titers, with a NORMAL B-cell count: B cells fail to become plasma cellsIgM 450 (high); age 14 months
Selective IgA deficiencyUsually asymptomatic; otherwise recurrent respiratory/GI (giardiasis) or urogenital infection; anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood productsIgA alone low; IgG and IgM normalIgG 250: the deficiency is not isolated
Syndromic defects with an Ig signature (Wiskott-Aldrich · Job/hyper-IgE)WAS: eczema + microthrombocytopenia + infection, X-linked. Job: cold staphylococcal abscesses, retained primary teeth, pneumatocelesThe non-immunologic finding makes the diagnosis, not the panel: small platelets; IgE markedly highPlatelets 260,000 and normal-sized; no eczema or abscess history
Secondary immune defects (HIV; protein-losing states)Opportunistic infection, thrush, diarrhea, failure to thrive; in perinatal HIV, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and a mother with an acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)-suggestive illnessHIV: inverted CD4/CD8 with leukopenia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (IgG and IgA high, IgM normal or high); protein loss: low IgGIgG 250 (low); CD4/CD8 2.2, WBC (white blood cell count) 9,000
CVID or XLA Onset – XLA: boys at 4 to 6 months as maternal IgG wanes; CVID: after a normal childhood, at puberty or age 20 to 40 · B-cell count – XLA: absent; CVID: normal, but they fail to mature into plasma cells · Immunoglobulins – XLA: all isotypes and vaccine titers absent; CVID: low IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM, low vaccine titers · Family history – XLA: affected maternal male relatives; CVID: usually none · A few toddler ear infections that cleared promptly – ordinary childhood illness, not the start of XLA
Infection pattern → immune compartmentwhich arm of immunity is broken

Viral, fungal (Candida, Pneumocystis) and bacterial infection with failure to thriveBefore 4 to 6 monthsLow lymphocytes, ± low immunoglobulinsT cell or combined: DiGeorge syndrome, SCID, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia

Recurrent Neisseria infection; systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)-like autoimmunityVariableLow CH50 (total hemolytic complement); normal leukocytes and immunoglobulinsComplement: C5–C9 (terminal) for Neisseria; C1q for SLE

SCID: the newborn screen and the cure Defect – gene defects stop T-cell development; B cells fail without T-cell help, so antibody is low too; X-linked or autosomal recessive · Presentation – in the first months: severe viral, fungal (thrush) and opportunistic (Pneumocystis) infection, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive · Labs and exam – lymphopenia with low CD4 and CD8 counts, hypogammaglobulinemia, no palpable nodes or tonsils · Newborn screen – part of US newborn screening: absent T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) on the dried blood spot; lymphocyte flow cytometry confirms · Treatment – hematopoietic stem cell transplant as early as possible; no live vaccines · Not SCID – Bruton agammaglobulinemia has absent B cells but normal T cells and bacterial rather than fungal or opportunistic infection; CVID starts later with normal T- and B-cell counts; CGD has normal lymphocytes and immunoglobulins
Syndromic immunodeficiencies: the tell off the panel Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – WATER: Wiskott-Aldrich, Thrombocytopenia with small platelets, Eczema, Recurrent infections; X-linked; bleeding at circumcision or from the umbilical stump in early infancy; T-cell dysfunction and low immunoglobulins worsen with age; stem cell transplant · Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome – FATED: coarse Facies (broad nose, prominent forehead), cold staphylococcal Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, high IgE with eosinophilia, Dermatologic eczema; autosomal dominant; impaired Th17 signaling; skin care and antibiotic prophylaxis · Ataxia-telangiectasia – autosomal recessive defect in DNA break repair; early childhood progressive cerebellar ataxia and poorly coordinated eye and head movements, then telangiectasias of the conjunctivae and face; recurrent sinopulmonary infection; high malignancy risk; genetic testing confirms · Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with polyendocrinopathy – AIRE deficiency breaks thymic negative selection, giving a T-cell defect against Candida plus autoimmunity; chronic Candida of skin, mouth and nails with hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcemia, seizure), adrenal insufficiency, type 1 diabetes and thyroiditis
Management, in one line Management is to replace what is missing and cover what the defect exposes. Give immunoglobulin replacement in XLA, CVID and CD40 ligand deficiency; in CD40 ligand deficiency, add TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) prophylaxis against Pneumocystis. In severe antibody deficiency, avoid live vaccines such as MMR (measles, mumps and rubella); in T-cell defects, avoid all live vaccines. In selective IgA deficiency, IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) does not help, and transfusions use washed or IgA-deficient products. Allogeneic HSCT (hematopoietic stem cell transplantation) is the curative therapy for CD40 ligand deficiency.
Long-term treatment: match it to the defect CVID and XLA – lifelong IVIG: the B cells cannot make antibody, so it is supplied; infections fall, but the autoimmune and malignancy risk of CVID remains · SCID – hematopoietic stem cell transplant, as early as possible · Complete DiGeorge syndrome (no thymus) – cultured thymus tissue transplant · CGD – interferon gamma, the immunomodulator, plus TMP-SMX and itraconazole prophylaxis · Cellular (T-cell) defects – antiviral and antifungal prophylaxis · CVID, an antibody defect with normal T cells – needs antibody replacement, not a transplant or an immunomodulator, although each is right for some other defect
Decision spine Is this beyond normal childhood illness? – ICU pneumonia, perforated tympanic membranes, weight <3rd percentile → yes, work it up as primary immunodeficiency · Are B cells / lymphocytes present? – Normal → not XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) · Is IgM high, normal, or low? – High with everything else low → class-switch failure → CD40L deficiency · Is any isotype normal or high? – IgG normal with IgA alone low → selective IgA deficiency; IgE very high → Job · Is every isotype high? – IgG, IgA and IgM all high is polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The primary antibody deficiencies all lower IgG or IgA. With thrush, adenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly, test for HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) · Any finding off the panel? – Small low platelets → Wiskott-Aldrich; inverted CD4/CD8 → HIV · Now use the pattern: – which organisms and which treatment does this specific block predict?

Scenario bank
  1. 11 mo M with newly diagnosed CD40 ligand deficiency, started on monthly immunoglobulin replacement → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis → Hyper-IgM syndrome
  2. 12 mo M with X-linked agammaglobulinemia on immunoglobulin replacement, presenting for the 12-month visit → Measles-mumps-rubella vaccine → X-linked agammaglobulinemia
  3. 23 yo F, sinopulmonary infections since age 16, bronchiectasis on computed tomography, IgG/IgA/IgM all low, normal CD19+ B cells → Immunoglobulin replacement therapy → Common variable immunodeficiency
  4. 24 yo M with known selective IgA deficiency, upper GI bleed, hemoglobin 6.5, requires transfusion → Transfuse washed red blood cells → Selective IgA deficiency
  5. 9 yo M, recurrent nontender staphylococcal skin abscesses, chronic eczema, retained primary teeth, lung cyst after pneumonia, IgE 4,200 → Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome → Antistaphylococcal prophylaxis and skin care
  6. 3 yo M, eczema, recurrent otitis media, bloody diarrhea, platelets 38,000 and small on smear → Refer for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation → Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
  7. 18 mo M with hyper-IgM syndrome, 2 weeks of dry cough, hypoxemia, diffuse interstitial infiltrates, elevated lactate dehydrogenase → Pneumocystis jirovecii → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treatment
  8. 10 mo M, recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections, IgG, IgA and IgM all markedly low → Flow cytometry for CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia if B cells are absent
  9. 4 yo M with CD40 ligand deficiency on immunoglobulin replacement → Boiled or filtered drinking water → Cryptosporidium and sclerosing cholangitis
  10. 7 mo M, third otitis media, thriving, IgG mildly low with normal IgA and IgM, normal B cells, protective tetanus titers → Reassurance and repeat immunoglobulin levels → Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
  11. 7 mo M with two otitis media episodes and prior bronchiolitis, growing at the 65th percentile, facial eczema, IgG low for age with normal IgA and IgM, normal leukocytes, and elevated tetanus- and diphtheria-specific IgG → Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy → a normal vaccine response is the discriminator
  12. 7 mo M with transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy, thriving, with two otitis media episodes → Observation with repeat immunoglobulin levels → it self-resolves by early childhood
  13. 4-month-old foster child with oral thrush, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly → Perinatal HIV infection → HIV DNA PCR
  14. 3-month-old with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, absent thymic shadow on chest x-ray, absent T cells on flow cytometry → Severe combined immunodeficiency → hematopoietic stem cell transplant
  15. 6-month-old born to a mother with unknown prenatal care, recurrent oral candidiasis, bilateral otitis media, CD4 count 180 → Perinatal HIV infection → start antiretroviral therapy
  16. 12 mo M, two prior pneumonias, chronic thrush, tympanostomy tubes, 2nd percentile height and weight, now intubated; lymphocytes 5%, CD3+ absent, CD19+ low, IgG 220, HIV antibody negative → Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation → the only definitive therapy in SCID
  17. 10 mo M with newly diagnosed severe combined immunodeficiency presenting for catch-up immunizations → The live attenuated rotavirus vaccine → live vaccines can cause fatal disseminated disease
  18. 14 yo boy with severe left ear pain and a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane; a few ear infections as a toddler cleared promptly, but over the past 3 years he has had recurrent otitis media, often with sinusitis, and pneumonia last year; fully vaccinated; IgG 258 mg/dL (768 to 1,728) and IgA 28 mg/dL (99 to 396) are low, IgM 40 mg/dL (38 to 266) is low-normal; tetanus, diphtheria and pneumococcal antibody titers are low → Impaired B-cell differentiation into plasma cells → Common variable immunodeficiency; B-cell count is normal
  19. 16 yo boy, healthy through early childhood, with recurrent sinusitis and two pneumonias over the past 3 years and a recent episode of giardiasis; IgG and IgA low, IgM low-normal, CD19+ B cells normal in number, poor antibody response to tetanus and pneumococcal vaccines; no affected relatives → Common variable immunodeficiency → Immunoglobulin replacement therapy
  20. 17 yo boy admitted with his second episode of meningococcal meningitis; no history of sinopulmonary, skin or opportunistic infections; CBC with differential and serum immunoglobulins are normal → Total hemolytic complement (CH50) → Terminal complement deficiency (C5 to C9)
  21. 5 mo M with 2 days of fussiness and fever; earlier otitis media, oral candidiasis and rotavirus gastroenteritis; weight at the 3rd percentile; T 39.3; bulging red right tympanic membrane; no palpable lymph nodes and tonsils not visible; platelets 240,000; WBC 7,500 with 5% lymphocytes; IgG 210, IgA 35 and IgM 14 mg/dL, all low; CD4 80 and CD8 70 cells/µL, both low → Severe combined immunodeficiency → absent TRECs on the newborn screen; hematopoietic stem cell transplant
  22. 5 yo boy who walked on time but over the past 2 years has developed a progressively unsteady, wide-based gait and poorly coordinated eye and head movements; dilated small vessels on both bulbar conjunctivae; three pneumonias and recurrent sinusitis; platelets normal in number and size; no eczema → Ataxia-telangiectasia → DNA break repair defect; high malignancy risk
  23. 9 yo girl with oral thrush and thick, discolored fingernails since age 3 despite repeated antifungal courses, now brought in after a seizure; serum calcium 6.8 mg/dL with a low parathyroid hormone; normal facies, no heart murmur, and no skin abscesses → Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 → AIRE deficiency; watch for adrenal insufficiency and type 1 diabetes
  24. 12 yo F with 2 weeks of nasal congestion, now thick green discharge, fever today and maxillary tenderness; two prolonged sinusitis episodes this year, a recent Giardia infection and Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteremia last year; asthma since age 3; normal milestones and fully immunized; height and weight at the 5th percentile; Hb 12 g/dL, platelets 180,000, WBC 7,500 → Intravenous immunoglobulin infusion → Common variable immunodeficiency; low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM and a normal B-cell count
  25. 4 mo F with truncus arteriosus repaired as a newborn, hypocalcemic seizures, recurrent oral thrush and no thymic shadow on chest x-ray; flow cytometry shows almost no CD3+ T cells; 22q11.2 deletion confirmed → Cultured thymus tissue transplant → Complete DiGeorge syndrome: without a thymus, T cells cannot mature
  26. 2 yo girl admitted with pneumococcal bacteremia; in the past year three otitis media episodes, two bacterial pneumonias and recurrent thrush; mother has persistent oral candidiasis, chronic diarrhea and a 9-kg weight loss; weight 5th percentile, height 50th percentile; white oral plaques, 2-cm nontender axillary nodes, spleen 2 cm and liver 3 cm below the costal margins; WBC 5,000, platelets 95,000; IgG 2,200, IgA 420 and IgM 400 mg/dL, all above normal → HIV infection → Perinatally acquired; confirm with an HIV viral load, then start antiretroviral therapy
  27. 20 mo boy with recurrent otitis media, two bacterial pneumonias and chronic diarrhea; generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly; IgG, IgA and IgM all high; CD4/CD8 ratio inverted → Perinatal HIV infection → Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio
  28. 14 mo boy with Pneumocystis pneumonia after two pneumococcal pneumonias; IgM high, IgG and IgA low; normal lymphocyte count and CD4/CD8 ratio → CD40 ligand deficiency → Class-switch failure; low IgG and a normal CD4/CD8 ratio separate it from HIV
Decoy note Lymphocytes at 75% look alarming but are expected. Lymphocytosis accompanies active infection. It also confirms that lymphocyte numbers are intact, which excludes XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia). The three bronchiolitis episodes read as ordinary infant viral illness but support CD40 ligand deficiency, which impairs viral defense as well as opsonization. Up-to-date vaccination converts the pneumococcal ICU admission into vaccine failure, an immunodeficiency finding rather than a gap in care.
Pearls High IgM with low IgG/IgA is class-switch failure. Absent B cells is XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia). Low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM and B cells present is CVID (common variable immunodeficiency). · Read the panel in a fixed order: B cells, then IgM, then IgG/IgA/IgE. · The missing isotype predicts the organism. No opsonizing IgG → encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae). A broken CD40 ligand–CD40 axis also breaks T-cell licensing of macrophages → Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium. · Neutropenia alongside hypogammaglobulinemia points at CD40L deficiency rather than XLA. · Selective IgA deficiency is the defect whose management is what you withhold: no IVIG, and washed or IgA-deficient blood products for transfusion. · A severe antibody deficiency contraindicates live vaccines such as MMR, and a defective T-cell limb contraindicates all of them; and replacement IgG likely interferes with later vaccine-titer testing. · A mildly low IgG at 6–9 months in a thriving infant with normal IgM, normal B cells, and protective vaccine titers is transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy: recheck levels, and treatment is conservative. · How NBME framed it: the lead-in asks for a mechanism but lists diseases, and the mother's thrush, chronic diarrhea and weight loss hold the deciding clue.
The physiologic IgG nadir The nadir – maternally derived IgG wanes after birth and troughs at 3 to 6 months, when the infant's own synthesis takes over · Transient hypogammaglobulinemia – that synthesis is delayed and the nadir is prolonged beyond 6 months, with recurrent respiratory infection and atopy · Vaccine response is the most discriminating line on the panel – a normal response excludes common variable immunodeficiency and X-linked agammaglobulinemia at once, whatever the isotype levels say
Pairs with Part I Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease shares the complaint of recurrent otitis media and pneumonia in a child. Ask: does the immunoglobulin panel explain it, or does the anatomy? When the panel is normal, that brief covers the structural and mucociliary axis; when an isotype is out of step, this one does. Part I Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function covers the phagocyte defects: chronic granulomatous disease, leukocyte adhesion deficiency and Chédiak-Higashi. Ask: are the immunoglobulins normal, and is there pus? Part I 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome covers the thymic T-cell defect with hypocalcemia (CATCH-22); ask: is there a conotruncal heart lesion? Part II Infectious Diarrhea follows a patient with common variable immunodeficiency on immunoglobulin replacement who develops Salmonella gastroenteritis. Ask: does the organism point to the immune defect, or to the food it came from?
Transferable rule With recurrent sinopulmonary infection and an immunoglobulin panel, read the pattern rather than recall a disease. Count the B cells, then ask which isotype is preserved. The preserved isotype names the block, and the missing isotypes name the organisms you must cover.
Unchecked attributeWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: eczema plus recurrent infection fits its pattern, but it requires small, low platelets. A normal count excludes it, and atopy is itself a feature of transient hypogammaglobulinemia.
Class-vs-memberBruton agammaglobulinemia: That member of the class requires absent B cells and low IgM; IgM is 450 and the lymphocyte compartment is intact
True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency: CVID leaves IgM low or normal but never high, and presents in adolescence or later, not at 14 months
Salient decoyHIV infection: HIV would show leukopenia and a low CD4/CD8 ratio; here the ratio is 2.2 and WBC 9,000. HIV raises IgG in a polyclonal rise, while this panel has IgG 250.
True-fact-wrong-slotIgA deficiency: Isolated IgA deficiency requires normal IgG and IgM; IgG 250 makes the deficiency global-with-a-block, not selective
Class-vs-memberWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: The syndromic member is defined by microthrombocytopenia; platelets are 260,000 and normal-sized, and there is no eczema
Class-vs-memberSevere combined immunodeficiency: It presents in early infancy with lymphopenia, low immunoglobulins and no palpable nodes. A 2-year-old with every isotype high and 2-cm axillary nodes does not fit.
Unchecked attributeWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: Platelets of 95,000 are the lure. It classically has eczema and small platelets, and it is X-linked, while this patient with every isotype high is a girl.
True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency: It lowers IgG along with IgA and/or IgM, and it usually starts after puberty. Here every isotype is high at age 2.
True-fact-wrong-slotChronic granulomatous disease: It causes catalase-positive abscesses and granulomas with an abnormal DHR (dihydrorhodamine) test. Immunoglobulins are normal or high in it, so this panel does not exclude it; the thrush, the adenopathy and the mother's illness point to HIV.
Unchecked attributeChédiak-Higashi syndrome: It needs oculocutaneous albinism and neuropathy, and neither is described in the girl with every isotype high.
True-fact-wrong-slotTerminal complement deficiency: It causes recurrent Neisseria infection, not pneumococcal disease with thrush and every isotype high.
Salient decoyCystic fibrosis: Recurrent pneumonia and low weight fit. It causes lung and pancreatic disease, without thrush, adenopathy or a mother with an AIDS-suggestive illness.

edits.html:
Stool Changes in a Well Infant

dyschezia, allergic proctocolitis, secondary lactase deficiency · ill-appearing mimics · reassure, eliminate, or work upIs the infant well and thriving, and what do the stool and its timing after the trigger show?

Source vignette Pt – 4 mo M, thriving, screams and strains for 10 minutes several times daily then passes a soft yellow stool, normal examination · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned reassurance and parental education, a glycerin suppository and switching to an extensively hydrolyzed formula
The decision point

Three benign stool complaints occur in a thriving, well-appearing infant or child whose parents are worried. Straining and screaming for minutes, followed by a normal soft stool in an infant under 9 months, is infant dyschezia → reassurance only. Painless blood-streaked stools in a well infant under 6 months are food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis. Treat it by removing cow's milk and soy from the maternal diet, or by using an extensively hydrolyzed formula. Watery diarrhea and bloating after dairy is reintroduced following gastroenteritis are secondary lactase deficiency → temporary lactose avoidance, with no workup.

Two mimics present with an ill-appearing infant. FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome) causes profuse vomiting and lethargy 1–4 h after the trigger; it is not immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated and needs fluids. IgE-mediated allergy causes urticaria, wheeze or anaphylaxis within minutes and needs epinephrine. Reassure the parents; a thriving infant needs no formula change, suppository or stool workup.

Defining criteria Infant dyschezia – under 9 months, strains and cries for minutes, then passes a normal soft stool, thriving; hard stool means constipation instead · Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis – well-appearing infant under 6 months, painless blood-streaked stools, insidious onset; non-IgE · Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome – under 12 months, profuse vomiting with diarrhea, dehydration and lethargy within hours (1–4 h) of the trigger, ill-appearing; non-IgE · IgE-mediated food allergy – urticaria, vomiting, wheeze, angioedema or hypotension within minutes (under 1 h), any age · Osmotic diarrhea – stops with fasting, raised stool osmotic gap, acidic stool pH
The well-appearing infant with a stool complaint – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Infant dyscheziaUnder 9 months; cannot coordinate a Valsalva with pelvic-floor relaxation; resolves spontaneouslyScreams and strains, then a normal soft stool; reassurance, nothing else
Functional constipationInfrequent, hard or pellet stools, often at a diet transitionHard stool – the one word that converts dyschezia into constipation
Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis (FPIAP)Under 6 months, breastfed or formula-fed; cow's milk or soy protein; resolves by about 1 yearPainless blood streaks in a well infant; eliminate cow's milk and soy, no scope
FPIESUnder 12 months; non-IgE; classic triggers include cow's milk and soyProfuse vomiting, lethargy, dehydration 1–4 h after feeding, ill-appearing; fluids, not epinephrine
IgE-mediated food allergyAny age; minutes after exposure; may progress to anaphylaxisUrticaria or wheeze within an hour; epinephrine, strict avoidance, allergist
Secondary lactase deficiencyBrush-border lactase lost after gastroenteritis or with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD); osmotic diarrheaDiarrhea and bloating when dairy is reintroduced after a resolving gastroenteritis; no fever, no vomiting
Necrotizing enterocolitis Can't miss PreemiePreterm infant on enteral feeds; bacterial invasion of an ischemic bowel wallDistension, bloody stools, pneumatosis intestinalis in a preemie – never a well-infant diagnosis
Scenario bank
  1. 4 mo M, thriving, screams and strains for 10 minutes several times a day, then passes a soft yellow stool, normal exam → Reassurance and parental education → infant dyschezia resolves by about 9 months
  2. 5 mo F, passed meconium on day 1, now hard pellet stools every 3 days with straining since starting solids, thriving → Functional constipation → dietary change, then an osmotic laxative
  3. 6 wk F, exclusively breastfed, thriving, blood-streaked soft stools for a week, comfortable and well → Eliminate cow's milk and soy from the maternal diet → food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis
  4. 3 mo M on cow's milk formula, well-appearing, gaining weight, blood streaks and mucus in soft stools → Extensively hydrolyzed formula → soy cross-reacts, so it is not the substitute
  5. 2 mo F, breastfed, with food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis; the recommendation to avoid → Stop breastfeeding and start a soy-based formula → soy protein triggers the same reaction and breastfeeding need not stop
  6. 7 mo M, 2 hours after his first cow's-milk formula, repetitive profuse vomiting, pale, limp and lethargic, no urticaria or wheeze → Intravenous fluid resuscitation → food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome is non-IgE, so epinephrine does nothing
  7. 9 mo F, hives and wheezing within 15 minutes of her first scrambled egg → Intramuscular epinephrine → IgE-mediated food allergy, strict avoidance and allergist referral
  8. 6 yo M, viral gastroenteritis 10 days ago that was improving, now watery diarrhea and bloating since milk was reintroduced, afebrile, no vomiting → Temporary lactose avoidance, then reintroduce → secondary lactase deficiency needs no workup
  9. 5 yo F, diarrhea after a resolving gastroenteritis that stops when she fasts, acidic stool pH, raised stool osmotic gap → Transient loss of brush-border lactase → colonic bacteria ferment the unabsorbed lactose
  10. 5-day-old born at 32 weeks, bilious and coffee-grounds emesis, distended tender abdomen, pneumatosis intestinalis on abdominal x-ray → Blood cultures and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics with bowel rest → necrotizing enterocolitis
Exceptions Reassurance or trigger elimination before testing applies only to an infant who is well-appearing and thriving. Lethargy, dehydration, or profuse vomiting is FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome). Urticaria or wheeze is IgE-mediated allergy. A preterm infant with distension and bloody stools has necrotizing enterocolitis. A child with fever, vomiting, or weight loss after gastroenteritis does not fit secondary lactase deficiency and needs a workup. Formula changes, rectal stimulation, and laxatives are wrong for dyschezia; a laxative is right only when the stool is hard.
Pearls Dyschezia is a coordination failure: raised intra-abdominal pressure without pelvic-floor relaxation, and inadequate abdominal tone for an effective Valsalva · FPIAP (food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis) is non-IgE and self-limited. The mother eliminates both cow's milk and soy, and FPIAP resolves by about 1 year · FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome) is also non-IgE but ill-appearing: onset hours after the trigger, no urticaria, treated with fluids · Only IgE-mediated disease gets epinephrine · Secondary lactase deficiency is osmotic (stops with fasting, acidic stool, no fever); IBD (inflammatory bowel disease) also causes brush-border loss
Pairs with Part II Feeding an Infant or Toddler covers the age for starting cow's milk; this brief covers the stool effects of cow's-milk protein before that age. Part I Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant has the necrotizing enterocolitis item: bloody stool in an ill preemie is not proctocolitis. Ask: is the infant well-appearing, and is the stool soft? Part I Constipation in a Child covers the same complaint in toddlers, where the withholding cycle, not milk protein, is the cause.
Transferable rule In a thriving child with worried parents, base management on the stool, the timing after the trigger, and the child's appearance. Reassure or eliminate the trigger before testing.
Uniform-answer doubtReassurance feels like doing nothing, but for dyschezia every active option is a named wrong answer.
Class-vs-memberSoy formula removes cow's milk, but soy protein cross-reacts.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpinephrine treats IgE-mediated food allergy; FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome) vomiting hours later is non-IgE and needs fluids.
Sequencing trapA stool workup is the tier above dietary change in a well child whose diarrhea followed dairy.

edits.html:
Kawasaki Disease

CRASH and Burn criteria · incomplete disease · intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and aspirin within 10 days · echocardiogram · coronary complicationsHas fever lasted 5 days with 4 criteria, and is the child still inside the 10-day window?

ScriptStem cuesDiagnosisManagementPreventionComplicationsPractice
Bottom line

Diagnosis is clinical: fever for 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 CRASH criteria. IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) must be given within 10 days of fever onset, with aspirin, and an echocardiogram is obtained at diagnosis. Treat now; do not delay it for a workup. Sterile pyuria is a feature of Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease causes urethritis, giving urinary white blood cells with no bacteria.

Exception: with only 2 or 3 criteria (incomplete disease, especially in infants under 6 months), use CRP (C-reactive protein) and ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), supplemental labs and echocardiography, and treat if they are supportive.

Illness script
Kawasaki disease
What it isMedium-vessel vasculitis that targets the coronary arteries
DriverImmune-mediated arteritis; the cause is unknown
TriggersNone proven; age under 5 and Asian ancestry, especially Japanese, raise risk (non-modifiable)
WhoYoung children; infants under 6 months have the most atypical presentations
LooksFever for 5 days or more with the CRASH findings; irritable
LabsAnemia, low albumin, high ALT (alanine aminotransferase), sterile pyuria; platelets high after day 7
CourseUntreated, coronary aneurysm risk is ~20–25%; IVIG within 10 days lowers it to ~3–5%
Chain: Kawasaki disease

Vasculitis

→ an immune response inflames medium-sized arteries

→ the coronary arteries are the main target

Structural

→ the inflamed coronary wall dilates into an aneurysm

→ the aneurysm can expand, rupture or clot

Clinical

→ myocardial ischemia or infarction

→ heart failure: fast breathing, fast pulse, low blood pressure, big heart

How it hides in a stem
History and examination: what each clue points to
ClueWhat it points to
Fever for 5 days or moreBurn: the gate; then count the criteria
"Pink eye"Nonexudative conjunctivitis: a criterion; pus points to adenovirus
Strawberry tongue, cracked red lipsOral criterion; ulcers point to Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Red swollen hands; later, peeling at the nailsExtremity criterion; the peeling comes in week 2 to 3
A single neck node 1.5 cm or largerAdenopathy, the least common criterion
Past high fever, red eyes, swollen red hands, big nodes, cracked lipsAn earlier Kawasaki illness: fever plus 4 criteria
That illness cleared on its own within 14 daysUntreated: no IVIG, so the coronary risk remained
The illness was 2 months beforeTime for aneurysms to cause heart failure ⚠︎ (role inferred)
A boy of 18 monthsThe usual age: most cases are under 5 ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Brought to the emergency department; 2 days of increasingly rapid breathing, irritableAn acute presentation; the symptom asked about: heart or lung? ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Now in obvious discomfortAn ill child; fits low cardiac output ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Vital signs, tests and pertinent negatives: what each clue points to
ClueWhat it points to
Temperature 38 C (100.4 F) two months laterLow grade: an ill child, not a new Kawasaki fever ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Pulse 150/min, respirations 60/minTachycardia, tachypnea: heart failure; tamponade shares them ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Blood pressure 60/40 mm HgHypotension: low output; tamponade also lowers it ⚠︎ (role inferred)
No other abnormal finding on examinationNo murmur: argues against mitral obstruction; no jugular distension or pulsus paradoxus argues against tamponade
Cardiomegaly on the chest x-rayA big heart; interstitial lung disease would show fibrosis
ST-segment depression in leads II and IIIIschemia from coronary disease ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Left ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviationVentricular strain in a failing heart ⚠︎ (role inferred)
White cells in the urine, no bacteriaSterile pyuria: part of Kawasaki disease, not a UTI (urinary tract infection)
Weeks after COVID-19, vomiting, low blood pressureMIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children), not Kawasaki disease
Diagnosis
Diagnostic criteria Kawasaki disease – fever for 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 CRASH criteria · Incomplete disease – fever for 5 days or more with only 2–3 criteria · Evaluate for incomplete disease – an infant 6 months or younger with fever for 7 days or more and no other explanation · IVIG resistance – fever persisting 36 h after IVIG
CRASH and Burn
  • Conjunctivitis – bilateral, nonexudative, limbal sparing
  • Rash – polymorphous, perineal accentuation with desquamation
  • Adenopathy – cervical ≥1.5 cm, usually unilateral (the least common criterion)
  • Strawberry tongue / cracked red lips – no ulcers, no exudate
  • Hands and feet – erythema and edema acutely, periungual desquamation in week 2–3
  • Burn – fever ≥5 days
First tests
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CRP and ESRFirstElevatedSupports Kawasaki
EchocardiogramFirstCoronary dilation or aneurysmBaseline at diagnosis; in suspected incomplete disease, coronary changes justify IVIG
CBC (complete blood count), albumin, ALT and urinalysisBy branchAnemia, low albumin, high ALT, sterile pyuria; platelets high after day 7Supportive labs for incomplete Kawasaki; in incomplete disease, a raised CRP or ESR triggers supplemental labs and echo
Rapid strep testBy branchPositive, with sandpaper rash and no conjunctivitisScarlet fever: penicillin
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsFever 5 days or more plus 4 of 5 criteriaTests support and stage it; IVIG within 10 days is not delayed for them
Urine culture for the pyuriaSkipSterile pyuria is part of KawasakiUrethritis from the disease; do not hold IVIG for a UTI workup
Kawasaki mimics and their discriminators
DiagnosisThe stem showsDecides itConfirms
AdenovirusFever, red eyes, sore throatExudative conjunctivitis and pharyngitis; Kawasaki's is nonexudativeViral testing of a throat or eye swab
Scarlet feverFever, strawberry tongue, responds to penicillinSandpaper rash, Pastia lines, no conjunctivitisRapid strep test; throat culture if negative
MeaslesCough/coryza, unvaccinatedKoplik spots, cephalocaudal rashMeasles antibody serology or viral testing
MIS-CPost-COVID, older children, prominent GI symptomsShockClinical criteria plus a positive COVID-19 test or antibodies
Toxic shock syndromeFever, rash, desquamation laterHypotension + multiorgan failureClinical criteria; negative cultures
Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysisTarget lesions, drug exposureMucosal erosions and ulcersClinical; skin biopsy
Staphylococcal scalded skinPerioral crustingNikolsky positiveClinical
Management and treatment
Management ladder
TierInterventionEscalate when
Diagnosis madeIVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin, within 10 days of fever onsetFever persisting 36 h after IVIG
Seen after day 10IVIG if unexplained fever or coronary changes persist with a raised CRP or ESRFever persisting 36 h after IVIG
IVIG resistanceSecond IVIG dose; steroids or infliximab as alternativesTop rung

Step down: high-dose aspirin acutely, then low-dose once afebrile for 48 to 72 hours (practice varies). Kawasaki is the exception to the rule against aspirin in children.

Follow-up and return precautions Echocardiogram – at diagnosis, then 1 to 2 weeks and 4 to 6 weeks after treatment in uncomplicated disease ⚠︎ (a 2024 guideline update may shorten the first recheck; unverified) · Return – fast breathing or irritability weeks later needs an ECG (electrocardiogram) and echocardiogram
Distractors
Salient decoyUrine culture and antibiotics: pyuria looks like a UTI; it is sterile and part of the disease.
Sequencing trapWaiting for a fourth criterion: coronary changes on the echocardiogram already justify IVIG.
Unchecked attributeNo IVIG after day 10: the 10-day mark is a target, not a cutoff; with persistent unexplained fever or coronary changes and a raised CRP or ESR, IVIG is still reasonable.
True-fact-wrong-slotAvoiding aspirin in a child: the Reye rule is real, but Kawasaki is the exception.
Prevention and screening
  • No vaccine or drug prevents Kawasaki disease; IVIG within 10 days prevents most aneurysms.
  • Live vaccines: MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) and varicella must be deferred 11 months after IVIG.
Complications and long-term sequelae
  • Coronary aneurysm: can expand, rupture or cause a myocardial infarction; infants under 6 months have the highest aneurysm risk.
  • Heart failure: tachypnea, tachycardia, hypotension, cardiomegaly and ischemic ST depression.
  • Pericardial effusion: a real complication; tamponade adds raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus.
  • Mitral valve: regurgitation, not stenosis.
  • Lungs and pulmonary vessels: rarely involved.
  • Workup: ECG and echocardiogram as soon as Kawasaki is suspected.
Practice
  1. 4-year-old boy brought in on day 12 of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands since the first week; CRP 12 mg/dL → IVIG now → give IVIG even beyond day 10 when unexplained fever or coronary changes persist with a raised CRP or ESR
  2. 18-month-old boy brought to the emergency department with 2 days of increasingly fast breathing and irritability; 2 months earlier he had a high fever, red eyes, cracked red lips, enlarged lymph nodes and red swollen hands, all of which cleared without treatment within 14 days; in obvious discomfort; T 38 C (100.4 F); HR 150/min; RR 60/min; BP 60/40 mm Hg; the rest of the examination is normal; chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly; ECG: ST-segment depression in leads II and III, left ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviation → Congestive heart failure → late cardiac complication of untreated Kawasaki disease: cardiomegaly with ischemic ST depression, and no murmur or signs of tamponade
  3. 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.5 C; bilateral conjunctivitis without discharge; strawberry tongue; a polymorphous rash; edema of both hands; one cervical lymph node 1.8 cm → Kawasaki disease → fever 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 criteria; IVIG plus aspirin
  4. 4-year-old boy with 5 days of fever; T 39.0 C; only 3 of the 5 criteria are present: bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips and a polymorphous rash; echocardiogram shows coronary artery dilation → IVIG and aspirin now → incomplete Kawasaki disease is treated on the coronary finding
  5. 4-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and sore throat; T 39.4 C; exudative pharyngitis; strawberry tongue; a fine sandpaper-like rash, densest in the skin creases; no conjunctivitis → Scarlet fever → a positive rapid strep test confirms it; penicillin
  6. 4-year-old boy who is unvaccinated; 4 days of fever, cough and runny nose; T 39.8 C; bilateral conjunctivitis; Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa; a red rash that began on the face and is spreading downward → Measles → Koplik spots and a descending rash decide it; measles antibody serology confirms
  7. 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen hands; IVIG and aspirin are ordered; urinalysis shows many white blood cells and no bacteria → Continue IVIG and aspirin as planned → sterile pyuria is Kawasaki urethritis, a feature of the disease, not a second diagnosis
  8. 9-year-old boy with 3 days of fever, abdominal pain and vomiting, 4 weeks after COVID-19; T 39.5 C; HR 168/min; BP 70/40 mm Hg; a diffuse red rash; cool hands and feet; creatinine 1.3 mg/dL; troponin raised → Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children → weeks after COVID-19, with prominent GI symptoms and shock
  9. 3-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.4 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands → Echocardiogram → baseline coronary assessment at diagnosis; IVIG is not delayed for it
  10. 2-year-old girl, 3 weeks after 7 days of fever with conjunctivitis, cracked lips, rash and hand swelling that were never treated; afebrile now; peeling skin around the fingernails; platelet count 780,000/mm³ → Coronary artery aneurysm → echocardiogram now; untreated aneurysms can progress to infarction or heart failure
  11. 5-year-old girl who received IVIG 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin for Kawasaki disease; the infusion ended 40 hours ago; T 39.3 C; conjunctivitis and rash persist → Second dose of IVIG → fever persisting 36 h after IVIG defines resistance
  12. 3-year-old boy at a well visit 2 months after he was given IVIG 2 g/kg for Kawasaki disease; afebrile; aspirin stopped after a normal echocardiogram; due for routine vaccines → Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines today → live vaccines are deferred 11 months after IVIG; inactivated vaccines are not
  13. 6-year-old boy treated with IVIG and aspirin for Kawasaki disease; afebrile since the day after the infusion; echocardiogram at diagnosis normal → Repeat echocardiogram at 1 to 2 weeks and 4 to 6 weeks → coronary changes can appear after a normal first study
How NBME framed it The untreated Kawasaki illness sits in the past history as an episode that resolved on its own, and the mechanism lead-in is keyed to heart failure. The criteria appear in lay words ("pink eye," swollen hands) and are never named.
Distractors: NBME question
True-fact-wrong-slotPericardial effusion: a real Kawasaki complication, but tamponade adds raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus; cardiomegaly with ischemic ST depression fits heart failure.
Unchecked attributeMitral valve obstruction: Kawasaki affects the mitral valve as regurgitation, not stenosis, and no stenotic murmur is heard.
Salient decoyChronic inflammatory interstitial lung disease: Kawasaki rarely involves the lungs, and the film shows cardiomegaly rather than interstitial fibrosis.
Class-vs-memberThickened internal layer of pulmonary arterioles: Kawasaki is a medium-vessel vasculitis that targets the coronary arteries and rarely involves the pulmonary vessels.
Pairs with Part I Heart Failure in a Child: is the failing heart from an untreated Kawasaki illness in the history or from an acute viral myocarditis?
Transferable rules

A candidate diagnosis that explains only a subset of the findings is wrong. A UTI (urinary tract infection) explains two of the findings; Kawasaki explains all of them. Check which findings a diagnosis leaves unexplained.

edits.html:
Liver Disease in Pregnancy

liver labs in normal pregnancy · liver disease by trimester · alkaline phosphatase · acute fatty liver vs HELLPDoes the gestational age fit a pregnancy-specific liver disease, or is this unrelated to pregnancy?

The decision point

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy, intrahepatic cholestasis and preeclampsia/HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) are all third-trimester diseases. A patient at 14 weeks with elevated transaminases, obesity, and diabetes has metabolic liver disease unrelated to pregnancy.

Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), bilirubin and alkaline phosphataseFirstAlkaline phosphatase raised alone, all else normalPlacental isoenzyme: physiologic, reassure
Serum bile acidsConfirmsRaised bile acids with itching of palms and solesIntrahepatic cholestasis: ursodeoxycholic acid, deliver at 36 to 37 weeks
Blood pressure, urine protein, complete blood count with smearConfirmsSchistocytes, low platelets, raised LFTs, hypertensionHELLP syndrome: delivery
Glucose, prothrombin time/international normalized ratio, ammonia and creatinineBy branchHypoglycemia with coagulopathy and a rising creatinineAcute fatty liver of pregnancy: emergent delivery
Hepatitis serologies and liver ultrasoundBy branchRaised ALT before 20 weeks, echogenic liverNot pregnancy-specific: metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease or viral hepatitis
Right upper quadrant ultrasound or bile acidsSkipAdds nothing when AST, ALT and bilirubin are normalIsolated alkaline phosphatase in late pregnancy needs no workup
Mnemonic HELLP – Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets
Scenario bank
  1. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intense palmar pruritus, raised bile acids and no rash → Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy → ursodeoxycholic acid
  2. 26 yo F at 36 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy and raised transaminases → Acute fatty liver of pregnancy → urgent delivery
  3. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with hypertension, hemolysis, high LFTs and platelets 68,000 → HELLP syndrome → delivery
  4. 26 yo F at 9 weeks with intractable vomiting, ketonuria and mildly raised transaminases → Hyperemesis gravidarum
  5. 26 yo F at 14 weeks, obese with diabetes and raised transaminases → Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease – the third-trimester diseases do not fit at 14 weeks
  6. 26 yo F at 30 weeks with an isolated alkaline phosphatase twice normal, all else normal → Placental alkaline phosphatase – physiologic → reassurance
  7. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intractable palmar pruritus and raised bile acids, taking ursodeoxycholic acid → Delivery at 36 to 37 weeks → intrahepatic cholestasis carries stillbirth risk
  8. 29 yo F at 35 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, raised ammonia and rising creatinine → Emergent delivery → acute fatty liver of pregnancy is treated by delivering
  9. 28 yo F at 32 weeks with alkaline phosphatase three times normal on routine labs; AST, ALT and bilirubin normal; no symptoms → Reassurance → the placenta makes alkaline phosphatase
Alkaline phosphatase in pregnancy Alkaline phosphatase normally rises in pregnancy because the placenta makes its own isoenzyme; levels run 2–4× normal. AST (aspartate aminotransferase), ALT (alanine aminotransferase) and bilirubin do not rise physiologically; any elevation is pathologic.
Liver labs in normal pregnancy
Rises physiologicallyFalls physiologicallyShould stay normal
Alkaline phosphatase (placental), WBC (to ~15,000), erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen and factors VII/VIII/X, total thyroxine and thyroxine-binding globulin, cholesterol, glomerular filtration rateHemoglobin (dilutional), platelets (mild gestational), creatinine and blood urea nitrogen, PaCO₂, thyroid-stimulating hormone in the first trimesterAST, ALT, bilirubin
Liver disease in pregnancy – by trimester
ConditionTimingThe tellManagement
Hyperemesis gravidarum1stVomiting, ketonuria, >5% weight lossSupportive
Intrahepatic cholestasis2nd–3rdPruritus of palms and soles, worse at night; ↑bile acids, ↑bilirubin; stillbirth riskUrsodeoxycholic acid; deliver 36–37 wk
Preeclampsia / HELLP Emergency>20 wkHypertension + proteinuria; Hemolysis, Elevated LFTs, Low Platelets, right upper quadrant pain, schistocytesDelivery
Acute fatty liver Emergency3rdHypoglycemia, ↑ammonia, coagulopathy, ↑Cr, encephalopathy; long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency linkEmergent delivery
AFLP vs. HELLP Hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, high ammonia and renal failure indicate AFLP (acute fatty liver of pregnancy). Hemolysis, thrombocytopenia and more hypertension indicate HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) syndrome. Both are treated by delivering. Cholecystectomy in pregnancy is safest in the second trimester.
Transferable rule Before diagnosing a pregnancy-specific liver disease, check that the gestational age fits it.
Salient decoy

edits.html:
Lymphadenopathy

tempo and laterality sort every neck node · acute and unilateral is bacterial · covering staph, strep, anaerobesHow fast did the node appear, on one side or both, and which organisms must the drug cover?

Source vignette Pt – 3 yo M, lump on the right neck noticed yesterday, today red, painful and larger; cough, rhinorrhea and low-grade fever a week ago, resolved; family reunion in eastern Arkansas with several cousins also coryzal · Exam – T 38.6, HR 98; 5 cm tender, warm, poorly mobile anterior cervical node with overlying erythema; no hepatosplenomegaly · Q – the most appropriate treatment; options spanned azithromycin, cefdinir, clindamycin, itraconazole, oseltamivir and supportive care only
The decision point

Sort the node by tempo and laterality. A node that appeared yesterday and is bigger, red and tender today is acute. A single inflamed node on one side is unilateral. Acute unilateral cervical lymphadenitis in a child under five is a bacterial infection of the node itself. The organisms are Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, with anaerobes when there is periodontal disease. Empiric therapy has to cover gram-positives including MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) plus anaerobes. Among the offered agents, only clindamycin does all three. The preceding viral illness is the portal of entry, not the cause, and it has already resolved.

Defining criteria Acute unilateral cervical lymphadenitis – child under 5; a 3 to 6 cm node, markedly tender, warm and erythematous, with or without fever; the child is usually well-appearing and the diagnosis is clinical · Empiric coverage required – S. aureus including MRSA, S. pyogenes, and anaerobes, which is clindamycin; amoxicillin-clavulanate is reasonable where community MRSA is low, a first-generation cephalosporin where periodontal disease is unlikely · Suppuration – fluctuance on examination signals abscess and adds incision and drainage · Observation gate – supportive care alone is defensible only in an afebrile child with minimal tenderness and minimal enlargement
Pertinent positives & negatives Onset yesterday, larger today – acute; excludes cat-scratch disease and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, both of which build over weeks · Unilateral – a node infection, not reactive adenopathy, which is bilateral · Tender, warm, erythematous – inflammatory; mycobacterial nodes are nontender and violaceous · T 38.6 – opens the antibiotic gate that observation would otherwise satisfy · 5 cm – large enough to risk suppuration; size is part of the treatment gate · Poorly mobile with overlying erythema – tethering from inflammation; malignancy is painless and not erythematous · URI (upper respiratory infection) a week ago, now resolved – the portal of entry, not the active illness · No hepatosplenomegaly or diffuse adenopathy – excludes disseminated histoplasmosis and mononucleosis
The inflamed cervical node – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Acute bacterial lymphadenitisUnder 5, after a URI; S. aureus and S. pyogenesAcute, unilateral, tender, warm, erythematous, with or without fever – (the answer)
Cat-scratch diseaseCat or kitten scratch or bite, or flea bite; Bartonella henselae; the inoculation papule is often small and not reportedTender regional node proximal to the scratch, arising over weeks, sometimes suppurative; fails antibiotics aimed at S. aureus and S. pyogenes; fever in someOnset yesterday; no animal exposure
Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitisAlso under 5, indolent courseChronic, violaceous, nontender; treated by excisionAcute, tender, erythematous and febrile
Reactive viral adenopathyConcurrent URI or influenzaBilateral, small, mobile, mildly tenderUnilateral and 5 cm; the URI has resolved
Disseminated histoplasmosisMississippi and Ohio River ValleysPulmonary disease with mediastinal adenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly with diffuse adenopathyIsolated neck node; no organomegaly or lung findings
Infected branchial cleft cystCongenital second-arch remnant that declares itself after a URI, often in later childhoodCystic lateral mass with a draining pit anterior to the sternocleidomastoidA solid tender node with no pit or sinus tract
The node pattern names the cause Acute, unilateral, tender, warm node – pyogenic: S. aureus or S. pyogenes; clindamycin · Tender regional node proximal to a scratch, failing antistaphylococcal antibiotics – Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease): ask about cats and kittens, send Bartonella serology; azithromycin speeds recovery · Chronic, single, nontender cervical node – mycobacterial: tuberculosis (TB) in an adolescent or adult with TB risk (interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test, then biopsy); nontuberculous mycobacteria in a child under 5, violaceous, excised · Generalized, painless adenopathy – systemic: HIV (antigen/antibody test), EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) with pharyngitis and splenomegaly, disseminated histoplasmosis in the immunosuppressed · Bilateral, symmetric, nontender nodes with cat exposure – toxoplasmosis; Toxoplasma serology · Bilateral, small, mildly tender nodes with a current URI – reactive viral adenopathy; supportive care
Decision spine Acute or chronic? – Days means bacterial; weeks means Bartonella or mycobacterial · Unilateral or bilateral? – Unilateral is a node infection; bilateral is reactive · Tender and erythematous, or violaceous and painless? – Tender means pyogenic · Febrile? Large? – Both means antibiotics, not observation · Fluctuant? – If yes, drain as well · Which agent covers S. aureus including MRSA, S. pyogenes and anaerobes? – Clindamycin
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsAcute, unilateral, tender, warm node in a child under 5Bacterial lymphadenitis; treat empirically; tests are for mimics and abscess
Neck ultrasoundBy branchFluctuance or no response by 48 hours: abscessIncision and drainage with continued antibiotics
Gram stain and culture of drained pusCauseGram-positive cocci in clustersS. aureus; identifies MRSA and narrows therapy
Bartonella henselae serologyBy branchTender regional node proximal to a scratch, not responding to antistaphylococcal antibiotics: positiveCat-scratch disease; the diagnosis is often clinical, serology confirms
Excisional biopsyBy branchChronic violaceous nontender node: granulomas, acid-fast bacilliNontuberculous mycobacteria; excision is also the treatment
Interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin testBy branchChronic, single, nontender cervical node with TB risk: positiveTuberculous lymphadenitis; confirm by node biopsy or aspirate with acid-fast culture
HIV antigen/antibody testBy branchGeneralized painless adenopathy: positiveHIV; a single tender regional node is not its pattern
Histoplasma testingSkipA single hot node is not histoplasmosisThe Arkansas geography is a decoy
Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo M with a 5 cm tender, warm, erythematous, poorly mobile right anterior cervical node appearing over 2 days, T 38.6, with a resolved upper respiratory illness a week earlier → Clindamycin → covers MRSA, S. pyogenes and anaerobes
  2. 4 yo with a 2 cm mildly tender unilateral cervical node, afebrile, well-appearing, no overlying erythema → Supportive care with reassessment → observation is appropriate below the treatment gate
  3. 3 yo who has taken clindamycin for 48 hours whose node is now fluctuant with spreading erythema → Incision and drainage with continued antibiotics → suppuration has developed
  4. 8 yo with a 3-week history of a slowly enlarging tender axillary node and a papule where his kitten clawed him → Cat-scratch disease → azithromycin
  5. 3 yo with a 6-week painless violaceous submandibular node, afebrile and otherwise well → Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis → surgical excision
  6. 3 yo with acute unilateral bacterial cervical lymphadenitis in a community with high MRSA prevalence → Cefdinir → no coverage of Staphylococcus aureus or anaerobes
  7. 5 yo from the Mississippi River Valley with cough, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse adenopathy → Disseminated histoplasmosis → itraconazole
  8. 2 yo with fever, cough and rhinorrhea with bilateral small mobile mildly tender cervical nodes → Reactive viral adenopathy → supportive care
  9. 4 year old with 1 day of fever and a red, tender, fluctuant 2 cm anterior cervical node; normal dentition, no animal contact, no rash → Staphylococcus aureus → With Streptococcus pyogenes – acute, unilateral, suppurative
  10. Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis and extensive dental caries → Anaerobic oral flora → Prevotella and relatives follow periodontal disease
  11. Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis after skinning a rabbit → Francisella tularensis → The exposure names the organism
  12. Child with bilateral tender cervical nodes, coryza and pharyngitis for 3 days → Acute viral adenitis → Bilateral and acute points at adenovirus and its relatives
  13. 3 yo with cough and rhinorrhea last week, now resolved, and a single neck node noticed yesterday that is 4 cm, tender, warm and red today; T 38.5 → Acute bacterial lymphadenitis → empiric clindamycin
  14. 12 yo M with a painful left neck lump a week after a febrile URI, now cystic, with a small pit anterior to the sternocleidomastoid draining mucopurulent fluid → Branchial cleft cyst → second-arch remnant infected after a URI; resect cyst and tract
  15. 8 yo with a tender midline neck cyst after a cold that rises when she sticks out her tongue → Thyroglossal duct cyst → follows the path of thyroid descent from the foramen cecum
  16. Adult trumpet player with a soft lateral neck swelling that enlarges when he bears down → Laryngocele → laryngeal mucosa pouching through the thyrohyoid membrane, inflated by pressure
  17. 16 yo F with a tender red lump at the left elbow 5 days ago, diagnosed as lymphadenitis and treated with clindamycin taken as prescribed; now fever and increasing swelling in the left armpit; T 38.3; a 1 cm tender mobile epitrochlear node and several 2 to 3 cm tender left axillary nodes; no other enlarged nodes → Bartonella henselae serology → cat-scratch disease; ask about cats; azithromycin speeds recovery
  18. 24 yo F who adopted a stray cat 2 months ago, with 3 weeks of fatigue and low-grade fever; 1 to 2 cm nontender, mobile posterior cervical nodes on both sides, symmetric; no pharyngitis, no splenomegaly, no skin lesions; heterophile antibody test negative → Toxoplasmosis → Toxoplasma serology; self-limited in an immunocompetent adult
  19. 26 yo M who moved from the Philippines 2 years ago, with a single firm, nontender, 3 cm right cervical node that has enlarged slowly over 2 months; no pain, no overlying warmth, no animal exposure; other node regions normal → Tuberculous lymphadenitis → interferon-gamma release assay, then node biopsy with acid-fast culture
Decoy note The location, eastern Arkansas, is genuinely endemic for histoplasmosis. Mentioned beside the sick contacts, it reads as an exposure history. It is not one: the cousins explain the resolved URI. The location explains nothing, because histoplasmosis does not present as a single hot node.
Congenital neck masses, sorted by location Midline, moves with swallowing or tongue protrusion – thyroglossal duct cyst, often found after a URI · Midline, does not move with the tongue – dermoid cyst, along an embryologic fusion plane · Lateral, anterior to the sternocleidomastoid, below the mandible – branchial cleft cyst, usually second arch, between the internal and external carotids; cured by resecting the cyst and its tract · Lateral, necrotic node with violaceous skin and a fistula – nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis · Posterior triangle, from birth or on prenatal ultrasound – cystic hygroma · Lateral, enlarges with Valsalva – laryngocele, through the thyrohyoid membrane; glassblowers and trumpet players · Submandibular sinus draining sulfur granules – actinomyces, after dental infection or trauma
Pearls Tempo and laterality sort neck nodes before anything else – acute and unilateral is bacterial, chronic and unilateral is Bartonella or mycobacterial, acute and bilateral is viral · Clindamycin is chosen for its spectrum, not its class – a cephalosporin that misses staphylococci fails · Violaceous and nontender is mycobacterial, and its preferred treatment is surgical excision rather than antibiotics · Fluctuance adds drainage – the drug stays the same · A resolved URI a week earlier is a portal of entry, not a competing diagnosis; a concurrent URI would point at reactive adenopathy instead
Pairs with Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the reactive-adenopathy end of this spectrum and the exudative pharyngitis fork. Ask: how fast did it appear, and is it one node or many?
How NBME framed it Scratches from a pet cat were planted beside a cat-scratch disease option, but acute midline pain that worsens with swallowing or tongue protrusion names an infected thyroglossal duct cyst.
Transferable rule When every option is a drug, name the organisms you must cover, then find the single agent that covers all of them. A geographic detail matters only when the syndrome matches the endemic disease, not merely the location.
Unchecked attributeSupportive care only: the observation gate requires an afebrile child with a small, minimally tender node; this is 38.6 with a 5 cm inflamed node at risk of abscess.
Unchecked attributeAzithromycin: correct for cat-scratch and part of mycobacterial therapy, but both are chronic and indolent; this appeared yesterday.
Class-vs-memberCefdinir: covers S. pyogenes but not S. aureus or anaerobes, and the two are clinically indistinguishable here.
Salient decoyItraconazole: eastern Arkansas is histoplasmosis country, but histoplasmosis presents with pulmonary or disseminated disease, not an isolated hot node.
True-fact-wrong-slotOseltamivir: influenza adenopathy is bilateral and accompanies active respiratory symptoms, which have resolved.

edits.html:
Fatty Liver Disease

aspartate aminotransferase (AST):alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ratio · causes to exclude · fibrosis staging · weight loss first · formerly nonalcoholic fatty liver diseaseIs the picture metabolic with ALT above AST, and have the other liver diseases been excluded?

The decision point

Metabolic syndrome (obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia) + transaminase elevation + hyperechoic liver on ultrasound. AST (aspartate aminotransferase) is below ALT (alanine aminotransferase), an AST/ALT ratio <1. Alcohol gives the opposite ratio: AST:ALT ≥2 ("t-oAST").

  • Most common chronic liver disease in the US; progression is steatosis → metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) → fibrosis → cirrhosis → hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and HCC can occur without cirrhosis
  • Exclude first: alcohol, hepatitis B/C, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, and drugs (steroids, amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen)
  • Stage fibrosis with Fibrosis-4 index (FIB-4) or transient elastography
  • Treatment: 7–10% weight loss reverses steatohepatitis; bariatric surgery if body mass index (BMI) ≥35; glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists; resmetirom for MASH with fibrosis
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
AST and ALTFirstALT higher, AST:ALT under 1Metabolic; a ratio of 2 or more points to alcohol
Liver ultrasoundFirstHyperechoic liverSteatosis
Hepatitis B and C serology, iron studies, ceruloplasminConfirmsAll normal, alcohol under the thresholdMetabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a diagnosis of exclusion; also exclude autoimmune hepatitis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, drugs
FIB-4 scoreStagingHigh scorePossible advanced fibrosis: elastography next
Transient elastographyStagingStiff liverAdvanced fibrosis or cirrhosis: hepatology, HCC surveillance if cirrhotic
Liver biopsy in every patientSkipInvasive; noninvasive staging comes firstReserved for an uncertain diagnosis or discordant staging
Scenario bank
  1. 48 yo M, BMI 34, type 2 diabetes, ALT 70, AST 45, hyperechoic liver → MASLD
  2. 48 yo M with AST 180 and ALT 70 and a history of heavy drinking → Alcohol-associated liver disease → AST:ALT of 2 or more
  3. 48 yo M with MASLD asking what most improves liver histology → 7 To 10% weight loss
  4. 48 yo M with MASLD and a high FIB-4 score → Assess fibrosis with elastography
  5. 48 yo M with MASLD and low-density lipoprotein 160 → Statins are safe and indicated
  6. 32 yo M with fatty liver, low ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings → Wilson disease
Pearls Significant alcohol intake threshold: >21 drinks/week (men), >14 (women) · gallstones in pregnancy are common (progesterone → gallbladder stasis) and usually incidental without wall thickening, fever, or pain · young patient with steatosis + tremor + Kayser-Fleischer rings → Wilson disease.
Pairs with Part II Wilson Disease covers the copper exclusion: is the patient under about 40, with a tremor, psychiatric change or Kayser-Fleischer rings, and is the ceruloplasmin low?

edits.html:
Bacterial Meningitis

cell type by glucose · organism by host · when computed tomography (CT) precedes the tap · antibiotics before imaging · when to add ampicillinAre the cells neutrophils or lymphocytes, and is the glucose low?

The decision point

Read the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) as a 2×2: cell type on one axis, glucose on the other.

CSF interpretation – the 2×2
Glucose LOWGlucose NORMAL
NeutrophilsBacterialEarly viral · parameningeal focus
LymphocytesTuberculosis · fungal (± partially treated bacterial)Viral
Organism by host
  • Neonate: group B Streptococcus · E. coli (K1 capsule) · Listeria  |  Unvaccinated toddler: Hib
  • Teen / dorm / military: N. meningitidis  |  Adult (most common): S. pneumoniae
  • >50, pregnant, immunosuppressed: + Listeria → add ampicillin
  • Ventriculoperitoneal shunt: S. epidermidis  |  Basilar skull fracture / CSF rhinorrhea: S. pneumoniae  |  Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) CD4 <100: Cryptococcus
Mechanism pearls Encapsulated organisms need opsonization, so they hit hardest in asplenia/sickle cell (lost filter), cirrhosis (lost complement synthesis) and complement deficiency. Complement deficiency means a lost MAC (membrane attack complex), which causes recurrent Neisseria infection; screen with CH50 (total hemolytic complement) · lipid A of LOS (lipooligosaccharide) triggers TNF (tumor necrosis factor) and IL-1 (interleukin-1) release → shock, DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation), Waterhouse-Friderichsen · Listeria escapes the phagosome with listeriolysin O and spreads via ActA-driven host actin polymerization; it has intrinsic cephalosporin resistance · conjugate vaccines convert T-independent polysaccharide into a T-dependent response, which is why they work under age 2.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Blood culturesFirstGrowth of the organismNames the organism if the tap is delayed; never delay antibiotics
Head CTBy branchOnly with a red flag: papilledema, focal deficit, seizure, obtundationGive antibiotics before the scan; an open fontanelle usually removes the need
Lumbar puncture: cell count, glucose, proteinNextNeutrophils with low glucoseBacterial; lymphocytes with normal glucose: viral
CSF Gram stain and cultureConfirmsOrganism seen or grownBacterial meningitis and the organism to target
CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for enterovirus and herpes simplex virus (HSV)By branchLymphocytic CSF, normal glucose: positive PCREnterovirus: supportive care; HSV: acyclovir
CSF cryptococcal antigen and acid-fast bacilli cultureBy branchLymphocytes with low glucose, HIV or basilar signsCryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis
Complement levels during the acute illnessSkipNot an acute studyCheck CH50 after recovery, for recurrent or unusual Neisseria infection
Scenario bank
  1. 22 yo M with fever and neck stiffness; CSF 3,000 neutrophils, glucose 25, protein 180 → Bacterial meningitis → dexamethasone with ceftriaxone and vancomycin
  2. 22 yo M with CSF 200 lymphocytes, normal glucose and mildly raised protein → Viral meningitis
  3. 35 yo M with HIV; CSF lymphocytes, very low glucose, high protein, basilar involvement → Tuberculous meningitis
  4. 22 yo M with suspected meningitis and papilledema on fundoscopy → CT head before lumbar puncture
  5. 22 yo M with suspected bacterial meningitis and a delayed CT scanner → Blood cultures and antibiotics before imaging
  6. 68 yo M with bacterial meningitis; what coverage must be added → Ampicillin for Listeria
  7. 8 yo M in summer, headache, fever, stiff neck, CSF with 200 WBCs and 85% lymphocytes, protein 60, glucose 55, Gram stain negative → Enteroviral meningitis → supportive care
  8. 5 yo F with fever and meningismus, CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein, well appearing → Supportive care and observation → viral meningitis
  9. The most common cause of aseptic meningitis in a child presenting during summer → Enterovirus → supportive care is sufficient
  10. 2 yo with fever, hypotension, lethargy and a purpuric rash on the legs; cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci → Serum fibrinogen → purpura signals disseminated intravascular coagulation
  11. When complement testing is indicated in a patient with meningococcal disease → After recovery, for recurrent or unusual-serogroup infection → terminal complement deficiency is C5 to C9, a predisposition rather than an acute study
  12. 1 year old with meningococcemia who develops large purpuric lesions and sudden vasomotor collapse and dies; the autopsy finding → Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage → Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
  13. Infant with fever, nuchal rigidity, spreading purpura and abrupt hypotension → Fulminant meningococcemia → 10 to 20% of infected infants; mortality approaches 100%
  14. 16 yo M, 8 hours of abrupt high fever and sore throat with severe diffuse leg pain, says he has never felt this terrible; pale, nonexudative pharyngitis, supple neck, mottled tender legs; rapid strep and influenza negative; complete blood count and blood culture drawn → Lumbar puncture → early meningococcal disease; no seizure, obtundation, focal deficit, papilledema or immunocompromise, so no CT first, and ceftriaxone does not wait
  15. Adolescent 10 hours into an abrupt febrile illness with severe leg pain, cold hands and feet and mottled skin, no rash yet → Meningococcemia → poor perfusion and severe myalgia arrive before the petechiae
Sequencing Get CT before LP (computed tomography before lumbar puncture) only if there is papilledema, focal deficit, seizure, immunocompromise, depressed consciousness or age >60. However, an open fontanelle in an infant generally removes the requirement, since it acts as a pop-off valve. Never delay antibiotics; draw cultures and treat. Empiric therapy is vancomycin + ceftriaxone (+ ampicillin for Listeria). Neonates get cefotaxime, not ceftriaxone (biliary sludging, bilirubin displacement). Dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose: give it to blunt the cytokine burst from bacterial lysis.
Early meningococcal disease Onset – nonspecific fever, headache, vomiting, myalgia or sore throat, easily mistaken for a viral or streptococcal pharyngitis · Red flags – severe myalgia such as leg pain, poor perfusion with pallor, mottling or cold hands and feet, and the worst illness the patient has ever felt · Tempo – petechiae, meningeal signs and altered mental status follow within 12 to 24 hours · Workup – blood cultures and lumbar puncture, with ceftriaxone given without waiting for either · CT first only for – recent seizure, obtundation, focal deficit, papilledema or immunocompromise · Complications – shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, adrenal hemorrhage · Prevention – droplet precautions and chemoprophylaxis for close contacts
Follow-up facts The classic triad is present in only 44% (van de Beek, NEJM 2004; n=696) · the most common sequela is sensorineural hearing loss; check hearing in every survivor · prophylaxis for meningococcus is rifampin, cipro or ceftriaxone; for Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) it is rifampin · eculizumab blocks C5, so meningococcal vaccination is mandatory first.
Pairs with Part I Seizure with Fever in a Child covers the decision to obtain the fluid; this brief covers interpreting it.
Salient decoyHeterophile antibody test: mononucleosis gives exudate and posterior cervical nodes, not leg pain, mottling and a collapse measured in hours.
Salient decoyCT scan of the neck: deep neck infection brings trismus, uvular deviation or a bulging pharyngeal wall.
Salient decoyThroat culture for diphtheria: needs a gray, adherent pharyngeal pseudomembrane.
Salient decoyHIV antigen/antibody test: acute HIV adds diffuse lymphadenopathy, rash and diarrhea.
