edits.html:
Microcytic Anemia

iron studies before electrophoresis · iron deficiency masks thalassemia trait · lead and chronic disease · the complete blood count (CBC) aloneIs the patient iron replete yet, and do the red cell distribution width (RDW) and red cell count fit deficiency or trait?

The decision point

Both iron deficiency anemia and beta-thalassemia trait produce a low MCV (mean corpuscular volume). Hemoglobin electrophoresis is not the first test, because iron deficiency lowers HbA2 (hemoglobin A2), the marker electrophoresis uses to diagnose beta-thalassemia trait. In an iron-deficient patient, a falsely normal HbA2 on electrophoresis will mask coexisting thalassemia. Order iron studies first, correct the iron, then electrophoresis.

Defining criteria Iron studies first – ferritin, serum iron, total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), transferrin saturation; iron deficiency must be corrected before electrophoresis is interpretable · HbA2 masking – iron deficiency suppresses delta-globin chain production, lowering HbA2 into the normal range · Beta-thalassemia trait HbA2 – elevated (>3.5%) only when iron stores are replete
Microcytic anemia – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellFirst testConfirms, then
Iron deficiency anemiaMenstrual loss, vegan/poor diet, GI bleed; low MCVLow ferritin, high TIBC, low transferrin satIron studiesLow ferritin; oral iron, then electrophoresis if the MCV stays low
Beta-thalassemia minorMediterranean/Asian, lifelong mild anemia, target cellsElevated HbA2 >3.5% on electrophoresis (only when iron-replete)Iron studies firstHbA2 over 3.5% once iron-replete; genetic counseling
Alpha-thalassemia minorSoutheast Asian/African, mild microcytic anemiaNormal electrophoresis; diagnosis by exclusion or gene testingIron studies → electrophoresis → gene analysisAlpha-globin gene deletion analysis
Lead poisoningChild in old housing, developmental delay, abdominal painBasophilic stippling; elevated lead levelLead levelElevated venous lead level; chelation if high
Anemia of chronic diseaseChronic infection, autoimmunity, malignancyLow iron, low TIBC (iron sequestered, not absent); ferritin normal/highIron studiesLow iron and TIBC with normal or high ferritin; treat the underlying disease
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo F vegan with heavy menses, MCV 68, hemoglobin 9.2 → Iron studies → iron deficiency must be assessed before electrophoresis is interpretable
  2. 15 yo F with confirmed iron deficiency anemia from heavy menses, hemoglobin 9.2, hemodynamically stable → Oral iron supplementation and reassess in 4 to 6 weeks
  3. 22 yo M of Mediterranean descent, MCV 64, hemoglobin 11.5, iron studies normal, HbA2 5.8% → Beta-thalassemia minor → genetic counseling
  4. Why hemoglobin electrophoresis can miss beta-thalassemia trait in an iron-deficient patient → Iron deficiency suppresses HbA2 production, normalizing a value that would otherwise be elevated
  5. 3 yo M in old housing with developmental delay, microcytic anemia, and basophilic stippling on smear → Lead poisoning → serum lead level and chelation if elevated
  6. 28 yo F of Southeast Asian descent, MCV 72, hemoglobin 11.0, normal iron studies, normal electrophoresis → Alpha-globin gene deletion analysis → alpha-thalassemia minor
  7. 18 yo F treated for iron deficiency with 3 months of oral iron, ferritin now 45, but MCV remains 66 and hemoglobin 10.8 → Hemoglobin electrophoresis → possible coexisting thalassemia trait
  8. 2 yo M, well-child visit, five 8-oz cups of whole cow milk daily, pale with tachycardia and a flow murmur, Hb 8, MCV 70, erythrocytes 3.1 million/uL, platelets and leukocytes normal → Elevated red cell distribution width → iron deficiency anemia
  9. 2 yo of Greek descent, MCV 65, Hb 10.2, erythrocytes 5.4 million/uL, RDW normal, ferritin and iron studies normal → Beta-thalassemia trait → a normal red cell count with a low MCV
  10. 2 yo M with Hb 8 and MCV 70 whose diet is cheese, yogurt and roughly 40 oz of whole cow milk daily → Limit cow milk below 24 oz per day and begin an empiric oral iron trial → iron deficiency from excessive milk intake
  11. Why the red cell distribution width rises in iron deficiency but stays normal in thalassemia trait → Iron available for erythropoiesis fluctuates, so cells are made at varying sizes → thalassemia produces uniformly small cells
  12. 16 yo F with heavy menses, a low MCV, a low erythrocyte count, an elevated RDW and a low ferritin → Iron deficiency anemia → oral iron
  13. 58 yo M with rheumatoid arthritis and a microcytic anemia; serum iron low, TIBC low, ferritin normal → Anemia of chronic disease → iron is sequestered, not absent
Pearls Iron studies → then electrophoresis: a required order, not a preference, because iron deficiency suppresses delta-globin chain production, lowering HbA2 (hemoglobin A2) into the normal range · Ferritin is the most specific single test for iron deficiency; TIBC (total iron-binding capacity) and transferrin saturation add sensitivity when ferritin is borderline (ferritin is an acute-phase reactant) · Alpha-thalassemia minor has a normal electrophoresis. It is diagnosed by exclusion or gene testing and is the one microcytic anemia that electrophoresis cannot diagnose · The Mentzer index is MCV (mean corpuscular volume) divided by RBC (red blood cell count). It is a screening heuristic: under 13 suggests thalassemia and over 13 suggests IDA (iron deficiency anemia). It is not diagnostic and is never the most appropriate test · If the anemia does not correct with iron, look for a second cause; that is when to order electrophoresis
Pairs with Sickle Cell Disease and Trait also uses hemoglobin electrophoresis. Ask: is the electrophoresis interpretable, or must iron be corrected first?
Telling them apart on the CBC alone RDW – elevated in iron deficiency because the iron available for erythropoiesis varies through the day, so cells are made at varying sizes; normal or low in thalassemia trait, where every cell is uniformly small · Erythrocyte count – low in iron deficiency because the marrow lacks substrate, but normal or elevated in thalassemia trait, which makes plenty of small cells · Mentzer index – MCV divided by RBC; over 13 favours iron deficiency and under 13 favours thalassemia trait · TIBC direction – elevated in iron deficiency as transferrin is upregulated, and low in anemia of chronic disease · mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration – low in both iron deficiency and thalassemia, and elevated in hereditary spherocytosis from loss of membrane surface area · Cow milk threshold – over 24 oz per day after age 1 is the named risk factor, because milk is iron-poor, its calcium and caseinophosphopeptide block absorption, and volume displaces iron-rich food
Transferable rule When two diseases share a lab value and one suppresses the marker used to diagnose the other, testing order is a dependency, not a preference. Correct the confounder first, then run the definitive test.
Sequencing trapHemoglobin electrophoresis: it checks for thalassemia, but iron deficiency makes it uninterpretable.
Class-vs-memberBone marrow biopsy: it can look like the definitive hematology test, but it is invasive and unnecessary when a dietary cause is obvious.

edits.html:
Heart Failure in a Child

the viral prodrome that is not bronchiolitis · gallop, apical murmur and weak pulses · cardiogenic shock: cautious fluidIs there a gallop or a new murmur, and are the pulses weak with a low pressure?

Source vignette Pt – 2 yo M, 4 days of rhinorrhea, congestion and low-grade fever, now tired with decreased urine output and labored breathing · Exam – T 38.2, HR 155, RR 48, BP 60/40, SpO2 91% on room air; scattered mobile subcentimeter anterior cervical nodes; gallop rhythm with a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex; brachial and femoral pulses 1+; nasal flaring, subcostal retractions and basal rales · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned acute rheumatic fever, bronchiolitis, glomerulonephritis, Kawasaki disease and myocarditis
The decision point

The respiratory findings are real, but every one of them is a consequence of the heart. Three cardiac findings decide the diagnosis: a gallop, a new holosystolic murmur at the apex, and 1+ pulses with a blood pressure of 60/40. A gallop is an S3, from a ventricle taking volume it cannot handle. In this setting, an apical holosystolic murmur is mitral regurgitation from ventricular dilation, not a primary valve lesion. Weak pulses with hypotension in a 2-year-old are shock. With basal rales and oliguria, this is acute left heart failure with pulmonary edema. That is why the lungs sound wet and the saturation is 91%. The viral prodrome is the cause, not a coincidence. The usual agents are coxsackievirus B and adenovirus. Myocyte injury is part direct and part immune-mediated.

Defining criteria Myocarditis – a viral prodrome, upper respiratory or gastrointestinal, then heart failure: respiratory distress, gallop, hepatomegaly, with or without arrhythmia, which is how it causes sudden death · Acute rheumatic fever gate – Jones criteria 2 to 4 weeks after untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis; a concurrent viral upper respiratory infection (URI) is the wrong illness at the wrong interval · Kawasaki gate – fever of 5 or more days plus 4 of 5 criteria, with a cervical node over 1.5 cm; four days of fever with no criteria does not open it · Workup – troponin, electrocardiogram (ECG) showing sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST change, chest film showing cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema, and echocardiography showing diffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fraction
Pertinent positives & negatives Gallop rhythm – an S3, the most specific finding in the stem for ventricular failure · Holosystolic murmur at the apex – functional mitral regurgitation from a dilated ventricle, new in a failing child · BP 60/40 with 1+ pulses – cardiogenic shock, an emergency · Basal rales with hypoxemia – pulmonary edema, not consolidation and not bronchospasm · No wheeze – argues strongly against bronchiolitis, whose classic finding it is · Decreased urine output – hypoperfusion; urine output reflects cardiac output · Subcentimeter mobile nodes – reactive to the viral illness and too small for Kawasaki, which requires over 1.5 cm · Fever 4 days with no rash, conjunctivitis or mucosal change – the Kawasaki gate fails on duration and on criteria count
Respiratory distress after a viral prodrome – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Viral myocarditis Can't missCoxsackie B or adenovirus; prodrome then failureGallop plus new apical holosystolic murmur plus poor perfusion after a URI – (the answer)
BronchiolitisRespiratory syncytial virus; first or second year, coryza then distressWheeze and hyperinflation; heart sounds normalNo wheeze; gallop and murmur unexplained by it
Acute rheumatic feverGroup A Streptococcus pharyngitis, then an immune sequelJones criteria 2 to 4 weeks later; migratory arthritis, choreaConcurrent viral URI and no Jones criteria
Kawasaki diseaseVasculitis of young children; can include myocarditisFever 5 or more days plus 4 criteria; node over 1.5 cmFour days of fever, no criteria, subcentimeter nodes
GlomerulonephritisPost-infectious or immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy; may follow a URIHematuria and Nephritic Syndrome, hypertension and edemaHypotensive rather than hypertensive; no hematuria
Management Treatment is supportive: diuresis, afterload reduction and inotropes. IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) is commonly given, but its benefit in children is not established. Do not treat the shock reflexively. This child's hypotension is cardiogenic, so a rapid large-volume bolus worsens pulmonary edema. Give fluid cautiously and in small aliquots, or not at all, while getting the echocardiogram.
Decision spine Is there a gallop or a new murmur? – Yes means the heart is the failing organ, whatever the lungs are doing · Wheeze or rales? – Rales means edema, not bronchiolitis · What is the blood pressure and what are the pulses? – 60/40 with 1+ means shock · How long has the fever run, and how many Kawasaki criteria? – Four days and none, so the gate is closed · Was the antecedent illness strep pharyngitis 2 to 4 weeks ago? – No, it is concurrent coryza, so not rheumatic fever · So what confirms it? – Echocardiography with troponin, ECG and a chest film
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
ECGFirstSinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST changesSupports myocarditis; watch for arrhythmia, the cause of sudden death
TroponinFirstElevatedMyocyte injury
Chest radiographSupportsCardiomegaly with pulmonary edemaRales are edema, not bronchiolitis or pneumonia
EchocardiographyConfirmsDiffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fractionMyocarditis with heart failure; excludes a structural lesion
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging or endomyocardial biopsyBy branchMyocardial inflammation or lymphocytic infiltrateTissue-level confirmation when the diagnosis remains uncertain
Antistreptolysin O titerSkipNo pharyngitis 2 to 4 weeks earlier, no Jones criteriaConcurrent coryza is the wrong illness at the wrong interval for rheumatic fever
Scenario bank
  1. 2 yo M, 4 days of rhinorrhea and low-grade fever, now tired with decreased urine output; HR 155, RR 48, BP 60/40, gallop rhythm with a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex, 1+ pulses, basal rales → Viral myocarditis → acute decompensated heart failure
  2. 2 yo with a 4-day viral prodrome who now has a gallop, basal rales and poor peripheral perfusion → Echocardiography with troponin and ECG → diffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fraction
  3. 3 yo with suspected myocarditis, hypotensive with a gallop, rales and hepatomegaly → A rapid 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus → the shock is cardiogenic, not hypovolemic
  4. 8 mo, 3 days of coryza, now wheezing with retractions and hyperinflation; heart sounds normal with no murmur → Bronchiolitis → supportive care and suctioning
  5. 6 yo with migratory polyarthritis and a new murmur 3 weeks after an untreated sore throat → Acute rheumatic fever → Jones criteria with an antistreptolysin O titer
  6. 4 yo with 6 days of fever, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips, a polymorphous rash and a 2 cm cervical node → Kawasaki disease → IVIG with aspirin
  7. The organisms most commonly responsible for myocarditis in children → Coxsackievirus B and adenovirus → direct viral injury plus immune-mediated myocyte necrosis
  8. 5 yo recovering from biopsy-proven myocarditis who has a syncopal episode and an irregular pulse → Continuous cardiac monitoring → arrhythmia is the mechanism of sudden death
Pearls S3 or new murmur in any child in respiratory distress – heart failure until an echocardiogram says otherwise, however viral the story sounds · A new holosystolic murmur at the apex in a failing ventricle is functional mitral regurgitation – a consequence, not a second disease · Hypotension in myocarditis is cardiogenic: fluid loading fills the lungs and is the commonest management error · Rheumatic fever is defined by its interval, 2 to 4 weeks after pharyngitis; a murmur appearing during a viral illness is myocarditis · Kawasaki's fever requirement is five days, and it is mandatory
Pairs with Part II Shock in Children covers the perfusion categories and the cardiogenic-versus-distributive fork. Part I Acute Rheumatic Fever covers Jones and the post-streptococcal interval. Kawasaki Disease covers the five-day fever requirement. Ask: is there a gallop or a new murmur, and how long has the fever run?
Transferable rule When respiratory findings are prominent and cardiac findings are subtle, read the cardiac findings first. A gallop, a new murmur or weak pulses point to the heart as the failing organ. The lung signs are then a consequence rather than a cause.
Unchecked attributeAcute rheumatic fever: fever with a new murmur after an infection is its exact shape, but the antecedent is coryza not pharyngitis, the interval is concurrent not 2 to 4 weeks, and no Jones criteria are met.
Unchecked attributeKawasaki disease: genuinely causes myocarditis, but fever is 4 days and no criteria are met; the nodes are subcentimeter against a 1.5 cm requirement.
True-fact-wrong-slotGlomerulonephritis: oliguria after a URI (upper respiratory infection) fits, but it presents with hematuria and hypertension, and this child is hypotensive with unexplained cardiac findings.
Salient decoyBronchiolitis: the whole respiratory picture and the age fit, but it explains nothing cardiac and the classic wheeze is absent while rales are present.

edits.html:
The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant

enterocolitis vs volvulus vs atresia · bilious emesis, bloody stool · the film tells you which one · excluding malrotationIs there air in the wall, air where bowel should be, or no air at all?

Source vignette Pt – 7-day-old term F with truncus arteriosus in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) awaiting repair, poor feeding and abdominal distension; T 35 C, BP 60/30, pulse 180, respirations 65, saturation 82% · Exam – lethargic and cyanotic, moderate distension, absent bowel sounds, bright red blood in stool; nasogastric tube returns bilious fluid · Imaging – abdominal x-ray · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), malrotation with volvulus, intussusception, milk protein proctocolitis and C difficile colitis
The decision point

The combination of temperature instability, abdominal distension with bloody stools, and pneumatosis intestinalis on the film indicates NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis). NEC is mainly a disease of prematurity, but this infant is term. In a term infant, cyanotic congenital heart disease and hypotension reduce mesenteric oxygen delivery and cause the same ischemic bowel injury.

The bilious return also fits volvulus, so rule it out. Volvulus gives abrupt vomiting in a previously well infant, with proximal gas and a gasless distal abdomen. NEC gives air in the bowel wall with gas still visible in the large bowel. Read the gas pattern first; if malrotation is still possible, only an upper GI (gastrointestinal) series excludes it.

Defining criteria Pneumatosis intestinalis – air within the bowel wall; highly specific for NEC, often with portal venous gas (branching lucencies over the liver) · Pneumoperitoneum – free air under the diaphragm; means perforation and an operation · NEC risk factors – prematurity (the most important), very low birth weight under 1.5 kg, enteral feeding (especially formula), prolonged antibiotics, and in term infants a hypoxic-ischemic insult such as cyanotic heart disease, hypotension or perinatal asphyxia · Volvulus film – proximal gaseous distension with a gasless distal abdomen · Intussusception age – 6 months to 3 years
The distended abdomen in a newborn or infant: the differentialtiming, the stool, and the gas pattern
DiagnosisThe pictureKey discriminatorWhat to do
Necrotizing enterocolitis EmergencyPreterm infant on enteral feeds; lethargy, apnea, hypothermia rather than fever, distension, feeding intolerance, bilious emesis, bloody stools (may be absent early); leukocytosis, metabolic acidosisPneumatosis intestinalis with or without portal venous gas; gas still present distallyNothing by mouth (NPO), nasogastric (NG) decompression, parenteral nutrition, broad-spectrum antibiotics now; surgery for perforation or worsening despite medical care
Malrotation with midgut volvulus EmergencyPreviously well, then abrupt bilious vomiting and pain; any age, most often the first month; older children can have intermittent pain and vomiting insteadProximal gas, gasless distal abdomen; upper GI series shows the ligament of Treitz on the right and a corkscrew or bird's-beak duodenumUpper GI series if stable; emergency laparotomy if not; the operation is the Ladd procedure
Duodenal atresiaBilious vomiting in the first 1 to 2 days, polyhydramnios, trisomy 21; abdomen not distendedDouble bubble with no distal gas, present from birth rather than abruptStop feeds, NG decompression, echocardiogram, then surgical repair
Hirschsprung diseaseNo meconium by 48 hours, poor feeding, distension, bilious vomiting; failed neural crest migration leaves an aganglionic segment, usually rectosigmoid, that cannot relax and stays contracted; usually isolated, but associated with Down syndromeNormal meconium once it passes; tight rectum with an explosive squirt of stool and gas on rectal exam; enema shows a rectosigmoid transition zone with dilated proximal colon; a newborn under 48 hours is not yet lateContrast enema, then rectal suction biopsy (absent ganglion cells confirms); surgical resection of the aganglionic segment
Meconium ileusNo meconium, distension, ± bilious vomiting; thick, sticky meconium obstructs the terminal ileum; cystic fibrosis in about 90%Dilated small bowel with little colonic gas; contrast enema shows a microcolon; empty rectum, no squirt; not a Down syndrome associationHyperosmolar contrast enema, which can also relieve it; surgery if it fails or for free air; sweat chloride test
IntussusceptionColicky pain, currant-jelly stool, right upper quadrant massAge 6 months to 3 years; target sign on ultrasoundAir-contrast enema
Milk protein-induced proctocolitisBlood-streaked stools at 2 to 8 weeksThe infant is well – thriving, undistended, normal vitalsMaternal dairy elimination or hydrolyzed formula
Clostridioides difficile colitisDistension with watery, sometimes bloody stoolNeonates are colonized but lack the toxin receptorsNot a neonatal diagnosis
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Abdominal radiographFirstPneumatosis intestinalis with or without portal venous gas, distal gas presentNEC: NPO, decompression, broad-spectrum antibiotics
Proximal gas, gasless distal abdomenVolvulus: upper GI series if stable, laparotomy if not
Double bubble, no distal gasDuodenal atresia: NG decompression and surgical repair
Diffusely dilated loops, distended abdomen, no air in the rectum, no free airDistal obstruction: Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus
Free air under the diaphragmPerforation: laparotomy
EchocardiogramBy branchDuodenal atresia with trisomy 21 featuresAbout half of infants with Down syndrome have heart disease (ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, atrioventricular canal); obtain before surgery, murmur or not
KaryotypeConfirmsTrisomy 21Confirms Down syndrome but is not urgent and does not change the operation
Upper GI series after a diagnostic double bubbleSkipFilm already diagnosticUpper GI is for malrotation, which has distal gas
Contrast enema, then rectal suction biopsyBy branchTransition zone; absent ganglion cellsHirschsprung disease: no meconium by 48 hours with distension
Contrast enema, then sweat chloride testBy branchMicrocolon with inspissated meconium in the terminal ileumMeconium ileus: a hyperosmolar enema can relieve it; about 90% have cystic fibrosis
Complete blood count, blood gas and blood cultureBy branchLeukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosisNEC: the platelet fall tracks severity; a rising count is often the first sign of improvement
Upper GI contrast seriesConfirmsLigament of Treitz on the right; corkscrew or bird's-beak duodenumMalrotation with midgut volvulus: Ladd procedure; skip it and operate if the infant is unstable
Abdominal ultrasoundBy branchTarget signIntussusception at 6 months to 3 years: air-contrast enema
C difficile toxin testingSkipNeonates lack the toxin receptorsNot a neonatal diagnosis
Scenario bank
  1. 7 day old term F with truncus arteriosus awaiting repair, temperature 35 C, lethargy, distended abdomen with absent bowel sounds, bilious nasogastric return and bright red blood per rectum → Necrotizing enterocolitis → Cyanotic heart disease is a term-infant risk factor – mesenteric hypoperfusion
  2. Preterm neonate on enteral feeds with abdominal distension and bloody stools → Pneumatosis intestinalis → Air within the bowel wall – specific for NEC; portal venous gas may accompany it
  3. Neonate with pneumatosis, distension and bloody stools, hemodynamically stable → Bowel rest, decompression and broad-spectrum antibiotics → Antibiotics immediately – septic shock is the lethal endpoint
  4. Neonate with NEC whose film now shows free air beneath the diaphragm → Laparotomy → Pneumoperitoneum means perforation
  5. 3 day old, well until now, abrupt bilious vomiting, abdominal pain and shock; film shows proximal gas and a gasless distal abdomen → Malrotation with midgut volvulus → Abrupt, previously well, and the mesenteric root twists around the superior mesenteric artery
  6. Stable infant with suspected malrotation → Upper gastrointestinal contrast series → Outlines the duodenojejunal junction and any corkscrew
  7. Newborn with bilious emesis from the first feeds, polyhydramnios in utero, trisomy 21 features, no distal gas on film → Duodenal atresia → Present from birth rather than abrupt – failure of recanalization
  8. 9 month old with intermittent colicky pain, currant-jelly stool and a right upper quadrant mass → Intussusception → Age 6 months to 3 years, target sign on ultrasound
  9. Thriving 5 week old, exclusively breast-fed, blood-streaked stools, no distension and normal vitals → Milk protein-induced proctocolitis → A well infant – the whole point is that nothing else is wrong
  10. Neonate with abdominal distension and bloody stools; which diagnosis should not be entertained → Clostridioides difficile colitis → Neonates are colonized but lack the toxin receptors
  11. 10-hour-old term boy with bilious vomiting, born to a 39-year-old mother without prenatal care; voided once, no meconium yet; hypotonia, flat facies, upslanting palpebral fissures, protruding tongue, single transverse palmar creases and a sandal gap; abdomen soft and not distended; loud holosystolic murmur with a thrill at the left lower sternal border; nasogastric tube in place; film shows a double bubble with no distal gas → Surgical repair → Duodenal atresia in Down syndrome; the echocardiogram comes first because of the likely VSD
  12. 1-day-old girl with trisomy 21 features and bilious vomiting since the first feed; film shows a double bubble with no distal gas; nasogastric decompression and IV fluids started; vital signs stable, no murmur heard → Echocardiography → About half of infants with Down syndrome have heart disease, often silent at birth
  13. 3-day-old term boy with trisomy 21 features, no meconium since birth, bilious vomiting and progressive abdominal distension; film shows diffusely dilated loops of bowel → Hirschsprung disease → Contrast enema, then rectal suction biopsy
  14. 12-hour-old term girl who has not yet passed meconium; breastfeeding well, voided twice, no vomiting, soft nondistended abdomen, patent normally placed anus → Observation → Most term newborns pass meconium within 24 hours and none by 48 hours is delayed; a well, undistended 12-hour-old is not yet late
  15. 52 hour old term girl delivered by cesarean for arrest of labor, voiding but has not passed stool, with a tense distended abdomen and no stool or gas on rectal exam; upright film shows many dilated small-bowel loops with little gas in the colon and rectum, and a decubitus film shows free air; at emergency laparotomy thick, sticky stool is evacuated from the ileum and the colon is diffusely narrow → Chronic rhinosinusitis → Meconium ileus from cystic fibrosis; nasal polyps and sinus opacification follow
  16. 2 day old boy with no meconium since birth, progressive abdominal distension and bilious vomiting; rectal exam finds an empty rectum with no release of stool or gas; film shows dilated small-bowel loops; contrast enema shows a narrow microcolon with pellets of inspissated stool in the terminal ileum → Meconium ileus → Sweat chloride test for cystic fibrosis
  17. 2 day old boy without dysmorphic features, no meconium yet, abdominal distension and bilious vomiting; rectal exam finds a tight anal canal and is followed by an explosive release of normal-appearing stool and gas → Hirschsprung disease → Contrast enema, then rectal suction biopsy
  18. 2 day old girl with distension and no meconium; contrast enema shows a microcolon with inspissated meconium in the terminal ileum; vital signs stable, no free air on film, no signs of peritonitis → Hyperosmolar contrast enema → Uncomplicated meconium ileus; sweat chloride test for cystic fibrosis
  19. 2-day-old term girl born to a 38-year-old mother after a fentanyl epidural; feeding poorly, spit up her last feed, has not passed meconium; firm distended abdomen; shallow 2-mm sacral dimple with intact skin and no hair; rectal exam finds increased tone followed by a release of stool; normal strength and reflexes; abdominal film shows dilated bowel loops with no air in the rectum → Failure of neural crest cell migration → Hirschsprung disease; contrast enema, then rectal suction biopsy
  20. 4-day-old girl without dysmorphic features, no meconium since birth, poor feeding and a distended abdomen; rectal exam is followed by an explosive release of gas and normal-appearing stool; contrast enema shows a narrow rectosigmoid with dilated colon above it → Rectal suction biopsy → Absent ganglion cells confirm Hirschsprung disease; treatment is resection of the aganglionic segment
  21. 3-week-old boy in the NICU born at 28 weeks weighing 900 g, extubated to nasal cannula last week, on continuous nasogastric formula feeds and gaining weight, with small yellow seedy stools until none in the past 24 hours, now has 6 hours of nonbloody bilious vomiting; temperature 35.6 C, BP 75/45, pulse 165, respirations 70; lethargic, with a tense distended abdomen and hypoactive bowel sounds; leukocytosis and metabolic acidosis → Abdominal x-ray with air in the bowel wall and portal veins → Necrotizing enterocolitis; stop feeds, NG decompression and broad-spectrum antibiotics
  22. Girl born at 27 weeks weighing 950 g, now 4 days old, stable on room air in the NICU and about to start enteral feeds; her mother is expressing milk → Exclusive feeding with breast milk → The most effective measure against necrotizing enterocolitis
  23. 7-month-old boy with 6 hours of persistent bilious vomiting, no fever, diarrhea or recent illness, last bowel movement 24 hours ago and no prior surgery; temperature 37 C, BP 70/50, pulse 180, respirations 65; moans with light palpation of a distended, hypertympanic abdomen with absent bowel sounds → Intestinal malrotation with midgut volvulus → Emergency laparotomy, Ladd procedure
  24. 5-week-old term girl with 4 hours of bilious vomiting and inconsolable crying; after a 20 mL/kg saline bolus, pulse is 190, BP 55/30 and capillary refill 4 seconds; abdomen distended and diffusely tender; film shows a dilated stomach and duodenum with little distal gas → Emergency laparotomy → Unstable malrotation with midgut volvulus; Ladd procedure without waiting for contrast
Exit ramps Free air – stop investigating and operate · Unstable with bilious vomiting – laparotomy without waiting for contrast · In a term infant with NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis), look for the perfusion insult: cyanotic heart disease, hypotension, sepsis · NEC worsening despite bowel rest and antibiotics: surgery · Late NEC sequelae – strictures and short-bowel syndrome · Bilious emesis in any infant, at any age, is malrotation until an upper GI (gastrointestinal) series excludes it
Decoy note: delayed meconium Maternal fentanyl epidural – maternal opioids can slow the newborn bowel and delay meconium, but they do not raise rectal tone or cause an explosive release of stool on rectal exam · Mother aged 38 – advanced maternal age raises the risk of Down syndrome, which goes with Hirschsprung disease; most Hirschsprung disease is isolated, so a nondysmorphic infant still fits · Shallow sacral dimple with intact skin and no hair – a normal finding; spina bifida occulta severe enough to cause a neurogenic bowel brings a hair tuft or neurologic deficits, and this exam has normal strength and reflexes · Tight rectum, then a release of normal stool – the squirt sign; meconium ileus gives normal tone, no release, and inspissated meconium in the ileum
Duodenal atresia in Down syndrome The order – stop feeds, NG (nasogastric) decompression and IV (intravenous) fluids, echocardiogram, then surgical repair · Echocardiogram – about half of infants with Down syndrome have heart disease. A loud holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border is a VSD (ventricular septal defect) · No distension – the block is proximal, so the rest of the abdomen stays flat; distension points to a distal obstruction · Meconium timing – about 99% of healthy term newborns pass meconium within 24 hours, so a distended infant with none by then needs evaluation; none by 48 hours is delayed and raises Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus; a well, undistended newborn a few hours old is not yet late · Pyloric stenosis – nonbilious projectile vomiting at 3 to 6 weeks, not bilious emesis on day 1
Pearls Pneumatosis – gas made by bacteria that have invaded the wall, which is why it is specific · Bilious vomiting means the obstruction is distal to the ampulla; it is urgent until an upper GI (gastrointestinal) series excludes malrotation · NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis) and volvulus both give a distended, bilious, unwell neonate; the gas pattern separates them · A well infant with blood in the stool is almost never surgical; distension and instability suggest a surgical cause · Prematurity is the commonest NEC risk factor, not a required one · Meconium ileus means cystic fibrosis – nearly all patients with cystic fibrosis develop sinopulmonary disease, including chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (sinus opacification by age 1); hypothyroidism and early-onset Alzheimer disease belong to Down syndrome, which goes with Hirschsprung disease
NEC severity and prevention Mild: lethargy, temperature instability, apnea, feeding intolerance, bilious residuals, heme-positive stool; labs and film normal or mild dilation · Moderate: adds absent bowel sounds, tenderness, abdominal wall erythema, thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis and pneumatosis · Severe: adds hypotension, peritonitis, DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) and pneumoperitoneum · Platelets: the fall tracks severity, and a rising count is often the first sign of improvement · Prevention: exclusive breast milk is the most effective measure; antenatal corticosteroids for a mother likely to deliver preterm within 7 days also lower the risk, along with respiratory distress syndrome and intraventricular hemorrhage
Malrotation beyond the newborn period Age: most present in the first month, but volvulus can happen at any age. In a 7-month-old with bilious vomiting, tachycardia and a silent distended abdomen, malrotation is still the first diagnosis · Older children: intermittent abdominal pain and vomiting, sometimes failure to thrive · Late signs: hematochezia, peritonitis and shock mean the bowel is already ischemic · Not NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis): a disease of preterm infants in the first weeks on feeds · Not pyloric stenosis: that vomiting is nonbilious and projectile at 3 to 6 weeks, in a well infant with an olive-shaped mass
Pairs with Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers the well infant with blood in the stool; this brief covers the sick one. Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia covers obstruction above the pylorus. Ask: is the infant well, and what is the gas pattern?
Transferable rule In a distended neonate, the stool and vital signs show severity and the gas pattern identifies the disease: air in the wall, air where bowel should be, or no air at all.
Unchecked attributeIf NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis) is filed under prematurity, a term infant is ruled out without checking perfusion.
Salient decoyBilious nasogastric return pulls toward volvulus before the film is read.
Class-vs-memberRight category of neonatal bowel emergency, wrong member of it.
Sequencing trapKaryotype confirms trisomy 21, but it is not urgent and does not change the need for repair.
Redundant workupAn upper GI (gastrointestinal) series adds nothing once the film shows a double bubble with no distal gas; it is for malrotation.
Unchecked attributeNo meconium sounds like Hirschsprung disease, but a 10-hour-old is not yet late and the abdomen is not distended.
True-fact-wrong-slotEarly-onset Alzheimer disease and hypothyroidism are real Down syndrome associations, but Down syndrome goes with Hirschsprung disease; thick meconium in the ileum with a microcolon is meconium ileus, which means cystic fibrosis and later sinus disease.
Class-vs-memberInspissated meconium is the other cause of no meconium with distension, but it obstructs the ileum with a microcolon, normal rectal tone and no squirt; it is cystic fibrosis, not Hirschsprung disease.
Salient decoyA shallow sacral dimple without a hair tuft is normal; spinal cord dysfunction would bring neurologic deficits, and strength and reflexes are normal.
Salient decoyA maternal fentanyl epidural can cause neonatal ileus, but not increased rectal tone with an explosive release of stool.
Salient decoyBilious vomiting pulls toward a proximal block, but air in the stomach and duodenum with no distal gas is duodenal atresia, which presents with the first feeds; an infant who has been passing yellow seedy stools on full feeds is not obstructed there.
Salient decoyNo stool for a day suggests Hirschsprung disease, but that shows no meconium by 48 hours or chronic constipation, not sudden hypothermia, acidosis and a tense abdomen in a 3-week-old preterm infant.
Unchecked attributeNEC is the right category of sick distended bowel, but it belongs to preterm infants in their first weeks on feeds; a term 7-month-old with bilious vomiting has volvulus.
Unchecked attributePyloric stenosis causes vomiting in infancy, but it is nonbilious and projectile at 3 to 6 weeks; bilious vomiting in any infant is malrotation until proven otherwise.

edits.html:
Jaundice in a Newborn

timing, direct fraction and Coombs · the sick neonate with a positive screenIs the infant well, and is any of it direct?

WorkupCausesSick neonatePractice
Bottom line

Physiologic jaundice is a conjugation lag: fetal hemoglobin breaks down quickly while hepatic uridine diphosphate (UDP) glucuronosyltransferase is still immature, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates. A raised direct fraction makes newborn jaundice urgent.

  • Physiologic jaundice: begins after 24 hours, peaks around day 3 to 5, predominantly indirect, resolving by 1 to 2 weeks.
  • Pathologic jaundice: within the first 24 hours, any raised direct fraction, or persistence beyond 2 weeks.
  • Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia: direct bilirubin above 1.0 mg/dL; never physiologic and never breast-milk jaundice.
  • Classic galactosemia: galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency; galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in the liver. Conjugated jaundice, a large liver and a non-glucose reducing sugar in the urine after milk feeds; it predisposes to Escherichia coli sepsis.
  • Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency: indirect jaundice with anemia and Coombs-negative hemolysis, often after an oxidant.
Workup
Causes: timing and the direct fraction
Well or sick, indirect or direct
CauseWhenThe tell
PhysiologicAfter 24 hours, peak day 3 to 5Well infant, feeding and voiding normally; indirect; nothing but time
Suboptimal-intake (breast-feeding) jaundiceDay 3 to 5Weight loss, few wet diapers; feed more often, lactation support
Breast-milk jaundiceDay 7 onward, peak about 2 weeks, can persist weeksThriving, indirect, normal GGT and stools; continue breast-feeding
Blood group or Rh hemolytic diseaseOften within 24 hoursCoombs positive; mother group O or Rh-negative; high reticulocytes
G6PD deficiency Can't missVariable, can be abruptCoombs negative, anemia, high reticulocytes, often an oxidant; X-linked, mostly boys; Mediterranean, African or Asian ancestry; remove the trigger, phototherapy
Biliary atresia Can't missWell at birth; jaundice and hepatomegaly at 2 to 8 weeksDirect, high GGT and ALP, normal reticulocytes; acholic stools, dark urine; reducing substances negative
PFICInfancyDirect with a normal GGT; gallbladder present; specialist evaluation
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosisInfancy, acuteFebrile and ill; direct and GGT high, cytopenias, low reticulocytes, normal gallbladder; urgent hematology
Crigler-Najjar or GilbertPersistent indirectThe same enzyme absent or reduced, not immature; depends on type
Classic galactosemiaWithin days of milk feedsSick; conjugated jaundice, hepatomegaly, urine reducing substances
Numbers and gates Visible – above about 5 mg/dL · Physiologic ceiling – peak around 14 to 15 mg/dL, indirect over 90% · Exchange range – generally above 20 mg/dL; kernicterus risk rises at 25 to 30 mg/dL · Under 24 hours – never physiologic: bilirubin with a direct fraction and a Coombs · Any direct fraction – not physiologic: consider obstruction or infection · Beyond 2 weeks – check the direct fraction and the stool color before reassuring · Phototherapy versus exchange – phototherapy first; exchange for the severe range or signs of encephalopathy, not a level near threshold · Feeding – almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding; more milk increases bilirubin excretion through the gut
The sick neonate with a positive screen
Galactosemia: act now Stop – all lactose and galactose immediately, without waiting for confirmation, because the injury is ongoing · Feed – soy-based formula in place of breast milk and standard formula · In parallel – blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid cultures and empiric neonatal antibiotics for Escherichia coli · Confirm afterwards – red cell GALT activity · Urine test – needs recent intake, so a negative test after feeds stop does not exclude galactosemia
Screen-positive and sick: the liver and the urine name it
DiagnosisThe tell
Galactokinase deficiencyCataracts in a well infant; no liver disease, no sepsis
Congenital rubella syndromeCataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, blueberry muffin rash; present at birth, not triggered by milk
Hereditary fructose intoleranceAldolase B; same liver picture plus hypoglycemia, at weaning with fruit, juice or sucrose
Maple syrup urine diseaseEncephalopathy without hepatomegaly or cholestasis; sweet-smelling urine, ketosis
Practice
  1. 4-day-old boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery is jaundiced breast-feeding without difficulty; eight wet diapers daily alert; Apgar scores 10 and 10 Afebrile · total bilirubin 11 mg/dL → Immature UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity → a well infant, feeding and voiding normally, jaundiced on day 4 at 11 mg/dL has physiologic jaundice: fetal hemoglobin breaks down quickly while the conjugating enzyme is still immature, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates. Enterohepatic circulation is increased in the newborn, not decreased, and ligandin is low at birth, not high: real mechanisms stated in the wrong direction. Cholestasis would make the bilirubin direct, and albumin displacement needs a displacing drug
  2. 3-day-old girl born at term is seen at a follow-up visit newborn screen reported positive for galactosemia by telephone asymptomatic and breastfeeding well Afebrile · weight 3% below birth weight · no jaundice → Stop breastfeeding and start soy-based formula pending confirmation → presumptive galactosemia: stop all lactose and galactose immediately, without waiting for confirmation, because the injury is ongoing; replace breast milk with soy-based formula and confirm afterwards with red cell GALT activity. Continuing feeds continues the injury, and intravenous antibiotics answer a febrile or septic neonate, not this well one
  3. 6-week-old girl: ultrasound shows no gallbladder stools pale gray since week 3; urine dark jaundice deepening over 4 weeks; exclusively breastfed liver 2 cm below the costal margin Well-appearing, afebrile · HR 148/min · total bilirubin 10.2 mg/dL → Direct bilirubin high, GGT high, reticulocyte count normal → pale stools and an absent gallbladder mean bile duct destruction, which raises the direct fraction and the GGT while the reticulocytes stay normal: biliary atresia. A direct rise with a normal GGT is progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, and an indirect rise with high reticulocytes is hemolysis. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis also raises both, but in a febrile, ill infant with low reticulocytes. Exclusive breastfeeding suggests breast-milk jaundice, but that is indirect and leaves the stools yellow and the gallbladder normal. Intraoperative cholangiography confirms, then Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy
  4. 9-month-old girl has vomiting and jaundice began after juice and fruit were introduced liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances Afebrile · glucose 38 mg/dL → Hereditary fructose intolerance → aldolase B deficiency gives the same hepatic picture as galactosemia plus hypoglycemia, but it starts with fruit, juice or sucrose at weaning, months old rather than days; remove fructose, sucrose and sorbitol. Glycogen storage disease type I brings hypoglycemia within hours of fasting with no dietary trigger; essential fructosuria is the benign cousin, a urinary sugar with no illness
  5. 2-day-old girl born at term has jaundice to the chest infant blood group B, mother group O direct Coombs test positive Alert and breast-feeding well Afebrile · total bilirubin 19 mg/dL · direct 0.6 mg/dL → Phototherapy → a positive Coombs test with a group O mother is isoimmune hemolysis, still below the exchange range. Phototherapy comes first; exchange transfusion is for the severe range (generally above 20 mg/dL) or signs of encephalopathy, not a level near threshold. Jaundice is almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding: more milk increases bilirubin excretion through the gut
  6. 2-week-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia last week parents ask what she can be fed jaundice resolving on her current feeds Mother hopes to resume breastfeeding Afebrile · weight gain 25 g/day → Breast milk → breast milk and standard formula carry lactose, so they are replaced with soy-based formula; the diet reverses the acute illness. An elemental lactose-free formula carries no lactose either
  7. 4-day-old girl born at term is jaundiced exclusively breast-fed weight 11% below birth weight three wet diapers in the past day Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL, direct 0.4 mg/dL → Suboptimal-intake jaundice → weight loss and few wet diapers in the first week are a hungry infant: too little milk, not the milk itself, raising bilirubin through increased enterohepatic reabsorption (also called breast-feeding jaundice). Feed more often, with lactation support. Breast-milk jaundice is a thriving infant still jaundiced in the second week, and biliary atresia raises the direct fraction
  8. 10-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances Newborn screen flagged a disorder of galactose metabolism Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3 mg/dL → Red cell GALT enzyme activity → red cell GALT activity names the enzyme defect: absent or near absent in classic galactosemia, and invalid after transfusion. Reduced red cell GALT activity establishes the diagnosis, so red cell enzyme analysis confirms it without hepatic tissue, and a serum galactose level only supports it
  9. 6-week-old girl born at term has jaundice acholic stools and dark urine liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin exclusively breast-fed; gaining weight Afebrile · total bilirubin 8 mg/dL · direct bilirubin 5 mg/dL → Biliary atresia → a direct fraction is never physiologic, and acholic stools with dark urine at 2 to 8 weeks in an infant well at birth is duct obstruction. An exclusively breastfed infant can still have it: breast-milk jaundice is indirect, peaks around 2 weeks and leaves the stools yellow. Physiologic jaundice is predominantly indirect and resolves by 1 to 2 weeks
  10. 5-day-old boy born at term has poor feeding and lethargy seizures today urine smells like maple syrup Newborn screen reported positive T 36.9 °C · glucose 72 mg/dL · no hepatomegaly or jaundice → Leucine-free formula with dextrose → branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency (signs from day 2 to 3) is encephalopathy without hepatomegaly or cholestasis, with sweet-smelling urine and ketosis: the right class of screen-flagged inborn error to confuse with galactosemia, but it carries ketoacids, not a reducing sugar. Soy formula, the galactosemia substitute, still contains protein, including the branched-chain amino acids, so it keeps feeding the block; protein is given as amino acids free of the branched chains, with isoleucine and valine added back, so the formula is leucine-free, and high calories come as dextrose and lipid. Antibiotics with observation do not lower plasma leucine
  11. 5-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced to the abdomen breast-feeding poorly with few wet diapers dry mucous membranes; weight 10% below birth weight Afebrile · total bilirubin 16 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL → Increased enterohepatic reabsorption → the newborn gut reabsorbs bilirubin, so anything that slows transit raises the indirect fraction: too little milk slows it and lets intestinal bilirubin return to the circulation. Conjugation is immature in every newborn, and albumin displacement requires a displacing drug
  12. 10-day-old girl born at term vomits after starting formula jaundiced, with the liver 4 cm below the costal margin bilateral cataracts urine positive for reducing substances Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3 mg/dL → Classic galactosemia → conjugated jaundice with hepatomegaly, cataracts and urine reducing substances within days of milk feeds: liver, kidney, brain and lens are affected; eliminate galactose and lactose. Glycogen storage disease type I has no galactose trigger and no cataracts; hereditary fructose intolerance appears at weaning
  13. 14-hour-old boy born at term has visible jaundice of the face and chest breast-feeding well Uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery; examination otherwise normal Afebrile · HR 140/min · transcutaneous bilirubin 9 mg/dL → Total and direct bilirubin with a Coombs test → onset inside 24 hours is never physiologic, so it is pathologic until proven otherwise: send bilirubin with a direct fraction and a Coombs test. Hepatic ultrasound and serum albumin cannot show hemolysis or immature conjugation
  14. 3-week-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia at 1 week bilateral cataracts seen on red reflex examination on soy formula; jaundice resolving Liver edge now 1 cm below the costal margin Afebrile · weight gain 30 g/day → Galactitol accumulation via aldose reductase → cataracts in both galactose disorders come from galactitol, made by aldose reductase, the same enzyme that makes sorbitol in the diabetic lens: an osmotic lens injury. Galactokinase deficiency makes cataracts without ever forming galactose-1-phosphate, so the lens injury is galactitol, not galactose-1-phosphate; sorbitol is the diabetic product
  15. 4-day-old term boy of Greek descent is jaundiced to the abdomen feeding well Mother and infant both group A, Rh-positive direct Coombs negative; no spherocytes on smear hematocrit 36% · reticulocytes high · bilirubin 17 mg/dL, direct 0.6 mg/dL → G6PD enzyme activity level → Coombs-negative hemolysis (anemia with high reticulocytes) in a boy of Mediterranean ancestry is G6PD deficiency: X-linked, so mostly boys, and often an oxidant trigger. Osmotic fragility testing looks for spherocytosis, which the smear argues against, and a liver panel answers a raised direct fraction
  16. 8-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced vomits after breastfeeds liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances, dipstick glucose negative Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL → Stop breast milk and start soy-based formula → a conjugated fraction, a large liver and a non-glucose reducing sugar after days of milk feeds indicate classic galactosemia: stop breast milk now and start soy formula. Phototherapy treats an indirect rise, and continuing feeds continues the injury; the diet reverses the liver disease, so transplant evaluation is not the step
  17. 3-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced to the chest a sulfonamide is proposed for a suspected urinary tract infection Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity is normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 15 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL → Displacement of bilirubin from albumin → free bilirubin crosses into the basal ganglia. Sulfonamides and ceftriaxone displace bilirubin from albumin, so they are avoided in jaundiced newborns; when G6PD is deficient a sulfonamide also causes hemolysis, a second way it harms, excluded here by the normal enzyme. Glucuronosyltransferase activity sets how much bilirubin is conjugated and heme breakdown how much is made; the sulfonamide instead competes with bilirubin for albumin, raising the unbound fraction.
  18. 6-week-old boy born at term is well and growing bilateral cataracts on red reflex examination no hepatomegaly; no jaundice urine positive for reducing substances Passed newborn hearing screen; no murmur Afebrile · weight at the 50th percentile → Galactokinase deficiency → a block one step earlier diverts galactose to galactitol: cataracts in a well infant, with no liver disease and no sepsis; lactose-free diet. Classic galactosemia traps toxic galactose-1-phosphate and makes the whole sick-neonate picture; congenital rubella brings cataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, present at birth and not triggered by milk
  19. 4-week-old boy born at term is well and feeding well jaundiced, with acholic stools urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · weight at the 40th percentile · total bilirubin 7 mg/dL · direct bilirubin 5 mg/dL → Abdominal ultrasound and HIDA scan → a direct fraction in a well infant with acholic stools and negative reducing substances is biliary atresia: image first, then intraoperative cholangiogram confirms, and Kasai follows confirmation, before about 60 days. Phototherapy treats an indirect rise
  20. 3-day-old boy, formula-fed, has increasing lethargy and vomiting breathing rapidly; no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, clear lenses Urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · arterial pH 7.50, low carbon dioxide · ammonia markedly elevated · glucose 80 mg/dL → Urea cycle disorder → very high ammonia with lethargy and respiratory alkalosis in the first days of feeding, with no jaundice, hepatomegaly or cataracts: hyperammonemia; stop protein and lower the ammonia. Classic galactosemia brings conjugated jaundice, hepatomegaly and urine reducing sugar; maple syrup urine disease brings sweet-smelling urine and ketosis
  21. 4-day-old girl born at term is jaundiced exclusively breast-fed; weight 9% below birth weight only three wet diapers today; alert and well Afebrile · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL · direct 0.4 mg/dL → Stopping breast-feeding → this is suboptimal intake, and jaundice is almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding: feed more often, not less, because milk intake drives bilirubin out through the gut. Lactation support with more frequent feeds, and phototherapy if the level crosses threshold, are both appropriate
  22. 3-month-old boy has a protuberant abdomen and doll-like facies massive hepatomegaly hypoglycemia after a 4-hour fast No cataracts; urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · lactate 6 mmol/L · triglycerides 450 mg/dL · glucose 35 mg/dL → Glycogen storage disease type I → hepatomegaly with fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis and hypertriglyceridemia, with hypoglycemia within hours of fasting, no galactose trigger and no cataracts; treat with frequent cornstarch feeds. Galactosemia needs milk feeds and urine reducing sugar; hereditary fructose intolerance starts with fruit or sucrose at weaning
  23. 6-week-old boy born at term, jaundiced since 3 weeks of age clay-colored stools, dark urine ultrasound: small gallbladder, triangular cord sign intraoperative cholangiogram: no contrast reaches the duodenum Afebrile · direct bilirubin 6 mg/dL · GGT high → Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy → no contrast reaching the bowel confirms biliary atresia: Kasai before about 60 days, best done early, and most eventually need a liver transplant, so transplant is the later step, not the first. Ursodeoxycholic acid is given after the Kasai, not in place of it
  24. 12-day-old girl was diagnosed with galactosemia on day 6 on soy formula since diagnosis now lethargic and feeding poorly Jaundice improving; liver smaller T 38.8 °C · HR 186/min · capillary refill 3 seconds → Blood, urine and CSF cultures, then IV ampicillin and gentamicin → galactosemia predisposes to Escherichia coli sepsis, and a neonate with suspected sepsis gets a lumbar puncture once able to tolerate it: culture blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid, then start empiric neonatal antibiotics. Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin, so it is avoided in a jaundiced newborn, and observing off antibiotics leaves the infection untreated
  25. 3-week-old girl born at term is still jaundiced to the chest exclusively breastfed and gaining weight well yellow stools and pale urine Seen at a routine visit; examination otherwise normal Afebrile → Serum total and direct bilirubin → jaundice past 2 weeks needs a direct fraction, and the stool color, before reassurance; an indirect result in a thriving infant is breast-milk jaundice. A transcutaneous reading gives no direct fraction, and a Coombs test answers jaundice inside 24 hours, not prolonged jaundice
  26. 9-day-old breastfed girl has 3 days of vomiting and poor feeding jaundiced; liver 4 cm below the costal margin bilateral cataracts Normal hearing screen, no murmur; mother 39, declined vaccines T 38.4 °C · blood culture: Escherichia coli → Inability to metabolize galactose in breast milk → a milk-fed neonate with conjugated jaundice, a large liver, cataracts and Escherichia coli sepsis has classic galactosemia: stop breast milk and start soy formula without waiting for confirmation, and treat the sepsis in parallel. Congenital rubella, the vaccine decoy, brings cataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, present at birth; a normal hearing screen and no murmur argue against it. Classic galactosemia is autosomal recessive, so the mother's age is a decoy
  27. 2-year-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia on newborn screening fed soy formula since day 5 parents ask about her long-term outlook Afebrile · height and weight at the 50th percentile → Speech and learning problems and ovarian insufficiency can occur despite the diet → even with an early, strict diet, children can have cognitive deficits and speech problems (verbal dyspraxia), and girls develop primary ovarian insufficiency. The diet reverses the acute liver, sepsis and cataract illness but does not prevent these, so normal fertility is not expected, and neither is progressive cirrhosis
  28. 3-week-old boy born at term is still jaundiced at a weight check exclusively breast-fed and gaining weight well yellow stools; thriving Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 13 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL → Breast-milk jaundice → milk beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin and increases enterohepatic circulation: from day 7, peaking around 2 weeks and able to persist for weeks, in a thriving infant with normal stools; continue breast-feeding. Suboptimal intake is a hungry infant losing weight in the first week, and biliary atresia raises the direct fraction and turns the stools pale
How NBME framed it: question 1

5-day-old boy of Mediterranean descent with 2 days of progressive jaundice Five yellow, seedy stools a day; 2 ounces of cow's milk formula every 2 hours Born at term to a 32-year-old primigravida, who took an old sulfamethoxazole prescription for cystitis in the third trimester Mother and infant both group O, Rh-positive examination normal except jaundice from the head to the upper thighs hematocrit 33% · total bilirubin 20 mg/dL, direct 0.9 mg/dL direct and indirect Coombs tests negative

Most likely explanation for the jaundice?

Competing answers
  • Dehydration: raises indirect bilirubin through enterohepatic reabsorption; but feeds every 2 hours and five stools a day argue against it, and it does not cause anemia.
  • Sepsis: can raise indirect bilirubin; but he is well on examination, and Coombs-negative anemia after an oxidant exposure points to hemolysis.
  • Milk protein allergy: the cow's milk formula is the decoy; allergy causes reflux, enterocolitis, enteropathy or urticaria, not hemolysis.

Down to two: enzyme deficiency or physiologic jaundice. Enzyme deficiency: a total of 20 mg/dL exceeds the physiologic peak of about 15, and a hematocrit of 33% points to hemolysis. A negative Coombs removes isoimmune hemolysis; Mediterranean ancestry and a maternal sulfonamide point to G6PD deficiency. G6PD makes NADPH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate), which keeps glutathione reduced; without it, sulfonamides and other oxidants cause hemolysis. The key named only the class.

Read three labs together Direct high, GGT high, reticulocytes normal – duct obstruction: biliary atresia in a well infant with pale stools · Direct high, GGT normal – progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis · Direct and GGT high, reticulocytes low, cytopenias – hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in a febrile, ill infant · Indirect, reticulocytes high – hemolysis · Indirect, everything else normal – breast-milk jaundice in a thriving infant; an exclusively breastfed infant can still have biliary atresia, so pale stools and a direct fraction decide it
The galactose pathway Reducing substances positive with dipstick glucose negative means galactose or fructose, because glucose is itself a reducing sugar, so read both tests. Galactokinase makes galactose-1-phosphate, and GALT converts it to uridine diphosphate galactose and glucose-1-phosphate. A galactokinase block leaves only galactitol, so cataracts alone; a GALT block traps toxic galactose-1-phosphate, so the whole sick-neonate picture, affecting liver, kidney, brain and lens. Cataracts in both come from galactitol via aldose reductase, the enzyme that makes sorbitol in the diabetic lens. Even with an early, strict diet, children can have cognitive deficits and speech problems, and girls develop primary ovarian insufficiency.
Common wrong answers Ligandin or enterohepatic circulation: real mechanisms stated in the wrong direction (ligandin is low and enterohepatic circulation increased in the newborn). Exchange transfusion at a level still in the phototherapy range. Maple syrup urine disease for a sick jaundiced neonate: the right class of screen-flagged inborn error, but no hepatomegaly, and ketoacids rather than a reducing sugar. Cystic fibrosis because the screen is positive: screened by immunoreactive trypsinogen, it presents with meconium ileus or quiet cholestasis, not fever with urinary sugar. Sickle cell or neonatal hyperthyroidism: screen-positive with no hepatic picture; sickle cell jaundice is unconjugated and silent at 10 days because fetal hemoglobin protects. Urea cycle disorder: very high ammonia with lethargy and respiratory alkalosis, but no jaundice, hepatomegaly or cataracts. Glycogen storage disease type I: hypoglycemia within hours of fasting with lactic acidosis, but no galactose trigger and no cataracts. Sulfonamides and ceftriaxone displace bilirubin from albumin, and a sulfonamide also causes hemolysis when G6PD is deficient.
Exam answer versus current evidence Board questions use 60 days as the Kasai cutoff, and the Kasai is ideally done before 60 days. The evidence shows no sharp cutoff: native-liver survival falls continuously with age at operation, and a 2023 meta-analysis found operating at 30 days or earlier still better than at 31 to 60 days. Use 60 days as the exam threshold, not as a deadline with room to spare.
Pairs with Part I Abnormal Liver Tests: the conjugated-versus-unconjugated workup in adults. Hereditary fructose intolerance has no brief of its own: did symptoms start with fruit or sucrose? Biliary atresia: is the infant sick or well, and are reducing substances present? Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism: another positive newborn screen, where the thyroid-stimulating hormone level and the neck locate the defect; in galactosemia, the enzyme deficiency and the organism locate it.
Transferable rule

When every option names a real mechanism, check which direction each one moves in this patient before choosing. A positive newborn screen never names the disease when every disorder under consideration is on the panel: the bilirubin fraction, the liver and the urine identify it, and a febrile neonate is cultured and treated for sepsis in parallel with the metabolic diagnosis, not after it.
