edits.html:
Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child

protein on a routine dipstick in a well child · nephrotic or nephritic · the lesion, and the age-directed search for its causeIs the protein still there in a first-morning urine, are there red cells and casts, and how old is the patient?

Routine dipstickWhich lesionMembranousPractice
Bottom line
  • Orthostatic proteinuria: protein in urine made while upright, with a normal first-morning sample after lying down all night; most common in adolescent boys.
  • Transient proteinuria: protein during fever, exercise, stress, cold or dehydration that is gone on a repeat once the trigger passes.
  • Persistent proteinuria: a first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio above 0.2 mg/mg (above 0.5 at 6 to 24 months), or protein with an abnormal urinalysis; it needs a renal workup.
  • Nephrotic syndrome: proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia; blood pressure and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) usually normal, which is what separates it from nephritic disease.
  • Minimal change disease: about 80% of nephrotic syndrome in children, and the default in a young child.
  • Membranous nephropathy: subepithelial immune deposits with granular immunoglobulin G (IgG) and complement component 3 (C3) along the capillary loops; usually primary in adults, rare and usually secondary in children.
Protein on a routine dipstick in a well child

A well child with protein on a routine dipstick most likely has transient or orthostatic proteinuria; both are benign, so the first step is to repeat the urinalysis, before any imaging, steroids or biopsy. Protein with blood, hypertension or edema points to glomerular disease from the start: that child goes straight to the renal workup.

Management ladder: incidental proteinuria in a well child
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Repeat the urine on a first-morning sample, after any fever or hard exercise has passed: dipstick, microscopy and protein-to-creatinine ratio; a bedtime sample alongside shows the orthostatic patternFirst-morning ratio above 0.2 mg/mg, or blood, casts, hypertension or edema
StopNormal first-morning sample (ratio 0.2 mg/mg or less, or 0.5 or less at 6 to 24 months, with a normal urinalysis): reassure and repeat a first-morning dipstick in 1 yearProtein returns on a first-morning sample
2Persistent proteinuria: complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine; add albumin, complement or renal ultrasound as the history and exam directHematuria, hypertension, low complement, falling kidney function or signs of vasculitis
3Pediatric nephrology referral; renal biopsy is considered for those featuresTop rung
Protein on a routine dipstick: the differential
DiagnosisThe tellIn a well adolescent
Orthostatic proteinuriaBenign upright leak; protein at bedtime, none on wakingCommon in adolescent boys; the timed repeat confirms it
Transient proteinuriaA trigger; gone on any repeat once wellNo recent trigger; the same repeat sorts it out
Nephrotic syndromeMinimal change disease in a young child; edema, 3+ to 4+ protein, ratio above 2 mg/mg, low albuminNormal examination, no edema
GlomerulonephritisPoststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy, lupus; blood and red cell casts, hypertension, rising creatinineNormal blood pressure; protein is the only urine finding
Edema and heavy protein: which lesion
The child with proteinuria: nephrotic versus nephritic, then which lesion
LesionMechanism and tellAgainst it when the biopsy shows membranous
Minimal change diseaseCytokine podocyte injury; abrupt onset, no hematuria, normal blood pressure; normal light microscopy, negative immunofluorescence, foot process effacement on electron microscopySubacute course and a positive immunofluorescence
Membranous nephropathyImmune complexes, the nephrotic exception; subacute; adult primary, child secondaryThe diagnosis; the question is its cause
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisImmune complexes about 2 to 4 weeks after strep pharyngitis, up to about 6 weeks after impetigo; nephritic: hematuria, hypertension, raised creatinine, low C3No red cells, normal blood pressure and creatinine
Alport syndromeX-linked type IV collagen defect; hematuria plus sensorineural hearing loss; family historyNo hematuria; membranous is not associated with deafness
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)Glomerular sclerosis; obesity, African ancestry, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV); segmental sclerosis on light microscopy; often hematuria, hypertension and steroid resistanceBiopsy already names membranous
AmyloidosisOlder adults; amyloid A (AA) after chronic inflammation, slowly progressive; amyloid light chain (AL) from a plasma cell clone; deposits can give a restrictive cardiomyopathy; apple-green birefringenceImmune deposits, not amyloid; wrong age, and rare in children
Membranous nephropathy: age directs the search

When the biopsy already names membranous nephropathy, only the search for a cause remains. In adults it is usually primary (autoantibodies to endogenous podocyte antigens) and once infection, autoimmune disease and drugs are excluded the search ends with malignancy screening for age; in children it is rare and usually secondary, so a pediatric case is secondary until proven otherwise, and finding the cause is the management. The highest-yield cause is hepatitis B: circulating immune complexes of hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) and anti-HBeAg deposit subepithelially and produce exactly this picture.

Practice
  1. 17-year-old boy has 1 month of facial puffiness and fatigue periorbital and pretibial edema urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells, no casts renal biopsy: subepithelial deposits, granular IgG and C3 BP 110/70 mm Hg · albumin 2.2 g/dL · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Hepatitis B serologies → membranous nephropathy in a child is usually secondary, so the biopsy names the lesion but obliges a search for its cause, and hepatitis B is the highest-yield cause to test. Antistreptolysin O chases poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which needs hematuria and hypertension, and strep is not associated with membranous; stopping leaves the cause unfound, and in a child finding it is the management
  2. 15-year-old boy at a sports physical afternoon dipstick: 2+ protein; a second afternoon sample a week later shows the same first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.1 mg/mg microscopy normal BP 116/70 mm Hg · examination normal → Orthostatic proteinuria → protein in urine made upright with a normal first-morning ratio (0.2 mg/mg or less) is orthostatic proteinuria: reassure and repeat a first-morning dipstick in 1 year. Transient protein follows fever, exercise or dehydration and is gone on any repeat; persistent proteinuria needs a first-morning ratio above 0.2 mg/mg or an abnormal urinalysis
  3. 11-year-old boy with 2+ protein and 2+ blood on a routine dipstick microscopy shows red cell casts no edema Well; no recent fever or hard exercise BP 138/90 mm Hg → Referral to pediatric nephrology → protein with blood, casts and hypertension is glomerular disease from the start, not a benign pattern, so it goes straight to the renal workup and pediatric nephrology. A first-morning repeat is for protein alone in a well child, and a prednisone trial treats nephrotic syndrome, while this boy has no edema and no diagnosis yet
  4. 4-year-old boy has periorbital swelling that began abruptly urinalysis: 4+ protein, no blood renal biopsy: light microscopy normal, immunofluorescence negative electron microscopy: diffuse foot process effacement Afebrile · BP 94/56 mm Hg → Minimal change disease → abrupt onset with normal light microscopy, negative immunofluorescence and foot process effacement on electron microscopy is minimal change disease; a typical young child is treated with empiric corticosteroids without a biopsy, which is kept for atypical features. Membranous shows subepithelial deposits with granular IgG and C3 and a subacute onset; focal segmental glomerulosclerosis shows segmental sclerosis on light microscopy
  5. 58-year-old man has 6 weeks of leg swelling biopsy: subepithelial deposits with granular IgG and C3 hepatitis B, hepatitis C and syphilis serologies negative antinuclear antibody and thyroid studies normal Takes no medications BP 128/80 mm Hg · albumin 2.4 g/dL → Malignancy screening for his age → with infection, autoimmune disease (lupus, thyroiditis) and drugs excluded, the leading remaining secondary association in an adult is malignancy, mostly solid tumors, so screen as appropriate for his age. A repeat biopsy names the same lesion again but not its cause, and stopping is almost never right while a secondary-cause list remains
  6. 9-year-old girl with acute otitis media has 1+ protein on a dipstick T 39.2 °C 2 weeks later she is afebrile afternoon and first-morning urines both negative for protein Otherwise healthy → Transient proteinuria → protein during a fever that is gone on a repeat once the trigger passes is transient proteinuria and needs no further testing. Orthostatic proteinuria keeps protein in the upright afternoon sample, and persistent proteinuria keeps it on the first-morning sample
  7. 4-year-old girl has 5 days of periorbital and ankle swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no blood creatinine and complement levels normal Previously healthy; growth normal Afebrile · BP 94/58 mm Hg · albumin 1.9 g/dL → Oral prednisone without a renal biopsy → a typical young child with edema, pure 4+ proteinuria and a normal blood pressure, creatinine and complement has presumed minimal change disease: corticosteroids without a biopsy, and most children remit. Biopsy is for an older child or atypical features, and furosemide alone with a repeat urinalysis delays the corticosteroids that bring the remission
  8. 8-year-old boy has cola-colored urine Sore throat 2 weeks ago No prior episodes of dark urine urinalysis: blood and red cell casts BP 140/90 mm Hg · creatinine 1.6 mg/dL · C3 low → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → a nephritic picture about 2 to 4 weeks after strep pharyngitis (up to about 6 weeks after impetigo), with hematuria, hypertension, a raised creatinine and a low C3, is poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis: supportive care and blood pressure control. Membranous is nephrotic, with protein and usually no red cells or casts; IgA nephropathy brings hematuria during or within days of a respiratory infection, not 2 weeks later
  9. 16-year-old boy with chronic hepatitis B has 1 month of leg swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells biopsy: granular IgG and C3 along the capillary loops electron microscopy: subepithelial deposits BP 112/70 mm Hg · albumin 2.0 g/dL → Deposited hepatitis B e antigen immune complexes → circulating immune complexes of hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) and anti-HBeAg deposit in the subepithelial space and give the granular IgG and C3 along the loops. That granular IgG is antibody in the deposits, so neither direct viral injury to the podocytes nor complement activation alone accounts for the picture
  10. 16-year-old boy with 1+ protein on a dipstick at a sports physical no blood in the urine No fever, illness or hard exercise this week Examination normal BP 114/70 mm Hg → First-morning urine protein-to-creatinine ratio → a first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.2 mg/mg or less on waking fits orthostatic or transient proteinuria. An afternoon sample is made upright, so it shows the orthostatic leak rather than excluding it, and the spot ratio replaces the 24-hour collection, which is impractical in children
  11. 5-year-old girl: serum albumin 1.7 g/dL; urine protein 4+ with no blood and no casts 2 weeks of swollen eyelids, pitting leg edema, mild ascites Body mass index 97th percentile before this illness BP 98/60 mm Hg · HR 96/min → Cytokine-induced glomerular injury → pure proteinuria with no blood, a normal blood pressure and dependent edema at age 5 is minimal change disease: T-cell cytokines such as interleukin 13 injure the podocytes. Obesity is a real focal segmental glomerulosclerosis association, but that lesion is far less common at age 5 and usually brings hematuria and hypertension; immune complex deposition (poststreptococcal, membranoproliferative) brings hematuria, and membranous, the immune complex exception without hematuria, is rare at age 5
  12. 13-year-old boy with 2+ protein on a dipstick at a well visit first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.6 mg/mg on two separate days microscopy: no blood or casts BP 108/66 mm Hg · no edema → Complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine → a first-morning ratio above 0.2 mg/mg is persistent proteinuria, which needs a basic renal workup; albumin, complement or a renal ultrasound are added as the history and examination direct. Reassurance is only for a normal first-morning sample, and biopsy is considered after hematuria, hypertension, low complement, falling kidney function or signs of vasculitis appear
  13. 12-year-old boy has persistent microscopic hematuria on repeated urinalyses Two maternal uncles have kidney failure No sore throat or recent illness; growth normal No edema; examination otherwise normal Afebrile · BP 108/66 mm Hg · creatinine 0.6 mg/dL → Audiology evaluation → persistent hematuria with kidney failure in maternal uncles points to Alport syndrome, an X-linked type IV collagen defect whose partner finding is sensorineural hearing loss, so test hearing. Hepatitis B serologies search for the cause of membranous nephropathy, which is nephrotic; antistreptolysin O chases poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows strep pharyngitis by about 2 to 4 weeks (impetigo by up to about 6) with hypertension and a raised creatinine
  14. 17-year-old girl has 5 weeks of facial and ankle swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells or casts biopsy: granular IgG and C3, subepithelial deposits No serologies sent yet BP 108/68 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Stopping the workup at the biopsy → membranous nephropathy in a child is usually secondary, so stopping at the biopsy leaves the cause unfound, and in a child finding the cause is the management. Hepatitis B and C serologies and an antinuclear antibody (for systemic lupus erythematosus) are the secondary-cause search and should go ahead
  15. 66-year-old man has 3 months of leg swelling and exertional dyspnea urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells echocardiography: restrictive cardiomyopathy renal biopsy: apple-green birefringence with Congo red stain BP 118/72 mm Hg · albumin 2.1 g/dL → Amyloidosis → nephrotic-range protein in an older adult with apple-green birefringence and a restrictive cardiomyopathy is amyloidosis, and echocardiography shows the cardiac involvement. The biopsy shows amyloid, not the immune deposits with granular IgG and C3 of membranous nephropathy or the normal light microscopy of minimal change disease
  16. 14-year-old boy with 3+ protein on a dipstick at a routine visit no edema no blood in the urine No repeat sample collected yet; feels well BP 110/68 mm Hg → Trial of oral prednisone → steroids treat nephrotic syndrome, not an unconfirmed dipstick finding; this boy has no edema and no diagnosis yet. A first-morning repeat and urine microscopy for red cells and casts are the right first steps
  17. 15-year-old boy with severe obesity has 2 months of leg swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein and microscopic hematuria no remission after a full course of prednisone Afebrile · BP 138/90 mm Hg → Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis → obesity with hematuria, hypertension and steroid resistance points to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (segmental sclerosis on light microscopy), and these atypical features earn a renal biopsy. Minimal change disease brings no hematuria, a normal blood pressure and a steroid response; membranous is subacute, usually secondary in a child, and its blood pressure is typically normal
How NBME framed it: question 1

12-year-old boy at a well-child visit No illnesses since his visit a year ago HR 102/min · respiratory rate 21/min · BP 102/60 mm Hg examination normal urinalysis: 3+ protein

Most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Intravenous pyelography: images the collecting system for anatomic lesions and strictures; but it cannot show whether the protein persists.
  • Trial of corticosteroids: treats nephrotic syndrome; but this boy has no edema and no diagnosis yet, and transient or orthostatic proteinuria is benign.
  • Renal biopsy: diagnoses persistent glomerular disease; but it is invasive and comes only after persistence or red-flag features are shown.

Down to two: repeat urinalysis at bedtime and on waking, or renal ultrasonography. Repeat urinalysis at bedtime and on waking: a well boy with protein on one dipstick most likely has transient or orthostatic proteinuria, and orthostatic proteinuria, common in adolescent boys, shows protein at bedtime and a normal first-morning sample. Ultrasonography looks for obstruction, abscess, cysts or masses and cannot show whether the protein persists; it is at most a later, selective test. The key named the timed procedure, not orthostatic proteinuria.

Membranous nephropathy Hepatitis B – evaluating every patient with membranous nephropathy for it is recommended; in a child it is close to mandatory · Secondary causes – infection (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis), malignancy (solid tumors in adults), autoimmune disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, thyroiditis), drugs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, penicillamine) · Tempo – gradual podocyte damage gives a subacute onset over weeks to a month; deposits accumulate slowly, while foot processes efface suddenly in minimal change disease · Course – blood pressure and GFR typically normal; partial or complete remission common, end-stage disease rare
Minimal change disease Mechanism – T-cell dysregulation releases cytokines such as interleukin 13 that injure podocytes; the capillary wall loses its charge selectivity, anionic albumin leaks, and low oncotic pressure gives dependent edema (periorbital, scrotal, pretibial) · Diagnosis – clinical; biopsy only for atypical features · Treatment – corticosteroids without a biopsy; most children remit, relapse is common, and the risk of chronic kidney disease is low when steroid responsive · Obesity – a real FSGS association, but FSGS is far less common at age 5 and usually brings hematuria and hypertension; no hematuria, a normal blood pressure and a pure 4+ protein urinalysis mean minimal change disease
Read the urine Nephrotic versus nephritic is settled on the urinalysis, not the protein: 4+ protein with hypoalbuminemia and edema, without red cells or casts and with a normal blood pressure and creatinine, is nephrotic; red cells, hypertension and a rising creatinine are nephritic. Deposits: subepithelial is membranous, subendothelial is lupus nephritis, mesangial is IgA nephropathy. Up to 10% of school-age children show protein on a single screen; with repeated testing, about 0.1% do. Orthostatic proteinuria affects about 2% to 5% of adolescents, more often boys, and long-term follow-up shows no progressive kidney disease. A first-morning spot ratio replaces the 24-hour collection, which is impractical in children. A dipstick can read falsely positive in very concentrated urine (specific gravity above 1.030) or alkaline urine (pH above 8).
Common wrong answers After a membranous biopsy in a teenager: no additional workup: the biopsy names the lesion but not the cause, and stopping is almost never right when a secondary-cause list exists. Antistreptolysin O: poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is nephritic, with hematuria, hypertension and a raised creatinine. Audiology: deafness belongs to Alport syndrome, which presents with hematuria, not nephrotic-range protein. Echocardiography: amyloidosis pairs nephrotic syndrome with cardiac disease, but a membranous biopsy shows immune deposits, and a teenager is the wrong age. Renal biopsy for a well child's dipstick: invasive, and only after persistence or red-flag features. Corticosteroid trial: treats nephrotic syndrome, and the well child has no edema and no diagnosis. Renal ultrasonography and intravenous pyelography: they look for obstruction, abscess, cysts, masses, anatomic lesions or strictures, and cannot show whether the protein persists.
Pairs with Part I Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome: the nephritic side of this fork, the Alport link, the parallel well child with isolated microscopic hematuria, and red cells, hypertension, a rising creatinine and a low C3 weeks after strep. Aquifer Child with Puffy Eyes: from the chief complaint to this diagnosis, with relapse, peritonitis, thrombosis and vaccines in the nephrotic child.
Transferable rule

In a well child with protein on a routine dipstick, repeat the urine on a first-morning sample before any imaging, steroids or biopsy; only protein that persists on waking, or protein with blood, hypertension or edema, needs a renal workup. When a biopsy diagnosis is given, decide what it obliges you to do next: ask what the disease is associated with, and let the patient's age decide whether that list is the priority or an afterthought.

Cyanosis in the Newborn

lung, heart or airway before a lesion · work of breathing, oxygen response, two limbs · normal exam: the trigger decidesIs he working to breathe, does oxygen help, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing?

Source vignette Pt – 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen · Imaging – ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned respiratory distress syndrome, d-transposition of the great arteries and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
The decision point

Three bedside findings settle the sort before any lesion is considered. He is working to breathe (grunting, flaring and retracting); cyanotic heart disease produces comfortable tachypnea, not distress. His saturation rises from 65% to 92% on oxygen. That cannot happen in d-transposition, where systemic flow bypasses the lungs entirely. The two limbs read the same, so nothing is shunting right-to-left across the duct. That leaves parenchymal disease. A 32-week infant with ground-glass opacification and air bronchograms has surfactant deficiency: respiratory distress syndrome.

Sometimes the examination is instead a list of normals: no murmur, symmetric pulses, equal four-extremity pressures, clear lungs, no retractions, no stridor. These normals already exclude lung and heart. The remaining finding is temporal. Ask: What brings the cyanosis on, and what relieves it? Cyanosis on latching that clears with crying is nasal obstruction, because neonates are obligate nasal breathers and crying opens the oral airway. The inverse pattern, cyanosis worsened by crying, is a tet spell.

Defining criteria Oxygen responsiveness – saturation rises substantially with supplemental oxygen in alveolar disease; it does not in d-transposition, because most systemic flow bypasses the pulmonary vasculature · Preductal vs. postductal – the right upper extremity is preductal and the lower extremities postductal; a higher preductal saturation means right-to-left ductal shunting · Ductal closure clock – the ductus arteriosus begins to constrict as early as 12 hours after birth, so ductal-dependent lesions declare after that, not at minutes · RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) risk – inversely related to gestational age, highest at ≤28 weeks; antenatal glucocorticoids reduce but do not eliminate it · Bilateral choanal atresia – incomplete canalization of the posterior nasal passage; cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying, with noisy breathing (stertor), symptomatic shortly after birth · Why crying relieves it – neonates are obligate nasal breathers; hypoxia and hypercapnia trigger crying, which opens the oral airway and temporarily bypasses the obstruction · The bedside test – inability to pass a catheter through the nares into the oropharynx, confirmed by CT (computed tomography) or nasal endoscopy · The stability gate – a cyanotic newborn whose hypoxemia does not correct on oxygen gets echocardiography, and prostaglandin E1 is added when the infant is hemodynamically unstable, because instability is what raises concern for a ductal-dependent lesion
Pertinent positives & negatives Grunting, flaring, retractions – work of breathing; this is lung disease, and it excludes the two structural cardiac options, which give tachypnea without distress · 65% → 92% on oxygen – the alveoli can be recruited; excludes d-transposition outright · Right upper and left lower extremity both 65% – no ductal gradient; argues against persistent pulmonary hypertension and against a coarctation presentation · Cyanosis at minutes of life – too early for ductal closure, which begins at about 12 hours; coarctation cannot yet have declared · 32 weeks, 1.7 kg – the base rate for surfactant deficiency; RDS incidence rises as gestational age falls · Ground-glass with air bronchograms and low lung volumes – RDS; transient tachypnea gives perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissures, and pulmonary hypertension a clear or oligemic film · Grade 1/6 systolic murmur – soft and non-specific, consistent with a physiologically open duct rather than a structural lesion · A dose of antenatal glucocorticoids – lowers the risk but never excludes the diagnosis · PPROM (preterm prelabor rupture of membranes) – raises concern for group B streptococcal pneumonia even after intrapartum penicillin; that pneumonia is clinically very hard to tell from RDS · Acrocyanosis – peripheral cyanosis of hands, feet, and circumoral area with pink mucous membranes is a normal finding in the first 24–48 hours of life; central cyanosis (mucous membranes blue) requires workup
Cyanosis in the newborn: sorting by physiology
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME (National Board of Medical Examiners) tellExcluded here by
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiency; alveolar collapse minutes to hours after birthDistress plus oxygen responsiveness plus ground-glass with air bronchograms in a preterm infant(the answer)
Transient tachypnea of the newbornRetained fetal lung fluid; term or late pretermMild distress and cyanosis; perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissuresSevere distress; the film is ground-glass, not streaky
Persistent pulmonary hypertension Can't missHigh pulmonary vascular resistance; right-to-left ductal shuntPreductal saturation above postductal; film often normal, poorly oxygen-responsiveEqual limb saturations; oxygen worked; the film is abnormal
d-Transposition of the great arteriesParallel circulations; deoxygenated blood to the bodyCyanosis without retractions, and oxygen does not helpGrunting and retractions; 65% to 92% on oxygen
Coarctation of the aortaDuctal-dependent systemic flow; shock when the duct shutsPostductal saturation below preductal, presenting after ~12 hoursEqual limb saturations at 30 minutes of life
Cyanosis with a normal examination: sorting by trigger
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Bilateral choanal atresiaPosterior nasal passage fails to canalize; the obligate nasal breather obstructs whenever his mouth closesWorse with feeding, better with crying; stertor; catheter will not pass(the answer)
Tetralogy of FallotRight ventricular outflow obstruction; a spell when systemic resistance fallsCyanosis worse with crying and agitation (the inverted trigger) plus a murmurCrying makes him pink; there is no murmur
Transposition of the great arteriesParallel circulations; deoxygenated blood to the bodyConstant cyanosis unchanged by feeding or crying, unimproved by oxygenThe cyanosis comes and goes with what he is doing
Tracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresiaAspiration through a fistula or from a blind pouchCoughing and choking with feeds, respiratory distress, a tube that coilsHe fed well without coughing; lungs are clear
LaryngomalaciaSupraglottic collapse on inspirationInspiratory stridor worse supine and with exertion; cyanosis uncommonNo stridor at all
Transient tachypnea of the newbornRetained fetal lung fluid after deliveryTachypnea with flaring, retractions and grunting in the first hoursNo respiratory distress of any kind
MethemoglobinemiaOxidized hemoglobin iron cannot carry oxygenPersistent cyanosis that does not improve with crying or with oxygenHis cyanosis clears every time he cries
Neonatal sepsisBacterial infection with varied, nonspecific signsTemperature instability, lethargy, poor feedingNormal temperature; vigorous; blue only at the breast
Intraventricular hemorrhageGerminal matrix bleed, mainly in preterm infantsLethargy, hypotonia, apnea, seizures; found on head ultrasoundTerm infant with a normal neurologic picture
Management, in one line Support RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) with CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure). Reserve mechanical ventilation and exogenous surfactant for severe or failing cases. In the heart branch, management is instead a prostaglandin infusion to hold the duct open; in the pulmonary-hypertension branch, it is oxygen and inhaled nitric oxide. For the nasal obstruction, the first step is an oral airway with orogastric feeding to bypass the obstruction, and definitive treatment is surgical repair.
Decision spine Is he working to breathe? – Grunting, flaring, retracting → lung, not heart · Does oxygen help? – 65% to 92% → not a fixed right-to-left shunt, so not transposition · Do the limbs differ? – No → nothing is shunting across the duct · How old is he? – Thirty minutes → the duct is still open; ductal-dependent lesions have not declared · What does the film show? – Ground-glass with air bronchograms in a 32-weeker → surfactant deficiency · If every examination finding is normal – sort by the trigger: worse with feeding and better with crying is nasal obstruction; worse with crying is a tet spell; unchanged by either is a fixed shunt.
FigureApproach to neonatal cyanosisshow

Redrawn rather than reproduced. The one deliberate change from the usual published version: echocardiography and prostaglandin are shown as separate steps with the stability gate between them, because bundling them is what makes the sequencing question hard.

Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Pulse oximetry, right hand and a footFirstPreductal higher than postductalRight-to-left ductal shunt: PPHN (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn), or coarctation after about 12 hours
Trial of 100% oxygenNextSaturation rises substantiallyLung disease; no rise means a fixed shunt such as transposition
Chest radiographNextGround-glass with air bronchograms and low volumesRDS in a preterm; streaking with fissure fluid is transient tachypnea of the newborn
Catheter through each narisBy branchCatheter will not passChoanal atresia when cyanosis worsens with feeding and clears with crying
CT or nasal endoscopyConfirmsPosterior nasal obstructionChoanal atresia; look for the rest of CHARGE
EchocardiographyConfirmsStructural lesion or high pulmonary pressuresHypoxemia that oxygen does not correct; prostaglandin E1 added only if unstable
Any testing for acrocyanosisSkipPink mucous membranesNormal in the first 24 to 48 hours: reassurance
Echocardiogram, methemoglobin level, blood cultures or head ultrasound for cyanosis only with feedsSkipNormal oximetry, pulses, heart exam and film; pink when cryingPass the catheter first; nothing in the exam points to the heart, the blood, infection or the brain
Scenario bank
  1. 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen, ground-glass with air bronchograms → Respiratory distress syndrome → Surfactant deficiency
  2. 32 wk with respiratory distress syndrome at 30 minutes of life, breathing spontaneously → Start CPAP → Surfactant and intubation are reserved for severe disease
  3. 32 wk on CPAP with a rising oxygen requirement and worsening retractions at 6 hours → Intubate and give exogenous surfactant → CPAP has failed
  4. Term newborn at 14 hours, cyanosis with comfortable tachypnea and no retractions, clear lungs, a loud single S2, equal pulses, saturation unchanged on 100% oxygen → Obtain echocardiography → an anatomic right-to-left shunt; prostaglandin is added only if the infant is unstable
  5. Term after meconium-stained fluid, distress, right hand 95% and foot 78%, film clear with decreased vascularity → Inhaled nitric oxide → Persistent pulmonary hypertension
  6. Why an infant with respiratory distress syndrome grunts → To generate end-expiratory pressure and keep alveoli open → Flaring lowers airway resistance
  7. 2-hour-old, cyanotic when latched at the breast, pink when crying, no murmur, clear lungs, normal four-extremity pressures → Bilateral choanal atresia → Obligate nasal breathing
  8. Newborn with cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying → Pass a catheter through each naris→ CT or nasal endoscopy confirms it
  9. 6-month-old with tetralogy of Fallot, sudden deep cyanosis and inconsolable crying → Knee-to-chest positioning with supplemental oxygen → A tet spell, triggered by crying
  10. Why crying temporarily relieves the cyanosis of bilateral choanal atresia → Crying bypasses the obstructed nose→ by opening the oral airway; Neonates are obligate nasal breathers
  11. Term newborn with cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen and a single S2, now with weak pulses, poor perfusion and a falling blood pressure → Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiography → instability licenses the drug before the picture
  12. Why supplemental oxygen fails to raise the saturation in transposition of the great arteries → Parallel circulations bypass the lungs→ systemic blood bypasses the lungs entirely; a fixed anatomic right-to-left shunt
  13. Term newborn cyanotic from the first hours with a loud single S2 and no murmur, unimproved on oxygen → Transposition of the great arteries → mixing flow is too low-velocity to make a murmur
  14. 1-day-old boy born at 39 weeks, feeding well. Heart rate 138/min, respiratory rate 42/min, afebrile. No murmur; femoral pulses 2+. Pulse oximetry: right hand 97%, right foot 93%. One hour later: right hand 97%, right foot 93%. → Echocardiography → a foot reading under 95% with a gap over 3% on two measures an hour apart fails the screen; with no other cause of hypoxemia found, echocardiography follows, and a second retest is not part of the algorithm
  15. Newborn at 5 minutes of life, heart rate 120/min, respiratory rate 50/min, vigorous cry, flexing extremities, cyanosis of hands feet and circumoral area with pink mucous membranes → Reassurance and routine care → acrocyanosis
  16. 6-day-old breastfed M, unconjugated bilirubin 14, weight 11% below birth weight, 3 wet diapers on day 5, nursing every 4 hours, mother milk just came in → Breastfeed every 2 to 3 hours and follow up in 1 day → lactation failure jaundice
  17. 10-day-old breastfed F, unconjugated bilirubin 16, weight appropriate, 8 wet diapers daily, nursing well every 2 to 3 hours → Breast milk jaundice → continue breastfeeding and monitor
  18. 2-day-old girl born at 40 weeks desaturates to 82% within moments of each breastfeed and recovers to 95% when she cries; afebrile, HR 144/min, lungs clear, no murmur; a soft catheter stops in the nasopharynx on both sides → Oral airway and orogastric feeding → Bilateral choanal atresia; confirm with CT or nasal endoscopy, then surgical repair
Decoy note Antenatal glucocorticoids are genuinely protective, but they only lower the risk of RDS (respiratory distress syndrome); they do not treat it away. A grade 1/6 murmur is soft and non-specific. In a 30-minute-old it is almost certainly a physiologically open duct rather than a lesion. PPROM (preterm prelabor rupture of membranes) raises concern for group B streptococcal pneumonia even after intrapartum penicillin; that pneumonia is clinically very hard to tell from RDS, so antibiotics are started empirically pending cultures. In the normal-examination case, six normal findings each exclude one diagnosis, and the only positive finding is the timing. A primigravida with an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, and an infant who voided and passed meconium, are inert findings. They only establish that the baby is well, which is the precondition for the sort.
Pearls Grunting with retractions that improves on oxygen is lung disease; in a preterm infant with ground-glass and air bronchograms that is surfactant deficiency. · Work of breathing is the first sort: grunting, flaring and retractions mean lung; comfortable tachypnea with cyanosis means heart. · Oxygen is diagnostic and therapeutic: it separates alveolar disease from a fixed shunt and treats RDS (respiratory distress syndrome). It is occasionally harmful: in hypoplastic left heart syndrome it lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and shifts right ventricular output to the lungs. · A lesion that depends on the duct presents when the duct closes, from about 12 hours onward. Cyanosis in the delivery room is lung disease, failed transition or transposition. · Antenatal glucocorticoids stimulate fetal surfactant synthesis and lower the risk of RDS; a dosed 32-week infant can still have it. · Hypoxia in RDS is self-amplifying. Collapse causes hypoxia, hypoxia constricts the pulmonary vasculature, and the resulting right-to-left shunt deepens the cyanosis. Shunt physiology can therefore be present without a shunt lesion. · Newborns are obligate nasal breathers. Nasal obstruction therefore gives cyanosis that worsens when the mouth is occluded by feeding and improves when it opens with crying. · The inverse pattern is the tet spell: cyanosis worsens with crying and agitation and is relieved by knee-to-chest positioning. · Pass a catheter through each naris first. It is a free bedside test, and imaging only confirms what the catheter suggested. · Choanal atresia may belong to CHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, atresia choanae, retardation of growth, genital and ear abnormalities). Unilateral disease often goes unrecognized until childhood, when it presents as chronic unilateral nasal discharge. · Tachypnea without distress points to the heart: fast breathing with no flaring, grunting or retractions, and clear lungs. Work of breathing points to the lung. · A loud single S2 with no murmur is characteristic of transposition. The absent murmur is a positive finding rather than a missing one, because flow through the mixing shunts is too low-velocity to generate sound.
Pairs with Part II Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers the film-based sort among the parenchymal causes. Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers the lesion catalog once the sort points to the heart. Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia covers the newborn clock (which diagnosis belongs at which hour) and includes choanal atresia in its minutes-to-hours group. Ask: is he working to breathe, does oxygen help, do the limbs differ, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing? Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers the step after a positive catheter test: which syndrome includes the choanal atresia. Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers acrocyanosis as the decoy beside a trisomy 18 murmur; ask: are the lips and tongue pink?
Transferable rule When a finding has both a lung and a heart cause, sort by physiology before naming a disease. The bedside triad of work of breathing, oxygen response and a pre-to-postductal difference decides which group of diagnoses to consider. When the sort finds nothing abnormal, the pattern in time is the key finding. A trigger that runs the opposite way excludes the lesion it resembles.
Unchecked attributeContinuous positive airway pressure: a respiratory rate of 66 reads as distress, but the stem negates flaring, grunting and retractions and reports clear lungs. The rate was checked and the work of breathing was not.
Salient decoyd-Transposition of the great arteries: Transposition gives cyanosis without grunting or retractions, and oxygen does not improve it; the stem shows both the retractions and a rise to 92%
True-fact-wrong-slotPersistent pulmonary hypertension: That is a consequence of the atelectasis, not the primary disease; PPHN (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn) gives a preductal-postductal gradient and a clear film, and neither is present
Mirror twinTransient tachypnea of the newborn: it is mild and gives perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissures; this infant has severe distress and a ground-glass film
Unchecked attributeCoarctation of the aorta: The duct does not begin to constrict until about 12 hours; at 30 minutes it is open, and coarctation would show a lower postductal saturation, not equal ones
True-fact-wrong-slotTetralogy of Fallot: its trigger is inverted. Tet spells come with crying and agitation, which is what turns this baby pink, and a murmur would be expected
Class-vs-memberTracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia: Aspiration through a fistula brings coughing, choking and respiratory distress; this infant latched, sucked well, and has clear lungs
Class-vs-memberLaryngomalacia: It obstructs at the larynx and announces itself with inspiratory stridor, which is explicitly absent; cyanosis is uncommon

Osteoarthritis

pharmacotherapy ladder · class right, member wrong · ketorolac's 5-day maximum · excluding inflammatory arthritisIs the offered drug the right member of the right class for a chronic condition in this patient?

The decision point

A drug class can be correct while the offered member is wrong. An NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) is first-line for knee OA (osteoarthritis). The NSAID ketorolac has a hard 5-day maximum because of GI (gastrointestinal), renal and bleeding risk. If it is the only NSAID offered, it is ruled out for a 6-month condition in a 72-year-old, and acetaminophen is the default choice.

Guideline currency The ACR/Arthritis Foundation 2019 (ACR: American College of Rheumatology) guideline strongly recommends topical NSAIDs for knee OA (upgraded from conditional in 2012). It also strongly recommends oral NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs). In the same guideline, acetaminophen was downgraded to conditional. It is framed for patients unable to take NSAIDs, and its effect sizes in trials are small. Older NBME (National Board of Medical Examiners) items still key acetaminophen. This patient's factors also favor it: age 72, with its GI (gastrointestinal), renal and CV (cardiovascular) risk, and pain rated 3/10.
Osteoarthritis pharmacotherapy ladder
TierIntervention
AlwaysExercise (strongly recommended) · weight loss – with body mass index 35, the highest-value intervention · self-management programs
First-line drug, kneeTopical NSAIDs – preferred in the elderly, minimal systemic exposure
NextOral NSAIDs – lowest effective dose, add a proton pump inhibitor if GI risk
ConditionalAcetaminophen (limited efficacy) · duloxetine · topical capsaicin
AdjunctIntra-articular glucocorticoid injection
Recommended againstOpioids · hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate (strongly against) · glucosamine · oral glucocorticoids (strongly against)
DefinitiveJoint replacement for refractory disease
Excluding inflammatory arthritis No fever, no morning stiffness, no synovitis, crepitus present: this pattern is mechanical, not inflammatory. It excludes hydroxychloroquine and prednisone. Oral steroids are strongly recommended against in OA (osteoarthritis); the accepted steroid route is intra-articular.
Scenario bank
  1. 68 yo F with knee osteoarthritis still limited by pain despite exercise and weight loss → Topical diclofenac → the first-line drug for knee OA
  2. Knee OA with chronic kidney disease or prior GI bleed → Topical NSAID or acetaminophen, avoid systemic NSAIDs
  3. Refractory pain despite NSAIDs and physical therapy → Intra-articular glucocorticoid
  4. Morning stiffness >1 hour with symmetric metacarpophalangeal/proximal interphalangeal synovitis → Rheumatoid arthritis → rheumatoid factor/anti-CCP, DMARDs
  5. Acute monoarticular knee with warmth and effusion → Arthrocentesis before any pharmacotherapy
  6. End-stage disease, failed all conservative measures → Joint replacement
Transferable rule When choosing initial pharmacotherapy, read which specific agent represents each class. A class can be right while the offered member is wrong: ketorolac for chronic OA (osteoarthritis), gentamicin for simple cystitis, chloramphenicol for otitis. Check the offered drug rather than rejecting the guideline.
Class-vs-member

edits.html:
GI Bleeding in a Child

both scopes first · pertechnetate scan in a child · capsule endoscopy in an adult · visible Meckel bleedingHave both scopes come back negative, and is the patient a child or an adult?

Source vignette Pt – 10-year-old boy, 2 months of exertional fatigue and exercise intolerance; no melena, hematochezia or abdominal pain; no medications · Exam – mucosal pallor, no lymphadenopathy, soft nontender abdomen, stool positive for occult blood · Labs – hemoglobin 9.4, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 74, platelets 380,000, leukocytes 7,500; erythrocyte sedimentation rate and coagulation normal; upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies unremarkable · Q – which study most likely reveals the diagnosis; options spanned computed tomography (CT) angiography, fecal calprotectin, fecal DNA, technetium 99m pertechnetate scan and tissue transglutaminase antibodies
Source vignette Pt – 2 yo M, dark red formed stool in the diaper; eating and drinking well but more tired than usual; lives on a ranch with cattle and goats; afebrile, pale; abdomen soft, nondistended, nontender, no masses; no anal fissures or hemorrhoids; stool occult blood positive · Labs – white blood cell count 8,000, Hct 27%, platelets 320,000 · Q – the study most likely to confirm the diagnosis; options spanned technetium-99m pertechnetate scan, abdominal CT, abdominal ultrasound, air contrast enema, bacterial stool culture, cow's milk elimination diet and upper endoscopy
The decision point

Iron deficiency anemia with a positive occult blood test and no visible bleeding is occult gastrointestinal bleeding. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are both unremarkable, so the source is in the small bowel, which neither scope reaches. In a child, the most common small-bowel bleeding lesion is a Meckel diverticulum. It is found by a technetium 99m pertechnetate scan, which images ectopic gastric mucosa rather than the bleeding.

An adult with the same negative workup gets capsule endoscopy, because adult small-bowel causes are angiodysplasia, neoplasia and ulcers.

A Meckel diverticulum can also bleed visibly. A toddler with painless dark red or maroon stool, pallor and a soft, nontender abdomen, without diarrhea, vomiting or fever, goes straight to the pertechnetate scan. Endoscopy is not done first. Pain suggests a complication or a different disease and changes the first test.

Defining criteria Occult GI bleeding – positive fecal occult blood and/or iron deficiency anemia without visible bleeding · First step regardless of age – upper endoscopy and colonoscopy · Child, source not found – technetium 99m pertechnetate scan for Meckel · Adult, source not found – capsule endoscopy, then CT or magnetic resonance (MR) enterography · Meckel – failed closure of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, the most common congenital GI anomaly, with ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates adjacent small bowel
Occult GI bleeding in a child: what each study answers
StudyWhat it detectsWho it is forWhy not here
Tc 99m pertechnetate scanEctopic gastric mucosaChild with small-bowel bleeding – (the answer)
Capsule endoscopyAngiodysplasia, neoplasia, ulcersAdult with small-bowel bleedingRight idea, wrong age branch
CT angiographyBrisk active bleedingHemodynamic instability with visible bleedingOccult bleeding is too slow to see
Fecal calprotectinIntestinal inflammationSuspected inflammatory bowel diseaseNo pain, diarrhea or weight loss; scopes and biopsies clean
Tissue transglutaminaseCeliac diseaseMalabsorptive iron deficiencyCeliac does not cause occult blood
Fecal DNA testingColorectal neoplasiaAverage-risk adults over 45Not a pediatric test
Upper endoscopyUpper GI sourceHematemesis or black, sticky melenaDark red or maroon stool without either is a lower source
Cow's milk eliminationMilk protein proctocolitisInfant, well, with blood-streaked stoolResolves by age 1; a toddler is past the window
Abdominal ultrasound, then air enemaIntussusceptionChild with intermittent severe pain, with or without bloody stoolThe Meckel bleed is painless
Bacterial stool cultureBacterial colitisBloody diarrhea with crampy pain and feverFormed stool, afebrile, no pain
Anal examAnal fissureBright red streaks on a hard stool, painful passageVisible on exam; none here
Abdominal CTBowel and mass lesionsAbdominal trauma, abscess or tumorCannot reliably tell the diverticulum from other bowel loops
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Complete blood count and stool occult bloodFirstMicrocytic anemia, occult blood positiveOccult GI bleeding
Upper endoscopy and colonoscopyNextUnremarkable, biopsies cleanSource is in the small bowel
Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanConfirmsEctopic gastric mucosaMeckel diverticulum, the child's small-bowel branch
Capsule endoscopyBy branchAngiodysplasia, neoplasia or ulcerAdult branch; then CT or MR enterography
Tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin ABy branchPositive, with occult blood negativeCeliac disease: iron deficiency from malabsorption, not bleeding
CT angiographySkipNeeds brisk active bleedingOccult bleeding is too slow to show
Abdominal ultrasoundBy branchTarget signIntussusception, when there is intermittent severe pain; air enema confirms and reduces it
Abdominal CTSkipCannot separate the diverticulum from bowel loopsThe pertechnetate scan answers the Meckel question
Scenario bank
  1. 10 year old with 2 months of exertional fatigue, pallor, hemoglobin 9.4 with MCV 74, stool positive for occult blood; upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies are unremarkable → Technetium 99m pertechnetate scan → Meckel scan – it images ectopic gastric mucosa
  2. How a Meckel diverticulum causes occult bleeding → Ectopic gastric mucosa secreting acid → Ulcerating adjacent small bowel
  3. Child with iron deficiency anemia and a positive fecal occult blood test; the first step → Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy → Localize before reaching for small-bowel studies
  4. Adult with occult gastrointestinal bleeding and a negative upper endoscopy and colonoscopy → Capsule endoscopy → Angiodysplasia, neoplasia and ulcers – the adult small-bowel causes
  5. Child with painless hematochezia and no abdominal pain, age under 2 → Meckel diverticulum → Failed closure of the vitelline duct
  6. Child with slow occult blood loss and stable vital signs; which study is least likely to help → CT angiography → It needs brisk active bleeding to see anything
  7. Child with microcytic anemia, chronic diarrhea and a negative fecal occult blood test → Celiac disease → Malabsorption, not blood loss – the occult blood is negative
  8. 2-year-old boy with dark red, formed stool in his diaper; eating and drinking well but more tired than usual; lives on a ranch with cattle and goats; afebrile and pale; abdomen soft, nondistended and nontender without masses; no anal fissures or hemorrhoids; stool positive for occult blood; hematocrit 27%, leukocytes 8,000/mm3, platelets 320,000/mm3 → Technetium 99m pertechnetate scan → Meckel diverticulum: ectopic gastric mucosa takes up the tracer; painless small-bowel bleeding in a toddler, and dark red stool without hematemesis or melena is not an upper GI bleed
  9. 10-week-old boy fed cow's milk-based formula with several days of mucus and streaks of blood in otherwise soft stools; feeding well, gaining weight, afebrile and playful; mild eczema on the cheeks; abdomen soft and nontender; no anal fissure on exam → Switch to an extensively hydrolyzed formula → milk protein proctocolitis: a non-IgE reaction in infants; bleeding clears once cow's milk protein is removed, and it resolves by age 1
  10. 2-year-old boy with 12 hours of sudden episodes of severe crying with his legs drawn up, quiet and sleepy between episodes; vomited twice; one stool of dark red blood and mucus (currant jelly); afebrile; a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant → Abdominal ultrasound → intussusception: pain is the tell; target sign on ultrasound, then air enema to confirm and reduce; a Meckel diverticulum can be the lead point
  11. 3-year-old girl with two episodes of painless maroon stool over the past month; pale, hematocrit 28%, vital signs normal; abdomen soft and nontender; technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows a focus of uptake in the right lower quadrant → Surgical resection → a symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is removed to stop the bleeding and prevent intussusception, diverticulitis and obstruction; iron treats the anemia, not the source
Stool color and bleeding source Stool color follows transit time, not only where the blood started. Dark red or maroon stool in a toddler is a lower source, usually the small bowel, because the blood passes quickly. The upper GI (gastrointestinal) picture is hematemesis with black, sticky melena, and it is more common in adults. This child had neither, so upper endoscopy is not the first test.
Gates Visible bleeding with instability – hematemesis, melena or hematochezia goes to CT (computed tomography) angiography, not a Meckel scan · Scope first for occult bleeding – small-bowel studies are for after a clean upper endoscopy and colonoscopy; a toddler with visible, painless dark red stool goes straight to the pertechnetate scan · Meckel is classically under 2 but presents into adolescence, so age does not exclude it · Balloon-assisted enteroscopy is the fallback when the source stays hidden
Pearls The Meckel scan detects gastric mucosa, not blood, so it works when the lesion is not actively bleeding · Occult bleeding is too slow for angiography · Celiac gives iron deficiency without occult blood; the FOBT (fecal occult blood test) separates them · Here, small bowel means the segment the two scopes cannot reach · Painless hematochezia in a toddler is Meckel until proven otherwise · Rule of 2s: often presents by age 2, usually under 2 inches long, within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve · The bleed is painless; pain comes from complications: intussusception with the diverticulum as lead point, diverticulitis that mimics appendicitis, obstruction or perforation · A symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is surgically resected to stop the bleeding and prevent those complications
Pairs with Part I The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers the obstructed and acutely bleeding infant gut. Part I Microcytic Anemia covers the iron-versus-thalassemia fork that precedes this workup. Ask: is the bleeding visible, and have both ends been scoped?
Transferable rule When an algorithm branches on age, the same negative workup can send a child and an adult to different tests.
Class-vs-memberCapsule endoscopy is the adult small-bowel study; a child gets the pertechnetate scan.
Sequencing trapOrdering a small-bowel study before upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are done.
Salient decoyMicrocytic anemia in a child pulls toward celiac serology, which the positive FOBT (fecal occult blood test) excludes.
Unchecked attributeMilk elimination fits painless blood in an infant, but milk protein proctocolitis resolves by age 1; a 2-year-old is past it.
Salient decoyRanch animals pull toward bacterial colitis, which needs bloody diarrhea, crampy pain and fever.
True-fact-wrong-slotEndoscopy is right for hematemesis and black melena; dark red stool without either points below.

edits.html:
Heart Murmurs in a Child

innocent vs pathologic murmurs · one pathologic feature buys the echo · louder on standing · the continuous murmur by locationIs any single feature pathologic, and does the murmur get louder or softer on standing?

The decision point

Innocent murmurs are turbulent flow through a structurally normal heart. They are grade 1–2, early or midsystolic, musical or vibratory, and softer with standing or Valsalva. Order ECG (electrocardiogram) and echocardiography for any single pathologic feature. Pathologic features are grade ≥3, holosystolic or diastolic timing, harsh quality, persistence upright, abnormal S2, weak femoral pulses, or symptoms. A murmur that gets louder on standing or Valsalva is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until proven otherwise.

Defining criteria Benign profile – grade 1–2, early/midsystolic, musical or vibratory, decreases with standing/Valsalva, normal vitals, S1/S2, and growth · Evaluation gate – any single pathologic feature → ECG + echocardiography · The reversal – intensity that increases with standing/Valsalva = hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded
Benign vs pathologic murmurs – the screening exam
AxisBenignPathologic
HistoryAsymptomatic, normal growthInfants: poor weight gain, feeding difficulty, respiratory distress; older: chest pain, syncope, exertional intolerance
MurmurEarly/midsystolic, musical or vibratory, grade 1–2, decreases uprightHolosystolic or diastolic, harsh, grade ≥3, persists upright
Other findingsNormal vitals, normal S1 & S2, symmetric pulsesCentral cyanosis, loud/fixed/single S2, weak femoral pulses, hepatomegaly
ManagementReassuranceECG & echocardiography
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Auscultation lying and standingFirstFull benign profile: grade 1 to 2, early systolic, softer standingInnocent murmur: reassurance, no testing
Murmur louder on standing or ValsalvaHypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded: hold sports, ECG and echo
Femoral pulses and four-extremity blood pressuresBy branchWeak femoral pulses with arm hypertensionCoarctation
ECGNextHypertrophy or conduction abnormalityPaired with echo whenever any pathologic feature is present
EchocardiographyConfirmsStructural lesion namedAny single pathologic feature, or a benign murmur outliving its window
Echocardiography for the full benign profileSkipNormal heartReassurance alone once every benign feature is named
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M, grade 2 vibratory murmur at the lower left sternal border, louder supine, vanishes on standing → Still murmur → reassurance
  2. 14 yo athlete, systolic murmur that grows louder with standing and Valsalva → Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → echocardiography before sports
  3. 6 yo F, continuous infraclavicular hum that disappears with neck rotation → Venous hum → reassurance
  4. 3 yo M, harsh grade 3 holosystolic murmur, otherwise well → ECG and echocardiography → one pathologic feature is enough
  5. Infant with weak femoral pulses and upper-extremity hypertension, continuous murmur over the back → Aortic coarctation → collateral flow murmur
  6. Well 4 yo, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border radiating to the axilla, normal S2 → Pulmonic flow murmur → innocent; a wide fixed split or ejection click would change the answer
  7. 4 yo with a soft continuous murmur under the right clavicle that fades with ipsilateral head rotation and when supine → Turbulent flow through the curved jugular and subclavian veins → venous hum, and why it is usually right-sided
  8. 3 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur under the left clavicle that does not change with head position or posture → Patent ductus arteriosus → echocardiography
  9. 9 yo with a continuous murmur heard best over the back, upper-extremity hypertension and diminished femoral pulses → Coarctation with intercostal collateral flow → echocardiography and four-extremity pressures
  10. 6-week-old with a large ventricular septal defect and tachypnea with feeds, the chamber that receives the increased preload → Left atrium → left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary venous return
  11. 2 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle that runs through S2, bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure → Patent ductus arteriosus → the machine-like continuous murmur, with a wide pulse pressure
  12. 6 do M, well and thriving, a soft 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, normal apical impulse, 2+ equal femoral pulses, saturation 98% → A large ventricular septal defect → soft because a wide defect creates little turbulence
  13. 3 wk old, well and feeding normally, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, normal S2 with symmetric pulses → Peripheral pulmonary stenosis → resolves by 6 to 12 months
  14. 5 yo F with a continuous grade 2 hum below the right clavicle that is louder when she sits up and disappears when she lies down → Venous hum → the one benign murmur that increases upright
  15. Why a venous hum is typically louder on the right than the left → The right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical → more turbulent flow into the superior vena cava
  16. 18 mo old whose neonatal murmur radiating to the axillae and back is unchanged, with normal growth and no symptoms → Echocardiography → peripheral pulmonary stenosis should have resolved by 12 months
  17. 7 yo F, well and growing normally, with a grade 2 vibratory midsystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that softens on standing; normal S2 and pulses → Reassurance → the full benign profile is present
  18. 15 yo soccer player, asymptomatic, with a grade 2 systolic murmur that grows louder when he stands from a squat → Hold sports pending ECG and echo → louder on standing is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded
The three innocent murmurs Still murmur – vibratory, lower left sternal border, louder supine · Pulmonic flow murmur – systolic ejection, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla · Venous hum – continuous, supra/infraclavicular, usually right-sided because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical, so flow velocity into the superior vena cava is higher; disappears with neck rotation or compression and when supine.
The continuous murmur A continuous murmur in a child has three causes, separated by location: Right infraclavicular and positional – venous hum, benign, fades with ipsilateral head rotation and when supine · Left infraclavicular and fixed – patent ductus arteriosus, machine-like, unchanged by head position or posture; runs through S2, with bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure · Over the back with weak femoral pulses – coarctation collateral flow, with upper-extremity hypertension · Normally split S2 – a fixed split is the atrial septal defect sign, so an S2 split that moves with respiration excludes atrial septal defect.
Pairs with Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers the cyanosis and single S2 of the pathologic column. Heart Murmurs in an Adult covers the pathologic counterpart of the innocent pulmonic flow murmur. Ask: "what does standing do to it?"
The four benign murmurs Still murmur – younger children, left lower sternal border, midsystolic, vibratory or musical, louder supine and softer standing; resolves by adolescence · Pulmonic flow murmur – childhood through adolescence, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla; appears or intensifies in high-output states such as fever, anemia and anxiety · Venous hum – continuous, supra- or infraclavicular, right louder than left because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical; the one benign murmur that increases sitting up, and it disappears supine or with ipsilateral head rotation · Peripheral pulmonary stenosis – the neonatal benign murmur, upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, from physiologically narrow proximal pulmonary arteries while fetal resistance is still falling; resolves by 6 to 12 months · Persistence past the expected age – a benign murmur that outlives its window is itself a pathologic feature · Intensity and defect size – a small ventricular septal defect is loud and a large one is soft or silent, because turbulence falls as the orifice widens
How NBME framed it A murmur new on day 3 after a normal birth examination pulls toward a ventricular septal defect or patent ductus arteriosus; its soft grade and spread to the axilla mark peripheral pulmonary stenosis. The options were the five common acyanotic lesions, so the key was the umbrella term, pulmonary stenosis.
Transferable rule In screening, reassurance requires the entire benign profile. One pathologic feature on exam, in the vitals or in the history is sufficient to start the workup.
Unchecked attributePatent ductus arteriosus: it is the right category for a continuous murmur near a clavicle. Check the side and the positional change; a ductus murmur does not change with head turning.
Unchecked attributeAtrial septal defect: the split S2 here moves with respiration, the opposite of the fixed split it requires.
Mirror twinHypertrophic cardiomyopathy: it is the dangerous mimic of the innocent murmur; the direction the murmur moves on standing separates them.
Uniform-answer doubtReassurance: accept it only after naming the full benign profile.

edits.html:
Acute Kidney Injury in a Child

the labs assign the compartment · prerenal pattern · ibuprofen with volume loss · sediment · fluids, stop the drugIs the kidney still concentrating, and what does the sediment show?

Source vignette Pt – 4 yo M, 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea, taking ibuprofen · Labs – blood urea nitrogen (BUN)/creatinine ratio 32:1, specific gravity 1.028, bland urinalysis · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned isotonic fluids with stopping the ibuprofen, furosemide and renal ultrasonography
The decision point

In any AKI (acute kidney injury), use the laboratory data to assign the injury compartment before using the drug to assign the mechanism. BUN/Cr >20:1 + specific gravity >1.020 + bland sediment = prerenal (BUN/Cr, blood urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio). In prerenal injury the kidneys are hypoperfused but intact and still concentrating. Ibuprofen acts hemodynamically. Hypovolemia makes GFR (glomerular filtration rate) prostaglandin-dependent, and COX (cyclooxygenase) inhibition constricts the afferent arteriole. The sediment and the 3-day timeline exclude drug-induced interstitial nephritis.

Defining criteria Prerenal pattern – BUN/Cr >20:1, specific gravity >1.020, bland urine sediment · acute tubular necrosis (ATN) pattern – muddy brown casts, specific gravity ≈1.010, BUN/Cr <20:1 · Mechanism here – volume depletion makes GFR prostaglandin-dependent; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) constrict the afferent arteriole
Pediatric oliguria – cause by compartment
CauseIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Prerenal (NSAID + hypovolemia)vomiting/diarrhea; NSAID constricts the afferent arterioleBUN/Cr >20:1 + specific gravity (SG) >1.020 + bland sediment
AINacute interstitial nephritisdrug hypersensitivity – NSAIDs after weeks, β-lactams, PPIsfever, rash, eosinophilia; white blood cells (WBCs)/WBC casts
ATNacute tubular necrosisischemia or direct toxins (aminoglycosides, contrast)muddy brown casts; SG ≈1.010
Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) Can't missShiga toxin E coli, 5–10 days after bloody diarrheaschistocytes + thrombocytopenia + hematuria/proteinuria
Immune-complex glomerulonephritispoststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathypost-streptococcal (2–4 wk) or gross hematuria with upper respiratory infection (URI)hematuria + proteinuria ± low C3
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
BUN and creatinineFirstBUN/Cr ratio over 20:1Prerenal pattern
Urinalysis with specific gravityNextSpecific gravity over 1.020, bland sedimentIntact tubules still concentrating: prerenal
Urine microscopyBy branchMuddy brown casts, specific gravity about 1.010Acute tubular necrosis
Urine sediment and complete blood count (CBC) with differentialBy branchWBC casts, with eosinophilia or rashAcute interstitial nephritis: stop the drug
CBC and peripheral smearBy branchSchistocytes with low plateletsHemolytic uremic syndrome after bloody diarrhea
Isotonic fluids and stopping the NSAIDConfirmsCreatinine falls with volumePrerenal AKI, confirmed by the response
Renal ultrasonographySkipUsually normal in prerenal AKIAdds nothing once the labs assign the compartment
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo M, 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea on ibuprofen, BUN/Cr 32:1, SG 1.028, bland urinalysis → Isotonic fluids and stop the ibuprofen
  2. 5 yo F, bloody diarrhea 6 days ago, now pallor, petechiae, oliguria, schistocytes on smear → Hemolytic uremic syndrome → supportive care; avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents
  3. 68 yo F on naproxen for 3 weeks, fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts → Acute interstitial nephritis → stop the NSAID
  4. 60 yo M after septic hypotension, SG 1.010, muddy brown granular casts, BUN/Cr 14:1 → Ischemic acute tubular necrosis
  5. 74 yo M on lisinopril and furosemide who starts ibuprofen, creatinine rising from 1.1 to 2.0 → Discontinue the ibuprofen and give fluids → the "triple whammy" of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID
  6. 16 yo M, gross hematuria 2 days into a URI, normal C3 → IgA nephropathy → timing with the URI and normal complement decide
  7. 7 yo M, cola-colored urine and periorbital edema 2 weeks after pharyngitis, low C3 → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → supportive care
Pearls Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole, and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole. An NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor drop GFR (glomerular filtration rate) from opposite ends. An NSAID plus an ACE inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin II receptor blocker) plus a diuretic is the "triple whammy" · FENa (fractional excretion of sodium) <1% supports prerenal but is unreliable after diuretics · the AIN (acute interstitial nephritis) triad is present in a minority; WBC (white blood cell) casts carry the diagnosis · PSGN (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis) vs IgA nephropathy is timing plus complement. PSGN comes 2–4 weeks after the infection with low C3; IgA nephropathy comes during the URI (upper respiratory infection) with normal C3.
Pairs with Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers sorting by smear and coagulation studies when renal failure comes with a falling platelet count.
Transferable rule Read the ratio, then the specific gravity, then the sediment, and only then the drug. When a full chemistry panel is given, read it before answering.
Salient decoyDrug-induced interstitial nephritis: the named drug draws attention to it, but the timeline and the sediment are wrong.
True-fact-wrong-slotHUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome): gastroenteritis cues it, but it needs bloody diarrhea, schistocytes and an active sediment.

edits.html:
Polymyalgia Rheumatica

aching with normal strength · sedimentation rate and creatine kinase · giant cell arteritis overlap · prednisone responseIs this pain and stiffness with normal strength after 50, and does low-dose prednisone clear it within days?

The decision point

Polymyalgia rheumatica presents at age >50 with bilateral proximal girdle aching with morning stiffness, systemic symptoms and ESR ≥50 (erythrocyte sedimentation rate). There is no true weakness and no muscle tenderness. "Can't get out of bed" here reflects pain and stiffness, not weakness; weakness points to myositis. Treatment is low-dose prednisone ~15 mg. A dramatic response within days is nearly diagnostic.

Defining criteria Diagnosis – age >50, bilateral proximal girdle aching with morning stiffness, ESR ≥50, with normal strength and no muscle tenderness · Response criterion – dramatic improvement on prednisone ~15 mg within days is nearly diagnostic · Rules out polymyositis – polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is pain with normal creatine kinase (CK); polymyositis is weakness with elevated CK
Proximal pain & stiffness – the differential
DiagnosisKey discriminatorLabsTreatment
Polymyalgia rheumaticaProximal pain/stiffness, strength normalESR/C-reactive protein (CRP) ↑, CK normalLow-dose prednisone
Giant cell arteritis EmergencyHeadache, jaw claudication, vision loss; coexists with PMR in ~50%ESR often >50–100High-dose prednisone; don't wait for biopsy if vision is threatened
PolymyositisProximal weakness > painCK ↑, anti-Jo-1High-dose steroids
Elderly-onset rheumatoid arthritis (RA)Small-joint synovitis (metacarpophalangeal [MCP]/proximal interphalangeal [PIP]), erosionsRheumatoid factor (RF) / anti-CCP +Methotrexate
FibromyalgiaDiffuse tender points, younger womenNormal ESR/CRPExercise, duloxetine, amitriptyline
Hypothyroid myopathyFatigue, weight gain, bradycardiaThyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) ↑, CK ↑Levothyroxine
Statin myopathyStatin exposureCK ↑Stop the statin
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
ESR and CRPFirstESR elevated, typically 50 or higherSupports PMR in the right clinical picture; normal values point toward fibromyalgia or another cause
CKFirstNormal CKPain without muscle injury; excludes polymyositis and statin myopathy
TSHFirstNormal TSHExcludes hypothyroid myopathy, which can mimic proximal aching
RF and anti-CCPBy branchNegative in PMRSwollen MCPs or PIPs: consider elderly-onset RA
Temporal artery biopsyBy branchGranulomatous arteritisHeadache, jaw claudication or vision change: giant cell arteritis (GCA); start high-dose prednisone before biopsy
Response to prednisone about 15 mg (clinical diagnosis)ConfirmsDramatic improvement within daysPMR; no response after a week means reconsider the diagnosis
Electromyography (EMG) and muscle biopsySkipNormal in PMR; strength is 5/5Reserved for true weakness with high CK (polymyositis)
Scenario bank
  1. 72 yo F, bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching, morning stiffness 90 min, ESR 62, strength 5/5 → Polymyalgia rheumatica → prednisone 15 mg daily
  2. 72 yo F with known PMR, new jaw claudication and temporal tenderness → Giant cell arteritis → high-dose prednisone immediately, biopsy after
  3. 68 yo M, progressive proximal weakness, CK 4,000, normal ESR → Polymyositis → EMG and muscle biopsy
  4. 70 yo F on atorvastatin, proximal aching, CK 900 → Statin myopathy → stop the statin and recheck CK
  5. 66 yo F, proximal aching, ESR 12, TSH 14 → Hypothyroid myopathy → levothyroxine
  6. 74 yo F with presumed PMR, no response after a week of prednisone 15 mg → Reconsider the diagnosis – PMR responds within days
  7. 63 yo F, widespread pain, non-restorative sleep, normal ESR and CK → Fibromyalgia
Pearls PMR (polymyalgia rheumatica) = pain with normal CK (creatine kinase); polymyositis = weakness with high CK · PMR responds to low-dose steroids, GCA (giant cell arteritis) needs high dose · every PMR diagnosis gets a GCA symptom screen, and ~50% of GCA patients have PMR · NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) fail in PMR; they are a close but inadequate therapy.
Sequencing trapTreat-the-number

edits.html:
Occupational Lung Disease

matching occupational exposure to lung disease · upper vs lower lobes · pleural plaques · cancer and tuberculosis riskWhat did the patient breathe at work, which lobes are involved, and is the pleura involved?

The decision point

The occupation identifies the dust, and the lobe distribution and pleural involvement confirm it. Asbestosis is the exception: it affects the lower lobes and involves the pleura. Everything else with a mining/quarry history affects the upper lobes.

Occupational lung diseases
DiseaseExposureLobesThe tellAssociation
AsbestosisBrake linings, shipyard, insulation, plumbing, roofingLOWERPleural plaques; ferruginous bodiesBronchogenic carcinoma > mesothelioma; smoking multiplies bronchogenic only
SilicosisSandblasting, mining, foundry, stone countertopsUPPEREggshell calcification of hilar nodes↑ tuberculosis (TB) risk – annual purified protein derivative skin test
Coal workers'Coal miningUPPERCoal macules → progressive massive fibrosisCaplan syndrome (+ rheumatoid arthritis nodules)
BerylliosisAerospace, nuclearDiffuseNoncaseating granulomas – sarcoid mimicResponds to steroids
ByssinosisCotton / textile mills – "Monday fever" – worse at the start of the work weekObstructive
Hypersensitivity pneumonitisMoldy hay, birds – Episodic fever/cough hours after exposureAvoidance cures
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Chest X-rayFirstUpper versus lower zones; pleural plaques; eggshell hilar nodesUpper: silica or coal; lower with plaques: asbestos
High-resolution computed tomography (CT) of the chestSupportsFibrosis pattern with or without pleural plaquesDefines distribution; plaques alone mark exposure and are benign
Pulmonary function testsStagingRestrictive pattern with a low diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxideSeverity of fibrosis; byssinosis is obstructive instead
None: exposure history plus imagingConfirmsNamed dust, typical distribution, latency of decadesBiopsy only when the picture is atypical
Beryllium lymphocyte proliferation testBy branchPositive in a granulomatous pictureBerylliosis rather than sarcoidosis
Tuberculin skin test, yearlyBy branchPositive in a patient with silicosisLatent TB, which silicosis makes more likely
CT and pleural biopsyBy branchPleural mass with an effusionMesothelioma after asbestos exposure
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo M shipyard insulator with lower-lobe fibrosis and pleural plaques → Asbestosis
  2. 55 yo M sandblaster with upper-lobe nodules and eggshell-calcified hilar nodes → Silicosis
  3. 58 yo M coal miner with upper-lobe nodules and black sputum → Coal workers' pneumoconiosis
  4. 50 yo M aerospace machinist with noncaseating granulomas on biopsy → Berylliosis
  5. 45 yo F cotton mill worker with chest tightness worst on the first day back at work → Byssinosis
  6. 40 yo M pigeon breeder with fever and dyspnea 6 hours after exposure → Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
  7. 62 yo M with asbestos exposure, a pleural mass and an effusion → Mesothelioma
  8. 55 yo M sandblaster and never smoker with silicosis → Annual tuberculin skin test → silicosis raises tuberculosis risk
  9. 66 yo M, retired shipyard worker, asymptomatic, with calcified pleural plaques and normal lung parenchyma on imaging → No treatment → plaques alone mark exposure and are benign
  10. 62 yo M with decades of asbestos exposure who also smokes heavily → Bronchogenic carcinoma → smoking multiplies bronchogenic risk only, not mesothelioma
  11. 50 yo M aerospace machinist with progressive dyspnea and noncaseating granulomas on biopsy, now removed from exposure → Oral corticosteroids → berylliosis responds to steroids
Mnemonic and timing Asbestos comes from the roof but affects the base; silica and coal come from the ground but affect the top. Latency is typically 20–30 years, so exposure that ended decades ago still counts. Pleural plaques alone are a marker of exposure, benign, and need no treatment.
Transferable rule Answering a long stem in under 40 seconds means one cue was pattern-matched and the verification pass was skipped. This costs the most in occupational stems. The lobe distribution usually decides the diagnosis, and it comes at the end of the stem.
