edits.html:
Polyuria

urine osmolality first · solute vs water diuresis · when water deprivation is indicated · desmopressin responseIs the urine dilute, and has the serum sodium already answered what the deprivation test would?

Source vignette Pt – 8 yo M, 2 months of excessive urination, drinking large volumes, irritable and restless; normal growth and milestones; no medications · Vitals – normal · Exam – physical and neurologic examination normal · Labs – Na 142, K 4.2, Cl 100, HCO₃ 24, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 30, creatinine 1.0, Ca 9.2, glucose 100 · Urine – specific gravity 1.001, no protein, blood, glucose or ketones; osmolality 120 mOsm/kg; 24-hour output 3.7 L · Q – the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned chest radiography, fractional excretion of sodium, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), an oral glucose tolerance test, renal ultrasonography and the water deprivation test
The decision point

Urine osmolality 120 is a water diuresis. The kidney is failing to concentrate, so solute diuresis and every test for it are excluded before any hormone is named. Then serum sodium 142, a normal value, makes the deprivation test necessary rather than redundant. A patient who drinks enough to hold his sodium normal has not yet shown the cause of the dilute urine. It may be a failure to make or to respond to vasopressin, or simply a normal kidney excreting a large water intake. Water deprivation is the manoeuvre that forces that distinction. It drives serum osmolality to the point where vasopressin secretion must be maximal, then shows whether the urine concentrates.

The two imaging studies are right tests in the wrong order. MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) localizes an established deficiency, and renal ultrasonography localizes an established resistance. Both wait on a diagnosis that has not yet been made.

Defining criteria Polyuria – urine output above 3 L/day in an adult, above 2 L/day/m² in a child · Dilute urine – urine osmolality under 300 mOsm/kg, specific gravity under 1.006 · Concentrated urine – 600 mOsm/kg or above, meaning the kidney can concentrate and the diuresis is driven by solute · Deprivation endpoint – water withheld until serum sodium exceeds 145 and serum osmolality exceeds 295, the point at which vasopressin secretion should be maximal · Deprivation result – urine above 600 is primary polydipsia, urine still under 300 is an arginine vasopressin (AVP) disorder · Desmopressin result – urine osmolality rises in deficiency and stays low in resistance
FigureWhen water deprivation testing is indicatedshow

Redrawn from the published indications flowchart. Two deliberate changes: the concentrated-urine branch is labeled with what it means – solute diuresis – rather than only with what not to do, and the indicated branch carries its own interpretation, because the exam asks what the deprivation test showed about as often as it asks whether to order it.

Polyuria with dilute urine – the differentialand the two mimics that never need the test
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Primary polydipsiaDrinking drives the urine; psychiatric illness, or a drug that creates thirstSerum sodium low or low-normal; urine concentrates above 600 after deprivationNot excluded – this is one of the two the test is between
AVP deficiency (central diabetes insipidus [DI])Impaired production or release: trauma, neurosurgery, craniopharyngioma or germinoma, hypophysitis, sarcoid or histiocytosis, a familial AVP mutation, pregnancyUrine stays dilute after deprivation, then rises with desmopressinNot excluded – the desmopressin step is what names it
AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI)The kidney ignores the hormone: AVPR2 or AQP2 mutation, hypercalcemia, severe hypokalemia, lithium, chronic tubulointerstitial diseaseUrine stays dilute after desmopressin too; in a child, usually hereditaryNot excluded – complete resistance leaves the osmolality unchanged, partial raises it slightly
Solute (osmotic) diuresisGlucosuria in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, or an osmotic diuretic such as mannitolPolyuria with a urine osmolality above 600; no deprivation test neededUrine osmolality 120, serum glucose 100, urine glucose negative
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)The mirror image – water retained rather than lost; malignancy, central nervous system and pulmonary disease, drugsConcentrated urine with hyponatremia, and no polyuriaDilute urine and a normal sodium – the opposite of the finding
Treatment, and the one child who must not be tested AVP deficiency – desmopressin in nearly all patients, oral, intranasal or parenteral; other agents are rarely needed · AVP resistance – remove the cause first (stop the lithium, correct the calcium and the potassium), then a thiazide with a low-sodium diet as first line; a low-protein diet cuts the solute load further; indomethacin is adjunct; amiloride is the one for lithium, because it blocks lithium entry into the collecting duct · Supervision – the deprivation test is performed in hospital in older children and adults, and is not performed in very young children, because the hypernatremia it deliberately produces is dangerous in a child who cannot ask for water
Decision spine

1. Is the urine dilute or concentrated? Urine osmolality of 600 or above means the kidney concentrates, so look for solute, not for a hormone. 2. Is there glucose in the urine? Glucosuria explains the whole picture without a hormone. 3. Is the sodium above 145 with osmolality above 295? Then the AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder is already proven; go straight to desmopressin. 4. Is the sodium frankly low? Polyuria with hyponatremia is primary polydipsia and needs no deprivation test. 5. Is the sodium normal? That is the only value that calls for the test. 6. After deprivation, did desmopressin raise the urine osmolality? If yes, it is deficiency, so image the brain. If no, it is resistance, so look at the kidney and the drug list.

Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Urine osmolalityFirstDilute, under 300 mOsm/kgWater diuresis; 600 or above means solute, such as glucose
Serum sodium and osmolalityNextSodium normalDiagnosis open: deprivation test; high sodium or low sodium has already answered it
Water deprivation test, inpatientBy branchUrine concentrates over 600Primary polydipsia; still under 300 means an AVP disorder
Desmopressin challengeConfirmsUrine osmolality risesAVP deficiency; unchanged means AVP resistance
MRI of the brainCauseSellar or hypothalamic lesionCause of AVP deficiency
Calcium, potassium and drug listCauseHigh calcium, low potassium or lithiumReversible AVP resistance
Serum vasopressin levelSkipToo unstable to measure routinelyThe desmopressin response is the assay
Scenario bank
  1. 8 yo M, 2 months of polyuria and polydipsia, normal growth and neurologic examination, Na 142, glucose 100, urine specific gravity 1.001 and osmolality 120, output 3.7 L/day → Water deprivation test → a normal sodium is what leaves the diagnosis open
  2. 10 yo M with polyuria, serum Na 149 and serum osmolality 302, urine osmolality 110 → Desmopressin challenge → the deprivation endpoint has already been reached spontaneously
  3. 12 yo F whose urine osmolality stayed at 150 through deprivation and then rose to 620 after desmopressin → MRI of the brain → AVP deficiency needs its cause localized
  4. 9 yo M whose urine osmolality is 140 after deprivation and unchanged after desmopressin, with normal calcium, potassium and no medications → A thiazide with a low-sodium diet → first line once resistance is established and reversible causes are excluded
  5. 8 yo M for whom water deprivation testing has been chosen → Admit for supervised inpatient testing → the test works by producing hypernatremia deliberately
  6. 20-month-old with polyuria and a serum sodium of 148 → Water deprivation testing → severe hypernatremia in a child who cannot obtain water
  7. 14 yo M with polyuria and weight loss, urine osmolality 650, serum glucose 420, urine glucose 4+ → Osmotic diuresis → a concentrating kidney moves the problem to solute
  8. 30 yo F on an antipsychotic with polyuria, urine osmolality 90 and serum sodium 128 → Primary polydipsia → polyuria with hyponatremia needs no deprivation test
  9. Child with polyuria whose urine remains dilute when fluids are withheld → Desmopressin after water deprivation → the hormone itself is too unstable in a sample to measure routinely; serial urine osmolality is what is read
  10. 17 yo F with polyuria, constipation and a serum calcium of 12.8 → Hypercalcemia blunts the response to vasopressin → an acquired, reversible AVP resistance; at the collecting duct
Pearls A sodium above 145 makes the test redundant. A sodium below normal already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test. · Serum vasopressin is not measured: its half-life is short and it is unstable in the sample, so the desmopressin response is the assay · AVP deficiency – the current name for central diabetes insipidus · AVP resistance – the current name for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus · Hypothalamic injury kills the magnocellular cell bodies and the deficiency is permanent; injury below the infundibulum is usually transient, because those cell bodies survive · Pregnancy can produce a transient deficiency through placental vasopressinase; it resolves with delivery and returns in the next pregnancy · Lithium causes resistance by inhibiting aquaporin-2, and amiloride is the agent that blocks lithium's entry into the cell
Pairs with Part I Enuresis already links a very low specific gravity to diabetes insipidus and to this test. This brief covers what happens after the test is ordered. Brain Tumors in a Child covers the causes of AVP (arginine vasopressin) deficiency and the post-operative case where the diagnosis is not in doubt. Hypercalcemia covers the commonest acquired resistance. Ask: is the serum sodium high, low, or normal?
Transferable rule When the kidney is making dilute urine, the serum sodium shows whether a water deprivation test is still needed. A high sodium already confirms an AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder; a low sodium already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test.
Sequencing trapMRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain: the right study once a deficiency is proven, and nothing has been proven yet.
Sequencing trapRenal ultrasonography: it images the kidney, which is implicated only if desmopressin fails.
Salient decoyA BUN (blood urea nitrogen) of 30 pulls toward renal disease, but the creatinine is 1.0 and the defect is concentration, not filtration.
True-fact-wrong-slotFractional excretion of sodium: it measures perfusion, and perfusion is not in question here.
Salient decoyChest radiography: it looks for SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), which produces concentrated urine and hyponatremia, both opposite to the findings here.

edits.html:
Preoperative Evaluation

numbers that gate procedures · platelet thresholds · low counts you do not transfuse · desmopressin treats function, not countDoes the count clear the threshold for this procedure, and is the low count real and worth transfusing?

The decision point

Specific values set the threshold for specific procedures. If the value clears the threshold, almost always proceed without further intervention.

Platelet count thresholds
Platelet countMeaning
<10,000Spontaneous bleeding risk → prophylactic transfusion even if asymptomatic
<50,000Transfuse only for active bleeding or before surgery/invasive procedures
≥50,000Adequate for nearly all surgery, including dental extraction and central lines
≥100,000Reserved for neurosurgery and posterior eye surgery
Scenario bank
  1. 60 yo M with a platelet count of 8,000 before elective surgery → Prophylactic platelet transfusion
  2. 60 yo M with a platelet count of 60,000 before a minor procedure → Proceed without transfusion
  3. 60 yo M with a platelet count of 40,000 before major surgery → Transfuse to at least 50,000
  4. 60 yo M needing neurosurgery with a platelet count of 80,000 → Transfuse to at least 100,000
  5. 28 yo F with immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), platelets 8,000 and petechiae, no surgery planned → Corticosteroids or IVIG → transfused platelets are consumed too
  6. 60 yo M with platelet clumping on the smear and a reported count of 40,000 → Pseudothrombocytopenia → repeat in a citrate tube
Variants Petechiae with a count of 8,000 in a healthy young woman → ITP (immune thrombocytopenia). Treat with steroids or IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin), not transfusion, because transfused platelets get consumed too · heparin day 5–10 with a 50% drop → HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia). Stop heparin, start argatroban and never transfuse · clumps on the smear → pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid). Repeat the count in a citrate tube; this is the one time "recheck the count" is correct · DDAVP (desmopressin) is for qualitative defects (von Willebrand disease, mild hemophilia A, uremic platelet dysfunction), not for a low count.

edits.html:
Primary Amenorrhea

pelvic ultrasound first · uterus present or absent, then read the follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) · Turner, agenesis, androgen insensitivityIs there a uterus, and if so is the FSH high or low; if not, is there pubic hair?

Source vignette Pt – 15 yo, no menses, distressed at looking younger than peers; no headache or visual change; mother and grandmother menarche at 13; height below the 3rd percentile, weight 20th · Exam – no breast development, normal external genitalia, Tanner 2 pubic hair; urine beta-hCG negative · Imaging – pelvic ultrasonography shows a prepubertal uterus with small ovaries · Labs – FSH 60 (normal under 40), luteinizing hormone (LH) 52 (normal 5–25) · Q – the next step in management, then the underlying cause; options spanned hormone measurements, imaging, karyotype and reassurance
The decision point

Primary amenorrhea is no menarche by 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by 13 without them. The first step is pelvic ultrasonography. The obstruction can sit anywhere from the hypothalamus and pituitary to the ovary, uterus and vagina. Imaging is the only test that answers the anatomical half of that chain in one move. Every hormonal test is interpretable only once you know whether there is a uterus. Uterus present → read the FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone). High FSH with high LH (luteinizing hormone) is primary ovarian insufficiency. With short stature, that is Turner syndrome: gonadal dysgenesis from loss of an X. Turner syndrome gives streak ovaries and absent oestrogen, while intact adrenals still produce pubic hair. Uterus absent → read the pubic hair. Pubic hair present means the androgen receptor works, so the diagnosis is 46,XX Müllerian agenesis. Absent pubic hair means it does not, so the diagnosis is 46,XY complete androgen insensitivity.

Defining criteria Primary amenorrhea – no menarche by age 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by age 13 without them · First step – pelvic ultrasonography, to establish whether a uterus is present before any hormone is measured · Uterus present, FSH high – primary ovarian insufficiency; with short stature, Turner syndrome (45,X on karyotype, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) if mosaicism is suspected) · Uterus present, FSH low or inappropriately normal – central: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for a hypothalamic or pituitary lesion, or GnRH deficiency, Cushing syndrome, functional hypothalamic amenorrhea · Uterus absent – serum testosterone: female-range with normal pubic hair is Müllerian agenesis (46,XX); male-range with absent pubic and axillary hair is complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY)
Primary amenorrhea – the two-step algorithmanatomy first, then the gonadotropins
StepFindingConclusionConfirms, then
Before step 1: urine hCGNegativePregnancy excludedThen the ultrasound
1. Pelvic ultrasoundUterus presentGo to the FSHAnatomy only; the FSH picks the branch
1. Pelvic ultrasoundUterus absentGo to the testosterone and the pubic hairAnatomy only; the karyotype settles the branch
2a. FSH high± short staturePrimary ovarian insufficiency → karyotype → Turner if 45,X45,X karyotype, FISH if mosaicism is suspected; then echocardiogram and renal ultrasound
2a. FSH low or normal± anosmia, weight loss, athlete, cushingoidCentral: MRI, or functional, Kallmann or CushingMRI shows a sellar lesion, or is normal with anosmia in Kallmann; check thyroid-stimulating hormone and prolactin
2b. Testosterone female-rangePubic hair presentMüllerian agenesis (46,XX) → evaluate the renal tract46,XX karyotype; then renal ultrasound
2b. Testosterone male-rangePubic hair absentComplete androgen insensitivity (46,XY)46,XY karyotype; then gonadectomy, usually after puberty, for tumor risk
Pertinent positives & negatives Height below the 3rd percentile – the key Turner clue; almost all patients develop short stature, often the only feature besides amenorrhea · No breast development with Tanner 2 pubic hair – oestrogen absent, adrenal androgens intact; the dissociation that points at the ovary rather than the axis · FSH 60 and LH 52 – loss of oestrogen negative feedback; hypergonadotropic hypogonadism · Prepubertal uterus with small ovaries – streak gonads; the uterus is present but was never stimulated · No headache or visual change – argues against a sellar mass, which is the central branch · Normal external genitalia – the genital tubercle is unaffected in every diagnosis on this list · Negative beta-hCG – pregnancy must be excluded before anything else
Decision spine Is the definition met? – No menarche by 13 without secondary characteristics → yes · What is the first test? – Pelvic ultrasound; anatomy before hormones · Is there a uterus? – Yes → read the FSH · Is the FSH high or low? – High → ovarian failure, not a central cause · Is she short? – Below the 3rd percentile → Turner · What confirms it? – Karyotype showing 45,X, with FISH for mosaicism if normal
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo with no menarche, no breast development, Tanner 2 pubic hair, height below the 3rd percentile, normal external genitalia and a negative urine beta-hCG → Pelvic ultrasonography → establish the anatomy before measuring hormones
  2. 14 yo with primary amenorrhea and no secondary sexual characteristics in whom ultrasonography has confirmed a uterus → FSH level measurement → it separates central (low or normal) from peripheral (high) causes
  3. 15 yo with primary amenorrhea, no breast development and short stature; ultrasound shows a prepubertal uterus with small ovaries and FSH is 60 with LH 52 → Turner syndrome → 45,X on karyotype
  4. 16 yo distance runner with primary amenorrhea, Tanner 4 breast and pubic hair, normal external genitalia; ultrasound shows normal ovaries and no uterus → Müllerian agenesis → failure of paramesonephric duct development
  5. 16 yo with primary amenorrhea, Tanner 4 breast development, absent pubic and axillary hair, tall stature and no uterus on ultrasound → Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome → 46,XY with male-range testosterone
  6. 15 yo with primary amenorrhea, a uterus on ultrasound, FSH 3 and LH 2, normal weight and normal sense of smell → MRI of the brain → a low FSH points centrally
  7. 16 yo newly diagnosed with Müllerian agenesis → Renal ultrasonography → renal tract anomalies are commonly associated
  8. 17 yo gymnast training twice daily with a body mass index of 16, primary amenorrhea, a uterus present, and low FSH and LH → Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea → energy deficit suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis
  9. Why girls with Turner syndrome develop pubic hair but no breast development → Adrenarche is intact while ovarian estrogen production fails → the adrenal glands are unaffected by loss of an X chromosome
Test order A 17-hydroxyprogesterone, a testosterone, a karyotype and an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) are each the right move in some branch of this algorithm. Each is uninterpretable until the ultrasound has shown whether there is a uterus, so ordering it first is one step too early. Reassurance is right for a girl under 15 who has secondary sexual characteristics. It is wrong here because the definition is already met and her height is below the 3rd percentile.
Pearls Ultrasound first, always – every hormone in this workup is uninterpretable until you know whether there is a uterus · Uterus present → FSH. Uterus absent → pubic hair. These two questions, in that order, resolve almost every case of primary amenorrhea · High FSH means ovarian failure; low FSH means a central cause – the gonadotropins tell you which end of the axis to investigate · Turner patients have pubic hair, because adrenarche is adrenal and the adrenals are normal; pubic hair without breast development points to ovarian failure · Müllerian agenesis and androgen insensitivity both present with an absent uterus and differ in pubic hair · Müllerian agenesis obliges a renal ultrasound – the ducts develop alongside the urinary tract, so anomalies travel together · An athlete with amenorrhea can still have a structural cause; functional hypothalamic amenorrhea never explains missing anatomy
Pairs with Part I Abnormal Uterine Bleeding covers the opposite complaint on the same axis, too much bleeding rather than none, and shares the immature-axis physiology. Part II Puberty covers the staging vocabulary this brief uses throughout. Ask: is there a uterus, and if so is the FSH high or low?
Transferable rule When a workup has an anatomical branch and a hormonal branch, image first. A hormone measured before you know the anatomy produces a number you cannot interpret.
Sequencing trap17-hydroxyprogesterone: real in the amenorrhea workup for congenital adrenal hyperplasia, but indicated only once a uterus is confirmed and with suggestive features.
Uniform-answer doubtReassurance and observation: the definition is already met, and height below the 3rd percentile is itself a finding.
Unchecked attributeAndrogen insensitivity: requires an absent uterus; she has one.
Mirror twinDevelopmental failure of the urogenital sinus: produces a vaginal dimple with a uterus present, the mirror image of Müllerian agenesis.
Salient decoyAbnormal GnRH pulsatility: twice-daily training is a real risk factor, but central causes give low gonadotropins and cannot remove a uterus.

edits.html:
Hyperprolactinemia

inferring the unnamed drug · antipsychotic ranking · causes by category · cheap tests before magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) · cabergoline firstIs the prolactin in the drug range or the prolactinoma range, and which drug is behind it?

The decision point

When a patient with a known illness remains on an unnamed medication, identify the drug by two-step inference. First identify the drug class the illness requires. Then choose the member whose side-effect profile matches the complaint. In psychosis, the class is an antipsychotic, and the member is the one with the highest prolactin liability.

The prolactin level separates drug-induced hyperprolactinemia from prolactinoma. Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia runs 25–100 and rarely exceeds 200; a prolactinoma typically produces >200. In this patient, a level of 70 is in the drug-induced range and excludes prolactinoma without any imaging.

Mechanism & the antipsychotic ranking Dopamine is prolactin-inhibiting factor. D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway removes that inhibition. Highest prolactin effect: risperidone and paliperidone, plus high-potency typicals such as haloperidol. Lowest: aripiprazole (a D2 partial agonist that can lower prolactin), quetiapine and clozapine. Aripiprazole is therefore the antipsychotic least likely to cause hyperprolactinemia and the one to switch to.
Hyperprolactinemia – causes by category
CategoryExamplesDiscriminator
PhysiologicPregnancy, nipple stimulation, stress, exercise, sleepPregnancy test first
DrugsAntipsychotics, metoclopramide, methyldopa, verapamil, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), opioids, estrogens, H2 blockersLevel 25–100
ProlactinomaMicro- or macroadenomaLevel >200; macroadenoma adds headache and bitemporal hemianopsia
Stalk effectAny sellar mass compressing the stalkModest elevation (<100) with a large mass on MRI
Hypothyroidism↑thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) stimulates lactotrophsThyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) elevated
Chronic kidney disease (CKD), cirrhosisReduced clearance –
Workup order & two pituitary pearls For elevated prolactin, first get a pregnancy test, TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), medication review and renal function. Order an MRI pituitary only if all are negative. Do not image before excluding the cheap causes. Hook effect: a very large prolactinoma can saturate the assay and give a falsely low value; repeat with dilution. Prolactinoma is the pituitary tumor you treat medically. First-line treatment is dopamine agonists (cabergoline > bromocriptine), even for macroadenomas, because they shrink the tumor. Surgery is for medical failure, intolerance, or apoplexy.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Serum prolactinFirstOver 200, or 25 to 100Over 200 suggests prolactinoma; 25 to 100 fits drugs or other causes
Pregnancy testNextPositivePhysiologic hyperprolactinemia
TSHNextHigh TSHPrimary hypothyroidism: TRH drives prolactin; treat with levothyroxine
Medication review and renal functionNextAntipsychotic, metoclopramide or other culprit; or CKDDrug-induced or reduced clearance; no imaging needed
Pituitary MRIConfirmsAdenoma once the cheap causes are excludedProlactinoma if level over 200; large mass with level under 100 is stalk effect
Prolactin repeated on a diluted sampleBy branchLevel much higher after dilutionHook effect in a giant prolactinoma
Serum follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormoneSkipLow from suppression, does not name the causeProlactin, pregnancy test and TSH come first
Scenario bank
  1. Prolactin >200 with bitemporal hemianopsia → Macroprolactinoma → MRI → cabergoline
  2. Patient needs continued antipsychotic coverage → Switch to aripiprazole or quetiapine
  3. Prolactin 60 + TSH 25 + fatigue and cold intolerance → Hypothyroidism → levothyroxine
  4. Prolactin 45 on metoclopramide for gastroparesis → Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia
  5. Large sellar mass with prolactin only 45 → Stalk effect → a non-functioning mass, not a prolactinoma
  6. Huge pituitary mass with a normal-looking prolactin → Hook effect → dilute and repeat
  7. Amenorrhea + galactorrhea + negative pregnancy test → Prolactin and TSH before imaging
  8. Years of untreated hyperprolactinemia → Hypogonadism → infertility and osteoporosis
  9. Woman on an SSRI with new galactorrhea → Modest drug-induced elevation
Pairs with Part I Brain Tumors in a Child covers the localization once the trophic-hormone pattern points to the region.
Transferable rule When a lab value has a well-known range that separates two candidate causes, use the value rather than the history to decide between them.

edits.html:
Scaly Rashes

psoriasis vs other scaly plaques · extensor vs flexural · the nails · exam findings outweigh the exposure historyWhere are the plaques, are the nails involved, and does the exam agree with the history?

The decision point

Nail dystrophy together with extensor-surface scaly plaques indicates psoriasis. An extensor distribution indicates psoriasis; a flexural distribution indicates eczema. An occupational "wet work" history does not override these findings. Psoriasis does show the Koebner phenomenon, so friction can localize it.

Scaly plaques – the differential
DiagnosisDistributionThe tellNails?
PsoriasisExtensor, scalp, trunkSalmon plaques, silvery scale, Auspitz sign, KoebnerYes – pitting, onycholysis
Atopic dermatitisFlexuralPruritus first, rash second; lichenification; atopy triadNo
Nummular eczemaExtremitiesCoin-shaped, intensely pruriticNo
Tinea corporisAnywhereAnnular with central clearing; potassium hydroxide (KOH) shows hyphaeSeparate (onychomycosis)
Seborrheic dermatitisScalp, nasolabial, browsGreasy yellow scale; MalasseziaNo
Pityriasis roseaTrunkHerald patch → Christmas-tree patternNo
Lichen planusWrists, ankles, mucosa6 Ps: pruritic purple polygonal planar papules; Wickham striaeCan
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
KOH preparation of the scaleFirstHyphae in an annular plaque with central clearingTinea corporis; a steroid would cause tinea incognito
Rapid plasma reaginBy branchReactive with a truncal or palm and sole eruptionSecondary syphilis, the mimic of pityriasis rosea
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsExtensor silvery plaques with nail pittingPsoriasis; the tests only exclude tinea and syphilis
Skin biopsy, only if atypicalSupportsParakeratosis with Munro microabscessesPsoriasis when the exam is not typical
X-ray of the handsBy branchPencil-in-cup erosions at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) jointsPsoriatic arthritis in a patient with dactylitis
Interferon-gamma release assay or purified protein derivativeNextLatent tuberculosis excludedRequired before the first dose of a tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) inhibitor
Wood lamp examinationSkipDoes not diagnose tinea corporisKOH answers the question at the bedside
Scenario bank
  1. 34 yo M with extensor-surface silvery plaques and nail pitting → Psoriasis
  2. 34 yo M with flexural lichenified pruritic patches and a history of asthma → Atopic dermatitis
  3. 34 yo M with an annular scaly patch with central clearing and an active border → Tinea corporis → KOH preparation
  4. 34 yo M with a herald patch followed by a Christmas-tree truncal eruption → Pityriasis rosea
  5. 34 yo M with purple polygonal pruritic papules and oral Wickham striae → Lichen planus
  6. 34 yo M whose plaques bleed at pinpoints when the scale is lifted → Auspitz sign
  7. 34 yo M with extensor-surface silvery plaques, dactylitis and DIP joint involvement → Psoriatic arthritis
  8. 34 yo M with a few silvery extensor plaques on the elbows and knees and nail pitting → Topical steroid plus calcipotriene → first rung before phototherapy and systemics
  9. 34 yo M with a single annular scaly trunk plaque with central clearing and an active border → KOH preparation → if tinea, a steroid causes tinea incognito
  10. 34 yo M with severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis about to start a TNF-alpha inhibitor → Test for latent tuberculosis → TNF blockade can reactivate tuberculosis
  11. 34 yo M with extensive plaque psoriasis who was started on oral prednisone for an asthma flare → Abrupt discontinuation of prednisone → abrupt steroid withdrawal can trigger a pustular flare
Psoriasis facts they attach Pathology: parakeratosis, acanthosis, Munro microabscesses, thinned suprapapillary plates (→ Auspitz) · immunology: Th17 / IL-17 / IL-23 (T helper 17 cell / interleukin 17 / interleukin 23) axis · drugs: secukinumab (IL-17), ustekinumab (IL-12/23), TNF-α (tumor necrosis factor alpha) inhibitors after screening for latent TB (tuberculosis) · associations: psoriatic arthritis with DIP (distal interphalangeal) joints, "pencil-in-cup," dactylitis; metabolic syndrome and CV (cardiovascular) risk · ladder: topical steroids + calcipotriene first, then narrowband UVB (ultraviolet B), then systemics · abrupt steroid withdrawal can trigger a pustular flare · for tinea, order a KOH prep (potassium hydroxide preparation), never a steroid (tinea incognito).
Pairs with Part I Hair Loss in a Child is the scalp version, where follicular invasion changes the therapy from topical to oral.
Transferable rule Exposures can suggest a diagnosis, but examination findings determine it. When the history and the exam conflict, rely on the exam.
Salient decoy

edits.html:
The Red Eye

three triage questions · conjunctivitis types · red eyes that cannot be missed · contact lens wearersIs acuity down, is the pain deep, or is the pupil, cornea or globe abnormal?

The decision point

1. Is visual acuity affected? 2. Is there true deep pain (not gritty or itchy)? 3. Is the pupil, cornea, or globe abnormal? Any "yes" means this is not simple conjunctivitis and points toward urgent ophthalmology.

Conjunctivitis types
TypeDiscriminatorTreatment
Viral (adenovirus)Watery, follicular tarsal conjunctiva, preauricular node, upper respiratory infection (URI) prodromeSupportive – cool compresses, artificial tears
BacterialPurulent, lids stuck shut on waking, papillaryErythromycin ointment or polymyxin-trimethoprim
Contact lens wearerAny red eye → think PseudomonasFluoroquinolone; remove lens; urgent ophtho if infiltrate
AllergicITCHING is the hallmark; bilateral, cobblestone papillaeOlopatadine, ketotifen
Gonococcal EmergencyHyperacute (<24 h), copious purulence – can perforate the corneaIntramuscular (IM) ceftriaxone + irrigation + urgent ophtho
ChlamydialChronic >3 weeks, follicular, sexually active adultOral azithromycin/doxycycline + treat partners
The can't-miss red eyes
DiagnosisThe tellAnswer
Acute angle-closure glaucomaSevere pain, halos, vomiting, mid-dilated fixed pupil, hard globe; triggered by dark rooms or anticholinergicsTimolol + apraclonidine + pilocarpine + IV acetazolamide → laser peripheral iridotomy
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) keratitisDendritic ulcer on fluorescein, ↓ corneal sensationTopical trifluridine or oral acyclovir – never steroids
Herpes zoster ophthalmicusV1 vesicles + Hutchinson signOral antivirals + ophtho
Anterior uveitisCiliary flush, cell and flare, consensual photophobia; human leukocyte antigen B27, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, sarcoidTopical steroid + cycloplegic – the one place prednisolone is right
ScleritisBoring pain that wakes from sleep, does not blanch with phenylephrine; rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitisSystemic NSAIDs/steroids
EpiscleritisSectoral, minimal pain, blanches with phenylephrineSupportive
EndophthalmitisPost-op or post-injection, pain + ↓visual acuity + hypopyonIntravitreal antibiotics – emergency
Orbital cellulitisProptosis, pain with extraocular movement, ophthalmoplegiaComputed tomography orbits + IV antibiotics (preseptal has none of those)
Scenario bank
  1. 24 yo M with bilateral watery red eyes, a preauricular node, recent URI and normal vision → Viral conjunctivitis → supportive care
  2. 24 yo M contact lens wearer with pain, photophobia and a corneal infiltrate → Bacterial keratitis → urgent ophthalmology, never patch
  3. 62 yo F with severe pain, halos, a mid-dilated fixed pupil and vomiting → Acute angle-closure glaucoma → topical agents plus acetazolamide
  4. 24 yo M with a dendritic corneal ulcer on fluorescein staining → HSV keratitis → topical antiviral, never steroids
  5. 30 yo M with ankylosing spondylitis, photophobia, ciliary flush, and cell and flare → Anterior uveitis → topical steroid plus cycloplegic
  6. 55 yo F with rheumatoid arthritis and severe boring eye pain that wakes her at night → Scleritis
  7. Newborn with purulent conjunctivitis on day 3 of life → Gonococcal conjunctivitis → parenteral ceftriaxone
  8. 9 yo M with bilateral eye itching, watery discharge, cobblestone papillae under the upper eyelids, nasal congestion each spring → Allergic conjunctivitis → olopatadine or ketotifen drops
  9. 5 yo F, 3 days of photophobia with lids crusted shut on waking, diffuse bulbar and palpebral erythema, mucopurulent discharge, acuity unchanged → Bacterial conjunctivitis → Mucopurulent discharge with normal acuity
  10. School-age child with mucopurulent conjunctivitis and no contact lens use; the likeliest organism → Haemophilus influenzae → With S pneumoniae and Moraxella catarrhalis
  11. Child with an undifferentiated red eye and mucopurulent discharge; which is contraindicated before slit-lamp examination → Topical corticosteroid drops → Steroid on an unrecognized HSV keratitis worsens it
Neonatal conjunctivitis by day of onset Day 0–1 chemical · day 2–5 gonococcal → IM/IV ceftriaxone + irrigation · day 5–14 chlamydial → oral erythromycin, or oral azithromycin as the alternative (counsel on pyloric stenosis with either) · day 6–14 HSV (herpes simplex virus) → IV acyclovir. Birth prophylaxis (erythromycin ointment) prevents gonococcal but not chlamydial disease.
How NBME framed it A home birth delivered by the father stood in for missing eye prophylaxis, and Kawasaki disease was listed under its formal name, mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome.
Pairs with Part II Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child covers the red eye that comes from a tender lump on the lid margin, and its lid-swelling mimics. Ask: is there a lump on the lid?
The steroid rule Steroids are indicated in anterior uveitis (topical) and scleritis (systemic). Topical steroids are catastrophic in HSV (herpes simplex virus) keratitis, bacterial/fungal keratitis, and undifferentiated red eye. If you cannot name the diagnosis with certainty, do not give steroids.

edits.html:
Rhinitis

the step-up ladder · nasal steroid after antihistamines fail · start 2 weeks before pollen · immunotherapy is the baitWhich step has the patient already failed, and how far off is the pollen season?

The decision point

For moderate-to-severe seasonal rhinitis that has failed antihistamines, step up to an intranasal corticosteroid. It is the single most effective drug class for allergic rhinitis. A visit in "late winter" points to prophylaxis: start it ~2 weeks before pollen season. The steroid suppresses the mucosal inflammatory response and needs lead time.

Option analysis – why each fails
ChoiceWhy it fails
Minimize outdoor activitiesImpractical for pollen (unlike dust mites or pets); inadequate once disease is complicated
Continue over-the-counter (OTC) antihistaminesAlready failing – and first-generation agents bring sedation and anticholinergic effects
Desensitization (immunotherapy)The real bait – the only disease-modifying option, but reserved for failure of maximal pharmacotherapy. He has never tried a nasal steroid
MontelukastLess effective than intranasal steroids; carries a Food and Drug Administration boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects
Oral prednisoneSystemic steroids for a benign chronic condition – never the answer
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F with moderate seasonal rhinitis failing OTC antihistamines → Intranasal corticosteroid
  2. 28 yo F seeking durable control after several drug classes have failed → Allergen immunotherapy
  3. 28 yo F advised to minimize outdoor activity for her pollen allergy → Impractical for pollen, unlike dust-mite control
  4. 28 yo F with rhinitis and asthma who wants a single oral agent → Montelukast – with neuropsychiatric counseling
  5. 28 yo F using oxymetazoline for 10 days with worsening congestion → Rhinitis medicamentosa → stop the spray
  6. 28 yo F with clear rhinorrhea, no itch or sneezing, triggered by temperature change → Vasomotor rhinitis
The ladder Start with allergen avoidance (when practical), then an intranasal corticosteroid. Next, add a second-generation oral or intranasal antihistamine. Use immunotherapy only after pharmacotherapy fails. Any first-generation antihistamine in a stem is usually there to be replaced, not continued.
Sequencing trap

edits.html:
Right Lower Quadrant Pain

appendix, ileocecum, or neither · Campylobacter and Yersinia · appendix-sparing imaging · when to treat CampylobacterIs there profuse mucoid diarrhea, and is there a sick contact?

Source vignette Pt – 17 yo, migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, sibling with the same illness · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Campylobacter infection, acute appendicitis and Escherichia coli O157:H7 infection
The decision point

Fever, right lower quadrant tenderness, and a neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis occur in both appendicitis and ileocecitis and do not discriminate. Two findings that appendicitis does not explain are twelve mucus-containing loose stools in 24 hours and a brother with the same illness. Both fit infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis) from organisms with an ileocecal predilection, Campylobacter jejuni and Yersinia enterocolitica. The migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain also fits: Campylobacter may infect the jejunum first and then spread to the ileum and cecum.

Defining criteria Infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis) – right lower quadrant pain from acute ileocecitis caused by organisms with an ileocecal predilection, specifically Yersinia enterocolitica and Campylobacter jejuni · The discriminating symptom – profuse watery or mucoid diarrhea, which acute appendicitis is not classically associated with · The imaging tell – ileocecal inflammation and mesenteric lymphadenopathy with sparing of the appendix · When Campylobacter earns antibiotics – duration beyond 7 days, bloody stools, high fevers, or a patient who is pregnant, immunocompromised, or elderly
Pertinent positives & negatives Twelve mucus-containing stools in 24 hours – profuse mucoid diarrhea, not a feature of appendicitis · A brother with the same illness, now improving – a shared exposure, which appendicitis does not explain; the sibling's course fits a self-limited enteritis · Migratory periumbilical → right lower quadrant pain – classic for appendicitis, but also explained by jejunal-then-ileocecal spread of Campylobacter · Right lower quadrant tenderness without rebound or rigidity – no peritonitis; this argues against an advanced or perforated appendix without excluding an early one · Fever 38.8 °C with WBC (white blood cell count) 13,700 and 80% neutrophils – present in both diagnoses; does not discriminate · Mucus in the stool – argues against norovirus, whose stools are watery without mucus · No hematochezia in the patient, with fever above 38.5 °C – argues against E. coli O157:H7, which usually brings hematochezia within 1–3 days and rarely high fever · Age 17 – diverticulitis is exceedingly rare at this age
Right lower quadrant pain in a young patient: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Infectious ileocecitis (Campylobacter, Yersinia)Undercooked poultry or a sick contact; ileocecal predilection; fever with mucoid or bloody diarrheaProfuse mucoid diarrhea with right lower quadrant pain; imaging spares the appendix(the answer)
Acute appendicitisLuminal obstruction; migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, anorexia, vomitingLittle or no diarrhea, progressive localized peritonitis, no sick contactsTwelve mucoid stools and an affected sibling
E. coli O157:H7Shiga toxin colitis; undercooked beef or a point-source outbreakHematochezia within 1–3 days and fever above 38.5 °C is rareThe patient has no bloody stools and a temperature of 38.8 °C
NorovirusCommon-source outbreak; prominent vomitingWatery stools without mucus, normal white blood cell countMucoid stools with a neutrophilic leukocytosis
Cecal diverticulitisRight-sided diverticular inflammationRight lower quadrant pain and fever in an adult; mild or no diarrheaExceedingly rare at 17; profuse mucoid diarrhea
Crohn ileitisChronic transmural ileal inflammationChronic, relapsing pain, weight loss, perianal diseaseThree days of illness with a sick contact
Management, in one line Campylobacter is treated supportively because it is usually self-limited within seven days. Antibiotics are reserved for the severe or high-risk cases listed above. In infectious ileocecitis, surgery is not required.
Decision spine Is there diarrhea, and how much? – Twelve mucoid stools → argues against appendicitis · Is there a sick contact? – A brother with the same illness → an infectious exposure, not a luminal obstruction · Are there peritoneal signs? – No rebound, no rigidity → not a surgical abdomen at this moment · What is the stool like? – Mucoid, with or without blood → invasive bacterial rather than viral · Which organisms live at the ileocecum? – Campylobacter and Yersinia
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Complete blood countFirstNeutrophil-predominant leukocytosisShared by appendicitis and ileocecitis; decides nothing
Ultrasound or computed tomography of the abdomenBy branchIleocecal inflammation with a spared appendixInfectious ileocecitis: supportive care, no surgery
Inflamed appendixAcute appendicitis: surgical consultation
Stool culture or polymerase chain reactionConfirmsCampylobacter or YersiniaNames the organism; a susceptibility panel alone is not a reason to treat
Colonoscopy with ileal intubationBy branchChronic ileal inflammation on biopsyCrohn ileitis: chronic, relapsing pain, weight loss, perianal disease
Diagnostic laparoscopySkipInvasive when imaging can decideImage first when the examination leaves the diagnosis unclear
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo with migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness → Campylobacter infection → Infectious ileocecitis
  2. A hemodynamically stable 17-year-old with migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness has had 3 days of symptoms without bloody stools. → Supportive care with stool studies → Usually self-limited within 7 days
  3. A 17-year-old with migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness now presents on day 9 with bloody stools and fever to 39.5 °C. → Start antimicrobial therapy → A high-risk criterion is met
  4. 17 yo with right lower quadrant pain, anorexia and vomiting but no diarrhea, with rebound tenderness → Surgical consultation for appendectomy → The classic script without the stool
  5. 17 yo with right lower quadrant pain and diarrhea in whom the diagnosis remains unclear after examination → Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen → Ileocecal inflammation with a spared appendix
  6. 16 yo with months of right lower quadrant pain, weight loss and a perianal fistula → Colonoscopy with ileal intubation → Crohn ileitis
  7. 6 yo with severe crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody stools, temperature 37.6 C, after a family cookout → Escherichia coli O157:H7 infection → Hematochezia early, high fever rare
  8. That 6 year old with suspected Shiga toxin producing E coli; which intervention should be withheld → Empiric antibiotics → Risk of precipitating hemolytic uremic syndrome
  9. Three weeks after a Campylobacter enteritis, ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia → Guillain-Barre syndrome → The classic post-infectious sequela
  10. Two weeks after a Campylobacter enteritis, asymmetric oligoarthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis → Reactive arthritis → The second named sequela
  11. 5 yo M, 4 days of mucoid diarrhea after a low-grade fever that has resolved, still 5 or 6 stools a day, well hydrated, afebrile, guaiac negative; stool culture grows Campylobacter coli, ciprofloxacin resistant, ampicillin and tetracycline sensitive → Symptomatic care only → mild and self-limited; the susceptibility panel is not an indication
  12. 6 yo with Campylobacter coli enteritis now on day 9 with bloody stools; ciprofloxacin resistant, erythromycin intermediate, ampicillin and tetracycline sensitive → Amoxicillin → sensitive, and safe under 8
  13. 4 yo in day care with high fever, bloody diarrhea and a brief generalized seizure; stool grows Shigella → Azithromycin → treating shortens illness and spread
Decoy note The brother's illness supports an infectious cause, but his bloody stools may prompt a diagnosis of Shiga toxin E. coli in a patient with no blood in his own stool. A contact's findings describe the exposure, not this patient's phenotype. The migratory pain is also explained by Campylobacter spread, so it does not confirm appendicitis.
Bacterial diarrhea: who gets antibiotics Campylobacter – self-limited within about a week; supportive care. Treat only for symptoms beyond 7 days, bloody stools, high fever, or pregnancy, immunocompromise or old age; choose by susceptibility · Stool culture – a positive culture with a susceptibility panel is not an indication. Culture is for protracted or severe illness and for outbreak control in day care and nursing homes · Shiga toxin-producing E. coli – bloody diarrhea with little fever; never give antibiotics, which can raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome · Shigella – high fever, bloody diarrhea, sometimes a febrile seizure; antibiotics (azithromycin) shorten illness and spread · Nontyphoidal Salmonella – supportive in a healthy child; treat infants under 3 months, sickle cell disease, immunocompromise or bacteremia, because treatment otherwise prolongs carriage · Yersinia – pseudoappendicitis like Campylobacter; supportive unless bacteremic or immunocompromised · Clostridioides difficile – recent antibiotics; oral vancomycin or fidaximicin · Doxycycline under 8 – avoided when another agent covers the organism, because of tooth staining
Pearls Appendicitis does not cause twelve mucoid stools or a sick sibling; ileocecal Campylobacter or Yersinia explains both. · Profuse watery-then-mucoid diarrhea or a sick contact alone should prompt reconsideration of appendicitis before surgery. · Campylobacter and Yersinia have an ileocecal predilection and mimic appendicitis; imaging shows ileocecal inflammation and mesenteric adenopathy with a normal appendix. · Campylobacter may infect the jejunum before the ileum and cecum, so the pain can migrate as in appendicitis. · The two tested sequelae of Campylobacter are Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis. · For Campylobacter, antibiotics are for illness beyond seven days, bloody stools, high fevers, or pregnancy, immunocompromise, or advanced age; otherwise the treatment is supportive. · Antibiotics are withheld for Shiga toxin E. coli.
Pairs with Part II Acute Kidney Injury in a Child has the Shiga toxin and hemolytic uremic syndrome row from the renal side, where the E. coli O157:H7 branch of this differential ends. Ask: whose stool was bloody, and how many days into the illness? Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers hemolytic uremic syndrome, which follows Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, not Campylobacter. Part II Infectious Diarrhea covers the organism by exposure: what did the patient eat, and when?
Transferable rule When a presentation fits a textbook script, look for the finding the script cannot explain, such as a symptom the disease does not produce or an exposure it cannot have.
Salient decoyAcute appendicitis is not associated with profuse watery then mucoid diarrhea and cannot explain a sibling with the same illness. There are no peritoneal signs.
True-fact-wrong-slotE. coli O157:H7 causes hematochezia in the patient within 1–3 days, and fever above 38.5 °C rarely occurs. The bloody stools are the brother's, not this patient's.
Class-vs-memberNorovirus gives watery stools without mucus, a normal white blood cell count, and prominent vomiting
Unchecked attributeCecal diverticulitis is exceedingly rare in children and adolescents and does not produce profuse mucoid diarrhea.
Test-overrides-findingsA susceptibility panel invites treatment, but a mild, improving, afebrile child is treated by the clinical picture, not the culture report.

edits.html:
Tick-Borne Illness

treat suspected rickettsiosis before confirming it · a rash from the extremities inward · the platelet, sodium and liver triadWhere did the rash start, and what did the platelets, sodium and transaminases do?

Source vignette Pt – 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, abdominal pain, body aches and headache with an unremarkable emergency department workup, now back with confusion and worse pain; lives by a lake surrounded by woods · Exam – T 39, BP 90/60, HR 120; new maculopapular rash on arms and legs, generalized abdominal tenderness without rebound, no neck stiffness, nonfocal neurologically · Labs – leukocytes 4,600, platelets 46,000, ALT (alanine aminotransferase) 158, AST (aspartate aminotransferase) 202, creatinine 1.1 · Imaging – abdominal CT (computed tomography) normal · Q – the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned amoxicillin, doxycycline, laparoscopy, prednisone, serum ceruloplasmin and stool ova and parasites
Source vignette · NBME Pediatrics CMS Pt – 6 yo F, previously healthy, seen in June with 4 days of persistent fever and severe headache and 1 day of a rash on the hands; lives in a rural area and is often bitten by mosquitoes; took corticosteroids for poison ivy a month ago; appears ill · Exam – T 39 C, HR 110, RR 22; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; scattered petechiae on the palms and distal arms · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned dengue fever, erysipelas, erythema infectiosum, exanthema subitum, Kawasaki disease, measles, meningococcemia, Rocky Mountain spotted fever and typhoid fever
The decision point

The picture is three to four days of undifferentiated fever, headache and myalgia, then a rash on the extremities, in a child with wooded exposure. With the laboratory triad of thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and hyponatremia, this is Rocky Mountain spotted fever. The management is empiric doxycycline started now. Diagnosis is made retrospectively by serology, and the disease progresses to vascular collapse and death if you wait for it. The abdominal pain is not a second problem: severe abdominal pain is part of RMSF (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) in children. It is the specific reason this boy got a CT rather than an antibiotic on his first visit.

Defining criteria Rocky Mountain spotted fever – Rickettsia rickettsii, a gram-negative obligate intracellular organism transmitted by tick bite, peaking in late spring and summer, most often in the southeastern and south-central United States despite the name; incubation 2 to 14 days; many patients never recall the bite, so its absence proves nothing · The rash – begins maculopapular on the wrists and ankles, spreads centrally, involves palms and soles, and evolves to petechiae · The laboratory triad – thrombocytopenia from intravascular platelet destruction, hyponatremia, and raised AST and ALT from hepatic endothelial injury · Treatment gate – doxycycline empirically on suspicion, in all patients including young children; a study found no staining of permanent teeth after short courses (5 to 10 days)
Pertinent positives & negatives Three days of nonspecific fever then a rash – the rickettsial tempo; the rash appears late, which is why the first visit was unremarkable · Rash on arms and legs – extremity onset, spreading centrally · Platelets 46,000 with raised transaminases – the vascular-injury signature, belonging to no isolated abdominal process · Lives near woods – the exposure; no recalled bite is typical, not exculpatory · Severe abdominal pain with a normal CT – the pediatric RMSF mimic of appendicitis; the negative scan closes the surgical option rather than opening a new one · Confusion with a nonfocal examination and no neck stiffness – early encephalitic involvement, not meningitis · BP 90/60 with HR 120 – early vascular compromise, and the reason waiting is dangerous · No adenopathy, clear oropharynx – argues against the viral exanthems and mononucleosis
Fever and rash after outdoor exposure – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Rocky Mountain spotted fever Can't missSummer, wooded exposure; R. rickettsiiExtremity rash spreading centrally, palms and soles; low platelets, low sodium, high transaminases – (the answer)
Lyme diseaseSame season and habitat; Borrelia burgdorferiErythema migrans – a single expanding annular lesion with central clearingMaculopapular extremity rash; cytopenias and transaminitis atypical
Ehrlichiosis / anaplasmosisSame tick exposure, similar prodromeSame labs, usually no rash; morulae in leukocytesA prominent rash is present
Dengue feverAedes mosquito; travel to or residence in the tropicsRetro-orbital pain, severe bone and muscle pain; leukopenia, low platelets; bleeding in severe casesNo tropical travel; mosquito bites at home in the US do not transmit it
MeningococcemiaNeisseria meningitidis; any seasonHours from fever to petechiae, purpura, shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation; meningismus in someDays of fever before the rash; rash began distally and spread inward
Kawasaki diseaseVasculitis of young childrenFever for 5 days or more plus 4 of 5: nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips or strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, hand and foot redness or swelling, cervical node; platelets risePetechial palm rash, low platelets; conjunctival injection alone does not make it
MeaslesUnvaccinated child; paramyxovirusCough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots; rash starts at the hairline and spreads down, sparing palms and solesRash began on the hands and wrists; no cough or coryza
Roseola (exanthema subitum)Human herpesvirus 6; under age 2Days of high fever in a well infant, then a blanching truncal rash as the fever breaksIll school-age child; petechial rash during the fever
Immune thrombocytopeniaPost-viral, otherwise well childIsolated thrombocytopenia, normal liver, afebrileFever, rash, transaminitis and hypotension
Wilson diseaseGenetic copper transport defectKayser-Fleischer rings; hepatic and neuropsychiatric disease over monthsAn acute febrile illness with a rash over days
AmebiasisFever, abdominal pain, liver abscessBloody diarrhea; abscess on imagingCT normal, no diarrhea, rash unexplained
Decision spine How long has the fever run and when did the rash appear? – Three to four days, then rash, the rickettsial tempo · Where did the rash start? – Wrists and ankles, spreading inward · What did the platelets, sodium and transaminases do? – Low, low, high, the triad · Any outdoor or wooded exposure? – Yes, and a recalled bite is not required · Is there abdominal pain? – In a child that is part of the disease, not a second one · So when do you treat? – Now; serology is retrospective and untreated disease kills
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Complete blood countFirstPlatelets low, white count normal or lowEndothelial injury; fits RMSF, not a surgical abdomen
Basic metabolic panel and liver enzymesFirstHyponatremia with raised AST and ALTCompletes the rickettsial triad; start doxycycline now
Peripheral smearBy branchMorulae in leukocytes, usually no rashEhrlichiosis or anaplasmosis; doxycycline treats it too
Rickettsia rickettsii serology, acute and convalescentConfirmsFourfold rise in immunoglobulin G titerRMSF, in retrospect; never delay treatment for it
Abdominal CTSkipNormalSevere abdominal pain is part of RMSF in children
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, headache and abdominal pain, now confused with a maculopapular rash on the arms and legs; platelets 46,000, AST 202, ALT 158; lives near woods; abdominal CT normal → Doxycycline → empiric treatment for Rocky Mountain spotted fever
  2. 10 yo with fever, an extremity rash, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis after wooded exposure; serology has been sent → Withholding antibiotics until serology returns → untreated disease progresses to vascular collapse
  3. 9 yo seen 10 days after a hike with a single expanding annular lesion showing central clearing and mild fatigue → Lyme disease → erythema migrans
  4. 4 yo with suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever whose parents decline doxycycline over concerns about dental staining → Give doxycycline → a study found no staining of permanent teeth after short courses (5 to 10 days)
  5. 40 yo with summer tick exposure, fever, headache, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases, with no rash → Ehrlichiosis → doxycycline treats it as well
  6. The mechanism of thrombocytopenia in Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Intravascular platelet destruction from infection of vascular endothelium → small-vessel vasculitis
  7. 12 yo with severe abdominal pain and fever, a maculopapular rash on the wrists and ankles, and a normal abdominal CT → Rocky Mountain spotted fever → abdominal pain in children mimics appendicitis
  8. Child already started on doxycycline for suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Rickettsia serology → confirmation is retrospective and never delays therapy
  9. 6 yo F, previously healthy, seen in June with 4 days of high fever and severe headache and 1 day of a rash on the hands; lives in a rural area, often bitten by mosquitoes; finished a steroid course for poison ivy a month ago; appears ill; T 39 C; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; scattered petechiae on the palms and distal arms → Rocky Mountain spotted fever → doxycycline now, without waiting for serology
  10. 10 yo F back 5 days from 2 weeks in the Dominican Republic; fever 39.5 °C, retro-orbital headache, severe bone and muscle pain; macular truncal rash; no outdoor exposure in the US; white blood cell count 2,800/µL, platelets 90,000/µL → Dengue fever → supportive care with fluids; avoid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
  11. 4 yo M on a Tennessee farm in July: 4 days of fever and headache; conjunctival injection; wrist and ankle macules, now petechial, spread to palms, soles and trunk; no cracked lips or hand swelling; platelets 85,000/µL, sodium 130 mEq/L → Start doxycycline → Rocky Mountain spotted fever; any age, treat on suspicion
Decoy note Two details suggest abdominal and hepatic causes. Worsening abdominal pain with a normal CT is the classic pediatric RMSF presentation that gets children taken to the operating room. Once the scan is negative, stop pursuing an abdominal cause. Confusion with transaminitis suggests Wilson disease, but confusion in RMSF is early encephalitis arriving over hours, not over months.
Decoy note: no tick in the stem No tick – most RMSF stems never mention one; the clue is season (late spring to summer), rural or outdoor life, days of fever and severe headache, then a rash that starts on the wrists, ankles, palms or soles and spreads inward, turning petechial · Mosquito bites – point to dengue only with tropical travel, and dengue brings retro-orbital pain and severe bone and muscle pain · Conjunctival injection – occurs in RMSF too; Kawasaki disease needs 5 days of fever plus its criteria, and measles needs cough, coryza and a rash from the hairline down · Steroids for poison ivy a month ago – irrelevant; they explain none of the fever, headache or petechiae
Pearls Treat on suspicion, confirm retrospectively – doxycycline treats the patient; serology only documents the diagnosis · Doxycycline is given to children of any age for RMSF – the staining concern applies to prolonged courses, and withholding it is the dangerous choice · Low platelets plus transaminitis plus hyponatremia after outdoor exposure – a rickettsial fingerprint the viral exanthems do not produce · The rash moves inward – extremity onset spreading centrally with palms and soles is a short differential: RMSF, secondary syphilis, coxsackie hand-foot-and-mouth · No recalled tick bite – does not lower suspicion; the exposure history is habitat, not bite · Abdominal pain in a febrile child with a rash is part of the illness – a normal CT should redirect you to a systemic diagnosis, not a more invasive abdominal one
Pairs with Part I Skin and Soft Tissue Infection covers the febrile-rash differential. Fever and Rash in a Child covers measles and roseola, and Kawasaki Disease covers the 5-day fever with red eyes. Related conditions without their own brief: Lyme disease and ehrlichiosis. Ask: where did the rash start, and what did the platelets and transaminases do?
How NBME framed it Kawasaki disease appeared under its formal name, mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, as a decoy for a child with 4 days of fever, red eyes and a petechial rash on the palms.
Transferable rule When the confirmatory test is retrospective and the untreated disease is lethal, treat on the clinical picture. Let the serology arrive whenever it arrives. A pending test is not a reason to wait; treatment should already have started.
Salient decoyStool for ova and parasites: fever with abdominal pain and liver enzymes fits amebiasis, but that causes bloody diarrhea and a liver abscess and explains no rash.
Treat-the-numberPrednisone: platelets of 46,000 invite ITP (immune thrombocytopenia), but ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child, not fever with rash, transaminitis and hypotension.
True-fact-wrong-slotAmoxicillin: correct for Lyme, same season and habitat, but Lyme rash is a single expanding annular lesion and it spares the platelets and liver.
Salient decoySerum ceruloplasmin: liver enzymes plus confusion reads as Wilson disease, a chronic disorder with Kayser-Fleischer rings, not four days of fever with a rash.
Sequencing trapLaparoscopy: the abdominal CT is already normal, which answers the surgical question.
Salient decoyDengue fever: mosquito bites suggest it, but without tropical travel dengue is not on the table. It brings retro-orbital and bone pain rather than a rash spreading in from the wrists.
Unchecked attributeKawasaki disease: red eyes fit, but fever has run 4 days, not 5, and the rash is petechial on the palms, not polymorphous with swollen hands.
Salient decoyMeasles: conjunctivitis tempts, but measles rash starts at the hairline, spares the palms and soles, and follows cough and coryza.

edits.html:
Adolescent Kyphosis

correction test · wedging on the lateral film · postural vs Scheuermann · observe, brace or fuse by curve sizeDoes the curve correct prone or in extension, and if not, is there 5 degrees of wedging in 3 consecutive vertebrae?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

A teenager with thoracic roundback: lie the patient prone or ask for active extension.

  • Corrects fully: postural kyphosis. Exercises and reassurance; a film, if taken, shows a smooth curve without wedging.
  • Stays rigid, often with activity-related mid-back pain: standing lateral film. Wedging of 5 degrees or more in 3 or more consecutive vertebrae is Scheuermann disease, most often in boys aged 12 to 17.

Treat by curve size and growth: observe and exercise a mild curve; brace a moderate curve (about 50 to 75 degrees; one source gives 60 to 80) or one that progresses, while growth remains; fuse a severe curve (over about 75 degrees) or refractory pain, even with growth remaining.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Rigid – over 40 degrees (normal 20 to 40); does not correct prone or in extension · Film – anterior wedging of 5 degrees or more in 3 or more consecutive vertebrae (Sorensen) · Schmorl nodes – disc herniation through the endplate; dramatic on film, not an emergency; support, not required
Mimics Compression fracture – trauma or osteoporosis; acute focal pain; height loss at one level, not three · Ankylosing spondylitis – young adult; sacroiliac pain, morning stiffness; not isolated thoracic wedging
Management and treatment
Management ladder: Scheuermann kyphosis
TierInterventionEscalate when
Mild curveObserve; exercise and stretchingCurve reaches the brace range or progresses, growth remaining
Moderate or progressing, still growingBrace until skeletal maturity; it halts progression, rarely correctsSevere curve (over about 75 degrees) or refractory pain
Severe or refractory painPosterior spinal fusionTop rung
Practice
  1. 17-year-old boy with 1 year of worsening thoracic roundback aching mid-back pain curve does not correct prone or in extension No morning stiffness or buttock pain Afebrile · lateral film: 8-degree anterior wedging of 3 consecutive mid-thoracic vertebrae, Schmorl nodes → Scheuermann disease → a rigid kyphosis with 5 degrees or more of wedging in 3 consecutive vertebrae is Scheuermann disease; Schmorl nodes support it
  2. 15-year-old girl whose parents worry about her upper back round shoulders for 2 years curve fully corrects lying prone and on active extension No back pain Afebrile · lateral film: smooth curve, no vertebral wedging → Postural kyphosis → a curve that fully corrects is postural kyphosis, the most common cause of adolescent roundback: postural exercises and reassurance; no structural vertebral change
  3. 16-year-old boy with 8 months of increasing thoracic roundback mild mid-back ache after sports curve does not correct in hyperextension No pain that wakes him from sleep or weight loss Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Standing lateral thoracic spine radiograph → a rigid kyphosis gets a standing lateral spine film first to measure the wedging and the Cobb angle; MRI is for pain that wakes from sleep, weight loss or neurologic signs
  4. 14-year-old boy was diagnosed with Scheuermann disease 1 year ago Cobb angle now 65 degrees, up from 52 about 2 years of growth remaining Doing his extension exercises Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Brace until skeletal maturity → a 65-degree curve sits in the brace range and is progressing; with growth remaining it is braced to halt progression until maturity; fusion is for a severe curve, over about 75 degrees, or refractory pain
  5. 17-year-old boy was diagnosed with Scheuermann disease at 13 Cobb angle 80 degrees skeletally mature; physes closed on film Back pain limits school despite a year of physical therapy Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Posterior spinal fusion → a severe curve (over about 75 degrees) or refractory pain at skeletal maturity goes to posterior spinal fusion; a brace no longer works once growth ends
Transferable rule

One bedside maneuver, whether the curve corrects, separates structural from postural kyphosis; the film confirms, it does not decide.

edits.html:
Scrotal Pain and Masses

painful scrotum and painless mass: separate workups · torsion vs epididymitis · the two hard pairs · tumor markersWas the onset sudden or gradual, and does the mass transilluminate or change with Valsalva?

The decision point

Separate torsion from epididymitis by timeline, location and infection signs. Torsion is sudden and maximal within minutes to hours. A 3-day escalating course with fever, dysuria and posterior tenderness is epididymitis, a clinical diagnosis. Ultrasound and urology are torsion steps; a clinical picture of epididymitis like this one does not need them.

The acute scrotum – the differential
ConditionOnsetThe tellCremastericNext step
Testicular torsion EmergencySudden, minutesHigh-riding transverse testis, N/V, no feverAbsentEmergent urology – salvage window ~6 h
EpididymitisGradual, daysPosterior tenderness, dysuria, fever; Prehn sign +IntactAntibiotics (clinical dx) + nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) + urinalysis
OrchitisDaysMumps history, unvaccinatedIntactSupportive
Torsion of appendix testisGradual, prepubertalBlue dot sign, superior poleIntactSupportive
Fournier gangrene EmergencyHoursToxic, crepitus, necrosis; diabetic – Emergent debridement
Scrotal mass (painless tree)
FindingDiagnosis
Bag of worms, ↑ standing/Valsalva, ↓ supineVaricocele – ~90% left-sided (left spermatic vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle)
Right-sided, sudden onset, or fails to decompress supineRetroperitoneal mass or renal cell carcinoma (RCC) invading the renal vein → abdominal imaging
Transilluminates, uniform, testis palpable withinHydrocele
Enlarges with Valsalva, reducible, doesn't transilluminateInguinal hernia
Firm, fixed, painless, on the testis, no transilluminationTumor → ultrasound + alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)/β-hCG/lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) → inguinal orchiectomy, never transscrotal biopsy
Testicular mass with gynecomastia, ↓ libido, or precocious puberty in a boy; markers normalLeydig cell tumor – a sex cord–stromal tumor secreting testosterone or estrogen. Reinke crystals on histology. Mostly benign; the hormonal syndrome is the tell, and AFP/β-hCG are negative
Testicular mass, heterogeneous with calcification and cystic areas on ultrasound; AFP and/or β-hCG elevatedTeratoma (nonseminomatous). In adults, malignant regardless of maturity; in prepubertal boys, benign – the one tumor whose behavior flips with age. Chemoresistant → resect residual masses after chemotherapy
Tumor marker logic AFP elevated → never a seminoma (AFP, alpha-fetoprotein; it indicates a yolk sac or embryonal/teratoma component) · β-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) can rise in seminoma and nonseminoma; only AFP is exclusionary · both markers normal with a solid mass → pure seminoma or a sex cord–stromal tumor (Leydig, Sertoli); a hormonal syndrome separates them · LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) tracks tumor burden, not histology · Sertoli cell tumor is, like Leydig, stromal and usually benign, but is typically hormonally silent.
Pearls Epididymitis treatment splits by age · <35 / sexually active → ceftriaxone + doxycycline · >35 / low STI risk (STI, sexually transmitted infection) → levofloxacin or TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) · varicocele is the most common correctable cause of male infertility; testicular size discrepancy in an adolescent is the surgical indication · seminoma never makes AFP (alpha-fetoprotein).
The two hard pairs
  • Varicocele vs. indirect inguinal hernia – both non-transilluminating, both enlarge with Valsalva. Separators: a hernia is reducible, feels like soft tissue or bowel, and you cannot palpate above it (it descends through the canal). A varicocele feels like worms, isn't reducible, and is confined to the scrotum.
  • Varicocele vs. spermatocele – both sit above and separate from the testis. Separators: the spermatocele transilluminates and does not change with position or Valsalva.
  • Femoral hernia presents below the inguinal ligament in the upper thigh, in older women, and anatomically cannot reach the scrotum – high incarceration risk.
Varicocele mechanism ~90% left-sided: the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle · possible "nutcracker" compression between the aorta and the SMA (superior mesenteric artery) · the right gonadal vein drains obliquely into the IVC (inferior vena cava) · subfertility comes from increased scrotal temperature impairing spermatogenesis; a varicocele may also cause ipsilateral atrophy · treatment: observation if asymptomatic · gonadal vein ligation or embolization for pain, >20% testicular volume discrepancy in adolescents, or abnormal semen analysis · scrotal support and NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) for older men not seeking fertility · a varicocele in a prepubertal child, right-sided, or persistent when supine is secondary until proven otherwise · in children think Wilms (with hypertension from renin secretion); in adults think RCC (renal cell carcinoma) invading the renal vein
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Exam with cremasteric reflexFirstAbsent reflex, high-riding transverse testis, sudden painTorsion: emergent urology; do not wait for imaging
Scrotal Doppler ultrasoundBy branchAbsent blood flow to the testisTorsion, used only when the exam is equivocal
Urinalysis and NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrheaSupportsPyuria or a positive NAATEpididymitis, a clinical diagnosis: treat without waiting on results
Transillumination of a painless massFirstMass glows, testis palpable within or separateHydrocele or spermatocele; a solid, dark mass needs ultrasound
Scrotal ultrasound with AFP, beta-hCG and LDHBy branchSolid intratesticular massTesticular tumor; an elevated AFP excludes pure seminoma
Radical inguinal orchiectomyConfirmsHistology names the tumorDiagnostic and therapeutic; never transscrotal biopsy
Ultrasound in gradual, febrile, posterior painSkipWould add delay, not a decisionEpididymitis is clinical; imaging is a torsion answer
Scenario bank
  1. Right-sided varicocele, sudden onset, or one that fails to decompress supine → Retroperitoneal mass or RCC invading the renal vein → abdominal computed tomography
  2. Mass transilluminates with the testis palpable within → Hydrocele → observe (infantile hydroceles usually close by age 1)
  3. Reducible mass extending from the inguinal canal, can't get above it → Indirect inguinal hernia → repair
  4. Firm, fixed, on the testis, no positional change → Ultrasound + AFP, β-hCG, LDH → radical inguinal orchiectomy (never transscrotal – it seeds lymphatics). Cryptorchidism is the biggest risk factor, for both testes
  5. Small transilluminating cyst at the superior pole, unchanging → Spermatocele → reassurance
  6. Adolescent with a varicocele and >20% testicular volume discrepancy → Refer for ligation
  7. Groin bulge below the inguinal ligament in an older woman → Femoral hernia → prompt repair
  8. Sudden severe pain, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex → Testicular torsion → emergent surgery
  9. 4 yo M, painless soft scrotal mass superior to the right testicle that does not decompress supine, blood pressure 160/96 → Secondary varicocele from an abdominal mass → abdominal ultrasonography
Transferable rules A 3-day timeline of scrotal pain excludes torsion. When the clinical findings confirm infection well enough, treat rather than image. Also, read the grammatical form of the answer choices before the stem. If every choice is an anatomic process, the question asks for mechanism; if every choice is a test, the next diagnostic step; if every choice is a drug, treatment.
