edits.html:
Brain Tumors in a Child

sellar and suprasellar masses that announce themselves on the growth chart, and posterior fossa masses that announce themselves on the neurologic examinationIs the abnormal finding endocrine or neurologic; for the sella, does the axis point at the stalk rather than the gland, and for the posterior fossa, which side and which structure?

DiagnosisPracticeWorkup and management
Bottom line

Ask where the abnormal finding sits. A falling height percentile or arrested puberty with a normal neurologic examination points to the sella; ataxia or crossed findings point to the posterior fossa, where you localize side first and structure second. Image with MRI (magnetic resonance imaging); with papilledema, never tap first.

  • Suprasellar mass: classically a normal neurologic examination (no dysmetria, gait abnormality, focal weakness or skin findings); height crosses downward through percentiles while weight holds, with Tanner 1 past the pubertal gate and papilledema. Growth failure with preserved weight is a hormonal deceleration, not a nutritional one; arrested puberty with it means more than one anterior pituitary axis has failed, and multiple axes point to the stalk, not the gland. Headache and disc edema from obstructive hydrocephalus make the mass midline and suprasellar.
  • Craniopharyngioma: from Rathke pouch remnants; cystic and calcified suprasellar mass: the cyst shows on MRI, the calcification mainly on computed tomography (CT); subtle for years before diagnosis.
  • Posterior fossa mass: 54 to 70% of childhood brain tumors but only 15 to 20% of adult ones, so in a child, ataxia with raised pressure is infratentorial until imaged. Cerebellar output decussates twice, so the crossings cancel and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral.
  • Hemisphere or vermis: limb dysmetria is hemispheric; a midline vermian lesion gives truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared. Both together mean a hemispheric mass large enough to disturb midline structures; ipsilateral facial numbness fits (the trigeminal system serves the face ipsilaterally), and papilledema comes from fourth-ventricular compression.
  • Crossed findings: a cranial nerve palsy on one side and long-tract weakness on the other mean brainstem.
Diagnosis
Localizing signs Cerebellar signs – ipsilateral; the patient falls and lists toward the side of the lesion; face also ipsilateral; body long tracts contralateral · Hemisphere – limb ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor · Vermis or midline – truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and titubation · Central nystagmus – direction-changing, gaze-evoked and unsuppressed; peripheral (vertigo) nystagmus is unidirectional and suppressed by fixation · Raised-pressure headache – daily or progressive, worse on waking or lying flat, poorly analgesia-responsive, with papilledema · Growth failure – downward crossing of height percentiles after a stable channel, weight preserved; endocrine causes such as growth hormone deficiency or hypothyroidism keep a normal or increased weight, and in poor nutrition weight loss comes before height loss · Pubertal delay – no breast development by age 13 in girls · Stalk pattern – multiple anterior axes down, with or without posterior failure (diabetes insipidus); stalk compression causes panhypopituitarism, most commonly growth failure from TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) or growth hormone deficiency; morning cortisol, free T4 (thyroxine), TSH and IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1) come back low in more than one axis · Gland pattern – a single hypersecreting axis with the others intact
Where is the mass
LocationTumorTell
Suprasellar, midlineCraniopharyngioma: Rathke pouch epithelial remnants in the stalk; the adamantinomatous type peaks at 5 to 14 and 50 to 74 yearsCystic and calcified; growth failure, pubertal delay, bitemporal hemianopsia; years of subtle symptoms
Suprasellar or pineal, midlineGerminoma (can't miss): germ cell tumor; adolescent, often maleDiabetes insipidus first, before the anterior axes; beta-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) and AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) usually negative in a pure germinoma, though low beta-hCG can be detected; radiosensitive
IntrasellarProlactinoma or other pituitary adenoma; adolescent or adultNon-calcified; one axis hypersecreting, others intact; galactorrhea and amenorrhea, or acromegalic features
Optic chiasm or nerveOptic pathway glioma (pilocytic astrocytoma); young child, often NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1)Café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling; visual loss and afferent pupillary defect precede endocrine failure; may cause diencephalic syndrome (emaciation with a normal appetite)
SellaRathke cleft cyst: same embryologic origin, benign, frequently incidentalNon-enhancing, non-calcified cyst; usually asymptomatic or mild headache
Pituitary stalkLangerhans cell histiocytosis; young childCentral diabetes insipidus with a thickened stalk; lytic skull lesions; seborrheic scalp rash
Cerebellar hemispherePilocytic astrocytoma most classicallyCyst with a mural nodule; ipsilateral limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia; falls toward the lesion
Cerebellar vermisMedulloblastoma; early fourth-ventricular obstructionTruncal and gait ataxia with a wide base, limbs relatively spared; typically hyperdense on CT (computed tomography), with restricted diffusion; seeds the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid)
Fourth ventricleEpendymomaTends to extend through the foramen of Luschka into the cerebellopontine angle; calcification and cysts common
Middle cerebellar peduncleCarries pontocerebellar inputAtaxia still ipsilateral: a right peduncle gives right-sided signs
PonsDiffuse intrinsic pontine gliomaCrossed findings: cranial nerve palsy one side (diplopia from an abducens palsy is often first), long-tract weakness the other; diffuse pontine expansion
Pineal regionGerminoma, adolescent boysParinaud syndrome: upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation
Frontal lobeSupratentorial gliomaContralateral weakness, personality change, expressive aphasia
Occipital lobeSupratentorial massContralateral homonymous hemianopia
Practice
  1. 14-year-old girl, a year of headaches, now worse height fell from 40th to 3rd percentile over 2 years weight steady at 70th percentile; Tanner 1 Skin, neurologic examination normal; no focal deficit Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · optic disc edema → Cystic, calcified suprasellar mass → height falling while weight holds is endocrine, and Tanner 1 at 14, with the mass signs, suggests a second failed axis, so the stalk is involved; with headache and disc edema the mass is midline and suprasellar, cystic and calcified: craniopharyngioma. A vermian tumor brings truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared, and this examination is clean; subependymal nodules belong to tuberous sclerosis, a skin-first diagnosis that does not arrest linear growth
  2. 9-year-old boy, 3 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting left-hand dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia gait lists to the left left facial numbness No weakness or sensory loss in the limbs BP 118/72 mm Hg · bilateral papilledema → A mass in the left cerebellar hemisphere → every cerebellar sign is on the left, and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral because the output decussates twice; limb dysmetria is hemispheric, the face is served ipsilaterally, and papilledema comes from fourth-ventricular compression. The right middle cerebellar peduncle is the right region on the wrong side, and a frontal lobe mass gives contralateral weakness
  3. 9-year-old girl, 2 months of bumping into door frames height fell from the 50th to the 10th percentile weight steady at the 55th percentile Misses fingers in the outer field of each eye Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg → MRI of the brain with contrast → a height percentile crossing with weight held and loss of the outer field in each eye is a suprasellar mass until imaged: MRI of the brain with contrast, sellar views. A bone age is nonspecific and delays the MRI, and a noncontrast CT shows the mass and its relation to the chiasm less well than MRI
  4. 6-year-old boy, 4 weeks of morning vomiting and unsteadiness truncal and gait ataxia; wide-based stance minimal limb dysmetria MRI: midline cerebellar mass filling the fourth ventricle, restricted diffusion, no extension through the fourth-ventricular foramina Afebrile · papilledema → Medulloblastoma of the vermis → truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and relatively spared limbs localizes to the vermis; a midline fourth-ventricular mass with restricted diffusion in a child fits medulloblastoma, which seeds drop metastases through the CSF. A cerebellar hemisphere pilocytic astrocytoma gives ipsilateral limb signs and is classically a cyst with a mural nodule; ependymoma tends to extend through the foramen of Luschka into the cerebellopontine angle, with calcification and cysts common
  5. 9-year-old boy is seen before planned surgery Imaging shows a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass Resection is planned for next week Height has slowed over 2 years; no medications BP 100/64 mm Hg · HR 88/min → Measure morning cortisol, free T4/TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery → stalk compression can leave several axes deficient, so measure morning cortisol, free T4 and TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery; secondary adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism are treated before the operation, glucocorticoid first. Growth hormone does not come before the axes that threaten the operation, and a planned resection is not a reason to wait 6 months for another MRI
  6. 5-year-old girl, 4 weeks of worsening double vision progressive left sixth and seventh nerve palsies right hemiparesis with brisk reflexes MRI: diffuse expansion of the pons Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg → Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma → a cranial nerve palsy on one side with long-tract weakness on the other is a crossed finding, which localizes to the brainstem; diffuse expansion of the pons in a child is a diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, and diplopia from an abducens palsy is often its first sign. Medulloblastoma and a cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma give ataxia rather than crossed findings
  7. 14-year-old boy, 3 months of polyuria and polydipsia urine osmolality 90 mOsm/kg non-calcified suprasellar mass CSF beta-hCG mildly elevated; serum AFP normal Growth and puberty normal so far; no rash or bone pain T 36.9 °C · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Suprasellar germinoma → diabetes insipidus first, before the anterior axes, with a mildly raised CSF beta-hCG and a normal AFP is a suprasellar germinoma (pure germinomas usually have negative markers, but low levels of beta-hCG can be detected), which is highly radiosensitive: radiation therapy, alone or after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Craniopharyngioma is cystic and calcified, and growth hormone and gonadotropin deficits are often its first endocrine failures; Langerhans cell histiocytosis thickens the stalk and brings lytic skull lesions and a seborrheic scalp rash
  8. 9-year-old boy, 2 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting wide-based gait; right-hand dysmetria bilateral papilledema A lumbar puncture is proposed to measure the pressure T 37.0 °C · BP 116/70 mm Hg → Obtain MRI of the brain instead → papilledema with cerebellar signs means a posterior fossa mass until imaged, and lumbar puncture risks herniation, so image first: MRI of the brain instead. Measuring an opening pressure does not remove that risk, and a noncontrast CT followed by a tap still ends in the tap that papilledema with a posterior fossa mass forbids
  9. 10-year-old girl, 1 day after resection of a suprasellar tumor urine output 350 mL/h serum Na 152 mEq/L urine osmolality 85 mOsm/kg Alert and thirsty BP 104/62 mm Hg · HR 112/min → Desmopressin → dilute polyuria with a rising sodium after the stalk has been handled is central diabetes insipidus: desmopressin. Fluid restriction worsens the hypernatremia, and hypertonic saline adds sodium to a patient whose sodium is already high
  10. 12-year-old boy, 2 months of headaches and trouble looking up upgaze palsy convergence-retraction nystagmus light-near dissociation of the pupils No head trauma; visual acuity normal Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · HR 76/min → MRI of the brain, then serum and CSF tumor markers → upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and light-near dissociation are Parinaud syndrome, a pineal-region mass; in an adolescent boy that is classically a germinoma, so obtain MRI of the brain first, then serum and CSF tumor markers, the CSF once imaging shows a tap is safe. This is not strabismus, and a noncontrast CT does not characterize the mass or the markers
  11. 8-year-old boy with a newly found suprasellar mass Vomiting and lethargic since this morning Free thyroxine low; cortisol result pending BP 84/50 mm Hg · HR 128/min · Na 128 mEq/L · glucose 52 mg/dL → Levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement → hypotension, hyponatremia and hypoglycemia with a new suprasellar mass is adrenal crisis; give IV hydrocortisone and isotonic saline, and avoid levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement, because thyroid hormone increases the clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate adrenal crisis
  12. 7-year-old boy with a right cerebellar hemisphere mass on MRI right-hand intention tremor and dysmetria falls toward the right Strength and sensation normal His parents ask why the signs are on the same side as the tumor → Cerebellar output decussates twice → cerebellar output decussates twice, so the two crossings cancel and the signs stay on the same side as the lesion. Cerebellar fibers do cross, and the cerebellum does not control the opposite limbs directly
  13. 15-year-old girl with amenorrhea and galactorrhea Normal growth; Tanner 4 MRI: 6 mm intrasellar lesion without calcification No headache; visual fields full BP 110/68 mm Hg · prolactin 180 ng/mL · TSH normal · urine pregnancy test negative → Prolactinoma → galactorrhea and amenorrhea with a raised prolactin, a normal TSH and pregnancy test, and a small, non-calcified intrasellar lesion with one axis hypersecreting is a prolactinoma; cabergoline is the preferred dopamine agonist. Craniopharyngioma is a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass, and a Rathke cleft cyst is a non-enhancing, non-calcified cyst that is usually asymptomatic
  14. 9-year-old boy admitted with headache and vomiting MRI: posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus Over the last hour he has become drowsy Pupils equal; no seizure BP 128/70 mm Hg · HR 64/min → Dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation → a posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus and a falling level of consciousness needs dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation, for CSF diversion then resection. Acetazolamide with outpatient follow-up, or observation, leaves the obstruction untreated
  15. 6-year-old boy with declining vision and nystagmus several café-au-lait macules; axillary freckling thin despite a good appetite Normal stools; no bone pain or fractures Afebrile · HR 96/min · weight below the 5th percentile → MRI of the brain and orbits → café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling point to neurofibromatosis type 1, and declining vision with emaciation despite a good appetite is an optic pathway glioma with diencephalic syndrome: MRI of the brain and orbits. Celiac disease is malabsorption and brings no visual loss, and a skeletal survey looks for bone lesions he does not have
  16. 7-year-old girl with newly confirmed medulloblastoma The tumor was resected 2 weeks ago Recovering well; no back pain Leg strength and bladder function normal Neurologic examination unchanged since discharge Afebrile · no papilledema → MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology → medulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so staging is MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology, the lumbar puncture done at least 10 to 14 days after surgery. Bone marrow and whole-body imaging do not look where it spreads
  17. 11-year-old girl with a known suprasellar mass Vomiting since last night now a depressed level of consciousness CT: dilated lateral and third ventricles BP 132/60 mm Hg · HR 58/min · pupils equal → Neurosurgical CSF diversion → a suprasellar mass that blocks CSF flow at the third ventricle causes obstructive hydrocephalus; a falling level of consciousness needs neurosurgical CSF diversion. Lumbar puncture risks herniation, and acetazolamide does not relieve an obstruction
  18. 4-year-old boy, 3 weeks of headache headache waking him from sleep morning vomiting Normal neurologic examination; no medications Growth chart normal; no recent head injury Afebrile · BP 98/60 mm Hg · HR 92/min → MRI of the brain → headache that wakes him from sleep, with morning vomiting, in a child under six is a red-flag headache: MRI of the brain, because a normal examination does not exclude a posterior fossa tumor. A diary or migraine prophylaxis delays the diagnosis
  19. 13-year-old girl with a suprasellar mass on MRI loss of both temporal visual fields A year of headaches; height has slowed Visual acuity normal; pupils equal Her parents ask why the outer halves of her vision are missing → Compression of decussating nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm → a suprasellar mass presses up on the optic chiasm, where the nasal retinal fibers, which carry the temporal fields, decussate: bitemporal hemianopsia. A lesion behind the chiasm, in the optic tract, gives a homonymous defect (the same hemifield lost in both eyes), and a Meyer loop lesion in the temporal lobe gives contralateral superior quadrantanopia
  20. 10-year-old boy treated 1 year ago with resection and radiation of a craniopharyngioma Currently asymptomatic Takes hydrocortisone and levothyroxine His parents ask what follow-up he needs BP 102/64 mm Hg · height 25th percentile → Serial growth velocity with annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields → after a craniopharyngioma, surveillance is lifelong and endocrine and visual: serial growth velocity with an annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields. Audiometry does not watch the axes or the visual fields this tumor threatens, and AFP and beta-hCG are germ cell tumor markers
Workup and management
Decision spine Is the neurologic examination focal? If not, the lesion is not hemispheric or in the posterior fossa. Plot the growth chart: height falling with weight holding is endocrine. Count failed axes: growth and puberty together are panhypopituitarism, which localizes to the stalk. Is there posterior pituitary failure? Polyuria makes germinoma or histiocytosis more likely. Is there raised pressure or a field cut? Papilledema or bitemporal hemianopsia makes the mass midline and suprasellar, and the imaging descriptor is cystic and calcified (calcification mainly on CT). If the examination is focal, find the side, then the structure.
Management Before surgery – treat secondary adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism before the operation, glucocorticoid before levothyroxine: thyroid hormone increases the clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate adrenal crisis in an unrecognized cortisol deficiency. Replace cortisol before thyroid hormone in any new panhypopituitarism. · After surgery – diabetes insipidus can develop in 70% after craniopharyngioma surgery; expect the sodium to rise, not fall, when the stalk has been handled, and treat hypotonic polyuria with desmopressin, not fluid restriction · Obstructive hydrocephalus – a posterior fossa mass with drowsiness needs dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation, for CSF diversion then resection; a suprasellar mass with a depressed level of consciousness needs neurosurgical CSF diversion, not lumbar puncture · Germinoma – highly radiosensitive: radiation therapy alone, or neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by response-based radiation therapy, which has been explored to reduce radiation doses and neurodevelopmental harm · Prolactinoma – cabergoline, the preferred dopamine agonist · After craniopharyngioma – lifelong endocrine and visual surveillance, with surveillance MRI
Papilledema forbids the tap With a posterior fossa mass, lumbar puncture risks herniation. Image first.
Reading a sellar vignette Height crossing down through percentiles with weight steady is endocrine growth failure; it excludes undernutrition, which costs weight first. Tanner 1 past age 13 in a girl is delayed puberty; with growth failure and signs of a mass (headache, disc edema), it suggests a second failed axis, which can indicate hypopituitarism rather than short stature alone. Optic disc edema without fever or neck stiffness is raised intracranial pressure without meningitis, from obstructive hydrocephalus at the third ventricle. A normal neurologic examination, including finger-nose-finger testing and gait, excludes the cerebellar compartment and with it medulloblastoma. Normal skin excludes tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas) and neurofibromatosis type 1 (café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling), the two phakomatoses whose intracranial lesions are on option lists. No focal deficit and no fever exclude brain abscess, which comes with focal findings and usually fever. A year of headaches before worsening is a slow-growing lesion, not a reassurance; the normal blood pressure and temperature exclude infection and crisis but say nothing about the pituitary; a morning cortisol would.
Pearls Height falling away from a stable weight with Tanner arrest and headache is a suprasellar mass until MRI says otherwise. Plot the growth chart before you order the headache imaging: a height percentile crossing is a localizing sign, and it remains detectable when the neurologic examination is normal. The exception to preserved weight is the diencephalic syndrome of a hypothalamic glioma: emaciation with a normal appetite. Diabetes insipidus first and anterior axes later makes germinoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis more likely than craniopharyngioma; send serum beta-hCG and AFP, and CSF levels once imaging shows a tap is safe, before assuming craniopharyngioma. Boundary: untreated acquired primary hypothyroidism reproduces this growth pattern exactly (height arrest, preserved or rising weight, delayed puberty) but does not produce papilledema; check TSH and free T4, and disc edema separates the two. Red-flag pediatric headache: wakes from sleep, worse on waking, morning vomiting, progressive over weeks, any focal sign, or a child under six. Medulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so staging requires neuraxis MRI and CSF cytology.
Common wrong answers Subependymal nodules in the lateral ventricles: tuberous sclerosis is a skin-first diagnosis and does not arrest linear growth. Tumor in the cerebellar vermis: truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared; it does not touch the pituitary. Parietal lesion with air-fluid levels and a hyperdense rim: abscess is acute, febrile and focal; a year of headaches with growth arrest is not an infection. Enhancing lesion in the internal auditory canal: acoustic neuroma is an adult disease of hearing loss and tinnitus, with no endocrine consequence. Right middle cerebellar peduncle for left-sided signs: the right region on the wrong side. Pineal mass: common in children, but it produces Parinaud syndrome. Germinoma when the anterior axes failed first and there is no polyuria; adenoma when two axes are down, there is no galactorrhea, and CSF flow is blocked; optic glioma with normal skin, normal pupils and weight preserved; Rathke cleft cyst for progressive panhypopituitarism with raised pressure, too much disease for a simple cyst; histiocytosis with normal skin, no polyuria and no bone pain.
Pairs with Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment: the same complaint, a 13-year-old girl with worsening headaches, with the red-flag gate answered in the opposite direction. Ask: is anything abnormal outside the headache history (the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination)? If yes, image and look at the sella; if no, explain the change in pattern. Headache in a School-Age Child: the workup before localization; is the headache primary or secondary, and do the fundi show raised pressure? Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: posterior fossa tumor as the can't-miss cause of acquired head tilt; this brief supplies the localization. Hyperprolactinemia: the intrasellar adenoma in the adult. Polyuria: the step before this one; is the polyuria water or solute, and is the deprivation test still needed?
Transferable rule

When a mass sits on a midline structure, the localizing finding may be endocrine rather than neurologic: a growth chart and a Tanner stage are examination findings, and in the sellar region they appear years before the field cut and the papilledema. When the finding is neurologic, localize side first and structure second; the cerebellum is the one place where signs stay on the same side as the lesion.

edits.html:
Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

six weeks of arthritis, then joints and fever set the subtype · mimics · the treatment ladder · marrow before steroidsHow many joints, does the fever spike daily, and are two or more cell lines low?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Arthritis for 6 weeks or more, before age 16, with no other cause is JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis). The diagnosis is clinical.

Set the subtype by the first 6 months:

  • Systemic: any joints, plus daily fever spikes for 2 weeks or more, with an evanescent salmon rash, nodes, big liver or spleen, or serositis
  • Polyarticular: 5 or more joints, symmetric; no fever or rash
  • Oligoarticular: 4 or fewer, usually a knee or ankle

Treat with an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) first, such as naproxen; weekly methotrexate when arthritis persists. Systemic: NSAID and steroids, then a biologic.

Slit lamp every 3 months if oligoarticular or RF (rheumatoid factor) negative polyarticular, ANA (antinuclear antibody) positive, onset before 7 and within 4 years of onset; otherwise every 6 to 12 months.

Low counts in two or more cell lines in a child labeled systemic JIA: bone marrow before any steroid.

Diagnosis
JIA subtypes All – true swelling, morning stiffness that eases, 6 weeks, no other cause · Systemic – fever 2 weeks or more plus rash, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy or serositis; boys and girls equally · Polyarticular – 5 or more joints; peaks at 2 to 5 and 10 to 14; girls more · Oligoarticular – 4 or fewer joints; ages 2 to 4; girls more
Mimics: what the stem shows instead
MimicThe tellTreat
Gonococcal arthritissexually active; one joint or a few, asymmetric; tenosynovitis; vesiculopustulesCeftriaxone
Lyme arthritisone large joint, usually the knee, after erythema migrans in an endemic areaDoxycycline
Hypothyroidismaches and fatigue, no true swelling; height velocity fallsLevothyroxine
Vitamin D deficiencydiffuse bone pain, same all day; no swellingVitamin D and calcium
Leukemiacytopenias, bone painBone marrow first
Dengue, malariaacute fever after travel; dengue lowers the counts and bruises; malaria has no rashInfection workup, not JIA therapy
Management and treatment
Management ladder: JIA
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineNSAID such as naproxen; steroid injection into a few jointsArthritis persists on the NSAID
PersistentWeekly methotrexateMethotrexate fails
RheumatologyA biologicTop rung
By situation Systemic – NSAIDs and steroids, then a biologic · MAS – ferritin in the thousands, high triglycerides, falling ESR and fibrinogen, DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation): high-dose steroids, after a marrow if two lines are low · Uveitis – oligoarticular highest, polyarticular too, systemic lowest; enthesitis-related (older boys, HLA-B27 (human leukocyte antigen type B-27)) gives a red, painful eye · One hot joint – in a child on methotrexate it is septic until the fluid says otherwise
Practice
  1. 5-year-old girl with 6 weeks of swollen knees and wrists 3 weeks of fever to 39.5 °C each evening, normal by morning salmon-pink rash with each spike that fades hepatosplenomegaly WBC 21,000/mm³ · platelets 610,000/mm³ · ANA low-titer positive · RF negative → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis → quotidian fever with an evanescent rash and 6 weeks of arthritis, with high counts: systemic JIA; a low-titer ANA does not exclude it, lupus lowers counts, and rheumatic fever's fever is persistent with a rash whose margin expands
  2. 5-year-old girl with 2 weeks of daily fever and 3 weeks of a swollen right knee parents' log: spikes to 39.8 °C each evening rash with each spike Seen in the afternoon, well appearing T 37.0 °C · ESR 64 mm/h → Continue the evaluation for systemic JIA → quotidian fever returns to normal between spikes, so a normal clinic temperature excludes nothing; no focus and well between spikes is not a bacterial infection
  3. 6-year-old boy diagnosed with systemic JIA a year ago, now persistently febrile oozing at venipuncture sites hepatosplenomegaly WBC 6,000/mm³ · platelets 92,000/mm³ · ferritin 18,000 ng/mL · fibrinogen 110 mg/dL · ESR 6 mm/h (70 last month) · AST 220 U/L · triglycerides 380 mg/dL → Macrophage activation syndrome → in systemic JIA, persistent fever with ESR and fibrinogen falling as ferritin, triglycerides and AST climb, and oozing from consumed clotting factors: macrophage activation syndrome; with only platelets low, high-dose steroids
  4. 4-year-old girl diagnosed 1 month ago with arthritis of the left knee and right ankle ANA positive no eye pain, redness or blurred vision Knee swelling improving on naproxen Afebrile · visual acuity 20/30 both eyes → Slit-lamp exam for asymptomatic uveitis → young, ANA positive and few joints carries the highest uveitis risk, and it is silent: slit-lamp exams every 3 months
  5. 4-year-old boy with 6 weeks of evening fever spikes since a trip to Costa Rica pink rash with each spike, gone by morning right knee swollen 6 weeks; spleen tip palpable Well between spikes hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL · platelets 640,000/mm³ → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis → weeks of quotidian fever with an evanescent rash, mild anemia and high platelets: systemic JIA; dengue and malaria are acute and usually lower platelets, and malaria has no rash
  6. 7-year-old boy with 4 weeks of daily evening fevers to 39.6 °C normal temperature each morning salmon rash during fevers; both knees and the left wrist swollen for 7 weeks pericardial rub Afebrile in clinic → High WBC and platelets, high ferritin; ANA and RF negative → systemic JIA is inflammation without autoantibodies: high WBC, platelets, ESR and ferritin; ANA and RF usually negative
  7. 3-year-old girl with 8 weeks of a swollen, warm left knee limps after waking, better by afternoon right ankle also swollen No fever or rash; lives in a nonendemic area; no tick bites Afebrile · ANA positive → Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis → 4 or fewer joints for 8 weeks with morning stiffness: oligoarticular JIA; nonendemic with no tick bite argues against Lyme; ANA positive and young: slit-lamp exams
  8. 13-year-old girl with 2 months of aching legs, hips and back pain the same all day; no morning stiffness no joint swelling; tibias tender to pressure Strict vegan diet without fortified foods Afebrile · height and weight steady → Vitamin D deficiency → diffuse bone pain that never eases and no swollen joints, on an unfortified vegan diet: vitamin D and calcium
  9. 14-year-old girl, ankles aching 3 months since starting daily walks this month knees, elbows, wrists; all swollen bilaterally stiff mornings that ease Tired despite 9 hours' sleep; new plant-based diet Afebrile · weight 95th to 90th percentile · height steady · chest normal → Naproxen → 5 or more joints within months, symmetric, stiff in the morning and easing: polyarticular JIA; naproxen first, methotrexate if it persists; deficiency pain never eases or swells joints, and falling weight with steady height is not hypothyroidism
  10. 4-year-old girl labeled systemic JIA 6 weeks ago, joints improving on naproxen now pale, with petechiae on her trunk and legs lymph nodes enlarged in the neck and groin T 39.4 °C · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL · WBC 2,100/mm³ · platelets 38,000/mm³ → Bone marrow aspiration → low counts in two or more cell lines in a child labeled systemic JIA: bone marrow first; leukemia mimics JIA, and a steroid can mask it and change the marrow
  11. 9-year-old boy with 3 weeks of a swollen right knee stiff after waking, better by noon no preceding diarrhea, urethritis or rash; nonendemic area No injury; walks with a slight limp Afebrile · WBC normal · ESR 32 mm/h → Naproxen and reassess at 6 weeks → JIA needs 6 weeks of arthritis with no other cause: treat the pain and reassess before labeling it or starting methotrexate
Pairs with Acute Leukemia in a Child: the marrow comes before the steroid. Septic Arthritis in a Child: one hot joint on methotrexate. The Limping Child: sick or well, then age and time.
Transferable rule

Before naming JIA, time the arthritis, chart the fever and look at every cell line.

edits.html:
Preventive Care: Ranking Interventions

rank by magnitude of benefit · smoking cessation first · blood pressure, statin, glucose · organ-specific exceptionsWhich option has the largest mortality benefit, and is the outcome limited to one organ?

Source vignette Pt – 58 yo M smoker with hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidemia · Q – the intervention that most reduces mortality; options spanned smoking cessation, a statin and lisinopril
The decision point

When every option is guideline-supported, rank them by magnitude of benefit. Smoking cessation reduces all-cause mortality more than any drug on the list. It cuts CV (cardiovascular) risk substantially within 1–2 years and approaches never-smoker risk over ~15 years.

Ranking preventive interventions – why each loses
ChoiceLegitimate claimWhy it loses
Smoking cessation – Largest mortality benefit of any intervention
LisinoprilDiabetic + hypertension → angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACE-I) preferred, especially with albuminuriaBP only mildly elevated, no proteinuria – real but smaller
StatinDiabetic 40–75 → indicated regardless of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levelTrue indication, but ~25% relative risk reduction – cessation dwarfs it
↑ hydrochlorothiazideBP above goalMarginal, and worsens glucose and lipids in a diabetic
↑ MetforminA1c above targetGlycemic control reduces microvascular complications; weak macrovascular effect (UKPDS)
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo M smoker with hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidemia; which most reduces mortality → Smoking cessation
  2. 58 yo M who has already quit; which intervention is next → A statin
  3. 58 yo M asking how soon quitting helps → Cardiovascular risk falls within 1 to 2 years
  4. 58 yo M ready to quit within the month → Varenicline plus behavioral support
  5. 58 yo M who is not ready to quit → Motivational interviewing
  6. 58 yo M with 30 pack-years who quit 5 years ago → Annual low-dose CT screening
The hierarchy to bank For macrovascular outcomes, the order of benefit is smoking cessation > BP (blood pressure) control > statin > glycemic control. If the patient smokes and smoking cessation is an option, choose it. The exception is an outcome limited to a specific organ. For risk of nephropathy progression, choose an ACE-I (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor) and BP control. For microvascular complications, choose glycemic (A1c) control. Lifestyle advice ranks low when vague ("recommend exercise") and high when specific and high-magnitude (smoking or alcohol cessation).

edits.html:
SSRI Adverse Effects

name the effect, then take the next stepOn the drug or after stopping it, and which phase of sexual response is affected?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Sexual dysfunction affects more than half of patients on a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) and can reach desire, arousal or orgasm.

Persistent, distressing low desire: lowering the dose is the common first step, especially with the depression in sustained remission. If that fails:

  • one episode in sustained remission: consider tapering off
  • staying on an antidepressant: reasonable options are adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine)

Another SSRI carries a similar risk. Sildenafil can help arousal problems and anorgasmia; no effect on desire has been shown.

FINISH symptoms typically within 3 days of a stop or a taper are discontinuation syndrome, not relapse: once other serious causes are ruled out, reassure.

Diagnosis
Which effect Sexual dysfunction – decreased desire, arousal problems or anorgasmia during SSRI therapy; increased serotonin likely explains it · Discontinuation syndrome – FINISH symptoms, typically within 3 days of stopping or starting a taper (FINISH) · Serotonin syndrome – mental status changes, autonomic hyperactivity and neuromuscular changes, rapid onset after a medication change
FINISH
  • F – flu-like symptoms: fatigue, lethargy, malaise, muscle aches, headaches, diarrhea
  • I – insomnia
  • N – nausea
  • I – imbalance: gait instability, dizziness or lightheadedness, vertigo
  • S – sensory disturbances: paresthesia, "electric shock" sensations, visual disturbance
  • H – hyperarousal: anxiety, agitation
Management and treatment
Persistent, distressing low desire on an SSRI
TierInterventionEscalate when
Common first stepLower the SSRI doseStill persistent and distressing at the lower dose
ThenOne episode, sustained remission: consider tapering off. Staying on an antidepressant: reasonable options are adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine)Top rung
By situation Bulimia or seizure-prone – not bupropion (contraindicated); mirtazapine has fewer sexual adverse effects than SSRIs · Arousal problems or anorgasmia – sildenafil can help; not shown to help desire · Unlikely to help or not recommended – another SSRI (similar risk; unlikely to resolve it); propranolol (unlikely to help sexual dysfunction; not helpful for depression); weekend drug holidays (not commonly used, and they interfere with the antidepressant effect)
Discontinuation syndrome
TierInterventionEscalate when
Other serious causes ruled outReassure: reversible, not serious, runs its course in 1 to 2 weeks; then consider restarting with a slow taper, or support if the patient prefers not to restartSymptoms arose during a taper
During a taperConsider restarting the original dose, then taper more slowlySlow tapering poorly tolerated
Slow taper failsConsider substituting fluoxetine for the short half-life drugTop rung
Prevention Before stopping – forewarn the patient; a supervised taper over 6 to 8 weeks may be required (another source: about 25% of the dose each week) · Choice of drug – fluoxetine, with its long half-life, is less likely than paroxetine to cause discontinuation symptoms · How long – after a first mild or moderate episode, about 6 more months after remission, then a taper over 2 months
Practice
  1. 34-year-old man, one depressive episode in remission 7 months on sertraline 150 mg daily low sexual desire since starting it it is straining his marriage no suicidal ideation · euthymic, full affect, linear thought · HR 72/min, BP 124/76 mm Hg → Lower the sertraline dose → persistent, distressing low desire in sustained remission: lowering the dose is the common first step; drug holidays are not commonly used and interfere with the antidepressant effect
  2. 31-year-old man, one moderate depressive episode in remission 10 months on sertraline dose cut from 150 to 100 mg 2 months ago for low desire still distressed; would rather stop euthymic, full affect, linear thought · no suicidal ideation · HR 70/min → Taper sertraline off gradually → a lower dose failed, and one episode in sustained remission allows stopping; an SSRI is tapered, not stopped abruptly
  3. 27-year-old woman, one depressive episode, in remission 14 months escitalopram lowered 8 weeks ago for low desire desire still low and distressing wants to stay on an antidepressant No seizures, eating disorder or heart disease euthymic, reactive affect · HR 68/min → Add bupropion to escitalopram → a lower dose failed and she prefers to stay on medication: reasonable options are adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine); sildenafil has not been shown to affect desire
  4. 45-year-old man, one depressive episode, in remission 9 months sertraline cut 150 to 100 mg 3 months ago wants to stay on it desire intact; erection trouble since starting it; bothers him euthymic · HR 72/min, BP 126/80 mm Hg → Add sildenafil to sertraline → desire is intact and the problem is arousal, which sildenafil can help; propranolol is unlikely to help, and another SSRI carries a similar risk
  5. 24-year-old woman with bulimia nervosa one depressive episode, in remission on fluoxetine after a dose reduction, desire still low and distressing wants to stay on an antidepressant BMI (body mass index) 21 kg/m² · HR 66/min · potassium 3.9 mEq/L · euthymic → Switching to bupropion → bupropion has no sexual adverse effects but is contraindicated in bulimia; mirtazapine has fewer sexual adverse effects than SSRIs
  6. 38-year-old woman ran out of paroxetine 4 days ago after 2 years for remitted depression 2 days of nausea, dizziness, unsteady gait, poor sleep brief electric-shock sensations in arms T 37.0 °C · reflexes normal, no clonus · anxious, irritable; mood fine → SSRI discontinuation syndrome → FINISH symptoms, typically within 3 days of stopping a short half-life drug; relapse comes 2 to 3 weeks or more later, and normal reflexes without clonus argue against serotonin syndrome
  7. 52-year-old man stopped sertraline on his own 3 days ago after 1 year; depression in remission mild nausea, lightheadedness, trouble sleeping wants to stay off T 36.9 °C · reflexes normal, no tremor or clonus · euthymic, mildly irritable · no suicidal ideation → Reassure; it resolves in 1 to 2 weeks → with other serious causes unlikely (afebrile, normal reflexes, no clonus), discontinuation symptoms after an abrupt stop: begin with reassurance that they are reversible and run their course in 1 to 2 weeks; restarting with a slow taper is considered, or support if he prefers not to restart
  8. 35-year-old woman, depression in remission 8 months 2 weeks into a paroxetine taper, 40 mg to 20 mg daily 3 days of dizziness, nausea, electric-shock sensations irritability keeps her from work T 37.1 °C · no clonus · anxious; mood not depressed → Resume 40 mg and taper more slowly → symptoms during a taper: consider restarting the original dose and tapering more slowly; fluoxetine is for a slow taper that is poorly tolerated
  9. 42-year-old man, depression in remission 1 year two tries to come off paroxetine, each tapered over 8 weeks both times: dizziness, nausea, electric-shock sensations relieved by resuming the full dose euthymic · no suicidal ideation · T 36.8 °C → Switch to fluoxetine, then stop → slow tapering is poorly tolerated: consider substituting fluoxetine, whose longer half-life makes discontinuation symptoms less likely
  10. 58-year-old woman taking sertraline got tramadol for back pain this morning 5 hours later: agitated, sweating, nauseated T 38.4 °C · HR 122/min · BP 162/94 mm Hg · dilated pupils · tremor, hyperreflexia, ankle clonus · hyperactive bowel sounds · oriented to person only → Serotonin syndrome → tramadol added to an SSRI, then clonus, hyperreflexia and mydriasis within hours; neuroleptic malignant syndrome builds over days with lead-pipe rigidity and slow reflexes
How NBME framed it: question 1

23-year-old woman at a follow-up visit first major depressive episode 1 year ago; fluoxetine 40 mg daily since depression well controlled: enjoys social activities more, more productive at work Reports no suicidal ideation new relationship; concerned about her limited sexual desire vital signs normal · smiling, euthymic affect

Most appropriate next step?

Competing answers
  • Initiate propranolol: an add-on that leaves the antidepressant alone; but it is unlikely to help sexual dysfunction and is not helpful for major depressive disorder.
  • Initiate sildenafil: a treatment for sexual dysfunction; but it helps arousal problems and anorgasmia; no effect on desire, her complaint, has been shown.
  • Recommend weekend drug holidays: they seem to spare the relationship; but they are not commonly used and interfere with the antidepressant effect.
  • Replace fluoxetine with citalopram: a switch sounds like progress; but citalopram carries a similar risk of sexual dysfunction.

Down to two: lowering the dose or switching to citalopram. Lower the dose: her low desire is persistent and distressing, and the explanation says initial management commonly involves decreasing the SSRI dose, especially with sustained remission. If that fails: one episode in sustained remission, so stopping can be considered; or, if she prefers to stay on medication, adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine).

Pairs with Bipolar Disorder: did the mood rise, not fall, after the SSRI started? (antidepressant-induced mania is rare) Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety: is the anxiety new within 3 days of a stop, a hyperarousal symptom of discontinuation?
Transferable rule

Name the effect and its timing before changing the drug. During therapy, with persistent, distressing low desire, lowering the dose is the common first step; typically within 3 days of a stop or a taper, think discontinuation, not relapse.

edits.html:
Tuberculosis

screen, sort, treat · skin test thresholds · latent vs active by film and symptoms · isolate first · four-drug toxicitiesAre there symptoms or an abnormal chest film, and must the patient be isolated before any drug?

The decision point

No test distinguishes latent from active TB (tuberculosis); the CXR (chest X-ray) and symptoms do. A positive test with a normal CXR and no symptoms means latent TB → monotherapy. A positive test with symptoms or an abnormal CXR means active TB. For active TB, isolate first, then give four drugs.

Purified protein derivative (PPD) positivity thresholds by risk group
PPD is positive at…Group
≥5 mmHuman immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection · recent TB contact · fibrotic changes on CXR · transplant, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) inhibitor, prednisone ≥15 mg/day
≥10 mmHealthcare workers · immigrants <5 yrs from endemic areas · prisoners · homeless · injection drug use · diabetes · chronic kidney disease · children <4
≥15 mmNo risk factors
Test mechanics BCG-vaccinated → IGRA: use an IGRA (interferon-gamma release assay), which BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) vaccination does not affect · anergy is a false-negative PPD (purified protein derivative) in HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), steroid use or sarcoid · PPD is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.
RIPE drug toxicities
RIPE drugToxicity
RifampinOrange secretions (benign – counsel, don't stop) · potent cytochrome P450 inducer → oral contraceptive pill failure, warfarin; use rifabutin with HIV protease inhibitors
IsoniazidPeripheral neuropathy → give B6 · hepatitis · drug-induced lupus · sideroblastic anemia
PyrazinamideHyperuricemia / gout · hepatitis
EthambutolOptic neuritis – red-green vision lost first. "Eye-thambutol"
The costumes – how the same question keeps showing up
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
PPD or IGRA (IGRA if BCG-vaccinated)ScreenPositive at the risk-group thresholdInfection, latent or active; the test cannot tell which
Symptom review and chest radiographNextNormal radiograph, no symptomsLatent TB: single-drug regimen; abnormal: airborne isolation, then sputum
HIV testScreenPositiveChanges the PPD threshold, drug interactions and antiretroviral therapy (ART) timing
Sputum AFB smear, three samplesBy branchAcid-fast bacilliActive, infectious pulmonary TB
Sputum nucleic acid amplification testSupportsM. tuberculosis DNA, with rifampin resistance resultRapid diagnosis and first resistance check
Sputum mycobacterial cultureConfirmsGrowth of M. tuberculosisActive TB, with drug susceptibility
Repeat PPD or IGRA to judge activitySkipCannot separate latent from activeThe radiograph and symptoms decide
  1. Booster / two-step: health care worker with a negative first PPD, positive on repeat 1–3 weeks later = old memory, not conversion → Treat as latent
  2. Window period: contact of an active case → PPD now and at 8–10 weeks → the only time "repeat later" is correct
  3. Before biologics: starting a TNF-α inhibitor (rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease stem) → Screen for latent TB first
  4. Sequencing trap: coughing + cavitary CXR → Airborne isolation → before any medication is started
Reference notes
  • HIV co-infection: PPD ≥5 mm = treat · TB drugs first, ART at 2–8 weeks (immediate risks immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome) · rifabutin with protease inhibitors
  • Extrapulmonary: Pott (spine) · scrofula (cervical node) · meningitis (↑protein, ↓glucose, basilar) · sterile pyuria · miliary CXR · adrenal insufficiency
  • Location logic: primary = lower/mid lobe (Ghon complex); reactivation = apices (highest pO₂)
Treatment Latent: rifampin ×4 mo (preferred) · isoniazid (INH) ×9 mo + B6 · INH + rifapentine weekly ×3 mo. Active: RIPE ×2 mo → INH + rifampin ×4 mo; reportable; directly observed therapy if nonadherent.
Sequencing trap

edits.html:
Teratogenic Exposures

the teratogen from the malformation pattern · critical periods · phenytoin vs alcohol · anticoagulation in pregnancyWhich single malformation belongs to only one agent, and when in pregnancy was the exposure?

Source vignette Pt – newborn male, growth restricted at 2.5 kg at 38 weeks, mother 29 with no prenatal care, forceps delivery for fetal heart rate abnormalities, Apgars 6 and 8 · Exam – microcephaly, a wide anterior fontanelle, cleft palate, and hypoplasia of the distal phalanges · Q – which maternal history would be found; options spanned alcohol use, cocaine use, lisinopril use, phenytoin use and untreated syphilis
The decision point

Cleft palate and distal phalangeal hypoplasia are the two findings that alcohol does not cause. Together they are fetal hydantoin syndrome, from in utero exposure to a folate-antagonizing antiepileptic, classically phenytoin. The drug crosses the placenta and produces low fetal folate with high oxidative metabolites. The wide anterior fontanelle and microcephaly complete the pattern. Fetal alcohol syndrome shares the microcephaly and the midface hypoplasia but has no association with clefting. Its signature is a smooth philtrum with a thin vermilion border and short palpebral fissures, none of which is described in this newborn.

Defining criteria Critical periods – 0–2 weeks all-or-none (death or no effect); 3–8 weeks organogenesis, the structural-malformation window; beyond 8 weeks growth restriction, central nervous system and functional deficits rather than structural defects · Fetal hydantoin syndrome – microcephaly, wide anterior fontanelle, cleft lip and palate, distal digit and nail hypoplasia, cardiac defects, neural tube defects · Fetal alcohol syndrome – smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, short palpebral fissures, midface hypoplasia, microcephaly, and no clefting · Antiepileptic management – switch to a lower-risk agent such as levetiracetam 6 months before conception, 4 mg folic acid from 3 months before conception, and make no changes after conception; screen with alpha-fetoprotein and anatomy ultrasonography
Teratogenic medications – drug to signaturethe malformation that belongs to only one agent
DrugSignature defect
PhenytoinDistal digit and nail hypoplasia, cleft lip/palate, wide fontanelle, microcephaly, cardiac, neural tube defects
ValproateNeural tube defects – the highest-risk antiepileptic
CarbamazepineNeural tube defects, less than valproate
TopiramateOral clefts, growth restriction, neurodevelopmental effects
PhenobarbitalCardiac, orofacial and urogenital malformations
IsotretinoinMicrotia and small ears, microcephaly, cleft palate, cardiac, thymic hypoplasia, hydrocephalus
MethotrexateLimb and craniofacial defects, cranial ossification defects, neural tube defects, abortion
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors / ARBsRenal dysgenesis → oligohydramnios → Potter sequence, growth restriction
WarfarinNasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses, limb hypoplasia; fetal hemorrhage later
LithiumEbstein anomaly
MethimazoleAplasia cutis, esophageal atresia, facial anomalies
TetracyclinesTooth discolouration, inhibited long-bone growth
FluoroquinolonesCartilage and bone toxicity
DiethylstilbestrolClear cell adenocarcinoma of vagina and cervix, uterine malformation
ThalidomidePhocomelia
Pertinent positives & negatives Cleft palate – present in hydantoin and absent in fetal alcohol syndrome; the single most discriminating finding in this newborn · Hypoplasia of the distal phalanges – near-specific for antiepileptic exposure · Wide anterior fontanelle – part of the hydantoin pattern, and easily overlooked · Symmetric growth restriction with microcephaly – shared by alcohol, phenytoin, isotretinoin and cocaine, so it discriminates nothing · No smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border or short palpebral fissures – the fetal alcohol facial triad is absent · No prenatal care – explains why a maternal medication history was never taken · No snuffles, hepatomegaly or maculopapular rash – congenital syphilis is excluded on its own features
Decision spine Is there a structural malformation? – Yes → exposure fell in the 3–8 week window · List the findings that only one agent causes. – Cleft palate and distal digit hypoplasia · Which agent causes both? – Phenytoin · Check the nearest mimic. – Alcohol shares the microcephaly but never the cleft · Is there an alternative explanation for the growth restriction? – It is nonspecific and belongs to every option · What would have prevented it? – Pre-conception switch plus 4 mg folate
Scenario bank
  1. Newborn male, growth restricted at 38 weeks to a mother with no prenatal care, with microcephaly, a wide anterior fontanelle, cleft palate and hypoplasia of the distal phalanges → Maternal phenytoin use → fetal hydantoin syndrome
  2. Child with a smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, short palpebral fissures and midface hypoplasia with microcephaly, and no cleft lip or palate → Fetal alcohol syndrome → alcohol is not associated with clefting
  3. Newborn with severe oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, flat facies and positional limb deformities; the mother took an antihypertensive throughout pregnancy → Maternal ACE inhibitor use → renal dysgenesis causing Potter sequence
  4. Newborn with Ebstein anomaly on echocardiography whose mother is treated for bipolar disorder → Maternal lithium use → apical displacement of the tricuspid valve
  5. Newborn with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses on radiograph; the mother has a mechanical mitral valve → Maternal warfarin use in the first trimester → low molecular weight heparin should have been substituted
  6. 26 yo on valproate for epilepsy who hopes to conceive in about a year → Switch to levetiracetam now and begin 4 mg folic acid → change the regimen before conception, not after
  7. 28 yo on carbamazepine who presents newly pregnant at 9 weeks gestation → Switching to a different antiepileptic now → organogenesis is largely complete and overlapping agents doubles exposure
  8. 22 yo about to start isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne → Two negative pregnancy tests 19 or more days apart with two forms of contraception → iPLEDGE risk-management requirements
  9. 2-week-old boy born at 38 weeks to a 27-year-old first-time mother after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with no prenatal exposure history recorded; birth weight about 2.3 kg; length, weight and head circumference at the 5th percentile; short palpebral fissures, flat midface, small jaw and thin upper lip; soft systolic murmur with normal femoral pulses; mild hypotonia → Fetal alcohol syndrome → the face and growth decide without an exposure history; the palpebral fissures are short, not upslanting
Anticoagulation in pregnancy Low molecular weight heparin and unfractionated heparin have no fetal effects; warfarin is teratogenic to bone and cartilage. Heparins do not cross the placenta, and warfarin does. Patients with mechanical valves therefore take low-molecular-weight heparin in the first trimester, warfarin in the second and third, and unfractionated heparin near delivery.
Pearls Cleft plus distal digit hypoplasia is phenytoin; alcohol affects the philtrum and the palpebral fissures, not the palate or the fingertips · Timing predicts the kind of damage – before 2 weeks all-or-none, 3–8 weeks structure, after 8 weeks growth and brain · Change antiepileptics before conception, never after; once pregnancy is recognized organogenesis is mostly done, and switching adds seizure risk plus a second teratogen · Valproate is the worst antiepileptic and levetiracetam the usual substitute · Oligohydramnios with Potter sequence should suggest ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors as well as renal agenesis, two different first causes of the same cascade · Lithium → Ebstein anomaly is the one psychiatric-drug-to-cardiac-lesion pairing worth memorizing outright
Fetal alcohol syndrome without an exposure history FAS (fetal alcohol syndrome) can be diagnosed from the examination when no exposure history is given. The 2016 revised Institute of Medicine criteria require all four of these. First, 2 of 3 facial features: short palpebral fissures (at or below the 10th percentile), a thin upper lip vermilion and a smooth philtrum. Second, height or weight at or below the 10th percentile. Third, a head circumference at or below the 10th percentile, a structural brain anomaly, or recurrent nonfebrile seizures. Fourth, neurobehavioral impairment, which under age 3 means developmental delay. Confirmed alcohol exposure is not required; a confirmed absence of exposure excludes the diagnosis. Short fissures point to FAS. Upslanting fissures with epicanthal folds, a flat facial profile and a single palmar crease point to Down syndrome.
How NBME framed it No maternal alcohol history was given; the face, with length, weight and head size at the 5th percentile, made the diagnosis in a hypotonic 2-week-old. Short palpebral fissures separated it from Down syndrome, whose fissures slant upward; trisomy 13, fragile X, Klinefelter syndrome and congenital toxoplasmosis were the other decoys.
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves covers the oligohydramnios cascade that this brief reaches from the drug side. Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers Ebstein anomaly. Ask: which single malformation does only one drug on the roster cause?
Transferable rule To identify a teratogen, find the one malformation that belongs to only one agent. Ignore the shared features that every candidate agent can produce.
Unchecked attributeAlcohol use: shares microcephaly and growth restriction, but has no association with cleft lip or palate, and none of the facial triad is described.
True-fact-wrong-slotCocaine use: causes preterm delivery, abruption and growth restriction, but no congenital defects.
Class-vs-memberLisinopril: a named teratogen, but it produces renal failure and Potter sequence, not clefting or digit hypoplasia.
True-fact-wrong-slotUntreated syphilis: symptomatic cases show snuffles, hepatomegaly and a maculopapular rash, none present here.
Unchecked attributeDown syndrome: hypotonia and a soft murmur fit, but Down syndrome gives upslanting palpebral fissures with epicanthal folds, a flat facial profile and a single palmar crease. These fissures are short.
True-fact-wrong-slotTrisomy 13 syndrome: it causes cleft lip and palate, holoprosencephaly, small eyes, scalp defects and extra digits, none of which this newborn has.
Unchecked attributeFragile X syndrome: the long face, large ears, prominent jaw and large testes appear later in childhood and after puberty; this newborn has a small jaw.
Unchecked attributeKlinefelter syndrome (seminiferous tubule dysgenesis): boys with 47,XXY look normal at birth; small testes, tall stature and gynecomastia appear at puberty.
Salient decoyCongenital toxoplasmosis: growth restriction fits, but it brings chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, scattered intracranial calcifications and an enlarged liver and spleen, not a facial pattern.

edits.html:
Tics and Tic Disorders

classify the movement first · motor and vocal tics · Tourette criteria · tic vs compulsion · habit reversal, then medicationIs the behavior involuntary, or is it neutralizing an obsession?

Source vignette Pt – 7 yo M, behavioral concerns at school; repeats exactly what other children say, and last year raised his hand repeatedly then said he was just stretching when called on; plays alone to avoid bullying, prefers books and jigsaw puzzles; says he tries not to be bad but sometimes cannot help it · History – father has obsessive-compulsive disorder; growth tracking at the 60th percentile · Exam – frequent head turning and shoulder shrugging; remorseful and anxious on mental status examination · Q – the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned atomoxetine, exposure and response prevention, fluoxetine, methylphenidate, parent management training and risperidone
The decision point

Three of the described behaviors are tics. Head turning and shoulder shrugging are motor tics. Repeating exactly what other children say is echolalia, a vocal tic. The hand-raising, explained away afterward, is a motor tic he covered for; this is how school-age children manage tics. Multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic, present over a year with onset before 18, is Tourette syndrome. Among the offered options, the therapy that targets tics is the antidopaminergic risperidone. It is a second-generation antipsychotic, preferred over first-generation agents for its adverse-effect profile.

Defining criteria Tourette syndrome – multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, not necessarily concurrent, present over 1 year, with onset before age 18; more common in boys, typically presenting age 6 to 15 · Motor tics – facial grimacing, blinking, head or neck jerking, shoulder shrugging, tongue protrusion · Vocal tics – grunting, sniffing, snorting, throat clearing, barking, yelling, echolalia, coprolalia · Compulsion – the mimic's gate: a repetitive behavior performed in response to an obsession to reduce anxiety; absent an obsession, a repetitive movement is a tic · Treatment tiers – habit reversal training is behavioral and first-line; antidopaminergic agents when tics impair function, meaning second-generation antipsychotics, dopamine depleters such as tetrabenazine, or alpha-2 agonists such as guanfacine and clonidine
Pertinent positives & negatives Head turning and shoulder shrugging – two motor tics, the examination finding that names the disorder · Echolalia – the required vocal tic; without it this is a chronic motor tic disorder, not Tourette · Symptoms over more than a year – meets the duration criterion, and the waxing and waning course is itself characteristic · Reads books, completes jigsaw puzzles, plays alone quietly – sustained attention, which argues against ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) despite the classroom referral · Remorseful, says he cannot help it – insight and distress consistent with tics, not oppositional defiance · No obsessional thoughts described – closes OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder), and with it both exposure therapy and fluoxetine · Bullied and avoiding peers – functional impairment, the gate that licenses pharmacotherapy · Father with OCD – a family-history decoy; OCD and Tourette are comorbid and heritable together, which is why it is plausible and why it is not diagnostic
Repetitive behavior in a school-age child – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Tourette syndromeBoys 6 to 15; waxing and waning; comorbid ADHD and OCDMultiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic over 1 year – (the answer)
Obsessive-compulsive disorderObsessions driving compulsions that relieve anxietyA named obsession; the behavior neutralizes itNo obsessional thought anywhere in the stem
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorderInattention or hyperactivity across settingsFidgetiness, cannot sustain attention, impairment in two or more settingsReads and completes puzzles alone; behavior is school-confined
Oppositional defiant disorderAngry mood, defiance and vindictiveness toward authorityDeliberate defiance without remorseHe is remorseful and distressed by the behavior
Provisional tic disorderTics present less than 1 yearSame movements, shorter durationSymptoms span more than a year
Management, and the option list that was not offered Behavioral therapy with habit reversal training is first-line and is the choice whenever it is offered. When tics impair function, add an antidopaminergic or an alpha-2 agonist. Clonidine and guanfacine are both guideline-supported for tics and ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) together. Guanfacine is often preferred first for its milder sedation profile; this is clinical practice, not a guideline ranking. When the guideline first-line treatment is not on the option list, choose the best offered treatment for the diagnosis you made. Do not change the diagnosis to fit an offered drug.
Decision spine Describe the movements. – Head turning, shrugging, hand-raising are motor tics · Is there a sound? – Echolalia is a vocal tic · How long? – Over a year and waxing and waning, so Tourette rather than provisional · Is any behavior neutralizing an obsession? – No, so not OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder), and the exposure therapy and fluoxetine options fall · Can he sustain attention? – Books and puzzles, so not ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder), and the stimulants fall · Is function impaired? – Bullied and isolated, so pharmacotherapy is licensed
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo M with head turning, shoulder shrugging and repetition of classmates' words for over a year, now bullied and socially isolated → Risperidone → Tourette syndrome with functional impairment
  2. 8 yo M with mild motor and vocal tics who is performing well academically and has friends → Habit reversal training → behavioral therapy precedes medication when tics are mild
  3. 9 yo M with motor tics who also describes intrusive thoughts of contamination relieved only by repeated handwashing → Comorbid obsessive-compulsive disorder → exposure and response prevention
  4. 7 yo M with head jerking and eye blinking for 8 months and no vocal tic → Provisional tic disorder → duration under 1 year with no vocal tic
  5. How antipsychotic agents suppress tics in Tourette syndrome → Dopamine receptor blockade → tetrabenazine instead depletes presynaptic dopamine
  6. 8 yo with Tourette syndrome and inattention impairing him at home and at school → A stimulant for the comorbid ADHD → stimulants are not contraindicated in Tourette – methylphenidate reduces ADHD symptoms without worsening tics (American Academy of Neurology (AAN) 2019)
  7. 7 yo with Tourette syndrome whose parents request medication to reduce the tics → Fluoxetine → a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) treats comorbid OCD, not tics
  8. 10 yo with moderate impairing tics whose parents decline an antipsychotic because of weight-gain concerns → Guanfacine → alpha-2 agonists are an accepted alternative
Decoy note Family history of obsessive-compulsive disorder in the father is the strongest decoy. It is true in a way that makes it worse: obsessive-compulsive disorder and Tourette syndrome are comorbid and co-heritable. So this history is consistent with Tourette syndrome while pointing toward obsessive-compulsive disorder. The child's own words describe the involuntariness of a tic, not the anxiety relief of a compulsion.
Pearls Describe the movement before you name the disorder – a family history does not change what a movement is · A compulsion requires an obsession; with no obsessional thought, a repetitive behavior is a tic and exposure therapy is the wrong tool · Echolalia is a vocal tic, and it upgrades a chronic motor tic disorder to Tourette syndrome. It is the criterion most often missed, because repeating words does not seem like a vocal tic · tics wax and wane, so a behavior that stopped last year and was replaced by a new one is natural history, not improvement · stimulants for comorbid ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) are not contraindicated in Tourette, despite older teaching
Pairs with Part II School Difficulty in a Child is the nearest relative. It shares the same referral route, a school behavior complaint. The resolution is opposite: there the private interview reveals a learning disorder, and here the examination reveals tics. Ask: what exactly is the child doing, and is it involuntary?
Transferable rule A family history raises the prior probability, but the phenomenology decides. When a relative's diagnosis and a child's behavior are both given, first describe the behavior in neutral terms. If the behavior is involuntary and stereotyped, it is a tic, whatever the family carries.
Salient decoyExposure and response prevention: the father's OCD and the anxious remorseful affect sell it, but exposure therapy treats compulsions driven by obsessions and no obsession is described.
True-fact-wrong-slotFluoxetine: first-line for pediatric OCD and depression, but the same category error, and an SSRI does not suppress tics.
Class-vs-memberParent management training: targets oppositional defiant disorder; he is remorseful rather than defiant, and it does nothing for tics.
Class-vs-memberMethylphenidate and atomoxetine: ADHD is genuinely comorbid with Tourette, but these behaviors are tics and sustained attention on books and puzzles argues against ADHD.

edits.html:
Transfusion Reactions

onset and company · urticarial vs anaphylactic · hemolytic and bacterial emergencies · when to resume · most need nothingWhat are the vitals, and what else is on the skin besides hives?

Source vignette Pt – 12 yo F with idiopathic aplastic anemia, new petechiae and bruising over a week; during a platelet transfusion a chest rash spreads over the body · Labs – absolute neutrophil count 420, platelets 7,000 · Exam – T 37.2 °C, blood pressure (BP) 110/82 mm Hg, heart rate (HR) 90/min, respiratory rate (RR) 18/min, saturation 98%; oropharynx normal, lungs clear; diffuse urticarial rash on trunk and limbs plus pinpoint nonblanching macules and bruises at the extremities · Q – the best next step in evaluation of the reaction; options spanned culture of the product, direct Coombs test, no additional evaluation, peripheral smear and coagulation studies
The decision point

Blood pressure is normal, there is no wheeze, the lungs are clear and the oropharynx is normal. This is isolated urticaria in a hemodynamically stable patient. The rash improved after an antihistamine, with an hour of stable observation. It is an urticarial transfusion reaction, caused by preformed immunoglobulin E (IgE) reacting against a soluble allergen in the donated plasma, or the reverse. Management is what has already been done: stop the transfusion, give an antihistamine and observe. Improvement with the antihistamine confirms the diagnosis, and the transfusion may be resumed without additional evaluation.

Defining criteria Urticarial reaction – hives and itching only, onset hours into the transfusion, from preformed IgE against a soluble plasma allergen; stop, antihistamine, resume if otherwise asymptomatic, no workup · Anaphylactic reaction – onset seconds to minutes, from antibodies to immunoglobulin A (IgA) in an IgA-deficient recipient reacting to donor IgA; respiratory distress or wheeze, angioedema, hypotension; epinephrine, and washed products thereafter · Acute hemolytic reaction – ABO incompatibility from clerical error; fever, flank pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, direct Coombs positive · Transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection – fever, chills, hypotension, most common with platelets; culture both the recipient and the product
Transfusion reactions: timing, company and the movethe vitals sort them faster than the rash does
ReactionOnsetThe company it keepsWhat to do
UrticarialHoursHives and itching, nothing else; vitals normalStop, antihistamine, resume; no workup
Anaphylactic EmergencySeconds to minutesWheeze, angioedema, hypotension; IgA-deficient recipientEpinephrine; future transfusions washed
Acute hemolytic EmergencyMinutes to hoursFever, flank pain, hypotension, dark urineStop; direct Coombs, smear, prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT); supportive
Bacterial contamination EmergencyMinutes to hoursFever, rigors, hypotension; platelets most oftenCulture recipient and product; empiric antibiotics
Febrile nonhemolyticDuring or within 4 hFever and chills without hemolysisStop, antipyretic; leukoreduction reduces its incidence
TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) / TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury)TRALI within 6 h; TACO within 12 hRespiratory distress: volume overload vs noncardiogenic edemaStop; diuretic for TACO, supportive care for TRALI
Pertinent positives & negatives BP 110/82 mm Hg, HR 90/min, saturation 98% – hemodynamically stable, which excludes anaphylaxis, hemolysis and sepsis · Lungs clear, oropharynx normal – no bronchospasm, no angioedema; the two findings that would make this anaphylaxis · Afebrile at 37.2 °C – excludes both a febrile reaction and bacterial contamination · Rash improved with diphenhydramine and stayed stable for an hour – confirms the diagnosis · Petechiae and bruises were present before the transfusion – they reflect a platelet count of 7,000 from aplastic anemia, not a new consumptive process · No flank pain, no dark urine – the findings of a hemolytic reaction are absent · It was a platelet transfusion – platelets are the product most associated with bacterial contamination; without fever, culture is not indicated
Decision spine What is the blood pressure and the saturation? – Normal → the dangerous reactions are out · Is there a fever? – No → not hemolytic, not bacterial, not febrile · Wheeze, angioedema or hypotension? – None → urticaria is isolated, so not anaphylaxis · How fast did it start? – Late, not in the first minutes → urticarial · Did it respond to the antihistamine? – Yes → that is the confirmation · So what is needed? – Nothing further; the transfusion may be resumed
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Vital signs, lung and airway examFirstNormal vitals, clear lungs, hives onlyThe dangerous reactions are excluded
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsHives improve with an antihistamine, vitals stay stableUrticarial reaction; resume the transfusion, no tests
Direct Coombs test, smear, PT and PTTBy branchFever, flank pain, dark urine: Coombs positiveAcute hemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility
Blood cultures of the recipient and the productBy branchFever, rigors, hypotension: growth in bothBacterial contamination, most often a platelet unit
Serum IgA levelBy branchAfter anaphylaxis: IgA absentAnti-IgA anaphylaxis; wash future products
Coombs test or product culture for hives aloneSkipAfebrile and stable: no indicationNothing to find; pre-existing petechiae come from the low platelets
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo F with aplastic anemia developing a diffuse urticarial rash late in a platelet transfusion; BP 110/82 mm Hg, saturation 98%, afebrile, lungs clear; rash improves after diphenhydramine and vitals stay stable for an hour → No additional evaluation is indicated → urticarial reaction; the transfusion may be resumed
  2. 30 yo F who develops wheezing, facial angioedema and a blood pressure of 70/40 mm Hg two minutes into a red cell transfusion → Intramuscular epinephrine → anaphylactic transfusion reaction
  3. Patient with selective IgA deficiency and a history of transfusion anaphylaxis who now requires red blood cells → Transfuse washed red blood cells → washing removes donor plasma IgA
  4. 45 yo who develops fever, flank pain, hypotension and dark urine 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion → Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction → ABO incompatibility from a clerical error
  5. 60 yo M who develops fever to 39 °C with rigors and hypotension 30 minutes into a platelet transfusion → Culture the recipient and the transfused product and start empiric antibiotics → bacterial contamination, most common with platelets
  6. The mechanism of an isolated urticarial transfusion reaction → Preformed IgE reacting against a soluble allergen in donor plasma → or donor IgE against a recipient allergen
  7. 12 yo with aplastic anemia and platelets of 7,000 who develops hives during transfusion; pinpoint nonblanching macules were documented on her limbs before the transfusion began → Pre-existing thrombocytopenia → the petechiae are not part of the reaction
  8. IgA-deficient patient with prior transfusion anaphylaxis who urgently requires red blood cells → Standard unwashed packed red blood cells → residual donor plasma IgA triggers anaphylaxis
Decoy note The petechiae and ecchymoses look like a new hemorrhagic complication, and they appear in the skin examination beside the urticaria as though they arrived together. They were present before the transfusion: she had bruising a week ago, and her platelet count is 7,000. A finding documented before the intervention cannot be a reaction to it.
Pearls Vital signs: normal blood pressure, no fever and no hypoxia eliminate anaphylaxis, hemolysis, bacterial contamination and TRALI · Isolated urticaria is the only reaction in which the transfusion may continue: stop, give an antihistamine, observe, then resume the same unit · Timing separates the two allergic reactions: seconds to minutes with wheeze and hypotension is anaphylaxis; hours with hives alone is urticarial · Anaphylaxis to blood suggests IgA deficiency; the long-term fix is washed products · Platelets carry the bacterial risk because they are stored at room temperature; fever and rigors during a platelet transfusion call for cultures
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers selective IgA deficiency and already keys washed red cells; this brief covers the same topic from the transfusion side. Ask: what are the vitals, and what else is on the skin besides hives?
Transferable rule When a treatment has already been given and the response is reported, the response serves as the diagnostic test, and usually nothing further is needed. Check the reported response before ordering anything.
Redundant workupDirect Coombs test: answers "is this hemolysis?", already excluded by normal vitals, no fever, no flank pain and no dark urine.
Salient decoyPT and PTT: indicated only for hemolysis complicated by disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC); her bruising is thrombocytopenic and predates the transfusion.
Redundant workupPeripheral smear: would show schistocytes if microangiopathy were present; there is no hemolysis to look for.
Unchecked attributeCulture of the product: platelets do carry the bacterial risk, but culture requires fever, chills or hypotension; she is afebrile and stable.
